1|1: For most TrueNAS setups, creating a separate pool for irreplaceable data is less beneficial than ensuring you have robust, independent backups of that data. A separate pool can help with organizational separation, different vdev layouts, and tailored performance or redundancy profiles, but it does not meaningfully change your overall data risk if the system itself is lost to fire, theft, power events, or major hardware failure.  If you stay on a single chassis, the big risks are common mode failures: PSU blowout, bad HBA, firmware bug, user error like rm -rf, ransomware, or catastrophic pool misconfiguration. A second pool in the same box shares all of those risks. ZFS is excellent for integrity and local redundancy, but it is not a substitute for independent backups.  The really important choices for irreplaceable data are usually these:  Use a more conservative RAID layout for that dataset, for example RAIDZ2 or mirrors rather than RAIDZ1, and avoid mixing it into risky vdev designs.  Enable robust snapshotting and replication so you can roll back from user error, corruption, or ransomware. Frequent snapshots replicated to another system beat a separate pool in the same box.  Have at least one backup target that is physically and logically separate: another TrueNAS box, a different host using ZFS replication, external drives that are periodically connected and then offline, or cloud/object storage via something like rclone. Ideally one of these is offsite.  A second pool might be useful when you need different disk types or behaviors: for example, an all SSD mirror pool for critical VM images plus a big HDD RAIDZ2 pool for bulk media. Or if you want to keep irreplaceable data on a conservative, well tested pool and experiment on another pool with new features, new disks, compression settings, or sVDEVs. But that is mostly about performance, growth strategy, and risk isolation for experimentation, not about ultimate survivability of that critical dataset.  So if your goal is to protect irreplaceable data, it is almost always better to:  Keep it on a robust, boring layout within your main pool, with good ECC RAM and UPS protection.  Configure frequent snapshots with sensible retention.  Add at least one additional backup destination that is off the main box, ideally also offsite and disconnected or immutable between backup runs.  A separate pool can be useful, but it is a secondary optimization. Real protection for irreplaceable data comes from multiple, independent copies stored on different systems and ideally in different locations, not from rearranging how many pools exist on the same hardware.
2|1: If you have to choose between a separate pool and an additional backup for irreplaceable data, the extra backup almost always provides more real protection than just splitting pools. A separate pool can help with certain risks, but it does not replace proper backups.  A second pool on the same physical server mainly gives you: - Some logical separation and possibly different vdev layouts or performance/feature tunings for that data - Isolation from corruption or mistakes that affect one pool but not the other (e.g., a bad scrub or a messed-up reconfiguration)  But it does not fundamentally protect you from the big risks: - Hardware failure at the host level: bad PSU, motherboard, HBA, RAM, or power event - Physical damage: fire, water, theft, surge - Admin error: rm -rf, zfs destroy, bad script, ransomware with access to both pools - Software bugs that could affect all pools on that system  A real backup (ideally a separate machine, and even better if off-site or at least off-line some of the time) directly addresses many of those. With ZFS, that generally means: - Using zfs send | zfs receive to replicate your important dataset to another TrueNAS or ZFS box - Or backing it up to a different system / cloud using a backup tool that understands snapshots or at least does versioned backups  Where a separate pool can still make sense: - You want your irreplaceable data on more conservative hardware or layout (e.g., all mirrored vdevs, lower capacity but higher redundancy), while the main pool might use RAIDZ2/3 for bulk media - You want to use different compression, deduplication, recordsizes, or special vdevs for that dataset and prefer pool-level tuning - You want to place the irreplaceable data only on a known-good set of disks and keep cheaper/less-trusted disks for noncritical data  Even then, that is more about service quality and risk reduction around disk failure than true data safety. You still need backups.  For most home or small-office TrueNAS users, the practical priority list is usually: 1) A robust pool design with enough redundancy for your risk tolerance (mirrors or RAIDZ2/3, ECC RAM, decent HBA, etc.) 2) Snapshot schedules for quick rollback against accidental deletions or ransomware 3) Replication or backup of critical datasets to another system or external drive 4) Only then, if your budget and complexity tolerance allow, consider additional pools for special workloads  So: if you are choosing between a separate pool versus a proper additional backup for irreplaceable data, put your effort and budget into the backup. If you have room for both, use the separate pool to tune reliability/performance, but treat it as complementary to, not a substitute for, backups.
3|1: For most TrueNAS setups, creating a separate pool for irreplaceable data is usually less beneficial than making sure you have a solid, independent backup strategy for that data. A separate pool on the same box still shares many of the same failure domains: the same chassis, power supply, controller, firmware bugs, user mistakes, malware, natural disasters, and sometimes even the same batch of drives. So while splitting things into multiple pools can help with some risks, it does not solve the core problem of data loss for truly critical data.  Where a separate pool can help is in how you architect redundancy, performance, and workloads. For example, you might want your irreplaceable data on a more conservative pool layout: mirrors instead of RAIDZ2 or RAIDZ3, higher-quality or enterprise drives, stricter scrubbing and SMART monitoring, and no risky experiments with compression, deduplication, or new features. You also might keep that pool relatively quiet: fewer writes, fewer jails/VMs, minimal tinkering. This can reduce wear and operational risks compared to a large, mixed-use pool that sees constant churn. Separate pools can also help with administrative safety boundaries: different datasets, different ACLs, and even different sets of users and services, making it a bit harder for a mistake in one environment to touch the other.  However, none of that replaces backups. If data is truly irreplaceable, you want at least one additional copy that is:  – On a separate physical system, ideally – Preferably in a different physical location (off-site or at least in another room/building) – Ideally using a different storage stack (another TrueNAS, a different NAS, cloud, external drives periodically rotated off-site)  The more independent the backup environment, the better. ZFS replication to another TrueNAS box, a secondary system with encrypted snapshots, or a cloud sync target all give you resilience against more failure modes, including the big ones like fire, theft, catastrophic PSU/controller failure, or major user error (rm -rf on the wrong dataset, for instance). Versioned snapshots on the backup side add protection against silent corruption and ransomware.  So in practice, a good approach is usually:  – Keep irreplaceable data on a well-designed, conservative pool with strong redundancy and monitoring. – Add robust, automated backups of that data to at least one other device or location, with snapshots/versions. – Use a separate pool only if it gives you clearer operational benefits: different drive classes, different usage profiles, isolation from experimental workloads, or simplified administration.  If you have to choose only one improvement, spending effort and money on an independent backup is almost always more valuable than carving out a separate pool on the same hardware. A separate pool is an optimization; a truly independent backup is what actually protects irreplaceable data.
4|1: For most home or small lab TrueNAS setups, you get more real protection by keeping a single well-designed main pool and adding at least one truly independent backup than by carving out a separate pool just for irreplaceable data.  A separate pool can make sense in a few narrower cases: for example, if you want different redundancy levels or performance characteristics (e.g., a mirror or RAIDZ2 pool for photos and RAIDZ1/striped vdevs for less important media), or if you physically separate the disks for risk isolation. But by itself, a second pool on the same machine is not a backup. It is still subject to the same controller, power, PSU, firmware, human error, malware, and environmental risks.  For irreplaceable data, the priority should be:  – Strong redundancy on the main pool: e.g., mirrors or RAIDZ2/3, scrub schedule, SMART monitoring, ECC RAM if possible. – Multiple independent backups: at least one offline or offsite. For example, regular ZFS replication to another machine, plus periodic snapshots backed up to an external drive that is disconnected most of the time, or cloud/object storage if feasible. – Good snapshot policy: frequent local snapshots protect against accidental deletion and some ransomware scenarios and make replication efficient.  Creating a separate pool only meaningfully improves safety if you are also changing the underlying risk profile: using different hardware, different power, a different chassis, or at least different classes of disks and vdev setup. Otherwise, you mainly add complexity: more pools to manage, more room for misconfiguration, and no real improvement against the big threats.  So, unless you have a very specific reason to tune redundancy or performance independently, it is usually better to:  Keep a single, robust main pool Use dataset-level snapshots and replication for the irreplaceable dataset Invest effort and money in an additional backup target or two, ideally offsite or offline  In that model, the main pool provides availability and quick restore, and the separate backup(s) provide true resilience against catastrophic or operator-level failures. That gives you much more practical protection than simply splitting the same disks into multiple pools.
5|1: For most home or small lab TrueNAS setups, a separate pool for irreplaceable data is usually less valuable than strong, independent backups of that data. ZFS redundancy (mirror/RAIDZ) protects against disk failure within a pool, but it does not protect you from user error, ransomware, silent controller corruption, software bugs, fire, theft, or the whole chassis dying. Backups do.   A second pool on the same box still shares a lot of the same risks: same power, same controller, same OS, same physical location, usually even the same user mistakes. So while you might gain a bit of logical separation and be able to tune vdev layout or datasets differently, the core risk to truly irreplaceable data is not much lower if everything lives in one physical server.  Generally, you get more real protection by:  – Keeping the irreplaceable dataset in a well-designed main pool (e.g., mirrors or RAIDZ2 with good drive selection and scrubbing) – Sending regular ZFS snapshots to a different system (TrueNAS replication to another box) – Having at least one backup that is offline or offsite (USB disks periodically synced and stored elsewhere, cloud backup, remote TrueNAS box) – Using snapshot schedules and retention policies that cover accidental deletions, ransomware, and gradual corruption  A separate pool for that data can still make sense in specific cases, for example:  – You want different vdev geometry or different size/brand of drives for that data, like using only high-end enterprise disks in a mirror pool for your most critical data – You want to isolate performance characteristics, e.g., a small SSD mirror pool for critical docs and a large spinning pool for bulk media – You want operational separation, like being able to export/import or move that pool independently  But in terms of protecting irreplaceable data, a well-architected backup strategy (ideally 3–2–1: three copies, two media types, one offsite) beats splitting pools on the same machine. The most sensible approach for most users is: keep everything on a robust main pool, and then add at least one more independent backup target for the irreplaceable dataset, ideally in a different location or at least on removable media or a separate powered-off device when not in use.
6|1: For most home or small lab TrueNAS setups, you gain more by investing in additional, independent backups for irreplaceable data than by creating a special separate pool for it.  A separate pool primarily gives you:  - Different redundancy profile: for example, you might use RAIDZ2 or RAIDZ3, or pairs of mirrors, only for your most important data while using a less redundant layout for bulk media. This can reduce the risk that a single pool failure wipes everything. However, it also fragments capacity and can leave you with “stranded” free space you can’t easily reallocate between pools. - Different hardware or media: if the second pool is truly on different disks, shelves, or even a different type of drive (e.g., mirrored SSDs for critical data and large HDD RAIDZ for bulk), you reduce the chance of a single hardware issue taking everything down. But for this benefit to be meaningful, it’s often more powerful to put that money toward an entirely separate backup system. - Different performance and tuning: you can tune recordsize, compression, and even vdev layout strictly for that dataset’s workload. That can be useful, but it’s rarely as important as having real backups.  What a separate pool does not give you is protection from human error, malware, logical corruption, catastrophic controller or chassis failure, theft, fire, or site-wide disasters. ZFS redundancy is about availability and protection from disk failure, not a substitute for backup.  For irreplaceable data, the priority order usually looks like this:  - Start with a solid, well-redundant main pool (e.g., RAIDZ2 or mirrored vdevs) - Use ZFS snapshots and replication for versioned protection - Add at least one separate backup target, ideally on different hardware - If the data is truly critical, have a second backup that is offsite or at least offline  Instead of splitting your main storage into separate pools, a more robust design for important data is:  - Keep a single, well-designed pool with enough redundancy for your risk tolerance - Put the irreplaceable data into its own dataset(s) within that pool - Use frequent snapshots on those datasets and replicate them to:   - Another ZFS system (second TrueNAS box, another server, or a trusted remote host), or   - External drives rotated offsite, or   - Cloud backup that understands ZFS send/receive or at least receives encrypted incremental backups  Creating a second pool is worth considering only if you are also changing the physical failure domain: for example, a pool on a completely different HBA and disk set, or in a different chassis, where the failure of one set is unlikely to affect the other. But even then, that is still not a replacement for backup. If you have to choose, putting money and effort into a truly separate backup (and preferably offsite or at least periodically disconnected) is almost always a better use of resources than subdividing a single machine into multiple pools.  So, unless you have a very specific need for different performance characteristics or hardware separation, it is usually better to keep one well-built pool and add robust, independent backups for the irreplaceable dataset.
7|1: For most TrueNAS setups, you get more practical protection by keeping a single well-designed main pool and investing your effort into solid backups and off-site copies, rather than carving out a special pool just for irreplaceable data.  A separate pool only really helps with a narrow class of risks: failure or corruption that is isolated to a particular vdev layout or group of disks. If both pools live in the same chassis, on the same power, same controller, and same environment, they still share many common failure modes: PSU failure, motherboard issues, power surge, fire, theft, flooding, user error like rm -rf or zfs destroy, malware/ransomware, and TrueNAS or ZFS bugs that affect the whole system.  What actually moves the needle for irreplaceable data is:  – Strong redundancy on the main pool: a conservative RAIDZ level or mirrors, no mixing of sketchy hardware, ECC RAM, scrubs and SMART monitoring, and regular testing of backups.  – Multiple independent backups: at least one other dataset or pool on different physical hardware (not just another vdev in the same machine), plus an off-site or cloud backup for the truly critical stuff. ZFS send/recv or replication tasks are ideal.  – Versioned backups and snapshots: so you can roll back from silent corruption, ransomware, or accidental deletion. That gives you logical protection that a second pool alone does not provide.  A separate pool is still useful in certain scenarios:  – When you deliberately isolate failure domains: for example, keeping irreplaceable data on a small pool of high-quality, low-capacity enterprise drives, and bulk media on cheaper, larger disks. If the cheap-bulk pool experiences an issue, the critical pool might be unaffected.  – When you need very different performance or redundancy policies: e.g., irreplaceable data on mirrors with a stricter scrub schedule, and large media on RAIDZ2 or RAIDZ3 for capacity efficiency.  – When you do frequent destructive experimentation: you can keep experiments, jails, VMs, or scratch data on a separate pool and never touch the critical pool.  However, for most home and small-business users, the better trade-off is:  – One robust, well-planned pool for everything, with conservative redundancy and good hardware. – At least one secondary backup target (another NAS, external drives, or cloud) that receives regular, automated, and verified backups of the irreplaceable dataset. – Off-site or at least off-device storage for the most important data, to survive total system loss.  In other words, a second pool in the same box is not a replacement for true backups; it is just another on-the-same-system storage configuration. If you have to choose between building a separate pool vs. spending that money on additional backup media or an off-site/cloud backup, the backup investment almost always provides more real protection for irreplaceable data.

A separate pool primarily gives you isolation of failure domains and sometimes performance characteristics, but it does not replace the role of backups.  Reasons to favor additional backups over a separate pool:  You still have a single box risk. If the whole system dies (power surge, fire, theft, catastrophic hardware failure), multiple pools on that same chassis don’t help at all. An off-site or at least off-machine backup does.  Backups protect against more failure types. Snapshots and replication to another system, external disk, or cloud storage protect you from accidental deletion, corruption, ransomware, and admin mistakes, in a way that just having another pool in the same box does not.  Operational simplicity. Managing one main pool and a clear backup pipeline (periodic snapshots, replication tasks, external drives, another TrueNAS box, or cloud targets) is often simpler and less error-prone than juggling multiple pools with different properties and vdev layouts.  That said, a separate pool can be useful in some situations, but it is more about engineering tradeoffs than about making data irreplaceable:  Different vdev types or media. You might want a separate pool for SSD-only high-IOPS workloads or for large, slow disks optimized for cold storage, or to keep mirrors separate from RAIDZ, etc. That can indirectly help protect irreplaceable data by making its storage more conservative or more robust.  Failure domain separation at the disk level. If you absolutely must stay on a single chassis, putting irreplaceable data on a pool backed by completely separate disks from your “bulk” pool ensures that losing a vdev in one pool doesn’t immediately threaten the other. But this is still weaker than a true backup on another system.  Different policies. A separate pool can have different compression, recordsize, deduplication (usually not recommended), or special-vdev layouts. That might be relevant if your critical data is small, random I/O (e.g., databases) and you want to tune that differently from large media files.  Even in these cases, though, you generally still want backups. A common practical approach is:  Keep one main pool tuned for your general workloads. Use datasets for logical separation of data, with ZFS snapshots and replication. Add at least one independent backup target for irreplaceable data: another TrueNAS box, a USB disk rotated off-site, cloud object storage, or a remote rsync/ZFS target.  If you can choose only one improvement for irreplaceable data, choose robust, tested backups (including an off-site or at least off-box copy) over making a second pool in the same machine. A second pool can be a nice complement for performance or organizational reasons, but it’s not a substitute for real backup.
9|1: For irreplaceable data, a separate pool can help in a few niche ways, but it is almost never a substitute for a proper additional backup. A separate pool on the same machine still shares most of the same risks: theft, fire, power events, severe hardware failure, user error, malware, or catastrophic OS/ZFS configuration mistakes. Another backup, ideally on a different system and preferably offsite or at least offline some of the time, gives you protection against all of those in a way that a second pool simply cannot.  Where a separate pool can make sense is for risk compartmentalization and operational reasons:  You can build that pool with more conservative settings specifically tailored to the critical data. For example, mirrors instead of RAIDZ for simpler recovery, more redundancy (RAIDZ3 or three-way mirrors), different vdev sizes, or higher quality drives (or mixed vendors) so that a failure pattern in one set of disks is less likely to affect everything.  You can separate workloads so that experimental things you do on one pool are less likely to affect the “precious” pool. For example, testing new features, encryption schemes, iSCSI, or heavy VM workloads on one pool while the other pool is kept boring and stable.  You can tune datasets and pool properties differently: recordsize, compression, sync, dedup (usually off), special vdevs, SLOG, etc., with the irreplaceable pool optimized more for safety and reliability than for performance or capacity efficiency.  However, if you have to choose between spending the money on a separate internal pool vs. a real backup, the backup is almost always the better investment. The 3-2-1 rule is a good guiding principle: at least three copies of your data, on two different types of media, with one copy offsite. Within that framework, your TrueNAS pool is one copy; a second pool on the same server is still only marginally more protection than more redundancy in the main pool, whereas a second TrueNAS box, a cloud backup, or periodic offline snapshots to USB disks are qualitatively better protection.  So for irreplaceable data: use a solid, well-designed main pool with appropriate redundancy, then prioritize an additional backup (or two) over creating a separate pool on the same box. Only add a separate pool if you have clear reasons, such as different reliability/performance requirements or operational isolation, and treat it as part of your primary storage strategy, not as a replacement for backups.
10|1: Creating a separate pool for irreplaceable data can make sense in a few specific scenarios, but it is not a substitute for having an additional backup. A separate pool affects how the data is stored and protected on that particular TrueNAS system; a backup affects whether you can recover from failures of that system, from user error, or from larger disasters.  Reasons you might create a separate pool for irreplaceable data:  You want a different redundancy profile: For example, bulk media might live on a RAIDZ1 or fewer drives to maximize capacity, while critical photos or documents live on a smaller pool of mirrors or RAIDZ2/3 for better fault tolerance. This can reduce risk that a failure mode in a high‑capacity, more aggressive pool layout also affects your most critical data.  You want physical separation: Using different drive models, different ages, or even different HBA or backplane for the irreplaceable pool can reduce the chance of correlated failures. If your main pool is a bunch of large SMR drives, you might prefer your important data pool live on a set of smaller, high‑quality CMR drives, or even SSDs.  You want different performance or feature choices: A dedicated pool lets you tune recordsize, compression, special devices, or SLOGs specifically for that critical dataset without having to compromise with other workloads. For example, you might put business documents on a small mirrored SSD pool with aggressive sync and snapshots, while media lives on a large HDD RAIDZ pool.  You want simpler management and risk isolation: Destroying the main pool, testing new features, or doing experimental vdev layouts becomes less nerve‑racking if your most important data is completely isolated in a separate, conservative pool.  However, all of that is still just primary storage engineering. It does not protect you from:  Accidental deletion or corruption that replicates to that same pool Pool‑wide failures like catastrophic controller failure, bad firmware, or power events that damage multiple drives Theft, fire, flood, or other site‑level disasters Malware or ransomware that encrypts data in place  For those threats, additional backups are strictly more important than carving out another pool. Ideally, you want at least:  Versioned backups or snapshots that are not trivially overwritten by user error or ransomware At least one physically separate backup target, like another TrueNAS box, a USB disk stored offsite, or a cloud backup If possible, an offline or immutable backup (e.g., periodic offline disks, or a locked backup dataset with limited write access)  If you have to choose between:  A single TrueNAS box with two pools (one special “safe” pool) but no real backup, versus One well‑designed pool plus a separate backup destination (second box, external drives, or cloud),  the second option is far safer for irreplaceable data.  So the hierarchy of decisions is usually:  First, ensure you have at least one solid independent backup of irreplaceable data, preferably versioned and not always online. Then, if you also have the budget and complexity tolerance, consider a separate pool with a more conservative layout, better drives, and tuning suited for that critical data.  In short: A separate pool can improve reliability and management on the main system, but it is a secondary optimization. The real benefit for irreplaceable data comes from adding independent backups, not just rearranging vdevs into another pool on the same box.

If you’re backend, go deep on databases, indexing strategies, query optimizers, caching, distributed systems primitives, and observability stacks. Read high-quality engineering blogs from companies that build large-scale systems and then re-implement or prototype small versions of the patterns they describe. Do focused, project-based learning: instead of scanning docs, build a small but complete experiment, like a feature-flag system, a custom caching layer, or a design system library, and run it end to end.  To avoid plateauing, deliberately adopt practices from senior and staff-level engineers. Make architecture design a conscious skill: write design docs before major changes, enumerate trade-offs, and ask senior peers to review them. Learn to assess costs and risks, not just code-level correctness. Improve your debugging and operational skills by owning systems in production: handle on-call, examine incidents deeply, and write postmortems that identify root causes in design, not just bugs in code. Invest in observability: logs, metrics, tracing, and how to turn vague symptoms into concrete hypotheses and fixes.  You can significantly improve by expanding into technical leadership even if you do not want a formal manager role. Practice mentoring less-experienced developers, reviewing code with an eye for teaching, and breaking work into clear, manageable units. Own cross-cutting concerns like security, performance baselines, accessibility, or developer experience. Improve communication: learn to write clear, concise technical documents, argue for a design calmly with data and reasoning, and tailor explanations for different audiences like product, design, or executives. These are the skills that allow you to have outsized impact without necessarily writing more lines of code.  Stay current, but be intentional about it. Instead of trying to chase every new framework, pick a strategic area where the ecosystem is evolving and that aligns with your interests and your market, such as modern frontend architectures, edge computing, cloud-native infrastructure, or AI-assisted development. For that area, pick a small real-world problem, build something, then measure and polish it. Use this to deepen not only your tool knowledge but also your understanding of patterns like modular architectures, incremental migration, or continuous delivery.  Finally, deliberately expand beyond pure coding. Learn enough about product thinking to ask why, not only how: understand business metrics, user research, and the trade-off between speed and quality. Volunteer to own a feature end to end, from requirements to rollout to iteration, and track its impact. Improve your own workflows by automating repetitive tasks, refining your testing strategy, and integrating tools like linters, formatters, and local observability. Over a few years of focused practice, these compounded improvements in depth, architecture, debugging, leadership, and product sense will give you a step change in skill rather than just another year of similar experience.
6|2: With a decade of experience you’re likely already strong at shipping features and maintaining systems, so the biggest gains usually come from moving up a level of abstraction: work on depth, breadth, and leverage. For depth, pick one or two areas that you already touch and push them toward expert level: for example become the go-to person on performance optimization, frontend architecture, backend scalability, or DevOps/CI-CD. Take real problems from your current codebase and treat them like case studies: profile bottlenecks, redesign a flaky module, or refactor a legacy area into a cleaner architecture, and document your decisions and results. For breadth, systematically cover the parts of web development you’re weak in: if you are mostly frontend, build and deploy a small backend-heavy side project with a proper database, caching, observability, and tests; if you are mostly backend, design and implement a small SPA with a modern framework, state management, accessibility, and solid UX practices. Use each side project to learn a nontrivial concept, like implementing background jobs, websockets, or a complex form with offline support, rather than just cloning a tutorial. To increase leverage, practice skills that scale your impact: learn to design systems through architecture diagrams, ADRs, and clear design docs; review others’ code regularly and intentionally, focusing on teaching and spotting patterns rather than just nits; mentor juniors or mid-level developers, which forces you to articulate and refine your own reasoning; and get comfortable with communication: writing concise technical documents, leading discussions, and aligning technical work with business goals. Finally, choose at least one axis of long-term differentiation: maybe you become the person who deeply understands security and threat modeling in web systems, or the one who can take a feature from vague product request through discovery, design, implementation, measurement, and iteration. Set concrete 6–12 month goals around that, like giving a talk, writing a series of internal posts, or leading a cross-team initiative. With 10 years in, deliberate practice is less about learning random new tools and more about repeatedly solving slightly harder real problems with better architecture, better tradeoffs, and better collaboration than you did a year ago.
7|2: At the 10-year mark, the biggest jumps in skill usually come less from learning yet another framework and more from deliberately reshaping how you learn, build, and collaborate. Some practical directions you can take:  Go deeper, not just broader  Pick a few core areas where you already work and push them to a more expert level. For example, if you are a full‑stack web developer, you might go deep into:  Backend internals: understand how your framework actually handles routing, middleware, async I/O, connection pooling, and error propagation. Read parts of the framework source code. Reimplement small pieces of it as practice. Performance and scalability: learn to use profilers, APM tools, and browser dev tools at a very detailed level. Practice diagnosing slow queries, memory leaks, high CPU, and network bottlenecks on real or synthetic systems. Security: systematically study OWASP Top 10, secure coding guidelines, and common vulnerabilities for your tech stack. Do code reviews with a security lens and run security scanners. Testing and reliability: get very good at test design, property‑based testing, contract testing, resilience patterns like circuit breakers and bulkheads.  Sharpen fundamentals  Solidify the underlying concepts that survive framework churn:  Networking and HTTP: caching, keep‑alive, TLS, HTTP 2 and 3, REST vs RPC, WebSockets, CDNs. Databases: indexing strategies, query planning, normalization vs denormalization, transaction isolation levels, eventual consistency, and how ORMs actually work. System design: design systems that can handle more users, more data, and more failure. Practice with system design prompts, then compare your designs to real architectures from engineering blog posts.  Improve code quality and architecture sense  At 10 years, the main differentiator is your ability to design and sustain complex systems.  Study and apply design patterns and anti‑patterns in moderation: understand when a pattern actually solves a problem you have, and when it is overengineering. Focus on modularity and boundaries: practice designing clear interfaces between services, modules, and layers. Think hard about where to put logic so that it is easy to change later. Refactor legacy code: pick nontrivial parts of your current codebase, write characterization tests, then refactor for clarity and testability. This builds strong engineering judgment. Do code reading: read high‑quality open source projects in your stack. Observe naming, file structure, abstractions, and error handling.  Level up in DevOps and delivery  Better engineers tend to own more of the lifecycle.  Learn CI/CD deeply: not just using a pipeline, but being able to design and debug it, optimize build times, and structure repos for fast, reliable delivery. Understand containers and orchestration: Docker, container images, health checks, environment configuration, basics of Kubernetes or your platform equivalent. Reliability in production: logging strategies, metrics, tracing, dashboards, alerting, on‑call best practices, SLOs and error budgets.  Deliberate practice and feedback  Skill does not automatically grow just because you are working.  Choose deliberate practice projects: small side projects or internal tools where you intentionally experiment with new techniques, patterns, or tools, and try to do them very well end‑to‑end. Seek strong code reviews: ask senior peers to be more critical; request focused feedback on architecture, naming, and simplicity; then apply the feedback and ask if your changes actually improved things. Mentor others: teaching juniors forces you to make your understanding explicit and reveals gaps. Practice explaining complex topics simply. Regularly reflect on mistakes: after incidents or failed projects, write short retrospectives for yourself. What early signals did you miss? How would you approach it now?  Upgrade your problem‑solving and communication  At this stage, your influence and impact matter as much as your raw coding skill.  Practice written communication: good technical docs, design proposals, and clear tickets reduce chaos and multiply your impact. Focus on requirements clarity: get better at asking the right questions to clarify what needs to be built and why. This reduces rework and leads to better designs. Learn to negotiate trade‑offs: performance vs complexity, speed vs safety, abstraction vs duplication. Being explicit about trade‑offs is a senior skill.  Stay current, but selectively  You do not need every new tool, but you should understand trends that affect how systems are built.  Choose 1–2 things per year to learn deeply, for example: a new programming language that shifts your mental model; a new architecture style like event‑driven or serverless; or a front‑end or backend framework that is becoming dominant in your ecosystem. Follow a few high‑signal sources: engineering blogs from well‑known companies, standards discussions, or a couple of curated newsletters rather than random social feeds.  Align growth with where you want to go  Ten years in, it helps to be intentional about your trajectory.  If you want to be a principal or staff engineer: double down on system design, cross‑team collaboration, long‑term thinking, and technical strategy. If you want to be an architect: focus on broad knowledge of tools and platforms, integration patterns, and nonfunctional requirements like security, compliance, and performance. If you want to lean toward management: build skills in planning, delegation, feedback, conflict resolution, and shaping technical work without having to write all the code.  Concrete steps you can start this month  Pick one area to go deep in and define a 3‑month mini‑curriculum for yourself: a book or course, 2–3 open source projects to study, and 1 practice project. Ask for a tough piece of work at your job that stretches you: rewriting a critical component, leading a cross‑team initiative, or designing a new service from scratch. Schedule regular learning time: even 3–5 hours per week of structured learning and deliberate practice compounds quickly. Find a peer group: meetups, online communities, or internal guilds where you can discuss architecture, review each others designs, and share lessons from production.  The key shift at your level is to move from accumulating experience to intentionally shaping it: choosing what you focus on, seeking feedback, and designing your own growth path instead of just reacting to whatever work arrives.

1|3: Animate the entire effect in one Blender scene by using the elevator doors themselves as a natural cut point. Put both environments in the same .blend file but in different locations or collections. Start with the camera in front of the elevator looking into Environment A. When the doors close, keyframe their movement so they fully seal the frame. At the frame where the doors are fully closed and the screen is entirely covered, instantly switch what is behind the doors: hide Environment A and show Environment B using keyframed visibility (render visibility or collection visibility), or move the camera and elevator to where Environment B is placed. Then continue animating the door opening to reveal Environment B. Because there is a full-frame occlusion while the doors are closed, the cut can be hidden entirely in that closed-door moment without using an external video editor.
2|3: Animate the entire thing in one Blender scene and treat the elevator doors as a practical transition. Set up your first environment on one side of the door and the second environment on the other, but control their visibility using collections and keyframed visibility rather than cutting in a video editor. Put all geometry for environment A in one collection and environment B in another. At the moment the elevator doors are completely closed, keyframe environment A’s collection to be disabled for viewport and render, and environment B’s collection to become enabled. Because the doors fully block the camera, the switch will be invisible in the final render. Make sure the camera stays in the same place between shots (parent it to the elevator cabin if the elevator moves) and that lighting and any shared objects like the cabin interior are in collections that remain visible the whole time. You can also fade lights or use different HDRIs by keyframing their strength or visibility during the closed-door frames, so when the doors open again you reveal the new environment with new lighting, all done in a single continuous animation without needing a video editor.
3|3: Animate the entire effect inside Blender by cutting between scenes on a specific frame where the elevator doors are fully closed, and use the Video Sequence Editor (VSE) that is already in Blender instead of an external editor. Set up two separate scenes, for example Scene_A for the hallway and Scene_B for the destination floor. In Scene_A, animate the doors closing and make sure that at a certain frame they fully overlap and no gap is visible. Render both scenes as image sequences or keep them unrendered and work directly in the VSE. Then open the Video Editing workspace, add Scene_A as a strip starting at frame 1, and Scene_B as another strip that starts exactly one frame after the door is fully closed in Scene_A. Instead of a dissolve, use a hard cut so there is no visible transition during the closed-door frames. If you want a smoother feel, add a few frames where the door is shut and nothing changes, then switch the scene strip during those frames. Alternatively, you can keep it all in a single scene and simply animate the camera and environment visibility: when the doors close, keyframe the visibility of the first environment (collections for floor A) to turn off and the second environment (collections for floor B) to turn on while the doors are fully closed, so that when the doors open again the new floor is already there. This uses collection visibility or material alpha keyframes, avoids any external video editor, and leverages Blender’s built-in tools to create a seamless behind-the-door scene swap.
4|3: Animate the elevator doors so that when they are fully closed, they completely occlude the camera’s view, then switch what the camera is looking at in that brief moment of total darkness. In practice, set up two separate environments: Scene A for the first location and Scene B for the second, or keep everything in one scene but put the second location on a different collection. Animate the doors closing in front of the camera so the screen becomes completely black (or at least fully covered by the doors). On the exact frame where coverage is 100%, move the camera instantly to the second location or keyframe its visibility: for example, have Collection A visible and Collection B hidden until that frame, then flip their render visibility switches so Collection A turns off and Collection B turns on from the next frame onward. Because the doors are blocking the view, the pop in between locations is invisible to the viewer. To smooth the effect, you can add a tiny bit of motion blur or keep the black screen for one or two frames before revealing the new environment by animating the doors opening again into Scene B. This way the entire transition is done inside Blender’s 3D scene and timeline, with no external video editing needed.
5|3: Animate the elevator doors to fully close, use that closed moment as a natural cut point, and switch scenes by changing what is behind the door within a single Blender file. One simple approach is to put both environments in the same scene but on different collections, and then animate collection visibility in the Outliner. 6|3: Animate the entire transition inside Blender so the shot is one continuous render instead of two clips you have to edit together. Parent your camera to an empty so you can keep framing consistent, then build both environments in the same .blend file on different layers of space, or in the same space but hidden with visibility controls.  Method 1: Two environments in one scene Place the elevator interior and the first environment (e.g., hallway) where the doors open initially. Somewhere else in the 3D space, place the second environment (e.g., different floor). Keep the elevator interior as a separate mesh that can physically move.  Have the elevator interior and camera parented to a main empty. At the moment the elevator doors close, animate:  - Doors closing as normal - Once fully closed, animate the main empty translating from the first environment to the second environment over a few frames while the doors are closed. Since the camera is inside and the doors are sealed, the viewer cannot see the world shifting. - Optionally fade the lights a bit or add a small camera shake during the transition to hide any small issues.  When the doors open again, the elevator is now located in front of the second environment. Because it is all one timeline, you can render the entire sequence in one go without a video editor.  To keep performance manageable, you can disable unnecessary objects with keyframed visibility (Disable in Viewports and Disable in Renders in the Outliner) so that the first environment is hidden after the doors close and the second only becomes visible right before they open.  Method 2: Scene strip in Blender Video Sequencer, but entirely inside Blender If you are allowed to use Blenders built-in Video Sequencer (still technically no external video editor), you can:  - Render the first part of the animation up to the door fully closing. - Render the second part starting from the door closed and opening to the new environment. - In the same .blend, go to the Video Sequencer workspace and add both as scene strips or as rendered image sequences. - Align them so the cut happens on the frame where the door is fully closed.  This gives you a perfect hidden cut behind the closed door with no external software. But if you want strictly one render without any compositor or sequencer steps, Method 1 is better.  Method 3: Use collections and visibility keys in a single scene Keep the elevator interior, camera, and both floors all in one place, with the floors overlapping exactly. Floor A and Floor B are separate collections.  - Animate the door closing. - When the doors are just one or two frames from being fully closed (so there is practically no gap), insert keyframes on the collections visibility in viewport and render.   - At frame N: Floor A visible, Floor B hidden.   - At frame N+1: Floor A hidden, Floor B visible. - The switch happens when the doors are practically shut so the viewer cannot see the pop.  Because the camera never moves and the elevator interior does not have to translate, this is simpler to manage. Just ensure that:  - Lighting is consistent between floors, or you animate lights slightly between frames. - Shadows, reflection probes, and baked lighting are updated or set up so the sudden swap does not look wrong.  Method 4: Mask with the door mesh in the compositor (only Blender) If you are comfortable with Blender Compositor instead of an external editor, do two renders from the same camera:  - Render pass A: Elevator and first environment, doors closing. - Render pass B: Elevator and second environment, doors opening.  Render the elevator doors with a pass that acts as a holdout or mask. For frames where the doors are fully closed, use them as a matte between the two renders, fading or switching in the second environment behind the closed door in the compositor, still fully inside Blender. This is more complex but still avoids external software.  The cleanest and least technical method is usually to keep everything in one scene and either move the whole elevator rig between different environments while the doors are shut, or hard-switch collection visibility exactly when the doors close so that the render is a single continuous animation with no external editing involved.

One straightforward approach:  Create your two environments: Scene A and Scene B, but keep them as collections in a single scene.  Place the elevator door mesh in front of the camera. No video editor is needed, and all switching is handled by in-scene animation, material keyframing, and simple rig movement inside Blender.

Set up two collections: one for the first environment and one for the second. At the frame where the doors are closed, keyframe the first collection’s visibility (in the viewport and render) to turn off, and at the same frame keyframe the second collection’s visibility to turn on. The camera and the elevator doors stay the same; only what exists behind the doors changes. When you animate the doors opening again, the camera will now reveal the second scene. To avoid any light or reflection pop, you can also keyframe things like environment textures or lights at the same closed-door frame so they swap seamlessly while the doors block the view. Render this as a single continuous animation, and you get an in-camera scene switch with no need for a separate video editor.

3|4: Here are some typical issues such a Factorio Lua control script might have, along with example fixes.  First, a common mistake is to assume you can directly share the same LuaInventory object between different entities. Factorio does not allow one inventory object to be assigned to another; instead, you must manually synchronize contents. A buggy pattern often looks like this:  local id = chest.get_inventory(defines.inventory.chest)[1].label if global.linked_chests[id] then   chest.get_inventory(defines.inventory.chest) = global.linked_chests[id] else   global.linked_chests[id] = chest.get_inventory(defines.inventory.chest) end  This is invalid because inventory objects are read-only references; you cannot assign to them. The fix is to store the entity or the inventory contents in a global table, and then copy items by transfering stacks manually. For example:  local function copy_inventory(src, dst)   dst.clear()   for i = 1, #src do     local stack = src[i]     if stack and stack.valid_for_read then       dst.insert{name = stack.name, count = stack.count}     end   end end  script.on_event(defines.events.on_gui_closed, function(event)   local player = game.get_player(event.player_index)   if not player or not event.entity or not event.entity.valid then return end   if event.entity.name ~= linked_chest_name then return end    local chest = event.entity   local id = chest.get_or_create_control_behavior().parameters.parameters[1].signal   if not id or not id.signal then return end    global.linked_chests = global.linked_chests or {}   global.linked_chests[id.signal.number] = global.linked_chests[id.signal.number] or {}   local group = global.linked_chests[id.signal.number]    if not group.master or not group.master.valid then     group.master = chest   end    local master_inv = group.master.get_inventory(defines.inventory.chest)   for _, other in pairs(group) do     if other ~= chest and other.valid then       local inv = other.get_inventory(defines.inventory.chest)       copy_inventory(master_inv, inv)     end   end    if not table.find(group, chest) then     table.insert(group, chest)   end end)  Second, reading an ID from an input field is usually done via control behavior or combinator parameters, not by assuming the first slot of the chest inventory is special. If the intention is to enter an ID as text via a constant combinator or via a custom GUI text field, the script must use the corresponding API.  For example, if using a constant combinator attached to the chest as the ID carrier, a buggy version might do:  local id = chest.get_inventory(defines.inventory.chest)[1].label  Instead, you should get the control behavior or the combinator parameters. For a chest with circuit behavior:  local cb = chest.get_or_create_control_behavior() if not cb or not cb.parameters then return end local param = cb.parameters.parameters[1] if not param or not param.signal or not param.signal.name then return end local id = param.count  This treats the count of the first signal as your numeric ID. Alternatively you can encode the ID in the signal index or name, but you must use the control behavior API, not inventory labels.  Third, global state must be initialized safely. Many mods crash on first load because they assume global.linked_chests exists. Before using it, always ensure it is initialized:  script.on_init(function()   global.linked_chests = {} end)  script.on_configuration_changed(function()   global.linked_chests = global.linked_chests or {} end)  Then in all event handlers:  global.linked_chests = global.linked_chests or {}  Fourth, events are sometimes attached incorrectly. For dynamic linking based on an ID in an input field, you must pick the right events:  on_built_entity and on_robot_built_entity to register new linked chests on_entity_died and on_robot_mined_entity and on_player_mined_entity to unregister them on_tick or GUI events to handle updates when the ID changes  A buggy approach is to do everything in on_tick unconditionally, which is wasteful, or to rely only on on_built_entity and never handle ID changes. A better pattern is:  script.on_event({defines.events.on_built_entity, defines.events.on_robot_built_entity}, function(event)   local entity = event.created_entity or event.entity   if not entity or not entity.valid then return end   if entity.name ~= linked_chest_name then return end    register_linked_chest(entity) end)  script.on_event({defines.events.on_player_mined_entity, defines.events.on_robot_mined_entity, defines.events.on_entity_died}, function(event)   local entity = event.entity   if not entity or not entity.valid then return end   if entity.name ~= linked_chest_name then return end    unregister_linked_chest(entity) end)  Where register_linked_chest and unregister_linked_chest update global.linked_chests by ID and remove invalid entities.  Fifth, code often forgets to check validity of entities every time they are accessed. Any entity stored in global can become invalid if removed, mined, or destroyed. Before using it, always check entity.valid. For instance, when iterating groups of chests:  for id, group in pairs(global.linked_chests) do   for i = #group, 1, -1 do     local ent = group[i]     if not ent.valid then       table.remove(group, i)     end   end end  Finally, if the mod tries to react to a changed ID by simply changing which global entry the chest is in, it must remove it from the previous group first. Buggy version:  local old_id = global.chest_ids[chest.unit_number] local new_id = read_id(chest) if old_id ~= new_id then   global.linked_chests[new_id] = global.linked_chests[new_id] or {}   table.insert(global.linked_chests[new_id], chest)   global.chest_ids[chest.unit_number] = new_id end  Fixed version:  local old_id = global.chest_ids[chest.unit_number] local new_id = read_id(chest) if old_id ~= new_id then   if old_id and global.linked_chests[old_id] then     for i, ent in ipairs(global.linked_chests[old_id]) do       if ent == chest then         table.remove(global.linked_chests[old_id], i)         break       end     end   end   global.linked_chests[new_id] = global.linked_chests[new_id] or {}   table.insert(global.linked_chests[new_id], chest)   global.chest_ids[chest.unit_number] = new_id end  To summarize the core fixes you likely need  Stop trying to assign inventories between chests; instead, copy contents manually Read the ID from a control behavior or GUI element, not from an inventory slot label Initialize and guard global tables such as global.linked_chests and global.chest_ids Always validate entities (ent and ent.valid) before use Properly register and unregister chests when built, mined, or destroyed, and correctly move them when their ID changes  If you paste the specific Lua snippet, I can rewrite it line by line using these patterns while preserving your intended behavior.
4|4: I’ll describe a set of common problems and concrete fixes, since you didn’t paste the actual code. You can compare each item with your script and adjust accordingly.  One Make sure you use a custom name for your linked chests, not an existing vanilla prototype name. If you try to place entities like linked-chest directly from script without a corresponding prototype or without allowing them in the mod, Factorio will complain or behave strangely. In control.lua you should only work with entities that exist in data.lua as prototypes. So if you haven’t already, define a prototype like:  – in data.lua local linked_chest = table.deepcopy(data.raw[container][steel-chest]) linked_chest.name = linked-chest-with-id linked_chest.type = linked-container linked_chest.icon = __yourmod__/graphics/icons/linked-chest.png linked_chest.minable = { mining_time = 0.2, result = linked-chest-with-id } linked_chest.inventory_size = 48 linked_chest.gui_mode = none  and then in control.lua only create_entity with name = linked-chest-with-id.  Two You need a reliable way to store, update, and look up the link ID for each chest. A common mistake is to keep per-entity data in a non-persistent local table or to forget to initialize the global table. Factorio clears all non-global Lua state between loads. Make sure you initialize global tables in on_init and on_configuration_changed, like this:  – in control.lua local function init_globals()   global.linked_chests = global.linked_chests or {}   – maps id -> { inventories = {entity, ...} }   global.entity_to_id = global.entity_to_id or {}     – maps unit_number -> id end  script.on_init(init_globals) script.on_configuration_changed(init_globals)  Three Do not use entity as a table key directly; use entity.unit_number. Entity objects are not stable across save/load and are not valid keys in serialized tables. A very common bug is doing something like:    global.entity_to_id[entity] = id  You must instead use:    if entity.valid and entity.unit_number then     global.entity_to_id[entity.unit_number] = id   end  Four Update links both ways when the user edits the ID. Many authors only update the source chest and fail to remove it from the old link group. When the ID in your GUI textfield or input field changes, you must:  – get the entity – remove the entity from its old group if it had one – add it to the new group  Something like:  local function set_chest_id(entity, new_id)   if not (entity and entity.valid) then return end    local unit = entity.unit_number   local old_id = global.entity_to_id[unit]    if old_id and global.linked_chests[old_id] then     for i, e in ipairs(global.linked_chests[old_id].inventories) do       if not e.valid or e.unit_number == unit then         table.remove(global.linked_chests[old_id].inventories, i)         break       end     end     if #global.linked_chests[old_id].inventories == 0 then       global.linked_chests[old_id] = nil     end   end    if new_id and new_id ~=  then     global.entity_to_id[unit] = new_id     global.linked_chests[new_id] = global.linked_chests[new_id] or { inventories = {} }     table.insert(global.linked_chests[new_id].inventories, entity)   else     global.entity_to_id[unit] = nil   end end  Then from your GUI handler do set_chest_id(entity, player_input_id).  Five Synchronize inventory contents correctly. A typical mistake is copying inventories only in one direction, or doing it in on_tick for every chest which is both slow and buggy. A better pattern for a linked chest group is:  – choose one chest as the canonical storage for that ID – mirror that inventory to all other chests with the same ID whenever something changes  You can do that in on_gui_closed or when the player changes content, but the most robust is using on_inventory_changed. In newer Factorio versions there is defines.events.on_player_main_inventory_changed etc., but for containers you can use on_entity_died and on_player_mined_entity to capture removal and manually resync when entities are added or removed.  Simplified approach:  local function get_group_main_entity(group)   – just pick the first valid entity as the source   for i, e in ipairs(group.inventories) do     if e.valid then return e end   end end  local function sync_group(id)   local group = global.linked_chests[id]   if not group then return end    local main = get_group_main_entity(group)   if not main then     global.linked_chests[id] = nil     return   end    local src_inv = main.get_inventory(defines.inventory.chest)   if not src_inv then return end    for _, e in ipairs(group.inventories) do     if e.valid and e ~= main then       local dst_inv = e.get_inventory(defines.inventory.chest)       if dst_inv then         dst_inv.clear()         for i = 1, #src_inv do           local stack = src_inv[i]           if stack.valid_for_read then             dst_inv[i].set_stack(stack)           end         end       end     end   end end  Then, whenever something relevant changes (chest built, chest removed, ID changed), call sync_group(id).  Six Use the correct inventory index defines.inventory.chest. A surprisingly frequent error is using the wrong inventory type (for example defines.inventory.player_main or defines.inventory.furnace_source) when calling get_inventory on a chest.  Correct usage:  local inv = entity.get_inventory(defines.inventory.chest) if inv then   – manipulate inventory end  Seven Always check entity.valid before accessing its fields. Many mods forget this in event handlers, which leads to script errors when entities are mined, destroyed, or invalidated by other mods.  Example corrections:  script.on_event(defines.events.on_entity_died, function(event)   local entity = event.entity   if not (entity and entity.valid) then return end   if entity.name ~= linked-chest-with-id then return end    local unit = entity.unit_number   local id = global.entity_to_id[unit]   if id then     – reuse the same removal logic as in set_chest_id     set_chest_id(entity, nil)   end end)  script.on_event(defines.events.on_player_mined_entity, function(event)   local entity = event.entity   if not (entity and entity.valid) then return end   if entity.name ~= linked-chest-with-id then return end    set_chest_id(entity, nil) end)  Eight Use on_built_entity and on_robot_built_entity to automatically register new chests and optionally open a GUI so the player can set an ID. A common bug is to forget one of these events, so robot placed chests never get IDs or vice versa.  Combined handler example:  local function on_built(event)   local entity = event.created_entity or event.entity   if not (entity and entity.valid) then return end   if entity.name ~= linked-chest-with-id then return end    – new chest starts with no ID   global.entity_to_id[entity.unit_number] = nil   – optional: open GUI for player if available end  script.on_event({   defines.events.on_built_entity,   defines.events.on_robot_built_entity }, on_built)  Nine When working with GUI textfields, convert the text to a normalized ID string or number, and handle empty fields correctly. Frequent bugs include:  – using tonumber on a non-numeric ID and getting nil – treating empty string as a valid ID – not trimming whitespace  Example GUI handler:  script.on_event(defines.events.on_gui_text_changed, function(event)   local element = event.element   if not (element and element.valid) then return end   if element.name ~= linked_chest_id_field then return end    local player = game.get_player(event.player_index)   if not player then return end    local entity = element.tags and element.tags.chest_entity and global.chest_by_tag[element.tags.chest_entity]   if not (entity and entity.valid) then return end    local text = (element.text or ):gsub(%s+, )   if text ==  then text = nil end    set_chest_id(entity, text)   if text then     sync_group(text)   end end)  Ten Do not create chests from inside on_tick in response to GUI input; use GUI events directly. If you placed your logic inside on_tick and reference some last_clicked_chest variables, it is easy to run into race conditions or nil accesses. Always store minimal state and react to explicit events.  If you compare your existing script with the patterns above, the most likely concrete mistakes are:  – using entity instead of entity.unit_number as a key in global tables – not initializing global tables in on_init / on_configuration_changed – not checking entity.valid before reading or writing inventory – using the wrong inventory index for chests – failing to remove chests from the old ID group when the ID changes – synchronizing inventory in only one direction or in the wrong event  Implementing the set_chest_id and sync_group helpers as shown, plus the correct event handlers, should fix the linking behavior so that all chests with the same ID always show exactly the same contents.
5|4: Since you did not include the actual LUA code, I can only give a generic description of what to check and how to fix typical mistakes in a Factorio mod that links chests by an ID typed in an inventory field.  First, a common conceptual problem is mixing runtime UI text with entity linking logic. Factorio entities do not natively have an input field you can just type into that then magically propagates. You usually need one of these approaches  Use the entitys unit_number as a key and store metadata like link_id in a global table, and provide a GUI or use an entitys combinator parameters or custom interface to set that link_id.  Or, if you are using a constant combinator or something similar as a proxy for the ID, read the signals from that combinator and interpret one of them as an ID.  Below is an example of how a minimal implementation could be structured, with explanations of typical mistakes and fixes.  Example control lua  local function ensure_global_tables()   global.linked_chests = global.linked_chests or {}   global.chest_by_id = global.chest_by_id or {} end  script on_init(function()   ensure_global_tables() end)  script on_load(function()   ensure_global_tables() end)  Mistake 1 using entity as a key directly without checking validity  A lot of code does something like    global.linked_chests[entity] = { id = id }  and later loops with    for chest, data in pairs(global.linked_chests) do     chest.get_inventory(defines inventory chest) insert{name  some item, count 1}  This breaks in two ways Factorio cannot serialize entity references as keys, and you also do not check chest.valid. Instead, use unit_number as the key and store the entity reference as a field.  Fix  local function register_chest(entity, link_id)   if not (entity and entity.valid) then return end   ensure_global_tables()    local unit = entity.unit_number   global.linked_chests[unit] = {     entity = entity,     id = link_id,   }    global.chest_by_id[link_id] = global.chest_by_id[link_id] or {}   global.chest_by_id[link_id][unit] = entity end  Mistake 2 not handling on_entity_died or on_player_mined_entity  If you never remove old references, later code may try to access an invalid chest entity, causing errors. You need to listen to events that remove chests.  Fix  local function unregister_chest(entity)   if not (entity and entity.valid) then return end   local unit = entity.unit_number   local data = global.linked_chests[unit]   if not data then return end    local id = data.id   global.linked_chests[unit] = nil    local by_id = global.chest_by_id[id]   if by_id then     by_id[unit] = nil     if not next(by_id) then       global.chest_by_id[id] = nil     end   end end  script on_event({defines events on_entity_died, defines events on_player_mined_entity, defines events on_robot_mined_entity}, function(event)   local entity = event.entity or event.created_entity or event.destination   if entity and entity.valid and entity.name == my linked chest name then     unregister_chest(entity)   end end)  Mistake 3 reading the ID from the wrong place or at the wrong time  Often people try to do something like read entity get inventory(defines inventory chest) or entity backer_name to interpret as an ID, but they never trigger a refresh when it changes. For example, if you want to use the name field of the entity to store the numeric ID, you must listen to the event when the player changes it.  However, normal chests do not have a backer_name editable in vanilla. Instead, many mods use  A GUI element that lets the player type an ID  Settings on an associated combinator  Custom input events  So, ensure you actually have a reliable source for the ID. Here is one plausible pattern using a simple textfield GUI opened when the player interacts with the chest.  script on_event(defines events on_player_opened, function(event)   local entity = event.entity   if not (entity and entity.valid) then return end   if entity.name ~= my linked chest name then return end    local player = game get_player(event.player_index)   if not player then return end    -- create or show GUIs textfield where player can type linked ID   -- when the player confirms, call set_chest_id(entity, text) end)  Then a function to set and update the ID  local function set_chest_id(entity, id_string)   if not (entity and entity.valid) then return end    local id = tonumber(id_string)   if not id then     -- maybe show message to player about invalid id     return   end    -- unregister from old id, if present   unregister_chest(entity)   register_chest(entity, id) end  Mistake 4 not synchronizing inventories between linked chests correctly  The usual approach is to choose one canonical inventory or aggregate items across all chests with the same ID, but naive code often double counts or loops infinitely. A clear simple approach is to treat the first chest with this ID as the canonical inventory, and mirror changes to others on certain events or on tick.  Here is a simple on tick example meant for small scale mods  script on_event(defines events on_tick, function(event)   if (event tick % 30) ~= 0 then return end  -- every 30 ticks   if not global.chest_by_id then return end    for id, chests in pairs(global.chest_by_id) do     local first     for unit, entity in pairs(chests) do       if entity and entity.valid then         first = entity         break       end     end      if first then       local ref_inv = first get_inventory(defines inventory chest)       if ref_inv then         local contents = ref_inv get_contents()          -- synchronize all other chests to match contents         for unit, entity in pairs(chests) do           if entity and entity.valid and entity ~= first then             local inv = entity get_inventory(defines inventory chest)             if inv then               inv clear()               for name, count in pairs(contents) do                 inv insert{name = name, count = count}               end             end           end         end       end     end   end end)  Common mistakes inside this sync logic are  Using entity get inventory(defines inventory chest) but using a wrong defines inventory value, like chest instead of defines inventory chest  Not checking inv is not nil before using it  Using contents as a local name but then writing content or items elsewhere  Not clearing the old contents first, leading to duplicated items every sync  Mistake 5 script event registration syntax errors  In Factorio 1.x the recommended style is  script on_event(defines events on_built_entity, function(event) ... end)  but many older guides show  script on_event(defines events on_built_entity, handler)  which is fine, but a typical mistake is writing  script.on_event({defines events.on_built_entity, defines events.on_robot_built_entity}, handler)  instead of  script on_event({defines events on_built_entity, defines events on_robot_built_entity}, handler)  Note the dots vs no dots, commas vs dots, etc. The correct syntax is  script.on_event({defines events on_built_entity, defines events on_robot_built_entity}, function(event)   -- code end)  or respectively with dot notation everywhere  script.on_event({defines events.on_built_entity, defines events.on_robot_built_entity}, function(event)   -- code end)  If your mod currently mixes both styles, fix it to the proper one so Factorio actually calls your handler.  Mistake 6 forgetting to filter to your custom chest prototype  When you handle on_built_entity, on_robot_built_entity, etc, you need to ensure you only register chests of your prototype, or you will try to treat normal chests or other entities as linked chests.  Fix  local linked_chest_name = linked-chest  -- replace with your actual prototype name  local function on_built_chest(event)   local entity = event.created_entity or event.entity   if not (entity and entity.valid) then return end   if entity.name ~= linked_chest_name then return end    -- maybe default ID, or wait for the user to set it   register_chest(entity, 0) end  script.on_event({defines events.on_built_entity, defines events.on_robot_built_entity}, on_built_chest)  Mistake 7 using non persistent local state instead of global  Any table that must persist between saves must be in global. A lot of code does  local linked_chests = {}  and modifies that directly. This is reset when the game is loaded or script is reloaded, so the links are lost. The fix is to always store runtime state in global, and copy a reference to a local variable inside functions only when you use it.  For example  local function some_logic()   local linked_chests = global.linked_chests   if not linked_chests then return end   -- use linked_chests here end  To summarize the kind of fixes you likely need in your existing LUA code  Replace entity keys in global with entity.unit_number keys, and always check entity.valid.  Add handlers for on_entity_died, on_player_mined_entity, and on_robot_mined_entity to unregister chests.  Use a reliable mechanism for players to set the ID, and when it changes, unregister then re register the chest with the new ID.  When syncing inventories, pick a canonical source, clear target inventories before inserting, and check for nil inventories.  Ensure script.on_event syntax and defines events usage is correct and that you filter by your specific chest prototype name.
