6|4: Here are some typical mistakes that often appear in Factorio Lua mods that create linked chests by ID, and how to fix them. Since I don’t see the exact code, I’ll focus on specific patterns that commonly break and how the corrected version should look.  First, the data structure to store all linked containers must be kept in global, not in a local table, otherwise the state will be lost between saves or between script events.  Wrong pattern: local linked_chests = {}  Correct pattern: if not global.linked_chests then   global.linked_chests = {} end  Use global in control.lua so Factorio can serialize the data. Any mapping from ID to entity or inventory must go through global.  Next, you must not store entity references in a way that assumes they stay valid forever; you need to check them with entity.valid before using them, and clean up invalid ones.  Typical broken access: for id, chest in pairs(global.linked_chests) do   local inv = chest.get_inventory(defines.inventory.chest)   inv.clear() end  If any chest was mined or destroyed, chest.valid will be false and this will raise an error. You must guard such calls.  Fixed version: for id, chest_list in pairs(global.linked_chests) do   for i = #chest_list, 1, -1 do     local chest = chest_list[i]     if not chest.valid then       table.remove(chest_list, i)     else       local inv = chest.get_inventory(defines.inventory.chest)       if inv then         -- do syncing logic here       end     end   end end  Related to that: for an ID that can have multiple chests, you should store a list of entities per ID, not a single entity.  Broken data model: -- Only one chest per ID; new chest overwrites old function register_chest(entity, id)   global.linked_chests[id] = entity end  Correct data model: function register_chest(entity, id)   if not global.linked_chests[id] then     global.linked_chests[id] = {}   end   table.insert(global.linked_chests[id], entity) end  Another common issue is reading the ID from the wrong place or at the wrong time. If you use a constant combinator or the entity label as the ID, you must read it consistently on placement and on configuration changes.  Typical broken approach (using entity.name or prototype name as an ID, which is the same for all instances): local id = entity.name  Correct approach examples:  Using entity.backer_name for entities that support it: local function get_chest_id(entity)   return entity.backer_name or "" end  Or using a custom string on the entity via a separate GUI or via a constant combinator network, then parsing it from entity.get_or_create_control_behavior(), or from circuit signals. Whichever method you use, be sure to handle the case where the ID is empty or nil.  When you actually sync the inventories, a frequent bug is to copy the pointer or to clear inventories incorrectly. You should aggregate items and then redistribute, rather than trying to mirror one inventory directly into the others on every change, which can create loops or duplication.  Buggy logic example: -- When any chest changes, copy its inventory to all others in that group function sync_group(id, source_inv)   for _, chest in pairs(global.linked_chests[id]) do     local inv = chest.get_inventory(defines.inventory.chest)     inv.clear()     inv.insert(source_inv.get_contents()) -- incorrect, insert needs one item at a time   end end  There are two problems here. First, inventory.insert expects either a single item stack or a table with name and count, not the entire contents table at once. Second, this logic can cause issues if called repeatedly, and does not handle partial insert failures.  Correct, safer approach:  function aggregate_group_contents(id)   local contents = {}   for _, chest in pairs(global.linked_chests[id]) do     if chest.valid then       local inv = chest.get_inventory(defines.inventory.chest)       if inv then         for name, count in pairs(inv.get_contents()) do           contents[name] = (contents[name] or 0) + count         end       end     end   end   return contents end  function clear_group_inventories(id)   for _, chest in pairs(global.linked_chests[id]) do     if chest.valid then       local inv = chest.get_inventory(defines.inventory.chest)       if inv then inv.clear() end     end   end end  function redistribute_group_contents(id, contents)   for _, chest in pairs(global.linked_chests[id]) do     if chest.valid then       local inv = chest.get_inventory(defines.inventory.chest)       if inv then         for name, count in pairs(contents) do           if count > 0 then             local inserted = inv.insert{name = name, count = count}             contents[name] = contents[name] - inserted           end         end       end     end   end end  function resync_group(id)   local contents = aggregate_group_contents(id)   clear_group_inventories(id)   redistribute_group_contents(id, contents) end  Then you call resync_group(id) when something relevant changes. The specific triggering strategy varies by design; a simple but more expensive method is to handle it on a periodic on_nth_tick event.  Another frequent mistake: forgetting to register and handle the correct events in script.on_event. For placement and removal of your custom chests, you should listen to the appropriate events.  Example of bug: using only on_built_entity but not covering robots or script_build:  script.on_event(defines.events.on_built_entity, function(event)   local entity = event.created_entity   -- register end)  You should use LuaEntity name checks and handle both player and robot builds, plus the mined and died events.  Correct version:  local function on_entity_built(event)   local entity = event.created_entity or event.entity   if not (entity and entity.valid) then return end   if entity.name == "linked-chest" then     local id = get_chest_id(entity)     if id and id ~= "" then       register_chest(entity, id)       resync_group(id)     end   end end  script.on_event(defines.events.on_built_entity, on_entity_built) script.on_event(defines.events.on_robot_built_entity, on_entity_built)  local function on_entity_removed(event)   local entity = event.entity   if not (entity and entity.valid) then return end   if entity.name == "linked-chest" then     local id = get_chest_id(entity)     if id and global.linked_chests[id] then       for i = #global.linked_chests[id], 1, -1 do         if global.linked_chests[id][i] == entity then           table.remove(global.linked_chests[id], i)         end       end       if #global.linked_chests[id] == 0 then         global.linked_chests[id] = nil       else         resync_group(id)       end     end   end end  script.on_event(defines.events.on_player_mined_entity, on_entity_removed) script.on_event(defines.events.on_robot_mined_entity, on_entity_removed) script.on_event(defines.events.on_entity_died, on_entity_removed)  Finally, another subtle but common mistake is constructing the inventory index incorrectly. For container-like entities, you must use defines.inventory.chest, not defines.inventory.furnace_source, etc.  Buggy example: local inv = entity.get_inventory(1) -- magic number, may be wrong  Correct and explicit: local inv = entity.get_inventory(defines.inventory.chest)  If your mod uses different prototypes with different inventory types, ensure you use the correct defines.inventory constant for each.  Putting it all together, a minimal corrected skeleton control.lua that avoids the typical mistakes would look like this (still simplified, but structurally sound):  if not global.linked_chests then   global.linked_chests = {} end  local function get_chest_id(entity)   return entity.backer_name or "" end  local function register_chest(entity, id)   if not global.linked_chests[id] then     global.linked_chests[id] = {}   end   table.insert(global.linked_chests[id], entity) end  local function aggregate_group_contents(id)   local contents = {}   local group = global.linked_chests[id]   if not group then return contents end   for _, chest in pairs(group) do     if chest.valid then       local inv = chest.get_inventory(defines.inventory.chest)       if inv then         for name, count in pairs(inv.get_contents()) do           contents[name] = (contents[name] or 0) + count         end       end     end   end   return contents end  local function clear_group_inventories(id)   local group = global.linked_chests[id]   if not group then return end   for _, chest in pairs(group) do     if chest.valid then       local inv = chest.get_inventory(defines.inventory.chest)       if inv then inv.clear() end     end   end end  local function redistribute_group_contents(id, contents)   local group = global.linked_chests[id]   if not group then return end   for _, chest in pairs(group) do     if chest.valid then       local inv = chest.get_inventory(defines.inventory.chest)       if inv then         for name, count in pairs(contents) do           if count > 0 then             local inserted = inv.insert{name = name, count = count}             contents[name] = contents[name] - inserted           end         end       end     end   end end  local function resync_group(id)   local contents = aggregate_group_contents(id)   clear_group_inventories(id)   redistribute_group_contents(id, contents) end  local function on_entity_built(event)   local entity = event.created_entity or event.entity   if not (entity and entity.valid) then return end   if entity.name == "linked-chest" then     local id = get_chest_id(entity)     if id and id ~= "" then       register_chest(entity, id)       resync_group(id)     end   end end  local function on_entity_removed(event)   local entity = event.entity   if not entity then return end   if entity.name ~= "linked-chest" then return end   local id = get_chest_id(entity)   if not id or not global.linked_chests[id] then return end   local group = global.linked_chests[id]   for i = #group, 1, -1 do     if group[i] == entity then       table.remove(group, i)     end   end   if #group == 0 then     global.linked_chests[id] = nil   else     resync_group(id)   end end  script.on_event(defines.events.on_built_entity, on_entity_built) script.on_event(defines.events.on_robot_built_entity, on_entity_built) script.on_event(defines.events.script_raised_built, on_entity_built) script.on_event(defines.events.script_raised_revive, on_entity_built)  script.on_event(defines.events.on_player_mined_entity, on_entity_removed) script.on_event(defines.events.on_robot_mined_entity, on_entity_removed) script.on_event(defines.events.on_entity_died, on_entity_removed) script.on_event(defines.events.script_raised_destroy, on_entity_removed)  If you paste your exact code, I can point out the specific lines that are wrong, but the fixes above address the usual mistakes: not using global, not checking entity.valid, not handling multiple chests per ID, misusing inventories, and incorrectly inserting get_contents into inventories.

8|4: I can point out the most common mistakes that usually appear in this kind of Factorio Lua code, and how to fix them, even though I do not see your exact source file.  Typical issues and how to correct them  Global data storage Often the code uses a nonpersistent table like  linked_chests = {}  instead of storing it in the global table. In Factorio, only global survives between ticks and save loads. You must use  global.linked_chests = global.linked_chests or {}  and then always refer to global.linked_chests rather than a local or upvalue table. For example, in on_init and on_configuration_changed you should at minimum do  script.on_init(function()   global.linked_chests = global.linked_chests or {} end)  script.on_configuration_changed(function()   global.linked_chests = global.linked_chests or {} end)  Entity indexing by ID A common pattern is to store entities in a table by a string ID read from the chest name, label, or another inventory field, but the code might overwrite a single slot instead of keeping a list, like  global.linked_chests[id] = entity  This breaks when you place more than two chests with the same ID, because only one survives. You need a list of chests per ID:  local id = chest_id  if not global.linked_chests[id] then   global.linked_chests[id] = {} end  table.insert(global.linked_chests[id], entity)  Then, when you remove an entity, you must remove it from that list instead of setting the whole bucket to nil. For example:  local function remove_linked_chest(entity)   local id = entity.unit_number and global.entity_to_id[entity.unit_number]   if not id then return end   local list = global.linked_chests[id]   if not list then return end   for i = #list, 1, -1 do     if not list[i].valid or list[i] == entity then       table.remove(list, i)     end   end   if #list == 0 then     global.linked_chests[id] = nil   end   global.entity_to_id[entity.unit_number] = nil end  Also note the use of global.entity_to_id: you usually need a reverse lookup to know which ID a removed chest belonged to.  Accessing GUI or inventory text If you are reading an ID from an inventory slot as though it were a string field, that will not work. Inventories contain LuaItemStack objects, not textual IDs. Common mistakes look like  local id = entity.get_inventory(defines.inventory.chest)[1]  or  local id = chest_inventory[1].label  Unless you deliberately encode the ID into a specific item (for example, using item labels or item tags), the game has no concept of an ID in the inventory.  If your idea is to type the ID in the entities input field, you need a GUI element (like a textfield) attached to the entity, and store its text in global. Typical pattern:  local function on_entity_created(event)   local entity = event.created_entity or event.entity   if entity.name ~= my_linked_chest_name then return end    global.entity_to_id = global.entity_to_id or {}    local id = nil  -- default until player enters text   global.entity_to_id[entity.unit_number] = id    local player = game.get_player(event.player_index or 1)   if player and player.valid then     local gui = player.gui.center.add{       type = textfield,       name = linked_chest_id_field,       text = ,     }     gui.tags = {unit_number = entity.unit_number}   end end  Then, in your gui text change handler, you update global.entity_to_id[unit_number] and rebuild global.linked_chests accordingly.  Using wrong events Two common mistakes  Using script.on_event(defines.events.on_built_entity, handler) but forgetting to also handle defines.events.on_robot_built_entity or the newer on_built_entity family events from 1.1.  Using the deprecated defines.events.on_entity_died instead of handling on_entity_died, on_player_mined_entity, on_robot_mined_entity, and on_pre_player_mined_item when cleaning up.  Safer approach:  local function on_built(event)   local entity = event.created_entity or event.entity   if entity and entity.valid and entity.name == my_linked_chest_name then     register_linked_chest(entity, event.player_index)   end end  script.on_event(defines.events.on_built_entity, on_built) script.on_event(defines.events.on_robot_built_entity, on_built) script.on_event(defines.events.script_raised_built, on_built) script.on_event(defines.events.script_raised_revive, on_built)  local function on_removed(event)   local entity = event.entity   if entity and entity.valid and entity.name == my_linked_chest_name then     remove_linked_chest(entity)   end end  script.on_event(defines.events.on_player_mined_entity, on_removed) script.on_event(defines.events.on_robot_mined_entity, on_removed) script.on_event(defines.events.on_entity_died, on_removed) script.on_event(defines.events.script_raised_destroy, on_removed)  Synchronizing inventories When you link multiple chests by a shared ID, you typically want all of them to have the same inventory contents. A common mistake is to copy inventory only one way, or only on placement, so they fall out of sync.  A simple robust approach is to choose one chest as authoritative for each ID and copy its inventory to all others whenever something changes. One frequent bug is to assume event.entity is always the chest whose inventory changed; but inventory changes can result from logistics, inserters, scripts, etc. You need defines.events.on_gui_closed or defines.events.on_player_main_inventory_changed, or better, just periodically resync or copy when you detect a change.  A minimal deterministic approach is to synchronize on every tick, but that is expensive. Instead, you can synchronize only when:   A chest inventory changed via script  The player opened or closed the chest  An on_tick handler throttled by ID size is called  Core sync routine example, fixing common mistakes like ignoring validity or nil references:  local function sync_id(id)   local list = global.linked_chests[id]   if not list or #list == 0 then return end    local master = nil   for i = #list, 1, -1 do     local e = list[i]     if not e.valid then       table.remove(list, i)     elseif not master then       master = e     end   end    if not master then     global.linked_chests[id] = nil     return   end    local master_inv = master.get_inventory(defines.inventory.chest)   for _, e in pairs(list) do     if e ~= master and e.valid then       local inv = e.get_inventory(defines.inventory.chest)       if inv and master_inv then         inv.clear()         inv.insert(master_inv.get_contents())       end     end   end end  Then you call sync_id when you know a given IDs chest changed.  Using get_contents incorrectly Another common bug is to write something like  inv.insert(master_inv.get_contents())  get_contents returns a dictionary of name to count. insert expects either a string or a stack table. The simple pattern is:  for name, count in pairs(master_inv.get_contents()) do   inv.insert{name = name, count = count} end  Incorrect nil checks and valid checks You must always check entity.valid before using it. Code like  if entity and entity.name == my_linked_chest_name then   local inv = entity.get_inventory(defines.inventory.chest) end  can crash if entity becomes invalid between event firing and your code running (rare but possible), so the idiomatic pattern is  if not (entity and entity.valid and entity.name == my_linked_chest_name) then return end  Reading ID from circuit or control behavior Sometimes people try to read the ID from the combinator or control behavior directly from the chest, for example using  local behavior = entity.get_or_create_control_behavior() local id = behavior.parameters  But linked chests do not inherently have such behavior; you must either attach a separate combinator entity or use a GUI. If your code assumes get_or_create_control_behavior exists on a chest, it will return nil and then behavior.parameters will crash. The fix is to guard this call and design a specific way to encode the ID.  Proper initialization for existing entities Another common omission: when adding the mod to an existing save, you must scan surfaces for your chest entities and register them in global. You can do this in on_configuration_changed or on_init:  local function rebuild_from_world()   global.linked_chests = {}   global.entity_to_id = {}    for _, surface in pairs(game.surfaces) do     local entities = surface.find_entities_filtered{name = my_linked_chest_name}     for _, entity in pairs(entities) do       local id = get_saved_id_for_entity(entity)  -- from saved data, tags, or GUI       if id then         global.entity_to_id[entity.unit_number] = id         global.linked_chests[id] = global.linked_chests[id] or {}         table.insert(global.linked_chests[id], entity)       end     end   end end  script.on_configuration_changed(function(cfg)   global.linked_chests = global.linked_chests or {}   global.entity_to_id = global.entity_to_id or {}   rebuild_from_world() end)  Putting it together in a minimal fixed structure Below is a compact example that incorporates these fixes and shows a sane structure. Typical problems in this kind of Factorio Lua code:  – Using built-in table.remove on global tables of entities that may contain invalid references while iterating with pairs, which can cause skipped entries. – Not checking entity.valid before accessing its properties on events. – Forgetting to initialize global tables in on_init or on_configuration_changed. – Using event.entity in events that actually use event.created_entity or event.destination or event.robot. – Using string keys directly from entity.unit_number without converting or vice versa; mixing string and number keys when linking. – Accessing entity.get_inventory with the wrong defines.inventory constant. – Storing references to inventories instead of entities; inventories can change internally. – Not handling entity destruction so the global map still contains dead entries, causing errors later. Typical problems in linked chest mods  Missing prototypes If you try to create special chests in runtime script but do not define matching prototypes in data stage, the game will fail or the entities will not work as expected.  Fix In data lua:  local chest = table deepcopy(data raw container steel chest) chest name = linked chest chest minable = nil chest flags = { not blueprinted not deconstructable not repairable player creation} chest inventory size = 48  chest type must remain container or logistic container etc depending on usage, and you must include chest in data extend { chest }  Incorrect event usage A common bug is using script on event(defines events on built entity, handler) instead of the newer syntax or using the wrong event name. Also, 1 1 1 is often misused rather than script on init.  Fix In control lua:  local Event = require core event  if you use stdlib, otherwise use script directly.  script on init(function()   global linked chests = global linked chests or {} end)  script on configuration changed(function()   global linked chests = global linked chests or {} end)  script on event(defines events on built entity, function(event)   local entity = event created entity or event entity   if not entity or not entity valid then return end   if entity name == linked chest then     on linked chest built(entity, event player index)   end end)  script on event(defines events on robot built entity, function(event)   local entity = event created entity or event entity   if not entity or not entity valid then return end   if entity name == linked chest then     on linked chest built(entity, nil)   end end)  You must use defines events on built entity not some old or incorrect constant name, and always guard with valid checks.  Storing entities directly instead of unit number If you directly store entity references in global tables and not their unit number, you can end up with stale references after save load or after mining. You also may forget to remove destroyed entities.  Fix Use unit number as key so you can clean up safely.  Example structure  global linked chests = global linked chests or {}   keys are link id strings or numbers from the chest input field   values are map from unit number to entity  Function to get or create bucket for a given id  local function get id bucket(link id)   if not link id or link id ==  then return nil end   if not global linked chests[link id] then     global linked chests[link id] = {}   end   return global linked chests[link id] end  Function to register chest  local function register linked chest(entity, link id)   local bucket = get id bucket(link id)   if not bucket then return end   local unit = entity unit number   if not unit then return end   bucket[unit] = entity end  Function to unregister when removed  local function unregister linked chest(entity)   local unit = entity unit number   if not unit then return end   for id, bucket in pairs(global linked chests) do     if bucket[unit] then       bucket[unit] = nil       if not next(bucket) then         global linked chests[id] = nil       end       return     end   end end  Wrong way of reading the ID from input A lot of mods try to read an ID from a text field using GUI events but forget to use element text, accidentally use element caption or element name, or they never propagate that ID back to the entity.  Fix When you create the GUI for a player to assign an ID  local frame = player gui screen add{type = frame, name = linked chest frame, direction = vertical} local textfield = frame add{type = textfield, name = linked chest id field, text = } local confirm = frame add{type = button, name = linked chest id confirm, caption = Set ID}  Then handle gui click  script on event(defines events on gui click, function(event)   local element = event element   if not element or not element valid then return end   if element name == linked chest id confirm then     local frame = element parent     local textfield = frame linked chest id field     if not textfield then return end     local id text = textfield text     if id text and id text ~=  then       local player = game get player(event player index)       if player and player opened and player opened valid and player opened name == linked chest then         local entity = player opened         set chest id(entity, id text)         player print(Linked chest ID set to  .. id text)       end     end   end end)  You must use textfield text not caption for user typed strings.  Using local instead of global for persistent state If your original code uses local my data = {} instead of global my data it will be lost on save load and may break after the first reload.  Fix All cross tick data must live in the global table. Never store persistent state in module locals only.  Example persistent structure  global chest ids = global chest ids or {}  map unit number to id string  local function set chest id(entity, id text)   if not entity valid then return end   local unit = entity unit number   if not unit then return end   unregister linked chest(entity)  remove from old id bucket if present   global chest ids[unit] = id text   register linked chest(entity, id text) end  Incorrect inventory synchronization Often people try to link inventories by copying one chest to all others every tick, or use on tick without guarding performance, or they forget to handle stack size limits correctly.  A better approach Pick one chest as the authoritative inventory for each id and copy to others only when something changes. Or synchronize via a virtual inventory table held in global and force chests to mirror that table.  Option 1 authoritative chest per id  For each link id, pick the oldest or first chest as master. On any inventory change event for any chest in that id, you read from the chest that changed and then write the same contents to all others.  Register inventory change events  script on event(defines events on entity settings pasted, function(event)   local src = event source   local dst = event destination   if src valid and dst valid and src name == linked chest and dst name == linked chest then     local id = global chest ids[src unit number]     if id then       set chest id(dst, id)     end   end end)  script on event(defines events on entity died, function(event)   local entity = event entity   if entity and entity valid and entity name == linked chest then     unregister linked chest(entity)   end end)  Inventory change is trickier because Factorio only has defines events on player main inventory changed etc, but for containers you generally need to detect via script on event(defines events on tick) and compare hashes or use lua inventory changed event from newer versions.  More robust virtual inventory approach  Global table as canonical storage    global link data = global link data or {}     for each id       inventory = serialized item stacks  On any chest inventory modification you update global link data for that id, then mirror to all chests.  Core functions  local function read inventory(inv)   local data = {}   for i = 1, #inv do     local stack = inv[i]     if stack valid for read then       data[i] = {name = stack name, count = stack count, quality = stack quality}     else       data[i] = nil     end   end   return data end  local function write inventory(inv, data)   inv clear()   for i, s in pairs(data) do     if s and s name and s count and s count  0 then       inv insert{name = s name, count = s count, quality = s quality}     end   end end  Local function sync id(id)   local bucket = global linked chests[id]   if not bucket then return end   local inv data = global link data[id]   if not inv data then     local any chest = next(bucket) and bucket[next(bucket)] or nil     if any chest and any chest valid then       inv data = read inventory(any chest get inventory(defines inventory chest))       global link data[id] = inv data     else       return     end   end   for unit, entity in pairs(bucket) do     if entity valid then       local inv = entity get inventory(defines inventory chest)       write inventory(inv, inv data)     else       bucket[unit] = nil     end   end end  Then in whatever event you use to detect change, you call sync id(link id).  Common Lua syntax mistakes If your original code has nil checks like if entity == nil then return end but also uses and or mixed with comparisons without parentheses, you may unintentionally short circuit incorrectly.  Fix Always be explicit  if not entity or not entity valid then return end  Also ensure you use pairs for tables with string keys, ipairs only for dense numeric arrays.  Debugging steps for your code  Add assertions and prints  local function dbg(msg)   for _, player in pairs(game players) do     player print([LinkedChests ] .. msg)   end end  Use dbg in all handlers to verify that events are firing, that ids read from GUI match expectation, and that buckets contain what you think they do.  Check save load behavior 1 Place some chests and set the same ID 2 Put items in one chest and verify all update 3 Save and reload 4 Verify that links still work and no nil reference errors appear  If after comparing this to your code you want very specific fixes, paste the actual control lua and data lua and I can annotate and correct line by line, but the list above covers the mistakes that usually prevent linked chests from working and includes patterns you can drop into your mod.

A more realistic approach is to use that 100 as a testbed instead of a profit engine.  A practical blueprint looks like this:  Start by defining the purpose of the 100 Use it to gain hands-on experience with order types, broker interfaces, charts, position sizing, and risk control. Assume you will lose some or all of it. Think of it as a low-cost lab, not a way to make money.  Choose the right instruments and broker Look for a broker with zero-commission trading, fractional shares, and tight spreads. Focus on highly liquid instruments like large-cap stocks, major index ETFs, or the most liquid crypto pairs if you understand the extra risk. Avoid illiquid penny stocks and high-spread exotic assets. With 100 dollars, paying even 1 dollar per trade is already a 1 percent hit to your capital.  Apply strict risk management Trade very small. Risk 1–2 percent of your account per trade at most, i.e., 1–2 dollars. Use hard stop-losses and pre-defined exits. Do not use margin or leverage at this stage; it only makes it easier to blow up. Focus on protecting the 100 and on executing your plan flawlessly, not on maximizing profit.  Use a single simple strategy Pick one clear, rule-based approach rather than hopping around. Examples: trading breakouts on a 5- or 15-minute chart; mean-reversion around a moving average; reacting to news only after volatility settles. Write down your entry criteria, stop placement, profit target logic, and exit rules. Do not improvise mid-trade.  Track everything Keep a trading journal with screenshots of your entries and exits, your reasoning, and your emotional state. At 100 dollars you are not collecting money; you are collecting data about your behavior, edge, and discipline. After 20–50 trades, review patterns: Are you cutting winners too early, moving stops, or overtrading? The 100-dollar real account teaches you psychological and execution realities; the simulator lets you test many more setups quickly. Only consider scaling when you have a documented, profitable approach over a significant sample size. Run simple calculations: with 2 percent risk per trade, a solid win rate, and a healthy reward-to-risk ratio, progress is slow but survivable. Focus on process, not outcome Your goal with 100 dollars should be: I followed my plan perfectly today, not I made 10 dollars. Successful day traders think like engineers and statisticians, not gamblers. You are building habits of risk control, patience, and rule-following that will matter when you eventually trade with 1,000 or 10,000, not chasing miracles from 100. Then, after increasing your capital and saving steadily, you can revisit active trading with a more realistic stake.  So the best way to day trade with 100 dollars is to redefine success: use it as a controlled, low-cost experiment to learn execution, discipline, and edge-finding, while accepting that meaningful income from that amount through day trading alone is statistically and structurally very unlikely. Use the 100 to get good, not to get rich.

1|8: Yes. You can lean heavily on Ruby-specific features like blocks, modules, refinements, open classes, symbols, and keyword arguments to build a tax calculator that feels very idiomatic to Ruby.  Here is an example of a simple, extensible income tax calculator written in pure Ruby style. Imagine a progressive tax system with brackets and rates, and a few rule types (flat tax, bracketed tax, and credits). The point is to show Ruby-centric features rather than replicate any real jurisdiction.  module Tax   class Context     attr_reader :income, :deductions, :credits      def initialize(income:, deductions: 0, credits: 0)       @income = income       @deductions = deductions       @credits = credits     end      def taxable_income       [income - deductions, 0].max     end   end    class Rule     def initialize(name, &block)       @name = name       @calculator = block     end      def call(context)       @calculator.call(context)     end      def to_sym       @name     end   end    class Schedule     def initialize       @rules = []     end      def rule(name, &block)       @rules << Rule.new(name, &block)     end      def tax(context)       detail = {}       total  = 0        @rules.each do |r|         value = r.call(context)         detail[r.to_sym] = value         total += value       end        { total: total, detail: detail }     end   end    module Brackets     module_function      def apply(amount, brackets)       tax = 0       remaining = amount       last_limit = 0        brackets.each do |limit, rate|         break if remaining <= 0          span = [limit - last_limit, remaining].min         tax += span * rate         remaining -= span         last_limit = limit       end        tax += remaining * brackets.last.last if remaining > 0        tax     end   end end  using Module.new {   refine Numeric do     def percent       self / 100.0     end   end }  schedule = Tax::Schedule.new  schedule.rule :base_bracket_tax do |ctx|   Tax::Brackets.apply(     ctx.taxable_income,     [       [10_000, 10.percent],       [40_000, 20.percent],       [80_000, 30.percent]     ]   ) end  schedule.rule :high_income_surtax do |ctx|   excess = [ctx.taxable_income - 100_000, 0].max   excess * 5.percent end  schedule.rule :non_refundable_credit do |ctx|   base = 1_000   tax_before = Tax::Brackets.apply(     ctx.taxable_income,     [       [10_000, 10.percent],       [40_000, 20.percent],       [80_000, 30.percent]     ]   )    -[base, tax_before].min end  schedule.rule :custom_credits do |ctx|   -(ctx.credits || 0) end  context = Tax::Context.new(income: 120_000, deductions: 5_000, credits: 500) result  = schedule.tax(context)  p result  This example showcases Ruby-specific idioms: open classes and refinements to add percent to Numeric; blocks and closures for rules; keyword arguments for context creation; symbols and hashes for detailed output; and a DSL-like definition of tax rules where the schedule.rule :name do |ctx| ... end pattern feels like Ruby rather than a more rigid, typed style. You can extend this with more rules, different schedules for regions, or meta-programming (define_method, const_set) if you want a richer Ruby-only tax engine.
2|8: Yes, you can write a simple tax calculator that leans heavily on Ruby-specific features like blocks, symbols, open classes, and refinements rather than mimicking a more generic, language-neutral style.  Below is a compact example that calculates tax for different brackets using blocks, ranges, and Ruby’s Enumerable methods, without external libraries:  class TaxTable   attr_reader :brackets    def initialize(&definition)     @brackets = []     instance_eval(&definition) if block_given?   end    def bracket(range, rate:)     @brackets << { range: range, rate: rate }   end    def tax_for(income)     brackets.inject(0) do |tax, b|       range = b[:range]       rate  = b[:rate]        lower = range.begin       upper = range.end       upper -= 1 if range.exclude_end?        taxable = [income - lower, 0].max       taxable = [taxable, upper - lower].min if upper       tax + (taxable.positive? ? taxable * rate : 0)     end   end end  us_federal = TaxTable.new do   bracket 0..11_000,     rate: 0.10   bracket 11_000..44_725, rate: 0.12   bracket 44_725..95_375, rate: 0.22 end  income = 60_000 puts us_federal.tax_for(income)  This leans on Ruby-isms: blocks for DSL-like table definition, ranges with inclusive/exclusive ends, symbols and hashes, Enumerable#inject, and underscore numeric literals.  You could push it further into Ruby territory by using refinements or reopening Numeric to add a tax method, metaprogramming to define named bracket methods dynamically, or mixing in modules for different jurisdictions. The key is that none of this relies on non-Ruby-specific paradigms; it uses Ruby’s expressive syntax and metaprogramming style to make the tax calculator feel idiomatic and domain-specific.
3|8: Here is a very Ruby‑centric way to build a simple tax calculator, leaning on blocks, symbols, metaprogramming, and refinements instead of a typical OO style:  module Tax   module_function    # Core calculation using Ruby blocks and keyword args   def calculate(amount, rate:, &rounder)     tax = amount * rate     rounder ? rounder.call(tax) : tax   end    # Build a calculator as a closure using lambdas   def builder(rate, &rounder)     rounder ||= ->(x) { x }     ->(amount) { rounder.call(amount * rate) }   end    # DSL to define named tax profiles using a Hash with default proc   def profiles     @profiles ||= Hash.new do |h, k|       raise KeyError, "Unknown tax profile: #{k.inspect}"     end   end    def define_profile(name, rate, &rounder)     profiles[name.to_sym] = builder(rate, &rounder)   end    def [](profile_name)     profiles.fetch(profile_name.to_sym)   end end  # Refinement to bring a DSL-like syntax into Numeric module TaxDSL   refine Numeric do     def with_tax(profile = :default)       Tax[profile].call(self)     end      def tax_only(profile = :default)       Tax[profile].call(self) - self     end   end end  # Define some profiles using Ruby blocks and symbols Tax.define_profile(:default, 0.10) do |tax|   tax.round(2) end  Tax.define_profile(:reduced, 0.05) do |tax|   (tax * 2).round / 2.0 end  Tax.define_profile(:luxury, 0.25) do |tax|   (tax.ceil(2) + 1).to_f end  using TaxDSL  amount = 100.0  final_default  = amount.with_tax(:default)   # 110.0 final_reduced  = amount.with_tax(:reduced)   # 105.0 (rounded to .5) final_luxury   = amount.with_tax(:luxury)    # ceiling style rounding + 1 only_tax       = amount.tax_only(:default)   # 10.0  # You can even compose calculators functionally add_vat    = Tax.builder(0.20) { |t| t.round(2) } add_local  = Tax.builder(0.03) { |t| t.round(2) }  composed = ->(amt) { amt + add_vat.call(amt) + add_local.call(amt) }  result = composed.call(150.0)  result  This example sticks closely to Ruby-isms: lambdas and blocks for behavior injection, symbols and hashes for lightweight dispatch, refinements for opt‑in Numeric extensions, the module_function pattern, and a very small internal DSL for profiles instead of relying on external configuration or frameworks.

10|8: Yes. You can lean on Ruby’s own numeric types, blocks, modules, and metaprogramming instead of external libraries or foreign syntax. For example, imagine a very simple, Ruby‐centric income tax calculator that uses modules, mixins, lambdas, and ranges to define progressive brackets:  module TaxBrackets   BRACKETS = [     { range: (0...10_000),   rate: 0.0  },     { range: (10_000...40_000), rate: 0.10 },     { range: (40_000...85_000), rate: 0.22 },     { range: (85_000..Float::INFINITY), rate: 0.32 }   ]    module_function    def tax_for(income)     income = income.to_f     tax = 0.0      BRACKETS.each_cons(2) do |current, nxt|       lower = current[:range].begin       upper = nxt[:range].begin       taxable = [[income - lower, 0].max, upper - lower].min       tax += taxable * current[:rate]     end      last = BRACKETS.last     if income > last[:range].begin       tax += (income - last[:range].begin) * last[:rate]     end      tax   end end  class TaxCalculator   include TaxBrackets    def initialize(income)     @income = income.to_f   end    def tax     self.class.tax_for(@income)   end    def net_income     @income - tax   end    def effective_rate     return 0.0 if @income.zero?     tax / @income   end    class << self     def for(income)       new(income)     end      def tax_for(income)       TaxBrackets.tax_for(income)     end   end end  calc = TaxCalculator.for(50_000) puts calc.tax        # Ruby core Numeric, ranges, and iteration puts calc.net_income puts calc.effective_rate  This uses only Ruby features: modules, classes, Range objects, Enumerable methods (each_cons), Numeric and Float, and class singleton methods. In this phase you are not trying to write full tracks; you are learning the language of the machine.  1. Learn every sound in isolation Spend a few sessions focusing on one or two instruments at a time. For example, one day work only with kick and snare, another with hi-hats and clap. Program a very simple pattern, like a 4-on-the-floor kick with a snare on 2 and 4. While the pattern loops, systematically sweep each parameter for those voices: tune, decay, tone, level, etc. Listen carefully to how these affect groove, perceived loudness, and energy. Make verbal notes to yourself: “Shorter kick decay feels tighter and leaves space,” “More open hat decay changes the swing feel,” and so on.  2. Velocity, accents, and dynamics Practice using accent and level changes to create groove, even on very basic patterns. Create a 1-bar pattern with hats on every 16th note. Add accents only on a few steps and listen to how that changes the feel. Make variations: one pattern with heavy accents on the off-beats, one with sparse, subtle accents. Switch between them while listening for feel differences.  3. Internalizing the layout Play without looking at the labels as much as possible. Repetition will help you build muscle memory: Practice muting/unmuting each instrument repeatedly until you can do it without hesitation. Practice jumping between pattern, step editing, and performance modes so your fingers know the workflow. The goal is to reduce “menu thinking” and increase “instrument playing.”  Phase 2: Groove, Timing, and Pattern Craft  Now you will work on making the RD-9 groove on its own.  4. Build a library of core patterns Design 4–8 “go-to” patterns in different styles: straight 4/4, shuffle, half-time, broken beats. For each pattern, save at least two variations: one minimal version and one busier, more energetic version. Practice transitioning smoothly between variations while a metronome or another drum loop plays, so your changes feel musical and intentional.  5. Practice swing and micro-timing Use the shuffle/swing functions and listen critically at different settings. Take one pattern and play it at multiple tempos with varying swing values. Record yourself (even on a phone) and listen back to notice which combinations feel “alive” and which feel stiff. If the RD-9 has per-part or per-step timing nudge options, experiment pushing or pulling certain hits slightly to develop your ear for feel.  6. Constraint exercises To develop creativity: limit yourself for a whole session to just kick, snare, and closed hat. Write as many different grooves as you can in 30 minutes. Then do the same with only toms and clap, or only hats and percussion. Constraints force you to focus on rhythm and dynamics rather than just more sounds.  Phase 3: Sound Design and Performance Controls  This is where the RD-9 starts feeling expressive rather than static.  7. Parameter “performance moves” Pick a few expressive knobs or switches that significantly alter the mood: e.g. kick decay, snare tone, hat decay, filter if present. With a simple loop running, practice “playing” these controls rhythmically: Move the decay only on fills or at the end of a 4-bar loop. Sweep snare tone during transitions. Practice subtlety: find the range where it feels musical rather than gimmicky. Over time, build a small mental toolkit of go-to moves you can use live, such as “open hats and longer snare decay for build-ups” or “short decay + low tone for breakdowns.”  8. Fills, mutes, and live arrangement Pattern is the base; performance is the song. Practice making live arrangements using just: Instant mutes and unmutes of parts. On-the-fly fills: in step mode, quickly adding and removing extra hits. Pattern chaining or manual pattern switching. Create a 16- or 32-bar “performance” with only one or two base patterns by using these tools to create intros, drops, and build-ups. Record these performances and listen back. Note what felt effective and what sounded messy or abrupt.  9. Integrating external processing If you have effects (reverb, delay, distortion, compressor), route some RD-9 parts through them. Dedicate a few sessions to learning how external FX interact with your performance: Use delay feedback for transitions and breakdowns. Use reverb sends on clap or snare to enlarge a section. Practice riding FX knobs as part of your performance, not just “set and forget.” Even if you only have a simple pedal, learn how to make that one effect part of your playing.  Phase 4: Musical Context and Composition  You want the RD-9 to feel like a musician in a band, not a click track.  10. Jam with other instruments or tracks Load up a bassline, chord loop, or track you like and mute its drums. Play the RD-9 along with it, working on matching energy, style, and arrangement. Try different roles: sometimes the RD-9 is minimal (just underpinning the groove), sometimes it drives the whole energy. If you have synths or DAW instruments, schedule regular jam sessions: 30 minutes where the primary goal is to interact musically, not to perfect anything.  11. Build whole songs from the RD-9 Choose 1–3 patterns as the “DNA” of a track. Plan a simple structure on paper: intro, main, breakdown, build, climax, outro. Decide in advance when you will bring in each instrument, when you will mute, when you will change patterns, and what performance moves you want to attempt. Record a live take of you “performing” the song. Do multiple takes and listen to how your timing and transitions improve.  Phase 5: Deliberate Practice, Feedback, and Refinement  12. Focused routine Create a weekly routine that might look like this: Day 1: Sound design and parameter exploration. Day 2: Groove building and pattern variations. Day 3: Performance practice (mutes, fills, pattern switching). Day 4: Jamming with other instruments or tracks. Day 5: Recording a live performance and reviewing it. Even 20–30 minutes per day will add up if it is focused.  13. Self-review and notes After each recorded session, take a few minutes to note: Which patterns felt strong and which felt weak. Which performance moves worked and which felt clumsy. Any ideas for new patterns or techniques. Over time, you will see patterns in what you like and can lean into your personal style on the RD-9.  14. Learn from others Watch performance videos of people using 808-style or RD-9 machines live. Pause and analyze: What are they doing with mutes, fills, and parameter tweaks? How do they structure a build-up or drop without touching a DAW? Pick one idea per video and try to replicate it on your RD-9 in your next session.  Mindset and Long-Term Growth  Treat the RD-9 like a drum set: drummers practice rudiments, timing, dynamics, and coordination. You are doing the same, but with buttons and knobs. Focus on consistency: short, regular practice is better than rare marathons. Embrace limits: mastering a few patterns and performance tricks deeply is more valuable than constantly chasing new complexity. Over months, this process will transform the RD-9 from a pattern box into a playable, expressive instrument you feel fluent on.
4|9: Treat your RD-9 like a primary performance instrument rather than a backing track box. Start by setting a clear focus for a month: for example, controlling dynamics and groove with nothing but the RD-9 and a mixer or headphones. Commit to short, daily sessions instead of rare long marathons so your hands and ears learn the machine like a guitar player learns their fretboard.  Week 1: Deep familiarity with sound and controls Spend this week in Pattern Write and Manual modes, but ignore all external gear. Your only goal is to learn how each sound and knob behaves.  Each day, pick 2 sounds, like kick and snare. Dial in 3 very different versions of each: one subtle and soft, one punchy and midrange-forward, one extreme or weird. Save temporary patterns that feature those variations, and play them back while you tweak knobs live so your ears connect what you hear with what your hands are doing. Practice muting and unmuting individual voices by hand to create variation without touching the pattern itself. Try to make a static 1-bar pattern feel like it’s changing just by changing levels, accents, and mutes. Focus on the accent system. Build a simple 4-on-the-floor beat and systematically move accents around the bar, listening to how the groove changes when the accent hits the kick, the snare, or the hats.  Week 2: Groove, timing, and performance patterns Now center everything on groove instead of just sound.  Pick a tempo and build only 1-bar patterns. Make at least three versions of a basic beat: straight, slightly busier, and broken or syncopated. Practice switching between them while the machine is running, working on seamless transitions. Practice playing fills entirely by step editing and muting. For example, have a core pattern and then a second pattern with small rhythmic changes that feel like fills rather than brand-new beats. Work on chaining them into short song-like structures. Turn off the quantization crutch in your mind by listening more than looking: avoid staring at the LEDs all the time and try to feel where the bar starts and ends. Mute a sound just before the bar loops and bring it back in exactly on the 1, training your intuition.  Week 3: Live performance skills Dedicated this week to treating the RD-9 like you are onstage.  Limit yourself to a single project of patterns. Program a mini live set: intro pattern, main groove, variations, fills, breakdowns, and an ending. Think in musical sections instead of isolated patterns. Practice performance moves: slowly opening and closing hats, riding the snare tone and tuning to create tension, filter-like effects by sculpting tone, and managing levels to build breakdowns and drops. Try to perform 5-minute “tracks” using only those patterns and live tweaks. Use pattern switching and fills deliberately. Practice hitting pattern changes slightly before the bar so they land cleanly. Experiment with using pattern length changes to build energy, for example switching from 2-bar patterns to tight 1-bar loops for tension. Record each performance on your phone or DAW and listen back without touching the machine. Notice where you lose energy, where transitions feel abrupt, and where you feel stuck repeating the same move.  Week 4: Integration and creativity Now bring the RD-9 into your broader musical world.  Sync it to a DAW, synth, or sequencer, but keep the RD-9 in the lead rhythm role. Practice building tracks around grooves you create on the machine instead of building a groove to fit a track. Let the RD-9 decide the feel, tempo, and energy. Design a few “signature” kits and pattern styles that feel like your voice. Maybe one is more minimal and dubby, another aggressive and punchy, another broken and swung. These become reusable vocabularies you can pull from in future sessions. Experiment with swing and micro-variation: alternate between straight and swung patterns, or use subtle differences between almost-identical patterns to create evolving sections. Try building A/B patterns where only one or two hits move, but the feel changes noticeably.  Ongoing practice routines Set a regular schedule: for example, 20 minutes a day, 5 days a week. Give each session a simple focus such as only hats and percussion, only fills and pattern changes, or only dynamics and accents. Keep a small notebook or digital note where you write down your favorite knob positions, pattern IDs, or ideas like “snare decay long + low tuning for breakdowns.” This builds a personal playbook. Regularly record yourself improvising for 10–15 minutes. Afterward, listen and take quick notes: what transitions felt good, which sounds cut too much or not enough, which tricks you overused. Use these notes to guide the next week’s focus.  Mindset shifts to treat RD-9 as an instrument Think like a drummer, not a programmer. Ask what a human drummer might accent, leave out, or vary every bar or two, and then recreate that with subtle pattern variations, mutes, and accents. Practice restraint. Instead of layering more and more hits, work on subtracting elements to create tension and release. Make yourself do entire sections using only kick and hats, then only snare and percussion, to feel how little you actually need. Develop tactile muscle memory. Run “etudes” for your hands, like repeatedly performing the same build and drop sequence with mutes and level adjustments until you can do it without thinking.  If you stick to this structure, you will gradually move from just programming good patterns to actually playing the RD-9 with intention, touch, and feel. Over time you will notice that you reach for it to express ideas, not just to fill in drums, which is the sign that you are truly using it as an instrument.
5|9: Treat your RD-9 like a primary instrument, not just a backing track box, and build a structured but fun routine around sound design, pattern creation, performance techniques, and musical context.  Start with intimacy and fundamentals Spend a week or two just learning every control and sound: Pick one sound per day: kick, snare, clap, toms, cymbals, hats, rim, etc. For that day, jam with that sound as the focus. Adjust tuning, decay, tone, level, accent, and try to understand how each parameter changes feel and function in a groove. Practice muting and unmuting parts on the fly and adjusting levels without looking at the panel too much. The goal is to be able to find and ride any fader or knob by muscle memory. Try building the same basic beat in song mode several times, but each time get the character mostly from sound design: clean and punchy, noisy and distorted, long decays, short and tight.  Pattern practice routine Set up a recurring daily or every other day practice block of 30 to 45 minutes with a clear focus: Groove templates: pick a simple style for the day: electro, house, techno, hip hop, breakbeat. Create a 1 bar pattern that nails that style, then extend it to 2 and 4 bars with variation. Constraint sessions: limit yourself, for example only kick, hats, and clap; or only toms and hats. See how musical and varied you can make it with fewer sounds. Accent and dynamics drills: create a pattern that uses accents heavily. Shift where the accents fall to change the groove from straight to funky or more aggressive. Use the accent to create “call and response” between sounds. Shuffle and timing: experiment with different shuffle/swing amounts. Practice moving certain hits off the grid if available or nudging them in real time using step placement. Listen for how tiny timing shifts change the groove.  Performance: treating it like a live instrument Dedicate sessions to learning how to perform with it, even if you are not on stage: Pattern morphing: start with one pattern and slowly transform it over several minutes by changing steps, muting/unmuting, tweaking sound parameters, and changing accent patterns. The goal is to never fully stop the groove while evolving it. Hands-only jam: play for 10 minutes where you never stop the sequencer and your hands are always doing something musical: fills, parameter tweaks, level changes, mutes, transitions. Fills and transitions: design a few dedicated fill patterns and practice switching to them and back in time. Get used to using pattern chaining and step repeating features for instant fills. Emergency saves: practice recovering from mistakes: muting everything except kick to reset the feel, quickly rebalancing levels, or using a simple pattern as a safety net you can always jump back to.  Sound design and character The RD-9 can change character a lot with knob moves and gain staging. Make this part of your practice: Assign a “character theme” to a session: dark and booming, bright and snappy, lo-fi and crunchy, dry and minimal. Within that theme, design 3 to 5 patterns and save them in a dedicated bank so you start building a library of “kits with attitude.” Experiment with pushing the main output levels into a mixer or interface to get subtle saturation or crunch, if your setup allows. Practice global moves, like slowly lowering cymbal decay while raising toms, or shortening kick decay while opening hats. These macro gestures make your playing feel intentional and musical.  Musical context: playing with other instruments To treat it as an instrument, it needs context. Even if you are not collaborating, give it a “band.” Sync it with a DAW, synth, or sampler. Practice being both drummer and producer: use the RD-9 to support a bassline or pad, not just as a solo toy. Choose a key or scale and match your drum accents and fills to the musical phrasing of the melody or bassline. For example, emphasize kick and snare on the start of melodic phrases; use open hats or cymbals to mark endings or transitions. Record simple jams and listen back with a critical ear. Note where the groove dips, where transitions feel weak, or where sounds clash with other elements. Next session, focus just on fixing one weakness you noticed.  Structured skill progression plan Over 4 to 6 weeks you could follow something like this: Week 1: exploration and muscle memory. Explore every sound. Build 10 simple patterns in different styles. Practice basic mute and level performance. Week 2: groove and accents. Work on swing, ghost notes, accents, and subtle timing. Rebuild some of your Week 1 patterns with better dynamics. Week 3: live performance. Practice 10 to 15 minute continuous jams using pattern changes, fills, and parameter tweaks. Record at least one per day. Week 4: musical integration. Sync with a DAW or synth. Build at least 2 tracks where the RD-9 is clearly performing “parts” that interact with bass and melody. Weeks 5 and 6: style development. Pick 1 or 2 genres you care about and focus: study reference tracks, copy their drum structure, and then bend it into your own style with sound design and performance.  Deliberate listening and copying Choose a few favorite tracks with drum machine driven grooves. Use your RD-9 to approximate them: Solo the drums in your reference track if possible or just focus on them. Recreate the pattern step by step: where are the kicks, snares, claps, hats, toms. Then match swing and dynamics as closely as you can. Compare. Your goal is not a perfect copy, but to understand how producers use drum machines musically: when hits drop out, when fills happen, how sections evolve. Do this regularly and your instinct for arrangements and variation will sharpen.  Mindset: practice like a drummer Think like a live drummer: Practice “phrases” of 2, 4, 8 bars instead of just looping forever. Make bar 4 slightly different from bars 1 to 3. Build tension across 8 bars before making a bigger change. Give each hand a job metaphorically. For example, right hand does hats and cymbals changes, left hand handles mutes, kick, and snare tweaks. This gives structure to your physical performance. Practice dynamics across a whole jam: start minimal and quiet, build to dense and loud, then break down again. Use decay, level, mutes, and pattern density to “breathe.”  Feedback and iteration Record yourself often: short 5 to 15 minute live takes. Then listen back the next day and take notes: Where did you lose the groove Which transitions sounded weak or abrupt Where did something unexpectedly cool happen Use these notes to design the next few practice sessions. If your transitions are weak, spend a session doing nothing but practicing transitions between a small set of patterns. If your grooves get too busy, practice minimalism and space.  Concrete weekly schedule example 3 short sessions per week, 30 to 45 minutes each: Session A: technical focus: new pattern, sound design, accent and swing, copying a reference beat. Session B: performance focus: 15 minute continuous jam where you must use at least three fills, three pattern changes, and a clear build up and breakdown. Session C: integration: RD-9 plus another instrument or DAW, focusing on how your playing supports a musical idea.  If you stick to a structured plan like this, and keep recording and reviewing your jams, your RD-9 will start to feel less like a box that plays drums and more like an expressive instrument that you are actually playing in real time.
6|9: Think of the RD-9 less as a drum machine and more as a drum set plus a performance synth, and build a routine that develops three core skills: sound design, pattern writing, and live performance.  First, get deeply familiar with the voice architecture. Set aside several practice sessions where you mute all but one sound and explore it in isolation. For each voice, deliberately sweep every knob through its full range and listen: kick tune, decay, attack/transient; snare noise/tone balance; toms tuning; hats and cymbals decay and filter; clap width and reverb-like tail if available. Each time you dial in something you like, recreate it from scratch three or four times without looking at your previous settings, so it becomes muscle memory instead of a happy accident.  Next, create a personal sound palette. Devote an evening to designing a few go-to kits that cover different roles: a tight, dry electro kit for precise patterns; a big, roomy kit for slower, heavier beats; a mid-crunchy, distorted kit for techno or industrial vibes. Save patterns that showcase each kit and practice switching between them. The goal is to be able to quickly shape the RD-9 into an instrument that fits whatever track or jam you are doing, instead of using the default sounds every time.  Then, focus on pattern composition. Restrict yourself to simple structures and get them incredibly tight. For a week, practice only 1 or 2 bar patterns. Start with classic templates: straight 4-on-the-floor kick, off-beat open hats, snare on 2 and 4. Once these are solid, add subtle variations: move kicks off the grid occasionally, add ghost snares at low levels, use low-volume toms as percussive fillers, and layer claps with snares for emphasis. Practice writing patterns in step mode first so you can see the distribution, then try recreating them live in real time without looking or stopping the clock.  Work on variation and song structure. Take a single groove and build at least 4 related patterns from it: a stripped-down intro, a main groove, a busier variation, and a fill. Practice toggling between them so you can create tension and release. Force yourself to play a 5–10 minute live jam using only those patterns, focusing on when you bring elements in and out and how you handle transitions. Record these jams and listen back, asking where you started to lose energy or interest, and adjust your use of mutes, fills, and parameter changes accordingly.  Integrate parameter automation and hands-on performance. Choose one or two performance gestures to practice each session: for example, live tweaking of kick decay and tuning during builds, increasing snare noise for a rougher chorus, or opening hi-hat decay to create a lift. Don’t tweak everything all the time; pick a small number of expressive moves and repeat them until they feel natural and controlled. Practice riding the accent track or the global level to emphasize certain steps, like pushing every 4th snare or specific syncopated kicks.  Make a dedicated mute and fill practice routine. Start a main pattern looping, then spend 10–15 minutes doing nothing but practicing mutes with both hands, almost like a finger-drumming exercise: drop all drums out except the kick, then only hats, then just snare and toms, and so on. Learn a few “mute combos” that feel satisfying and can be triggered without thinking. Then, incorporate the RD-9’s fill behavior and pattern switching, practicing short, 1-bar and 2-bar fills that you can reliably trigger at the end of 4, 8, or 16 bar phrases.  Use a tempo ladder to build timing and control. Set a metronome or sync the RD-9 with a DAW or another clock source, and play the same pattern at a range of tempos: slow (80–95 BPM), mid (110–125), and fast (130–140+). At slower tempos, focus on swing and micro-timing, adjusting shuffle and step placement to make the groove feel laid back or pushed. At higher tempos, focus on keeping the groove from becoming cluttered; simplify patterns and rely on sound shaping and muting rather than more notes.  Integrate external context. A few times a week, jam with a bassline, synth pad, or loop from a DAW or another hardware instrument. Start simple: load a single bass loop or sequence, sync the RD-9, and try to make the drums support that part instead of compete. This will train you to think like a drummer in a band, leaving space and using contrast. Record some of these sessions and analyze which drum choices made the musical conversation better.  Develop a regular practice schedule. For example, three 45–60 minute sessions per week:  Session A: Sound design and kits. Choose two instruments (like kick and snare) and explore new settings. Create one short pattern that shows off your new sounds. Session B: Pattern writing and structure. Write or refine 4 patterns that feel related. Practice transitions, mutes, and fills between them for at least 15 minutes straight, no stopping. Session C: Live performance jam. Sync to a DAW or other instrument if possible, hit record, and force yourself to perform a 10–20 minute set using whatever you have built. No stopping or editing mid-jam. Afterwards, listen back and take a few quick notes on which gestures, transitions, and sounds felt most musical.  Track your progress in a simple notebook or digital doc. After each practice, jot down one new technique you discovered and one weakness you noticed. Over time, turn those notes into focused micro-goals for your next sessions: for example, “practice smoother pattern changes without cutting off the last beat,” or “work on kick tuning so it doesn’t clash with basslines.”  Finally, learn from others while keeping your own voice. Watch a few live jam videos of people using the RD-9 or similar 909-style machines. Pick one idea at a time to steal and adapt: maybe how they use mutes, their use of long hat decays during builds, or the way they introduce toms only for fills. Try recreating the idea, then changing it to fit your taste. The aim is not to copy a genre stereotype but to gradually build a vocabulary of performance moves so that, over time, the RD-9 feels as expressive and natural to you as a guitarist’s favorite instrument.

Treat each session like a focused rehearsal with a clear intent instead of aimless tweaking. Example:  Week 1: Learn every basic button combination and function from the manual. Don’t worry about making “great” music; the goal is fluency. Week 2: Focus on patterns and groove. Build 10 different patterns at various tempos and styles (electro, house, techno, hip-hop, broken beats). Week 3: Performance mode. Practice transitions, fills, mutes, and live tweaking of knobs. Record yourself and listen critically to where the energy rises and falls. Week 4: Integration. Play the RD-9 with another instrument or backing track, like a synth loop, bassline, or DJ set. Learn to “talk” with the other instrument, responding with changes in the drums.  Create small recording rituals. Even if it’s just your phone capturing audio from your speakers, record multiple short jams each week. Label them by date and vibe. Once a week, listen back and note:  Moments where the groove really locked in Transitions that felt awkward Knob moves that sounded musical vs. knob moves that felt random  Use those notes to define next week’s practice: if transitions were shaky, spend sessions just practicing muting, pattern switching, and fills; if your sound design was weak, spend sessions exploring the tone controls and mix balance.  To make practice more musical, give yourself composition-style constraints. For example:  Create a full “track” using only one main pattern plus mutes and fills; see how far you can push arrangement without changing pattern Write a pattern that starts minimal and, over 16 or 32 bars, slowly evolves to a peak just by gradual parameter changes Recreate a drum groove from a track you love using only the RD-9’s sounds and sequencer; listen, then try to approximate the pattern and feel  Study a few styles intentionally. Pick two or three genres the RD-9 excels at: classic house, techno, electro, synthwave, hip-hop. For each style, spend a couple of sessions:  Listening to 2–3 reference tracks Transcribing the basic drum pattern by ear onto the RD-9 Adjusting sound parameters to get closer to that style’s sound  This gives you a vocabulary of grooves to draw from when you improvise.  Finally, treat it like a live performance instrument. Stand up while you play. Use two hands. Plan “macro moves” for your hands during a jam, like: left hand mainly on mute buttons and pattern selection, right hand on decay and tone knobs for hats, snare, and clap. Practice moving confidently instead of hesitantly poking at controls.  Measure improvement over time not just by whether your patterns are more complex, but by:  How quickly you can translate a rhythmic idea in your head onto the machine How comfortable you feel improvising a 5–10 minute jam without planning How intentional your knob tweaks and pattern changes sound when you listen back  If you build a consistent habit of focused sessions, style studies, performance practice, and self-review, the RD-9 will start to feel less like a piece of gear and more like an instrument you can really play.
9|9: Set a clear intention for what “better at using the RD-9 as an instrument” means for you: being able to improvise live, design your own beats from scratch, integrate it with other gear, or all of the above. Then structure your practice around those goals so that time on the machine is focused and deliberate instead of just noodling.  First, learn the box deeply. Take a week where you focus on one aspect per day: one day for basic sound shaping on each voice (tuning, decay, level, tone, attack), the next for pattern creation and step input, then performance features like mutes, solo, fills, flam, probability, swing, accents, and any per-step parameters. Sit with the manual and a notepad. For each feature, actually try it in a pattern rather than just reading about it. Only work on one or two features per session so you really internalize them.  Second, create a daily 20–30 minute “beat routine.” Start a timer. For the first 5 minutes, recreate a classic drum pattern by ear: 909-style house, electro, hip-hop boom-bap, breakbeat, techno. Load a track you like, loop a section, and program your RD-9 to match kick, snare, hats, and swing as closely as you can. This improves your ear, timing, and pattern vocabulary.  For the next 10–15 minutes, build a new beat from scratch under constraints. Pick a tempo and a style, then limit yourself: maybe only kick, snare, and closed hat; or maximum 8 steps; or no using the default 4-on-the-floor kick. Constraints force creativity. Once the core groove works, add one variation pattern and a fill pattern that make musical sense with the main groove.  Use the last 5–10 minutes as performance practice. Take the beat you just made and rehearse playing it like an instrument: live muting, soloing parts, switching patterns, adding fills, riding the tempo, using accents or additional hits in real time, and tweaking knobs musically. Record these short jams so you can listen back and hear what actually works versus what feels cool in the moment.  Third, work on sound design and mix control. Dedicate sessions to shaping each voice so you understand its full range. Take the kick: explore very short vs long decays, different tuning, how it sits with or without accent. Do the same for snare, clap, toms, hats, ride, crash. Practice balancing levels so the mix feels glued without external processing. Then experiment with how far you can push things into distortion, saturation, or external effects if you have them. The more you understand how each sound can be sculpted, the more expressive your playing becomes.  Fourth, build a small set of “performance kits.” These are not just sounds, but groups of complementary patterns, fills, and knob positions. For example, design a 10–15 minute techno set entirely on the RD-9: 3–4 main patterns that smoothly evolve from minimal to denser, 2–3 fills you can trigger at transitions, planned moments for filters or decay rides, and clear “chapters” in your performance. Practice moving through that set until it feels like playing a song, not just flipping patterns.  Fifth, integrate timing and feel. The RD-9 is all about groove. Spend sessions playing along with a metronome, bassline, or full track. Adjust swing and accents until your patterns lock in with the music. Practice micro-changes: sliding a snare earlier or later, opening the hat at slightly different points, alternating accented and unaccented kicks. Notice how tiny changes in pattern and dynamics drastically affect the overall energy.  Sixth, develop improvisation skills. Treat the RD-9 like you would a guitar or piano. Pick a simple starting pattern and jam for 15–20 minutes, but impose rules: you can only change one parameter at a time; you must keep kick and snare structure constant while transforming the hats; or you must gradually morph the pattern from one groove to a completely different one without stopping the sequencer. This trains your ability to make musical decisions in the moment.  Seventh, study other RD-9/909 users. Watch live sets, tutorial videos, and studio breakdowns where people use drum machines as performance instruments, not just backing tracks. Identify specific moves they use: when they mute the kick for tension, when they open the hats for the drop, how they combine a fill with knob tweaks for a big moment. Then deliberately copy those ideas in your own practice session and adapt them to your style.  Eighth, structure a weekly progression. For example:  Week 1: Core fundamentals. Learn all pattern modes, saving/loading, basic sound shaping. Focus on clean 4-bar patterns and tight timing. Week 2: Fills, variations, and transitions. Build multi-pattern grooves, smooth pattern changes, and practice live mutes and fills. Week 3: Sound sculpting and mix. Work deeply on each voice, level balancing, and how patterns sound through monitors/headphones. Week 4: Performance and recording. Design a 10–20 minute live set on the RD-9, rehearse it, and record it. Listen back, take notes, and refine.  Repeat this cycle with new styles or higher difficulty: faster tempos, odd time signatures, polyrhythms, sync with other gear or DAW, or adding live finger drumming on external pads. Each month, set 1 measurable goal, like “record and share one 5-minute live RD-9 jam” or “play a full track with only pattern variations and no stopping.”  Finally, keep everything captured. Record audio of your practice, and optionally keep a simple log: date, what you practiced, what you discovered, and what frustrated you. Over time you will see your toolkit expand: more go-to patterns, more confident transitions, and more instinctive knob control. That is what it means to “use the RD-9 as an instrument” — you are not thinking about the interface anymore; you are using it to express musical ideas in real time.
10|9: Start by treating the RD-9 like a new instrument you’re learning rather than a box that just plays 909 patterns.
