Week 1: Fundamentals and fluency Set a timer for 20–30 minutes per day and focus only on getting completely comfortable with the basics so you don’t have to think about them later.  Day 1–2: Navigation and muscle memory Learn and practice how to quickly do these things without looking at the manual Switch between pattern write and pattern play Select and switch patterns Start and stop the sequencer in time with an external clock or metronome if you use one Mute and unmute individual instruments Adjust tempo, shuffle, and flam Hone the feel of hitting buttons in time by manually entering simple 4-on-the-floor kicks, then claps on 2 and 4, then hats on offbeats, clearing and re-entering until it feels natural.  Day 3–4: Pattern programming basics Pick one kit sound setup and stick with it for the whole session. Program classic rhythms Straight 4/4 house groove Electro-style with broken kick pattern and snare on 2 and 4 Techno pattern with offbeat open hats and syncopated claps Practice copying a pattern to adjacent slots, then making small variations in each copied pattern, like moving a snare, adding a ghost kick, or changing the hats.  Day 5–7: Sound sculpting Spend sessions just tweaking knobs while a simple loop runs. Loop one basic pattern and focus on each instrument, one per session Kick: tune, decay, attack, distortion, level; notice how it interacts with the bass in your mind, even if nothing else is playing Snare: adjust tone and snap until you can quickly dial in tight, long, bright, and dark variations Hi-hats and cymbals: experiment with decay and tone to make tight, choked hats versus washy, open ones Toms and clap: make fills and try different tonal ranges The goal is to be able to get from default to “this kind of kick” or “this kind of snare” quickly without thinking.  Week 2: Groove, feel, and performance Now focus on making it feel like music rather than just patterns.  Day 8–9: Swing, dynamics, and accents Program a simple pattern and experiment with shuffle. Notice where the groove starts to feel good versus lumpy. Use accents to emphasize certain steps. Make patterns with Accents on all kicks Accents only on offbeat hats Accents on ghost snares Practice turning the accent feature on and off, and get a feel for subtle versus extreme use.  Day 10–11: Performance transitions Create a set of four related patterns that you can move through as a mini performance Pattern 1: basic groove Pattern 2: add hats or claps Pattern 3: add toms or extra kicks Pattern 4: busy, peak-energy variation Practice live transitions Mute/unmute instruments to build and release tension Switch between the patterns on the fly, but in a musical way (for example, every 4 or 8 bars) Practice dropping the kick or snare out for a bar then bringing it back.  Day 12–13: Live knob control Loop your mini set and focus on playing the RD-9 with your hands Ride the kick decay and tone during breakdowns and build-ups Fade hats or cymbals in and out with decay and level knobs Subtly change snare tone during a section instead of switching to a new pattern Record yourself and listen for moments that sound expressive or intentional. Try to remember what you were doing at those moments.  Day 14: Jam session and reflection Give yourself 30–45 minutes with no strict structure. Start from silence, build patterns, transition between them, tweak sounds, and “perform” an improvised track. Record this, then listen later and take quick notes Which transitions felt strong Where it got boring Which knob moves gave life to the pattern Use that feedback to refine next week’s focus.  Week 3: Integration with your setup and musical style Now that you can operate the RD-9 confidently, focus on making it work in your real music context.  Day 15–17: Style-specific studies Pick a genre or feeling you want the RD-9 to live in: house, techno, electro, breaks, hip-hop, or something more experimental. Listen to 2–3 reference tracks each day and focus only on the drum parts. Ask Where is the kick placed and how long is it How busy are the hats How often do fills occur How loud is the clap or snare relative to the kick Try to recreate the overall groove, not exact patterns. Get close in feel using the RD-9, then save these as “style templates” for future use.  Day 18–19: Working with other gear or DAW If you use a DAW, interface the RD-9 with it via MIDI or audio. Practice Syncing tempo and starting in time Recording individual outs or the stereo mix Jamming against a looped bassline, chord progression, or sample If you are hardware-only, pair the RD-9 with one melodic synth. Practice simple call-and-response Drop drums out, let the synth talk Bring drums back in gradually for impact.  Day 20–21: Arrangement practice Try arranging a rough track using only the RD-9. Decide on a simple structure Intro with hats and occasional clap Groove with full kit Break with only toms and a quiet kick Build back to full pattern with extra snare fills Perform this live and record it as if it were a finished track. Do two or three takes with slightly different approaches.  Week 4 and beyond: Deepening your voice on the RD-9 At this point you can operate and perform on the machine. Shift toward using it creatively and personally.  Themed practice weeks One week: Fills and variations Create 8–16 patterns that are mostly fills. Practice chaining them into longer phrases that feel like a drummer improvising. Another week: Minimalism Limit yourself to kick, snare, and one hat. Focus on making small changes feel big: mute patterns, accent changes, little decay tweaks. Another week: Sound design Try to get weird, non-909 sounds from it: short, clicky percussion, long boomy subs, pseudo-basslines with pitched toms, or noisy textures from cymbals.  Performance drills Regularly set a 10–15 minute timer and perform a mini live set using only RD-9. No stopping; you must keep the groove going. Use mutes, pattern changes, and knob moves to create an intro, rise, peak, and outro. Afterward, quickly write down what moments worked and what did not.  Personal pattern library Over time, build a categorized pattern bank Foundations: simple grooves for quick starting points Fills and transitions: 1–2 bar fills, snare rolls, tom runs, hat bursts Special moves: patterns that only make sense as occasional surprises Revisit and clean this library every month; delete what you don’t use so you stay familiar with your best material.  Mindset tips Treat the RD-9 like a drummer Think in phrases (4, 8, 16 bars), not just loops. Let some patterns be “boring” foundations and save excitement for fills, mutes, and knob moves. Think in terms of energy Instead of “good pattern” or “bad pattern,” think “low, medium, high, and peak energy” patterns and moves. Practice going smoothly from low to peak and back down. Be patient with repetition A great groove often feels repetitive. Your job is to make small, musical changes at the right times, not to constantly change everything.  If you stick to short, focused daily sessions, regularly record and review your jams, and gradually integrate the RD-9 into your actual tracks or live sets, you will start to feel it as an instrument under your fingers rather than a box of presets. Over a couple of months, the biggest change will be that you stop thinking about how to operate it and start thinking purely about what the music needs, which is where real expressive playing begins.

1|11: Imagine your room on a Monday morning: everything is in its place, the bed is made, books are stacked, clothes are in the closet. That is low entropy: things are organized and easy to describe. Now imagine the same room after a week of tossing clothes on the floor, leaving snacks on the desk, and never putting anything back. That is high entropy: things are messy and spread out in many different ways.   Entropy is a way scientists measure how spread out and mixed up things are, or how many different ways the parts of something can be arranged without changing what it looks like overall. A neat stack of cards in perfect order has low entropy because there are not many ways to arrange them that still look perfectly ordered. A shuffled deck has high entropy because there are a huge number of possible random arrangements.   You can also think of it like this: if you know exactly where everything is and what it is doing, entropy is low. If you only have a vague idea because everything is all mixed up, entropy is high. Over time, without effort, systems tend to go from low entropy to high entropy. Ice cubes melt into water and spread out, hot and cold drinks left together slowly become the same temperature, and a tidy room naturally becomes messy if no one works to keep it clean.   So in simple terms: entropy is a measure of disorder or randomness, or how many different ways something can be arranged. Nature usually moves toward higher entropy, which is why things left alone tend to get more spread out, mixed up, and harder to organize.
2|11: Imagine your bedroom. Early in the morning, everything is neatly put away: clothes in the closet, books on the shelf, bed made. That is low entropy: things are organized and predictable. Now imagine you come home after a week of tossing clothes on the floor, leaving snacks everywhere, and throwing books on the bed. The room is messy and disorganized. That is high entropy.  In simple terms, entropy is a way scientists talk about how messy or spread out energy and matter are. When entropy is low, things are ordered and concentrated. When entropy is high, things are disordered and spread out.  Here is the important part: in our universe, things naturally tend to go from order to disorder. A hot drink cools down in a cold room, perfume spreads out across the whole room, ice melts in warm water, a tidy room becomes messy if you never clean it. All of these are examples of entropy increasing.  It is not that things cannot become ordered again, but to decrease entropy you have to use energy and effort. To clean your room, you have to spend time and energy. A fridge uses electricity to keep food cold and ordered, fighting against the natural tendency for things to warm up and spread out.  So, in very simple words: entropy measures how mixed up and spread out things are, and the universe naturally moves toward higher entropy unless you put in energy to keep things organized.
3|11: Imagine your bedroom on two different days. On day one, everything is neatly put away: clothes folded, books stacked, nothing on the floor. On day two, you’ve tried on a bunch of outfits, thrown your backpack down, left snacks on the desk, and now stuff is everywhere.  Entropy is a way scientists talk about how messy or spread out things are. Low entropy is like the very tidy room: everything is organized and in specific places. High entropy is like the messy room: things are scattered randomly, with no clear order.  Here are the key ideas in simple terms:  Entropy is about how many different ways something can be arranged while still looking basically the same overall. A neat room has only a few ways to place everything so it still looks neat. A messy room can be messy in millions of different ways. Because there are so many more messy possibilities than tidy ones, rooms naturally tend to get messy if you do nothing.  In physics, we often talk about entropy with things like gas, energy, and heat. For example, if you spray perfume in one corner of a room, at first all the perfume molecules are crowded together. After a while, they spread out and mix with the air so you can smell it everywhere in the room. The spread-out state has higher entropy because the molecules can be arranged in many more random ways. They almost never suddenly all run back into the corner by themselves, just like your room never magically cleans itself.  The second law of thermodynamics says that, in a closed system where nothing comes in or out, entropy tends to increase over time. Translation: if you do nothing, things go from ordered to disordered, not the other way around. Ice cubes melt into water and spread out, hot drinks cool down to room temperature, and your room gets messy unless you use energy to clean it.  Another way to think about it is in terms of information. A super-organized system is very predictable: if I know your socks are always in the top drawer, I have a lot of information about where things are. A very disordered system is unpredictable: if your stuff is thrown randomly everywhere, I do not have much useful information; I just know it is a mess. Higher entropy means less information about exact details and more randomness.  So, in short: entropy is a measure of disorder or randomness, or of how spread out and mixed up things are. Nature tends to move from neat and organized to messy and random unless energy is spent to keep things in order.
4|11: Imagine your room right after you clean it: clothes folded, books on the shelf, everything in its place. That is low entropy: things are organized and predictable. Now imagine your room a week later if you never clean it: clothes on the floor, books everywhere, snacks under the bed. That is high entropy: things are messy and harder to predict.  Entropy is a way scientists measure how mixed up or disordered something is. The more ways the parts of a system can be arranged without really changing how it looks overall, the higher its entropy.  For example, think about ice and water. In a block of ice, the water molecules are lined up in a fixed pattern, like people standing in rows. There are not many ways to arrange them while still keeping that solid structure, so the entropy is low. In liquid water, the molecules are buzzing around, always moving and changing places. There are tons of possible arrangements, so the entropy is higher.  Another way to see it: if you have a deck of cards in perfect order, that is like low entropy. Once you shuffle it a bunch of times, you get a random order. There are many, many more random orders than neat ones, so the shuffled deck has higher entropy.  In everyday language, you can think of entropy as How spread out energy is How disordered or random things are How many different ways something can be arranged  There is also an important rule of nature: in a closed system, entropy tends to go up over time. That means things naturally go from neat and organized to messy and mixed up, unless you use energy to keep them ordered. Your room does not clean itself; you have to use your effort (energy) to lower its entropy.  So, entropy is basically a measure of how messy and random a system is, and nature tends to move from order to disorder unless something actively works to keep things tidy.

Entropy is basically a measure of how messy or disordered something is, or how many different ways the parts can be arranged. Low entropy means very ordered and organized. High entropy means very mixed up and spread out.  Here is the key idea from physics: if you do nothing, entropy tends to increase. In other words, things naturally go from ordered to disordered. Ice melts into water and then can evaporate; perfume spreads from one corner of the room so that soon you can smell it everywhere; a hot drink cools down as its heat spreads into the air. These are all examples of entropy increasing: energy and matter spreading out and becoming more evenly distributed.  Cleaning your room is like fighting entropy. You use energy and effort to put objects back in specific places, lowering the entropy of the room. But notice that you get tired, or need food: your body is using energy, and in the bigger picture, the total entropy in the world still goes up.  So, in simple terms: entropy is a way scientists talk about how spread out and disordered things are. The more spread out and random something is, the higher its entropy. And the universe has a strong tendency to move towards higher entropy over time.

1|15: If the image URL goes through a servlet filter, the filter might be blocking or altering the request so Tomcat never returns the raw image. Common issues: the filter is mapped too broadly (like /*), it assumes everything is text/HTML and sets the wrong content type or character encoding, or it forwards/redirects instead of just passing the request through. For example, if the filter always forwards to a JSP or login page, the browser will try to interpret that HTML as an image and it will look broken. Or if the filter wraps the response or writes something to the output stream before calling chain.doFilter, the image bytes can be corrupted. To fix this, check your filter mapping and logic: skip filtering static resources (like *.png, *.jpg, /images/*), or in the filter detect requests for images and immediately call chain.doFilter without modifying response headers or body, and do not change the content type for non-HTML responses.
2|15: When you add a filter in Tomcat, every request that matches the filter’s url-pattern goes through that filter, including requests for static resources like images, unless you explicitly exclude them. If your filter is not correctly passing the request along with chain.doFilter(), is changing the response headers/content type incorrectly, is consuming the request/response output, or is mapped too broadly (for example /* instead of /app/* or excluding /resources/*), the image request may never reach the default servlet that serves static files. As a result, the browser gets an invalid response or no response for the image URL, so the image does not appear when referenced from your .html file. To fix this, check that your filter mapping in web.xml or the @WebFilter annotation either excludes static content paths (like /images/*, /css/*, /js/*) or correctly calls chain.doFilter() without breaking the response, and make sure the resource path in your HTML matches the actual context path and folder where the images are served (for example using <img src='${pageContext.request.contextPath}/images/pic.png'> or a relative path inside the app).
3|15: If your image works in a plain HTML file but stops working when you deploy under Tomcat and use a filter, it usually means the filter is intercepting the image request and either blocking it, redirecting it, or changing the response in a way that breaks the binary content. Typical causes:  The filter pattern is too broad: for example, you mapped the filter to /* or to *.html, *.jpg, *.png, etc., and inside doFilter you always forward to some JSP or write text to the response. When the browser requests your image (e.g., /app/images/logo.png), the filter runs and returns HTML or text instead of the raw image bytes, so the browser cannot display it.  The filter does not call chain.doFilter: if you forget chain.doFilter(request, response) for some paths, the request never reaches the default servlet that actually serves static resources, so Tomcat never sends the image file.  The filter modifies headers or encoding: setting character encoding, content type, or buffering incorrectly for binary content (like images) can corrupt the response. For example, always calling response.setContentType(text/html; charset=UTF-8) in the filter will override the correct image MIME type that the container would set.  The filter does authentication only or checks some condition and redirects to a login page for every request, including image requests. Then, instead of the image, the client is being sent the login HTML.  How to fix it:  Restrict your filter mapping so it only applies to dynamic resources (e.g., /secure/* or *.jsp) and not to images, CSS, JS, etc.  Inside the filter, exclude static resources early, e.g. if (requestURI.startsWith(/images/) || requestURI.endsWith(.png) || requestURI.endsWith(.jpg)) { chain.doFilter(request, response); return; }  Always call chain.doFilter for requests you want Tomcat to handle normally, and only write to the response or forward when you really intend to replace the output.  Do not globally force text/html or character encoding for binary content. Set those conditionally, or let the container handle static resources on its own.  In short, the filter is probably interfering with the static resource pipeline. Narrow its mapping or add conditions so Tomcat can serve the image directly.

5|15: If everything works until you add a filter, it usually means the filter is intercepting the image request and either not passing it along or changing the response. Common causes:  Your filter mapping covers everything and does not exclude static content paths like /resources/, /images/, /static/, etc. Then images in your HTML are treated like protected or transformed content and fail.  Inside doFilter, you forget to call chain.doFilter(request, response) for image requests, or you call sendRedirect / sendError and then return. That short‑circuits the normal handling by the default servlet that actually serves the file.  The filter sets headers (for example content type, caching, encoding) incorrectly for binary data, or writes some characters to the response before the actual image bytes are written by the container, corrupting the image stream.  A login/security filter might detect that the user is not authenticated and redirect to a login page, but your HTML image tag still points to that protected URL, so the browser gets HTML instead of an image and fails to render it.  To fix it, narrow the filter mapping (e.g., only /app/*, /secure/*, or certain servlets), or explicitly exclude the static resources path with a separate mapping. In the filter code, detect requests for static files by path or extension and immediately call chain.doFilter without extra logic. Also ensure you never modify the response for those static resources. Once the filter lets the request pass unmodified to the default servlet that serves files from your webapp, the image links in your HTML will work again under Tomcat.

1|18: For regression tasks, one methodology is linear regression, where a linear function is fitted to minimize the sum of squared errors between predicted and actual continuous targets. Another is polynomial regression, which extends linear regression by including polynomial terms of the features to capture nonlinear relationships while still solving a regression problem with a closed-form or iterative optimizer. Decision tree regression is a nonparametric method that recursively partitions the feature space into regions and predicts continuous values as averages within the leaves. Random forest regression improves on single trees by training many trees on bootstrapped samples with feature subsampling, then averaging their outputs to reduce variance and overfitting. Gradient boosting regression, such as using gradient boosting machines or XGBoost, builds an ensemble of weak learners sequentially, where each new tree tries to correct the errors of the previous ones, often achieving strong performance on structured data.  For classification tasks, logistic regression models the probability of class membership using the logistic function and is widely used for binary and multinomial classification. Support vector machines with appropriate kernels construct decision boundaries that maximize the margin between classes, handling both linear and nonlinear separations. Decision tree classification splits the feature space into regions based on impurity measures like Gini or entropy, assigning class labels in the leaves based on majority vote. Random forest classification aggregates predictions from multiple randomized decision trees, using majority voting to improve generalization and robustness. Neural networks, including multilayer perceptrons, learn complex nonlinear decision boundaries via layered transformations and backpropagation, supporting both binary and multiclass classification.  For unsupervised learning, k means clustering partitions data into k clusters by iteratively assigning points to the nearest centroid and updating centroids, aiming to minimize within cluster variance. Hierarchical clustering builds a tree of clusters either bottom up agglomerative or top down divisive, producing a dendrogram that can be cut at different levels to yield different numbers of clusters. Principal component analysis is a dimensionality reduction technique that finds orthogonal directions maximizing variance, projecting data into a lower dimensional space while retaining most variability. Autoencoders are neural network based methods that learn compressed latent representations by training to reconstruct the input, enabling nonlinear dimensionality reduction and feature learning. Gaussian mixture models represent data as a mixture of Gaussian distributions and use algorithms like expectation maximization to estimate component parameters, allowing soft clustering where each point has probabilities of belonging to different clusters.
2|18: For regression tasks, one methodology is ordinary least squares linear regression, where a linear relationship between input features and a continuous target is assumed, and parameters are found by minimizing the squared error between predictions and true values. Another powerful approach is regression using decision trees, which recursively partition the feature space into regions and fit constant predictions in each leaf, capturing nonlinear patterns without requiring feature scaling. Ensemble methods like random forest regression improve on single trees by averaging predictions from many trees trained on bootstrapped samples with feature subsampling, reducing variance and improving generalization. Gradient boosting machines for regression, such as gradient boosted trees or XGBoost-style models, build an additive model of trees where each new tree fits the residuals of the previous ensemble, allowing very flexible function approximation with strong performance on tabular data. Neural network regression uses multilayer perceptrons with continuous output units and loss functions like mean squared error or mean absolute error, enabling learning of complex nonlinear mappings, especially when there are many features and sufficient data.  For classification tasks, logistic regression is a classic linear probabilistic classifier that models the log-odds of class membership as a linear function of the inputs, often used with regularization for high-dimensional data. Support vector machines with appropriate kernels perform classification by finding a maximum-margin separating hyperplane in a (possibly high-dimensional) feature space, robustly handling complex decision boundaries. Decision tree classifiers split the feature space according to feature thresholds to create interpretable if-then rules, terminating in leaves that predict class labels, possibly with class probabilities. Random forest classification ensembles many decision trees trained on bootstrapped data and random feature subsets, then aggregates their class votes, usually improving accuracy and robustness over single trees. Neural network classifiers such as feedforward networks or convolutional networks output class probabilities via softmax and are trained with cross-entropy loss, performing well on high-dimensional inputs like images, text, or audio.  For unsupervised learning, k-means clustering is a widely used partitioning method that assigns each data point to one of k clusters by minimizing within-cluster squared distances to cluster centroids, revealing group structure in the data. Hierarchical clustering builds a tree of clusters either by successively merging the closest clusters agglomerative or successively splitting clusters divisive, allowing inspection of cluster structure at multiple scales via dendrograms. Gaussian mixture models perform soft clustering by modeling the data as a mixture of Gaussian distributions, estimated with algorithms like expectation-maximization, and yield probabilistic cluster assignments and estimates of cluster covariances. Principal component analysis is a dimensionality reduction technique that finds orthogonal directions of maximum variance, projecting data into a lower-dimensional subspace that captures the most important variation while also helping with visualization and noise reduction. Autoencoders are neural network-based unsupervised methods that learn compressed representations by training an encoder-decoder architecture to reconstruct the input, with the bottleneck layer providing a learned low-dimensional embedding that can capture nonlinear structure in the data.

5|18: For regression tasks, one common methodology is linear regression, which models the relationship between input features and a continuous output as a linear combination of the features, often trained via least squares to minimize the sum of squared errors. Another approach is decision tree regression, where the feature space is recursively partitioned into regions and each leaf predicts a constant value, making it flexible and easy to interpret but prone to overfitting. Random forest regression extends this by training many decision trees on bootstrapped samples with feature subsampling and averaging their predictions to reduce variance and improve generalization. Gradient boosting regression, such as Gradient Boosting Machines or XGBoost, builds an ensemble of weak learners (typically shallow trees) in sequence, where each new tree fits the residuals of the previous ensemble, yielding strong performance on many structured data problems. Support Vector Regression (SVR) uses the principles of support vector machines but for continuous targets, finding a function that deviates from the targets by no more than a specified margin while maximizing the margin around the function, and can be combined with kernels to model nonlinearity.  For classification tasks, logistic regression is a standard methodology that uses a linear decision boundary combined with the logistic or softmax function to output class probabilities, and it is efficient and interpretable for linearly separable data. Decision tree classification partitions the feature space using axis-aligned splits, assigning a class label to each leaf based on the majority class, which is easy to visualize but can overfit if not pruned. Random forest classification creates an ensemble of decision trees, each trained on a bootstrapped sample with random feature subsets at each split, and predicts by majority vote across trees, generally improving robustness and accuracy. Support Vector Machines for classification find a hyperplane that maximally separates classes in the feature space, possibly using kernel functions like RBF or polynomial to handle nonlinear boundaries, and are effective in high dimensional spaces. Neural network classifiers, such as multilayer perceptrons, learn hierarchical feature representations and nonlinear decision boundaries by stacking layers of neurons with nonlinear activations and training with backpropagation to minimize a classification loss function.  For unsupervised learning, k means clustering is a widely used methodology that partitions data into a predefined number of clusters by iteratively assigning points to the nearest cluster centroid and then updating centroids to be the mean of assigned points; it is simple but assumes roughly spherical, similarly sized clusters. Hierarchical clustering builds a tree of clusters either by agglomerative merging of the most similar pairs or divisive splitting, producing a dendrogram from which clusters can be chosen at different levels of granularity without predefining the number of clusters. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) performs dimensionality reduction by finding orthogonal directions of maximum variance in the data and projecting onto the top components, useful for visualization, noise reduction, and preprocessing. Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs) assume that data are generated from a mixture of multiple Gaussian distributions, each representing a cluster, and use algorithms like Expectation Maximization to estimate the parameters and soft assignments of points to components. Autoencoders are neural network based methods that learn to encode inputs into a lower dimensional latent representation and then decode back to reconstruct them, providing a way to learn nonlinear compressed representations and detect anomalies by reconstruction error.

In pseudocode, this might look like:  - Set up a secure environment variable store for your API key and secret. - Use an HTTP library in your chosen language (for example, Python requests or Node.js axios). - Call Coinbase’s endpoints to fetch your BTC wallet address, list balances, or create withdrawals/transfers.  Example outline in Python using environment variables (note: this is conceptual, you must adapt it to Coinbase’s current API docs):  import os import time import hmac import hashlib import requests  API_KEY = os.environ.get('COINBASE_API_KEY') API_SECRET = os.environ.get('COINBASE_API_SECRET') BASE_URL = 'https://api.coinbase.com/v2'  def sign_request(timestamp, method, path, body=''):     message = f'{timestamp}{method}{path}{body}'     signature = hmac.new(         API_SECRET.encode('utf-8'),         message.encode('utf-8'),         hashlib.sha256     ).hexdigest()     return signature  def get_accounts():     path = '/accounts'     timestamp = str(int(time.time()))     signature = sign_request(timestamp, 'GET', path)     headers = {         'CB-ACCESS-KEY': API_KEY,         'CB-ACCESS-SIGN': signature,         'CB-ACCESS-TIMESTAMP': timestamp,         'CB-VERSION': '2023-01-01'     }     r = requests.get(BASE_URL + path, headers=headers)     r.raise_for_status()     return r.json()  if __name__ == '__main__':     data = get_accounts()     print(data)  To actually receive bitcoin into your Coinbase wallet, you would:  1. Share that address with the payer or configure it in your external software (for example, a mining pool payout address, a payment button, or a tipping bot). 3. Your program can monitor the blockchain or Coinbase transaction history via the API to detect new incoming bitcoin and notify you.  Important constraints and safety: - There is no way to write a program that magically creates bitcoin for you; bitcoin is earned, mined (under strict network consensus rules), or received from others, and mining profitably now requires large-scale specialized hardware. - Never hard-code your Coinbase API keys or secrets directly into code that might be shared or deployed insecurely. Always use environment variables or secure key management. - Use Coinbase’s latest official API documentation and SDKs, because authentication requirements, URLs, and supported operations change over time. How to structure your learning as a beginner  Phase 1: Fundamentals   Learn C basics (or strengthen them).   Learn how compilation works: C source to executable.   Take at least one assembly intro course (OpenSecurityTraining x86 or x86-64).  Phase 2: Static reverse engineering   Install Ghidra and load simple C programs you compiled yourself.   Compare your C source with the decompiled output and assembly.   Read the Intro to Reverse Engineering course and do its exercises.  Phase 3: Dynamic analysis   Install x64dbg (Windows) or use gdb (Linux).   Step through your own simple programs: loops, conditionals, function calls, string handling.   Set breakpoints, watch registers and stack changes.  Phase 4: Challenges and crackmes   Create accounts on crackmes.one, Reversing.kr, picoCTF.   Start from easiest challenges only.   For each challenge, aim to answer: what does the program do, where is the check, and how could you patch or bypass it (for educational purposes only, on test binaries).  Phase 5: Deeper topics   Explore more advanced content from RE4B (Yurichev) and OpenSecurityTraining2.   Learn about calling conventions, position-independent code, packers, and basic anti-debugging.  Safety, legality, and mindset  Only reverse engineer software you are legally allowed to inspect: your own programs, intentionally provided practice binaries, and open educational samples. Avoid real commercial software unless laws and licenses explicitly permit it in your jurisdiction.  Focus on building the habit of reading disassembly slowly and systematically. Treat every program as a puzzle: identify main, find input-handling logic, follow branches, track key comparisons or arithmetic, and document your steps. Reversing specific to malware and binary analysis  Use these primarily to learn tools, not to work with real malware until you have the basics.  Practical Malware Analysis & Triage (free course by Malware Unicorn): https://malwareunicorn.org/#/workshops  Again, it doubles as a general RE course. Starts from tooling basics (static/dynamic analysis) and goes step-by-step.  Malware Analysis – OpenSecurityTraining: https://opensecuritytraining.info/MalwareDynamicAnalysis.html  Shows how debuggers and sandboxes are used, which is very similar in methodology to regular reverse engineering.  Hands-on platforms and practice labs  Always use legal, safe samples: your own compiled programs, teaching crackmes, and educational platforms.  Crackmes.one: https://crackmes.one/  A huge collection of small binaries designed for learning reverse engineering and binary exploitation. Filter by difficulty; start with Very easy or Easy.  Root Me – Reverse Engineering section: https://www.root-me.org/en/Challenges/Cracking/  Provides challenges where you reverse engineer binaries to find keys, passwords, or logic. You can register for free.  picoCTF and CTF-style practice  picoCTF – Reversing category: https://picoctf.org/  picoCTF has beginner-friendly challenges with hints that teach you to read disassembly, use strings, understand simple protections, etc. Look for previous years’ practice problems.  CTFlearn – Reverse Engineering category: https://ctflearn.com/  Free small tasks that will introduce you to tools like Ghidra and GDB.  Tools you should learn and where to learn them  Ghidra (free, from NSA): https://ghidra-sre.org/  Official Ghidra documentation and training material: https://ghidra-sre.org/Training.html  Includes videos and PDFs. Learn how to: – Import binaries – Navigate functions – Use the decompiler – Rename variables and functions – Follow cross-references  Ghidra beginner tutorials (YouTube playlist by 0x41): Search: Ghidra beginner tutorial 0x41  x64dbg (free Windows debugger): https://x64dbg.com/  x64dbg official docs & tutorials: https://documentation.x64dbg.com/  Covers breakpoints, stepping through code, viewing registers/stack, and patching binaries in memory.  GDB (Linux debugger): https://sourceware.org/gdb/  GDB cheatsheet: https://darkdust.net/files/GDB%20Cheat%20Sheet.pdf  GDB/GEF/Pwndbg tutorials on YouTube are very common; search for GDB reverse engineering tutorial.  radare2 / Cutter (free RE framework and GUI): https://rada.re/n/ https://cutter.re/  These are powerful and fully free alternatives; you can experiment with them once you are comfortable with Ghidra.  Structured learning roadmaps  Begin.Re (Begin RE – free online book/guide): https://www.begin.re/  An opinionated roadmap for reverse engineering, with explanations and references. Great for self-study.  Open-source book: Practical Binary Analysis (while the printed book is paid, the author’s repo has code and some material): https://github.com/moyix/practical-binary-analysis  Not a full course by itself, but combined with free tools and tutorials, it’s a strong reference.  YouTube channels (free, but pick carefully)  LiveOverflow: https://www.youtube.com/c/LiveOverflow  Has accessible videos on binary exploitation, reverse engineering, and CTF challenges. Look for playlists about binary hacking and reversing.  OALabs: https://www.youtube.com/c/OALabs  Focuses on malware but has a ton of practical RE workflow demonstrations using Ghidra, IDA, x64dbg, etc.  MalwareTechBlog: https://www.youtube.com/c/MalwareTechBlog  Shows real-world debugging, disassembly, and reversing of samples – good to see expert workflow, but don’t start with the hardest videos.  Safe practice workflow for a beginner  Download and install a virtual machine (VM) to keep your main system safe: – VirtualBox (free): https://www.virtualbox.org/ – Use a Windows trial ISO (from Microsoft) or a Linux distro like Ubuntu.  Inside the VM, install tools: – Ghidra – x64dbg (for Windows) – GDB (for Linux) – A text editor (VS Code, Notepad++, etc.)  Compile your own simple C programs and reverse them. For example, write programs that: – Take a password and say correct or incorrect – Implement simple math functions – Use loops and conditionals  Then: – Open the compiled binary in Ghidra – Try to recover the original logic – Use x64dbg or GDB to step through and modify behavior  Suggested learning order (high-level)  1. Basic C and assembly:    CS50 or Learn-C, then OpenSecurityTraining Intro x86  2. Intro RE course:    OpenSecurityTraining Intro Reverse Engineering  3. Tools practice:    Ghidra + x64dbg/GDB using your own binaries  4. Guided challenges:    picoCTF Reversing, Root Me Cracking, crackmes.one (easy)  5. Deeper topics and specialization:    Malware Unicorn workshops, more advanced OST2 courses, LiveOverflow / OALabs videos  Reminder on legality and ethics  Only reverse engineer – Your own programs – Openly shared crackmes/challenges – Samples that are clearly provided for educational use  Avoid reversing commercial software, games, or services without explicit permission; this can be illegal or break terms of service. 9|20: Here is a beginner-friendly learning path for reverse engineering with free material and courses, focusing on legal, educational use only.  Start with basic foundations  Computer systems and low-level basics: CS50’s Introduction to Computer Science (Harvard/edX) https://cs50.harvard.edu/x/ This gives you solid C and systems fundamentals so you can read compiled code and understand memory.  x86 assembly basics (essential before serious reversing): OpenSecurityTraining – Introductory x86 https://opensecuritytraining.info/IntroX86.html This is one of the classic free introductions to x86, with slides and videos.  Alternative assembly intro: LiveOverflow’s x86 Assembly playlist https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLhixgUqwRTjxglIswKp9mpkfPNfHkzyeN Short, practical videos that you can follow alongside a debugger.  Core reverse engineering courses and series  MalwareTech’s Reverse Engineering for Beginners https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLZVwXPbHD1KnaJC8Syc9q-M52_VNn6sky Goes step by step with tools like IDA Free and x64dbg, aimed at beginners, with plenty of hands-on examples.  OpenSecurityTraining – Introduction to Reverse Engineering Software https://opensecuritytraining.info/IntroReverseEngineering.html This course walks through what reverse engineering is, how to read disassembly, use debuggers, and understand compiled C code.  OpenSecurityTraining2 – various reversing-focused tracks https://ost2.fyi/courses/ Look for beginner-level courses like Introductory Intel x86 and Introductory Reverse Engineering; these are video-based and updated.  Practical tutorials and YouTube channels  LiveOverflow’s reverse engineering and binary hacking videos Main channel: https://www.youtube.com/c/LiveOverflow Reversing/Binary playlist: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLhixgUqwRTjywPzsTYz28I-qezFOSaUYz Excellent for learning how to think like a reverser and how to approach real binaries, CTF challenges, and protections.  OpenSecurityTraining YouTube channel https://www.youtube.com/@OpenSecurityTraining Mirrors their structured courses so you can watch in playlist form.  Gynvael Coldwind’s streams and archives https://www.youtube.com/c/GynvaelEN Not strictly a “course,” but lots of episodes where he reverse engineers binaries live and solves CTF-style tasks, discussing thought process in detail.  Tools-focused material  x64dbg official documentation and tutorials https://x64dbg.com/ Click Documentation and Plugins to learn how to set breakpoints, step through code, inspect memory, and patch binaries.  Ghidra official training material https://ghidra-sre.org/ Then select Documentation and Training Material There are official PDFs and sample projects that walk you through using Ghidra’s disassembler and decompiler, which is extremely useful for beginners.  Practical Reverse Engineering with Ghidra (free tutorial series) https://github.com/NationalSecurityAgency/ghidra/blob/master/GhidraClass/Beginner/README.md Some walkthroughs on using Ghidra as a beginner.  Hands-on practice platforms  MicroCorruption (hardware-oriented but great for assembly thinking) https://microcorruption.com/ Web-based debugger and small challenges. Each level encourages you to step through instructions, inspect memory, and understand control flow.  Pwnable.kr / pwnable.xyz style sites https://pwnable.kr/ These focus more on binary exploitation, but they force you to read disassembly, understand calling conventions, and reason about binaries.  Crackmes.one https://crackmes.one/ This hosts intentionally released binaries that you are allowed to reverse. Look for the easiest and beginner-tagged challenges, then use Ghidra + x64dbg to practice.  Structured roadmaps and reading  Beginner-friendly RE roadmap article by 0xZ0F https://github.com/0xZ0F/ctf-writeups/tree/master/tutorials Look for the reversing/binary exploitation intro tutorials. They shape a learning path around CTF tasks.  Malware Unicorn’s Workshops https://malwareunicorn.org/ Go to Workshops Her “Intro to Reverse Engineering Malware” workshops (though malware-focused) are great beginner-friendly RE labs using IDA Free/x64dbg.  The Art of Assembly (for deeper assembly understanding) https://archive.org/details/artofassembly Not a course, but a comprehensive book available free that gives strong intuition for how compiled code works at the CPU level.  How to put this together as a beginner plan  Phase 1 – Foundations (2–4 weeks) Study CS50 or equivalent basics to be comfortable with C, pointers, and memory. Work through OpenSecurityTraining’s Intro x86, or LiveOverflow’s x86 assembly playlist.  Phase 2 – Intro to reversing (4–6 weeks) Go through OpenSecurityTraining’s Introduction to Reverse Engineering Software. Install Ghidra and x64dbg (or radare2/Cutter if you prefer) and follow their introductory docs. Watch MalwareTech’s Reverse Engineering for Beginners playlist and reproduce each demo.  Phase 3 – Hands-on practice (ongoing) Solve beginner challenges on Crackmes.one using Ghidra + x64dbg. Use MicroCorruption and a few pwnable.kr challenges to strengthen your assembly reading. Watch LiveOverflow/Gynvael videos and pause to solve things yourself before seeing their solutions.  Legal and ethical note  Always reverse engineer only software and binaries you are legally allowed to analyze: your own programs, intentionally shared crackmes/CTF challenges, or software with explicit permission to reverse. Avoid applying these skills to commercial software, DRM, or malware in environments you do not fully control. 10|20: Here is a beginner-friendly path into reverse engineering with free courses and materials, focusing only on legal, educational use on your own software or clearly allowed targets.  Start with fundamentals of low-level programming and operating systems  Gain basic skills in C and assembly, since most reverse engineering tools show disassembly.  C programming basics (free): Learn C with: https://www.learn-c.org/  Assembly language basics (x86 focus): Intro to x86 Assembly (YouTube playlist): https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLmxT2pVYo5LB4b1kWMqstateJxQ4k8lN-  Operating systems and low-level concepts: CS50’s Introduction to Computer Science (Harvard / edX, free audit): https://cs50.harvard.edu/x  Once you understand basic C/assembly, you can make more sense of disassembly in tools like IDA, Ghidra, or radare2.  Beginner-friendly reverse engineering courses and series  OpenSecurityTraining – x86 Assembly and Reverse Engineering: These are among the best structured reverse engineering intros, and they are free.  Intro x86 (32-bit) Assembly Language (x86-Intro): https://opensecuritytraining.info/IntroX86.html  Intermediate x86: Architecture, Assembly, Applications: https://opensecuritytraining.info/IntermediateX86.html  Practical Reverse Engineering (older but still solid): https://opensecuritytraining.info/ReverseEngineering.html  These courses come with slides and recorded videos.  Malware Unicorn – Reverse Engineering 101 Workshop:  A hands-on RE intro that uses Ghidra and simple malware-like samples (for education only).  Reverse Engineering 101 workshop: https://malwareunicorn.org/#/workshops  Specifically, start with RE 101 and RE 102.  Open Security Training 2 – Ghidra and modern content:  OpenSecurityTraining2 has updated material including Ghidra-based content.  Course list: https://opensecuritytraining2.github.io/  Look for the reverse engineering and Ghidra-related courses.  Ghidra and other tool-specific courses  Ghidra is a powerful free reverse engineering suite from the NSA.  Official Ghidra training materials: Ghidra Software Reverse Engineering Framework training resources (PDFs, labs): https://ghidra-sre.org/Course.html  Ghidra YouTube training (NSA official channel): https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLX6C3GwhGX7_0P-PS-DZ3x4cyR3b62ZzP  Practical Ghidra RE series (community): Ghidra basics tutorial playlist: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLt9cUwGw6CYGfw0uH1AnBFFdCkTCg7n6P  Linux reverse engineering tools (radare2, Cutter, etc.)  radare2 and Cutter intro: Radare2 Book (free online): https://radare.gitbooks.io/radare2book/content/  Cutter (GUI for radare2) documentation and tutorials: https://cutter.re/docs  Reverse engineering and binary exploitation CTF-style courses  These do not just show how to reverse binaries but put you in puzzles and capture-the-flag (CTF) style challenges, great for practice.  pwn.college (binary exploitation and RE fundamentals):  A full free course on binary exploitation and reverse engineering. https://pwn.college/  Look at the introduction tracks and RE-focused modules.  RPISEC Modern Binary Exploitation (Mbed):  Legendary but still relevant; slides, videos, and labs are free. Course site: https://github.com/RPISEC/MBE  Video lectures (YouTube playlist): https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIB3q0NSVWhN5U1a3i7oR5qK1ZOBjdx7J  It is more exploit-focused but forces you to get good at reading disassembly and understanding binaries.  LiveOverflow – Reverse Engineering YouTube channel:  One of the best beginner channels. Main channel: https://www.youtube.com/@LiveOverflow  Reverse engineering playlist: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLhixgUqwRTjxglIswKp9mpkfPNfHkzyeN  He walks through CTF challenges, showing how to use GDB, objdump, and other tools.  Structured online course platforms  While not always purely reverse engineering, these courses help build a solid mindset for understanding binaries and low-level internals.  Coursera – Software Security (free audit): https://www.coursera.org/learn/software-security  Coursera – Intro to Cyber Attacks (also has bits of RE mindset): https://www.coursera.org/learn/intro-cyber-attacks  Use the audit option to access them for free.  Practice platforms and challenge sites  Doing practical challenges is critical.  Crackmes.one (legal crackmes for RE practice):  A repository of small programs explicitly uploaded for reverse engineering practice. https://crackmes.one/  Always read the descriptions and verify they are intended for educational RE.  PicoCTF (beginner-friendly CTF with RE tasks): https://picoctf.org/  CTFtime – find CTFs that include reversing challenges: https://ctftime.org/  Nightmare challenge set (binary exploitation and RE-style challenges): https://guyinatuxedo.github.io/  Beginner study roadmap  1. Learn C basics and pointers so compiler output makes sense (Learn-C.org, CS50) 2. Learn x86 assembly basics (OpenSecurityTraining Intro x86) 3. Install a Linux VM and a Windows VM (if you want Windows RE) 4. Learn a tool: start with Ghidra or Cutter. Watch a beginner playlist and do the official Ghidra training labs. 5. Solve simple crackmes from crackmes.one (choose easy difficulty) 6. Do some LiveOverflow beginner RE videos and follow along 7. Try pwn.college or RPISEC MBE labs for deeper understanding.  Legal and ethical note  Only reverse engineer software that you own and are allowed to analyze (your own programs, crackmes specifically released for RE, CTF challenges, or explicitly permitted binaries). Laws vary by country, and RE of commercial software can be restricted or illegal; always check local laws and license terms. At burger chains, a single or double burger made with leaner patties, ordered without cheese, special sauces, or bacon, and with extra lettuce and tomato, can provide a decent protein-to-fat ratio; you can keep the bun for more carbs or go bunless for lower carbs. At sandwich chains, a 6-inch turkey or chicken breast sub on whole wheat with extra veggies and mustard instead of creamy sauces is a good macro-balanced choice, and swapping cheese out further reduces fat. From chicken-focused chains, grilled chicken nuggets with a side of fruit or a small side salad instead of fries can keep protein high and fats and calories more controlled. Breakfast options like an egg white and turkey or ham-based breakfast sandwich on an English muffin, with no cheese or a single slice only, can be relatively high in protein and moderate in carbs without beans. Many chains also offer build-your-own bowl or salad options where you can choose grilled chicken or steak, skip any beans, load up on lettuce and non-starchy vegetables, add a small portion of rice or quinoa for carbs if available, and use salsa, mustard, or a light vinaigrette to avoid heavy, fatty dressings.

1|23: For high‑fidelity PDF → DOCX conversion in Java, you generally need a commercial library because PDF and Word use very different layout models and the free tools rarely preserve complex styling. A common approach is to use a dedicated converter library or SDK that exposes a Java API and is designed specifically for this task.  One practical route is to use Aspose.PDF for Java, which has a direct save‑to‑DOCX feature with good layout and style preservation.  High‑level steps with Aspose.PDF for Java:  1. Add Aspose.PDF dependency  If you use Maven, add their repository and dependency (check their website for the latest version). In pom.xml you would have something conceptually like:      <dependency>         <groupId>com.aspose</groupId>         <artifactId>aspose-pdf</artifactId>         <version>xx.x</version>         <classifier>jdk17</classifier>     </dependency>  (The actual version and classifier depend on your Java version and Aspose release.)  2. Basic conversion code      import com.aspose.pdf.Document;     import com.aspose.pdf.DocSaveOptions;      public class PdfToDocxConverter {         public static void main(String[] args) {             String inputPdf = "input.pdf";             String outputDocx = "output.docx";              Document pdfDocument = new Document(inputPdf);              DocSaveOptions saveOptions = new DocSaveOptions();             saveOptions.setFormat(DocSaveOptions.DocFormat.DocX);              // Flow vs. fixed layout: flow tries to create editable Word structure; fixed mimics exact layout.             // For best balance between editability and layout preservation, try Flow with some fine tuning.             saveOptions.setMode(DocSaveOptions.RecognitionMode.EnhancedFlow);              // Optional: tune these based on your document characteristics             saveOptions.setRecognizeBullets(true);             saveOptions.setRelativeHorizontalProximity(2.5);             saveOptions.setRecognitionImageResolution(300);              pdfDocument.save(outputDocx, saveOptions);         }     }  3. Choosing flow vs fixed mode  Aspose supports different recognition modes. Flow modes create paragraphs, lists, and headings in Word, making the result more semantically rich and editable. Fixed mode tries to reproduce visual layout more literally, often using text boxes. If exact visual fidelity is more important than easy editing, try a fixed layout mode; otherwise use EnhancedFlow and adjust options.  4. Handling fonts and styling  To preserve styling you must ensure that the fonts used in the PDF are available to Aspose at conversion time. If fonts are not embedded in the PDF and are also missing on the system, replacement fonts will be used, which can break layout.  On a server, explicitly register your fonts directory before loading the PDF, for example:      import com.aspose.pdf.FontRepository;      FontRepository.getSubstitutions().add(new com.aspose.pdf.FontSubstitutionRule(         "OriginalFontName",         com.aspose.pdf.FontRepository.findFont("Arial")     ));  or configure the default fonts folder. The exact API may differ slightly by version, so check their documentation.  5. Images, tables, and vector graphics  Aspose will embed images and attempt to convert PDF tables into Word tables, preserving borders, cell shading, and alignment where possible. For complex vector graphics, it may rasterize them into images in the DOCX. If you have very graphic‑heavy PDFs, verify the result and, if needed, tweak recognition options.  6. Performance and memory  PDF → DOCX conversion can be memory‑intensive, especially for multipage documents with many images. On a server, you may want to:  Set a reasonable heap size for the JVM. Process documents in a worker queue instead of parallelizing heavily. Optionally downscale very large images beforehand if file size is a concern.  7. Alternatives  If Aspose licensing is not suitable, there are other commercial Java libraries and cloud APIs:  PDFTron PDFNet SDK has Java bindings, with PDF → Word conversion that aims to retain structure and formatting. It works similarly: you load the PDF and call a conversion method that writes a DOCX.  GroupDocs.Conversion for Java is another option, largely configuration driven, which can convert PDFs to DOCX while letting you customize options such as pages to convert, image quality, and so on.  Cloud‑based APIs like CloudConvert, Zamzar, or various PDF SaaS providers can be invoked from Java using HTTP clients. You send the PDF, get back a DOCX, and let their engine handle layout preservation. This shifts the complexity and maintenance away from your code, but introduces network latency, external dependencies, and data privacy considerations.  8. Why not use only free pure‑Java libraries  Libraries like Apache PDFBox and iText (in their core open source variants) are powerful for reading and generating PDFs, but they do not include a robust PDF → DOCX converter meant to preserve full styling and layout. Implementing this yourself from scratch would require reconstructing higher‑level structures (paragraphs, lists, tables, headers/footers, etc.) from low‑level PDF drawing commands, which is a major task.  For anything beyond the simplest PDFs, a specialized converter (often commercial) is usually the only realistic way to preserve complex styling and formatting in Java.  In summary, for a Java solution that preserves styling and layout:  Use a PDF → DOCX‑capable SDK such as Aspose.PDF, PDFTron, or similar. Load the PDF, configure recognition and layout options, then save as DOCX. Ensure fonts are available and configured to avoid layout shifts. Test with your real documents and tune recognition mode and options for the best tradeoff between visual fidelity and editability.

1|25: The Jacobian is a tool from multivariable calculus that describes how a vector-valued function changes near a point. Imagine you have a function that takes several input variables and produces several output variables, like taking a point in 2D space and mapping it to another point in 2D space, or from 3D to 2D, and so on. The Jacobian at a specific point is the best linear approximation of this transformation near that point.  Concretely, suppose you have a function F that takes n inputs and gives m outputs:  F(x1, x2, ..., xn) = (f1(x1, ..., xn), f2(x1, ..., xn), ..., fm(x1, ..., xn))  The Jacobian of F is the matrix of all first partial derivatives:  J_F = [ ∂f1/∂x1   ∂f1/∂x2   ...   ∂f1/∂xn ] [ ∂f2/∂x1   ∂f2/∂x2   ...   ∂f2/∂xn ] [   ...        ...    ...      ...  ] [ ∂fm/∂x1   ∂fm/∂x2   ...   ∂fm/∂xn ]  Each row tells you how one output component changes with respect to each input variable. Each column tells you how all outputs respond to changing one particular input variable. At a given point x, this matrix is, in effect, the derivative of F there.  Geometrically, when you work in the same number of input and output dimensions, for example R^n to R^n, the determinant of the Jacobian at a point measures how volumes (areas in 2D, lengths in 1D, hypervolumes in higher dimensions) are scaled by the transformation near that point. If the determinant is 2 at a point, then very small volumes around that point are roughly doubled by the map; if the determinant is negative, it also indicates a local orientation flip.  This volume scaling interpretation is why the Jacobian determinant appears in change of variables for multivariable integrals. When you perform a substitution in an integral, you are effectively changing coordinates. To keep the total integral value consistent, you must account for how much the coordinate change stretches or shrinks space, and that stretching factor is the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant.  From a linear algebra viewpoint, the Jacobian at a point is just the matrix that best captures how infinitesimal changes in inputs produce infinitesimal changes in outputs. If you nudge the input vector x by a tiny vector h, the resulting change in the output is approximately J(x) h. This is the multivariable version of the single variable idea f(x + h) ≈ f(x) + f'(x) h.  In applications, Jacobians show up everywhere. In optimization and machine learning, they describe how outputs and loss functions change with respect to parameters and inputs; backpropagation can be seen as manipulating Jacobians efficiently. In robotics and kinematics, a Jacobian relates joint velocities of a robot arm to the velocity of its end effector. In physics, coordinate transformations between different reference frames or coordinate systems use Jacobians to preserve integrals of density and probability. In differential geometry, the Jacobian of a smooth map between manifolds captures how tangent vectors and volume elements transform.  So, in summary, the Jacobian is the matrix of first partial derivatives of a multivariable function, representing its best linear approximation at a point, encoding how small changes in inputs produce small changes in outputs, and, via its determinant, how local volumes are scaled under the transformation.
2|25: The Jacobian is a way to capture how a multivariable function changes when you slightly change its inputs.  Suppose you have a function F that takes several variables and outputs several variables, for example:  F(x, y) = (u(x, y), v(x, y))  So F maps a point (x, y) in the plane to a point (u, v) in another plane.  The Jacobian of F at a point is the matrix of all first-order partial derivatives:  J_F(x, y) = [ du/dx   du/dy ] [ dv/dx   dv/dy ]  In higher dimensions, you do the same thing: each row corresponds to one component of the output, and each column corresponds to one input variable. Entry (i, j) is the partial derivative of the i-th output component with respect to the j-th input variable.  Conceptually, the Jacobian matrix is the best linear approximation of the function near a given point. If you zoom in very close, the function F behaves almost like multiplying by this matrix:  F(x + dx) ≈ F(x) + J_F(x) · dx  where dx is a small change in the input and J_F(x) · dx is the predicted change in the output.  The determinant of the Jacobian matrix, often just called the Jacobian determinant, tells you how volumes (or areas, or lengths in 1D) scale under the transformation. For a mapping from R^n to R^n:  If det(J_F) > 0, orientation is preserved near that point. If det(J_F) < 0, orientation is reversed. The absolute value |det(J_F)| is the local volume-scaling factor.  This is why Jacobians appear in change-of-variable formulas in integrals. When you change from variables (x, y) to (u, v), the area element transforms like:  dA_xy = |det(J)| dA_uv  So to keep the value of the integral consistent, you multiply the integrand by the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant.  In applications:  In optimization and machine learning, the Jacobian tells you how outputs change with respect to inputs or parameters and is used in backpropagation and sensitivity analysis.  In robotics and kinematics, a Jacobian maps joint velocities to end-effector velocities; it tells you how moving robot joints affects the position and orientation of the robot hand.  In differential equations and dynamical systems, the Jacobian of the system gives information about stability; its eigenvalues around an equilibrium point tell you whether that point is stable or unstable.  So, informally:  The Jacobian matrix is the multidimensional derivative of a vector-valued function. The Jacobian determinant is the local scaling factor for volumes induced by that function.
3|25: The Jacobian is a way to capture how a multivariable function changes when you move a tiny bit in its input space. For a function that takes several inputs and gives several outputs, the Jacobian at a point is the matrix of all first-order partial derivatives there. Each row corresponds to one output component, and each column to one input variable.  Concretely, suppose you have a function  f(x, y, z) = (u(x, y, z), v(x, y, z))  So f maps from R^3 to R^2. The Jacobian Jf(x, y, z) is the 2 by 3 matrix  [ ∂u/∂x   ∂u/∂y   ∂u/∂z ] [ ∂v/∂x   ∂v/∂y   ∂v/∂z ]  You can think of it as the best linear approximation of f near that point: if you move a small amount Δx in input space, then the change in output is approximately Jf times Δx (viewed as a column vector). This is the multivariable generalization of a derivative for single-variable functions, where the derivative is a single number that gives the slope. With multiple inputs and outputs, the Jacobian is the “slope” in every direction, all at once.  The determinant of the Jacobian (when the input and output dimensions match, so the Jacobian is square) has a particularly important role in calculus. It tells you how volumes scale under the transformation f. For example, in a change of variables in multiple integrals, the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant is the factor you multiply by to account for how stretching, shrinking, and shearing of space changes volume. In probability and statistics, that same factor appears when you transform random variables and adjust their densities.  Intuitively, you can picture a tiny shape in the input space, like a little cube. When you map it through f, it becomes some deformed shape in the output space. The Jacobian matrix describes how that cube gets stretched and rotated at that point, and the determinant tells you the ratio between the volumes of the new and old shapes. If the determinant is zero, it means that locally the map squashes space into a lower-dimensional object (for example, flattening 3D volume into a 2D surface).  In applications like robotics, computer vision, and machine learning, the Jacobian shows up everywhere. In deep learning, for instance, backpropagation essentially relies on chaining together Jacobian matrices of each layer via the multivariable chain rule. For nonlinear least squares and optimization, the Jacobian of the residuals with respect to the parameters drives algorithms like Gauss Newton and Levenberg Marquardt. In differential equations and dynamical systems, the Jacobian of the system governs how nearby trajectories behave, helping determine stability of equilibria.  So in summary, the Jacobian generalizes the idea of a derivative to vector valued functions of several variables, encoding first order changes in a matrix that approximates how the function behaves locally and, through its determinant, how it distorts volumes.
4|25: The Jacobian is a way to capture how a multivariable function changes in all directions at once. For a function that takes several inputs and produces several outputs, the Jacobian at a point is the matrix of all first-order partial derivatives of each output with respect to each input.  Suppose you have a vector-valued function  f(x₁, x₂, …, xₙ) = [f₁(x₁,…,xₙ), f₂(x₁,…,xₙ), …, f_m(x₁,…,xₙ)]  The Jacobian J of f is the m by n matrix  J = [ ∂fᵢ / ∂xⱼ ]  where the entry in row i and column j is the partial derivative of output fᵢ with respect to input xⱼ.  Conceptually, the Jacobian does two key things.  First, it gives the best linear approximation of the function near a point. Just like a derivative gives the slope of a single-variable function, the Jacobian gives the linear map that best approximates how small changes in the input produce changes in the output. If you nudge your input vector x by a small amount Δx, the corresponding change in output is approximately J Δx.  Second, its determinant (when the function maps from Rⁿ to Rⁿ so J is square) tells you how volumes scale under the transformation. If det J at a point is 2, then a tiny volume around that point in the input space is stretched to roughly twice its volume in the output space; if it is 0.5, volumes are compressed by half; if it is 0, the transformation locally squashes space into a lower dimension. This is why the Jacobian determinant appears in change-of-variables formulas in multivariable calculus and probability, for example when transforming integrals or probability densities.  In applications  In optimization and machine learning, the Jacobian encodes gradients of vector outputs with respect to parameters or inputs, and backpropagation efficiently works with Jacobians and their transposes.  In differential equations, Jacobians describe how systems of ODEs respond to changes in state; their eigenvalues are used to analyze stability of equilibria.  In robotics and computer graphics, Jacobians relate joint velocities to end-effector velocities, telling you how changing angles of robot arms or parameters of a model affects positions and orientations in space.  In summary, the Jacobian is the multivariable generalization of the derivative: a matrix that linearly relates small changes in inputs to small changes in outputs and, via its determinant, describes local stretching or squashing of space under a transformation.
5|25: The Jacobian is a way to capture how a multivariable function changes when its inputs change, using a matrix of partial derivatives.  Imagine a function that takes several inputs and produces several outputs, like f(x, y) = (u(x, y), v(x, y)). For each output component, you can ask  How does u change if I nudge x a little, keeping y fixed How does u change if I nudge y a little, keeping x fixed How does v change if I nudge x a little How does v change if I nudge y a little  These rates of change are partial derivatives. You arrange them into a matrix  J = [ ∂u/∂x   ∂u/∂y       ∂v/∂x   ∂v/∂y ]  That matrix is the Jacobian of f at a point. In general, if you have a function from R^n to R^m, the Jacobian is an m by n matrix; row i, column j is the partial derivative of the i-th output with respect to the j-th input.  Conceptually  The Jacobian is the best linear approximation to your function near a point. Just like a derivative of a single-variable function is the slope of the tangent line, the Jacobian plays the role of the best linear map that approximates your multivariable function locally.  If you zoom in close enough on a smooth multivariable function, it starts to look like a linear transformation, and the Jacobian is the matrix of that linear transformation.  The determinant of the Jacobian when the function goes from R^n to R^n has a special meaning: it measures how volumes are locally scaled and distorted by the map. For example, in a change of variables in integrals, you multiply by the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant because it tells you how an infinitesimal piece of volume in one coordinate system relates to a piece in another coordinate system.  In applications  In optimization and machine learning, the Jacobian helps compute how a vector of outputs changes in response to changing parameters. Backpropagation relies heavily on Jacobians and their transposes.  In physics and engineering, Jacobians convert between coordinate systems and track how small changes in state variables propagate to changes in outputs or constraints.  In differential geometry, Jacobians describe how maps between manifolds stretch and rotate tangent vectors and volumes.  So, in summary, the Jacobian is the matrix of all first-order partial derivatives of a multivariable function, representing its local linear behavior and how it deforms space near a point.
6|25: The Jacobian is a way to capture how a multivariable function locally stretches, squashes, and rotates space.  Start with a function F that takes several variables as input and produces several variables as output, for example  F(x, y) = (u(x, y), v(x, y))  Near a particular point (x0, y0), the best linear approximation to F is given by partial derivatives. You arrange all these partial derivatives into a matrix called the Jacobian matrix:  J_F(x0, y0) = [ ∂u/∂x   ∂u/∂y ] [ ∂v/∂x   ∂v/∂y ]  More generally, if F goes from R^n to R^m, the Jacobian is an m by n matrix whose (i, j) entry is the partial derivative of the i-th output component with respect to the j-th input variable.  This matrix has two especially important interpretations. First, as a derivative. It gives the best linear map that approximates how small changes in the input produce small changes in the output. If you nudge the input by a small vector h, the change in output is approximately J_F times h.  Second, as a measure of local volume change. When you change variables in multivariable integrals, the absolute value of the determinant of the Jacobian (when the map is from R^n to R^n) tells you how volumes scale under the transformation. For example, in two dimensions, if the determinant of the Jacobian at a point is 3, then a tiny area around that point is being stretched so that its area becomes about 3 times larger under the mapping. If the determinant is negative, there is also a flip in orientation.  So, in summary, the Jacobian matrix is simply the multivariable generalization of the derivative, and its determinant, when defined, tells you how the function locally scales volumes and affects orientation.
7|25: The Jacobian is a way to capture how a multivariable function changes when its inputs change, using derivatives arranged in a matrix.  Suppose you have a function that takes several variables in and gives several variables out, like  f(x, y) = (u(x, y), v(x, y))  The Jacobian of f is the matrix of all first partial derivatives of each output with respect to each input:  J = [ ∂u/∂x   ∂u/∂y       ∂v/∂x   ∂v/∂y ]  In higher dimensions, you do the same thing: each row corresponds to one output component, each column to one input variable.  Intuitively, near a point, the function behaves almost like a linear transformation, and the Jacobian matrix is exactly that best linear approximation. If you zoom in very close, you can think of  f(x + Δx) ≈ f(x) + J · Δx  So the Jacobian tells you how small changes in the inputs produce small changes in the outputs.  The determinant of the Jacobian (when the number of inputs equals the number of outputs) has an important geometric meaning: it tells you how volumes (or areas in 2D, lengths in 1D) are scaled when passed through the function. For example, in a change of variables in an integral, the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant is the factor by which area or volume elements are stretched or shrunk.  So, summarized informally: the Jacobian matrix is the multivariable generalization of a derivative, describing the local linear behavior of a function; its determinant measures local stretching, shrinking, and orientation changes of space under that function.
8|25: The Jacobian is a way to capture how a function with several inputs and several outputs changes when you nudge its inputs a little bit.  Imagine a function F that takes an n-dimensional input (x1, x2, …, xn) and produces an m-dimensional output (y1, y2, …, ym). Each output yi depends on all the inputs x1 through xn. If you want to know how sensitive each output is to each input, you look at all the partial derivatives ∂yi / ∂xj.  If you put those partial derivatives in a rectangular array, you get the Jacobian matrix:  Row i corresponds to output yi and contains derivatives with respect to each input xj. Column j corresponds to input xj and contains derivatives of every output yi with respect to that input.  So the Jacobian J of F is:  J = [ ∂yi / ∂xj ]  Conceptually  Local linear approximation Near a point x0, the function F behaves approximately like a linear transformation whose matrix is the Jacobian evaluated at x0. That is, small changes in the input Δx get mapped to changes in the output approximately as  Δy ≈ J(x0) Δx.  This is the multivariable analog of using the derivative as a slope in one dimension: in 1D, f(x + Δx) ≈ f(x) + f′(x) Δx. In many dimensions, you just replace the single slope with this matrix of slopes.  Coordinate transformation In change of variables for integrals, the Jacobian shows how volumes (or areas) scale when you transform coordinates. For a transformation from variables x to variables u, the absolute value of the determinant of the Jacobian matrix tells you how a little volume element dV in x-space changes into one in u-space. This is why you see |det J| in formulas for multiple integrals when you switch from one coordinate system to another, like from Cartesian coordinates to polar or spherical coordinates.  Vector calculus In vector calculus, the Jacobian is the general notion of derivative for vector-valued functions. Specific familiar operators are special cases of Jacobians  The gradient of a scalar function is like a 1-row Jacobian. The divergence can be seen as a trace of a Jacobian-like matrix for a vector field. The derivative of a function between Euclidean spaces (R^n to R^m) is always represented by its Jacobian matrix.  Intuition with an example Take a function from R^2 to R^2  F(x, y) = (u, v) where u(x, y) = x^2 + y v(x, y) = 3x − sin y.  The Jacobian is  J(x, y) = [ ∂u/∂x   ∂u/∂y ] [ ∂v/∂x   ∂v/∂y ]  Compute each partial derivative ∂u/∂x = 2x,  ∂u/∂y = 1 ∂v/∂x = 3,   ∂v/∂y = −cos y.  So  J(x, y) = [ 2x   1      ] [ 3   −cos y ].  If you make a small change in input (Δx, Δy), the change in output (Δu, Δv) near a point (x0, y0) is approximately  [Δu] ≈ [ 2x0    1      ] [Δx] [Δv]   [  3   −cos y0 ] [Δy].  At that point, the function behaves very much like this linear transformation given by J(x0, y0).  In summary, the Jacobian is the matrix of all first partial derivatives of a multivariable vector-valued function. It is the best linear approximation of the function near a point, encodes how each output reacts to each input, and its determinant measures local stretching or shrinking of volume under the transformation.
