It is the multidimensional analogue of the derivative of a single-variable function.  Intuitively  If you zoom in very close to a point, a smooth nonlinear function behaves almost like a linear function. The Jacobian is precisely that best linear approximation near the point. 10|25: The Jacobian is a way to describe how a multivariable function locally stretches, rotates, and shears space. Formally, suppose you have a function F that takes several variables as input and outputs several variables, like F(x, y) = (u(x, y), v(x, y)). In symbols, if F(x) = (f1(x), f2(x), ..., fm(x)) with x = (x1, x2, ..., xn), then the Jacobian matrix is  J_F(x) = [ ∂fi/∂xj ]  This matrix is the best linear approximation to the function F near that point, in the sense of multivariable calculus. If you zoom in extremely close to a smooth transformation, it behaves almost like multiplying by this matrix.  Two especially important uses are:  Change of variables in integrals: When you transform coordinates, volumes and areas change. The factor that tells you how much a little volume element changes is the absolute value of the determinant of the Jacobian matrix. This Jacobian determinant appears in the change of variables formula for multiple integrals.  Differential equations and optimization: The Jacobian is used for Newtons method in multiple dimensions, for analyzing stability of dynamical systems (through the eigenvalues of the Jacobian), and for computing gradients and sensitivities. 1|29: Pacing around your room to get more steps is usually not bad for your joints, and for most people it is actually beneficial. Gentle, frequent walking helps lubricate joints, strengthens supporting muscles, and can improve circulation and mood. As long as you are comfortable and not pushing through pain, this kind of low-impact movement is generally considered joint friendly.  There are a few things to keep in mind so it stays safe and comfortable:  – Surface: A flat, even surface like typical indoor flooring is usually fine. If your floor is very hard and you pace for long periods, supportive shoes or cushioned slippers can reduce impact on knees, hips, and lower back.  – Footwear: Walking barefoot on a hard floor for hours may cause discomfort in feet, ankles, or knees, especially if you have flat feet or existing issues. Supportive shoes with some cushioning and arch support are better if you do a lot of pacing.  – Repetitive pattern: Constantly turning around in a tiny space can put a bit of repetitive stress on the same joints if you always pivot the same way. You can occasionally change directions, vary your path slightly, or take some longer walks elsewhere when possible.  – Existing joint problems: If you already have knee, hip, ankle, or back issues, pay attention to how your body feels. Mild muscle tiredness is normal, but sharp, increasing, or lingering pain is a sign to ease up and maybe talk with a doctor or physical therapist.  – Duration and intensity: Short bouts spread through the day are generally kinder to joints than very long nonstop pacing sessions, especially if you are not used to a lot of activity.  If you feel fine during and after your pacing, and you are on a reasonably comfortable surface with decent footwear, it is unlikely to cause joint damage and is a useful way to increase daily movement. If you start to notice pain or stiffness that does not settle after rest, it is worth adjusting how you pace or asking a healthcare professional for personalized advice.

You can reduce that strain by making wider turns when you change direction, walking in a small loop rather than a strict back‑and‑forth line, or occasionally changing which way you turn so you are not always twisting the same joint in the same direction. From a broader health perspective, many people do exactly what you are describing to meet step goals when they work from home or have a sedentary lifestyle, and studies generally support that accumulating steps in small bouts, even indoors, is good for metabolic and cardiovascular health.  So pacing in your room is not inherently bad for your joints. With decent footwear, a reasonably forgiving surface, and attention to any pain or discomfort, it is a safe and useful way to boost daily activity. If anything starts to hurt consistently, that is your cue to adjust how much, how fast, or where you are pacing, or to get personalized advice from a healthcare professional.
3|29: Short, gentle pacing around your room is generally safe for most people’s joints and can actually be helpful, especially if you spend a lot of time sitting. Walking is a low-impact activity, and your joints are designed to move; regular movement can support joint lubrication, circulation, and overall mobility.  A few things to watch for:  Surface and footwear If you’re pacing barefoot on a hard floor (tile, concrete under thin carpet), that repeated impact can irritate feet, ankles, knees, or hips over time, especially if you are sensitive or have flat feet or previous joint issues. Supportive, comfortable shoes and, if needed, cushioned insoles make a big difference.  Direction and variety If you are always walking the exact same very short path, turning the same way at each end, your joints are repeating the same small stresses. This usually isn’t harmful at moderate volumes, but if you’re doing many thousands of steps this way every day, try to vary your route a little, change directions, and occasionally walk in larger loops or in different rooms or outside when possible.  Volume and pain signals Your joints adapt to gradual increases in activity. Problems are more likely if you drastically jump your step count overnight or push through pain. If you notice new or worsening pain in knees, hips, ankles, or lower back that doesn’t settle within a day or two of easing up, that’s a sign to back off and, if it persists, check in with a professional.  Noise and posture In a small room, people tend to hunch over their phone while pacing. Try to keep an upright posture, relax your shoulders, and look forward instead of down all the time. Also consider whether constant pacing might disturb others (neighbors below you if you live in an apartment).  When it might be problematic If you already have joint conditions like osteoarthritis, previous knee or hip injuries, or foot problems, even low-impact repetition on a hard surface might aggravate symptoms. In that case, shorter bouts, better shoes, and mixing in other low-impact activities (cycling, elliptical, swimming, gentle strength training) is wiser than relying only on room pacing.  Practical tips Try to increase steps gradually rather than going from, say, 2,000 to 12,000 in a week. Wear supportive shoes if the floor is hard. Change directions and routes often. Include some simple strength exercises for legs and hips a few times a week; stronger muscles reduce joint stress. Use pain and lingering soreness as feedback; discomfort that improves as you warm up is usually less concerning than sharp or worsening pain.  In summary, pacing around your room is not inherently bad for your joints and can be a perfectly fine way to boost step count, especially if life or weather limits outdoor walking. Just pay attention to surface, footwear, volume, and any pain signals, and try to mix in a bit of variety and strength work for the best long-term joint health.
4|29: Pacing around your room is generally not bad for your joints; for most people it is actually a gentle, low-impact way to get more steps in. Walking is one of the safest forms of exercise for joints because it does not involve sudden high forces like jumping or sprinting. As long as you feel comfortable and are not experiencing pain, stiffness that gets worse over time, or swelling, it is unlikely to be harmful.  There are a few things to watch for, though, because of the specific way you are walking:  If your room is very small and you are constantly turning sharply at each end, that repetitive pivoting could irritate knees, hips, or ankles over long periods, especially if you already have joint issues or flat feet. Increasing time and steps gradually, paying attention to any new discomfort, is safer. A simple rule is to increase total weekly steps or time walking by something like 5 to 10 percent per week rather than doubling suddenly.  If you notice pain during or after pacing that lasts into the next day, worsens over time, or is focused in one joint, it is a sign to ease back and possibly change how or where you walk. Sometimes just changing surfaces, wearing better shoes, or taking more frequent short breaks is enough to solve this.  To make pacing healthier and more joint-friendly, you can:  Use supportive footwear, even indoors. Walk a larger circuit if possible, or vary your route in the home to avoid constant sharp turns. 10|29: Pacing around your room to get more steps is generally not bad for your joints, and for most people it’s actually a net positive for health, as long as a few conditions are met.  In favor of it:  It’s low-impact: Walking on a flat, indoor surface is one of the gentlest activities you can do for your joints. It reduces stiffness: Regular light movement can help lubricate joints, improve circulation, and reduce stiffness from sitting too long. It helps your overall health: More steps usually correlate with better cardiovascular health, mood, energy, and sleep.  Possible downsides and what to watch for:  Surface: Very hard flooring (like concrete under thin carpet or tile) can be tougher on knees, hips, and lower back over long periods. If you have this type of floor, consider supportive shoes or a cushioned mat in the area where you walk the most. Repetition and tight turning: Constantly walking a short distance and pivoting at the ends can put a little extra stress on ankles, knees, and hips, especially if you always turn the same direction or make sharp turns. You can soften this by:  – Making your pacing path as long and straight as possible – Alternating the direction you turn – Slowing slightly at the ends and turning with multiple small steps instead of one hard twist  Footwear: Doing all your pacing barefoot or in unsupportive slippers can bother feet, knees, or lower back if you do a lot of steps. Supportive sneakers or at least shoes with some cushioning and arch support can help.  Volume and intensity: If you suddenly jump from almost no walking to many thousands of steps per day, your body may complain a bit. Gradually increasing your daily step count is easier on joints and tendons. Mild soreness or fatigue can be normal at first; sharp, persistent, or worsening pain is a sign to back off and reassess.  Existing joint issues: If you already have knee, hip, ankle, or foot problems (arthritis, previous injuries, etc.), pacing might still be fine, but it’s more important to:  – Keep sessions shorter and spread through the day – Use good shoes and a softer surface – Pay attention to whether pain appears or gets worse with pacing  When to be concerned or get advice:  Consider talking to a doctor or physical therapist if you notice:  – Pain that gets sharper or more frequent the more you pace – Swelling, warmth, or locking in a joint – Limping or needing to change the way you walk because of discomfort  Practical tips to make your indoor steps joint-friendlier:  – Wear comfortable, supportive shoes, not just socks on hard floors. – Use the longest straight path you have (hallways, around furniture, etc.). – Change direction regularly so you are not always pivoting the same way. – Break it up: short bouts throughout the day instead of one super-long pacing session. – Mix in some gentle mobility or stretching for hips, hamstrings, calves, and ankles.  Overall, for a healthy person with no serious joint conditions, pacing around your room is not inherently bad for your joints and is usually beneficial as a way to stay active. It is basically just walking. As long as you feel okay during and after, adjust for comfort, and increase your steps gradually, it is a perfectly reasonable way to raise your daily step count.
1|30: In SAP ERP (especially in the classic ECC / R3 world), orders such as sales orders and purchase orders are not stored as a single row in a single table. Instead, SAP uses a highly normalized, multi-table structure following its general principle of separating document headers from items and then extending them with additional detail tables.  Take a sales order as the most common example. The core technical object is called a document and it is primarily identified by the field VBAK-VBELN (the sales document number). SAP stores the sales order in several logically linked tables in the underlying relational database, for example an Oracle, HANA, SQL Server, or another supported DBMS. The database is not accessed directly by end users; instead, ABAP programs use Open SQL to work with these tables.  At the highest level, SAP splits the order into:  Header data: One row per order, containing information that is valid for the entire document. For sales orders, this is mainly table VBAK. Key fields include VBELN (document number) and other fields like AUART (document type), VKORG (sales organization), KUNNR (sold-to party), AUDAT (document date), WAERK (currency), and overall status fields. The header captures who the customer is, organizational data, document type, pricing date, and various control flags.  Item data: One row per item/position in the order, containing information valid at the item level. For sales orders this is table VBAP. Here the key is VBELN+POSNR (document number + item number). You find material number MATNR, requested quantity KWMENG, schedule line category, item category, plant, storage location, and references to pricing and schedule-line data. Each item row points back to its VBAK header through the same VBELN.  Schedule lines: For detailed delivery scheduling, SAP uses schedule line tables. For sales orders, that’s VBEP. Each schedule line is identified by VBELN+POSNR+ETENR. Fields include EDATU (schedule line date), confirmed quantity BDMNG, and schedule line category. This allows one sales order item to be delivered in multiple partial shipments on different dates.  Conditions/pricing: Pricing information is not denormalized into VBAK or VBAP, but stored separately in condition tables. For sales orders, the actual document-level pricing lines are in KONV. KONV is keyed by KNUMV (condition record number) which is referenced from the document header or item via fields like VBAK-KNUMV or VBAP-KNUMV. Each KONV entry represents a specific condition type (e.g., PR00 for base price, K007 for discount, MWST for tax), with value fields for amount, rate, condition currency, and calculation type. In S/4HANA, KONV is technically replaced by the pricing result table PRCD_ELEMENTS, but the same separation of pricing data from header/item persists.  Status and control data: SAP additionally stores detailed status information in dedicated status tables, such as VBUK (header status) and VBUP (item status) for sales documents. These tables are keyed again by VBELN (and POSNR for VBUP) and contain fields like overall processing status, delivery status, billing status, credit status, and so on. This separation allows SAP to update statuses frequently without touching the main business data tables as much.  Partners and addresses: Sales orders often involve multiple business partners: sold-to, ship-to, bill-to, payer, etc. SAP stores partner assignments in tables such as VBPA (partner data for sales documents). VBPA is keyed by VBELN, POSNR, and PARVW (partner function). The actual master data for business partners is in KNA1/KNB1 (classic customers) or the Business Partner tables (S/4HANA), and address details live in address tables like ADRC. The order records only store keys that reference the master data, not duplicate all address and master fields.  Texts and long data: Free-form text (e.g., header text, item text, shipping instructions) is managed through SAP’s generic text framework, stored in cluster or standard text tables like STXH/STXL. The order header or item stores only text IDs and language keys that point to those text entries.  Organizational referencing: Many fields in the order refer to customizing or master-data tables. For example, the sales organization VKORG in VBAK points to TVKO, distribution channel VTWEG to TVTW, division SPART to TVTA, customer number KUNNR to KNA1, material MATNR to MARA/MARC, and plant WERKS to T001W. This approach avoids redundancy and enforces data consistency across all orders.  Indexes and performance: Because orders are accessed from many angles, SAP defines numerous secondary index tables and database indexes. For example, there are transparent index tables like VBAK index on customer/date, or custom-defined secondary indexes created in SE11. These do not change the logical data model but influence how the DB retrieves order data. Additionally, in S/4HANA, performance is further optimized through HANA column-store indexes and CDS views on top of the basic tables.  Application-level document flow: SAP’s notion of an order being connected to subsequent documents (deliveries, invoices, returns) is represented via table VBFA (document flow). VBFA stores relationships like preceding document and subsequent document, with fields for source VBELV, target VBELN, document categories, and references to items. Thus the document flow is not directly part of VBAK/VBAP but a separate relational link structure.  Similar structures for other order types: Other business areas follow comparable header/item separation, but in different table namespaces:  Sales: VBAK, VBAP, VBEP, VBPA, KONV (or PRCD_ELEMENTS) Purchase orders: EKKO (header), EKPO (item), EKET (schedule lines), conditions in tables like KONV/PRCD_ELEMENTS and additional partner and text tables Production orders: AUFK (order master), AFKO/AFPO, AFVC (operations), and related status and assignment tables Maintenance/service orders: AUFK, AFIH, AFVC, and PM/CS-specific tables  In all cases, SAP stores the order as a cluster of related records across multiple tables, linked by shared keys such as the order/document number and item numbers. The application layer then reconstructs the business document by joining these tables logically, typically via ABAP Open SQL or CDS views rather than raw database joins written by users.  In modern S/4HANA, the physical storage still uses this header/item/schedule/pricing/status pattern, but some tables are simplified or replaced, and additional virtual views (CDS views) provide a more business-friendly data model. However, the underlying design principle remains: orders are decomposed into related, normalized tables instead of a single wide, denormalized record.
2|30: In classic SAP ERP (ECC) and in SAP S/4HANA, orders are not stored as one single big record, but are split across multiple related tables that together form the order object. The exact tables depend on the order type (sales order, purchase order, production order, etc.), but the principle is similar: there is always a header table for data that applies to the whole order and one or more item tables for line-level details, plus many auxiliary tables for conditions, schedules, statuses, texts, and so on.  For a sales order in SAP SD for example, the primary header table is VBAK. Each record in VBAK represents one sales document header and is identified by the document number field VBELN. This table holds data that is common to the entire order, such as the sold-to party, document type, overall dates, currency, sales organization, and reference information. You can think of it as the top-level object that all other parts of the sales order link back to.  The items of the sales order are stored in VBAP, which is the sales document item table. Each item line is again identified by VBELN plus a position number POSNR. VBAP contains information such as material number, quantity, plant, item category, and item-level controls. The header and item tables are linked by the shared VBELN key, forming a one-to-many relationship.  On top of header and items, SAP separates schedule information and delivery dates into schedule line tables like VBEP (sales document schedule lines). Each record in VBEP is keyed by VBELN, POSNR and the schedule line number ETENR. Here SAP stores confirmed quantities, requested and confirmed delivery dates, and availability-related data. This makes it possible to have multiple partial deliveries or different dates per line item.  Prices, discounts, and taxes are not duplicated in the item table but live in separate condition tables, most notably KONV in ECC. Each condition line is linked back to the sales document through keys such as KNUMV, which is a pricing document number referenced from the sales document header or item. In S/4HANA the pricing model has been simplified and technically changed, but conceptually it is still an external pricing layer linked to the order.  Status information is split into header and item status tables. For sales orders these are VBUK for document header status and VBUP for item status. They indicate whether the order is fully delivered, billed, blocked, or partially processed. This keeps frequently changing status flags out of the main header and item tables and allows SAP to update them without heavy locking on the core business data.  Texts (free-form notes) are managed in generic text tables such as STXH and STXL or in newer text frameworks. The sales order objects reference these texts using object keys and text IDs. This pattern is reused across many SAP applications, so the order header or item only stores keys that point to where the big text blobs are stored.  Customer or document-specific fields that users add via configuration or enhancements are stored in append structures on the main tables or in customer include tables (for example, VBAP append structures). In S/4HANA some extensibility is handled via extension tables that are automatically linked using a 1:1 relationship to the standard table key.  If you look at purchasing, the same conceptual pattern appears. Purchase order headers are in EKKO, and items are in EKPO, with schedules in EKET, conditions in EKKN and related tables, and statuses in additional technical tables. The key for a purchase order is EBELN, and item positions are EBELP. Again, header data that affects the whole document is in EKKO, while line-level data like quantity and material is in EKPO.  In production planning, internal production orders (PP) are stored in tables like AUFK for the order header and AFKO or AFPO for production-specific data and operation-level details. Service orders and maintenance orders in PM/CS follow a similar split: a generic order header in AUFK, and application-specific tables holding PM or CS data, with operations in AFVC and relationships to settlement, costs, and technical objects.  Underneath all of this, SAP uses foreign keys and standardized field names to link tables: VBELN for sales documents, EBELN for purchasing documents, AUFNR for order numbers, KUNNR for customer, MATNR for material, and so on. The application logic in ABAP and the business application layer interprets these linked records as a single business object called an order.  With the move to S/4HANA, the underlying database is usually SAP HANA, and some data models have been simplified. Redundant or aggregate tables have been removed, and some condition and status models have been adjusted. But the core idea remains: orders are logically one object, physically stored as multiple normalized tables with a stable key. CDS views and APIs then provide a virtual object view over these tables, so consumers can treat them as a unified entity even though the persistence is distributed.  In other words, when you open an order in the SAP GUI or Fiori app, the system is reading from a whole set of related tables: one for header, one for positions, one for schedules, one for prices, one for statuses, one for texts, and more. The relationships between these tables, plus the application layer logic, is how SAP represents and stores orders in its database structure.
3|30: In SAP ERP, orders are not stored as one big document in a single table, but as a set of related database records spread across several tables that follow a standardized structure. At a high level, SAP separates the business document into header data, item data, and various specialized detail tables, all linked together primarily through keys such as client, document number, and item number.  For sales orders in SD (Sales and Distribution), the core tables are:  VBAK: This is the sales document header table. Each record here represents one sales order header and contains information that applies to the whole order, such as the sales document number, document type, sales organization, customer numbers (sold-to, ship-to, bill-to, payer), overall status fields, currency, and high-level dates.  VBAP: This is the sales document item table. Each record here represents a single line item within a sales order. It is linked to the header via the sales document number and item number. VBAP holds data that is specific to an individual line, such as material number, order quantity, item category, schedule line category, plant, and pricing relevance flags.  VBEP: This is the schedule line table for sales orders. Not every implementation looks here in detail, but technically each item can have one or more schedule lines that determine confirmed quantities and delivery dates. VBEP is linked to VBAP by document number and item number, and then by schedule line number.  Pricing data for a sales order is stored separately in condition tables. The main ones at document level are:  KONV (in older ECC systems): Holds pricing condition lines such as base price, discounts, surcharges, taxes, and freight. Each condition is linked to the sales document and item. In S/4HANA, pricing is reorganized into new structures (for example PRCD_ELEMENTS), but the conceptual idea is the same: conditions are stored line by line with condition type, amount, and currency.  Texts, partners, and other extensions are also stored separately:  STXH and STXL (or their successors): Store long text lines for headers and items, such as header notes or item-specific notes.  VBPA: Contains partner functions (sold-to, bill-to, ship-to, payer, and many others) at header and sometimes item level. This allows multiple partners to be attached to the same order.  For purchase orders in MM (Materials Management), the pattern is analogous but with different tables:  EKKO: Purchasing document header. One record per purchase order, with vendor, purchasing organization, document type, overall status, currency, and key dates.  EKPO: Purchasing document item. One line per PO item, linked to EKKO by document number. It contains material, quantity, plant, delivery date, item category, account assignment category, and price-relevant fields.  EKET: Schedule lines for PO items. It specifies at what dates and in what quantities the material should be delivered.  Pricing and conditions in purchasing are stored in condition tables such as KONV (ECC) or successor structures in S4, again on a per-condition-line basis.  Financial and controlling documents are not physically embedded inside the order tables. When an order leads to posting in FI or CO, separate documents are generated and stored in their own tables, linked via reference fields. For example, an SD billing document produces accounting documents stored in BKPF (header) and BSEG (line items), which reference the billing and/or order number.  Technically, SAP uses a client field (for example MANDT) and a primary key such as sales document number or purchasing document number to identify each order. All related tables carry the same document number and are linked logically. There is usually no foreign key constraint in the database in the strict relational sense, but SAP enforces consistency at the application level.  Indexes and views are used heavily for performance and reporting. Transparent tables store the core data, while SAP delivers logical views and CDS views (particularly in S4HANA) that join header, item, schedule lines, partners, and pricing to present an order as an integrated business object. For instance, an SD order might be exposed to applications through a CDS view that reads from VBAK, VBAP, VBEP, VBPA, and pricing views, hiding the underlying complexity from the end user.  The general pattern therefore is:  Order header in a header table containing global document attributes Order items in an item table linked to the header Schedule lines in schedule tables for date and quantity confirmation Conditions (prices, discounts, taxes) in condition tables, one line per condition Partners, texts, and other attributes in separate tables linked by document and item  This modular structure allows SAP to handle many different order types (sales, purchase, production, maintenance, internal) with a consistent approach. For example, production orders use AUFK for the order header and AFKO/AFPO for additional production-specific header and item data, while maintenance orders use AUFK with PM-specific extension tables such as AFIH and operations in AFVC. In every case, one logical order document is realized as a cluster of related records across multiple tables, all keyed and linked via document number and client, and exposed as a single business object through the application layer.
4|30: In classic SAP ERP (ECC) and largely also in S/4HANA, business orders are stored following a highly normalized, header–item–schedule-line approach, implemented as sets of relational tables that are linked by key fields like client, document number, and item number.  For sales orders (SD), the core tables are:  VBAK – sales document header This table contains fields that apply to the entire order document. Key fields and examples:  Client (MANDT) Sales document number (VBELN) Document type (AUART) such as standard order, return Sales organization, distribution channel, division Sold-to party, ship-to party, payer, bill-to Overall status fields (e.g., delivery status, billing status) Document date, pricing date, requested delivery date Currency, overall net value, incoterms  VBAP – sales document item Each entry in VBAP represents one item (line) of a sales order. It is connected to VBAK by VBELN and identified by item number POSNR. Typical fields:  Client (MANDT) Sales document number (VBELN) Item number (POSNR) Material (MATNR) Plant, storage location Item category, schedule line category Order quantity and unit of measure Net price, condition indicators, pricing reference Item-level status (delivery status, billing status, rejection reason)  VBEP – schedule lines In many SAP processes, each item can have multiple delivery dates and quantities. These are stored in VBEP and are linked to VBAP by VBELN + POSNR, with an additional schedule-line number ETENR. Important fields:  Sales document number (VBELN) Item number (POSNR) Schedule-line number (ETENR) Requested delivery date, confirmed delivery date Schedule quantity (e.g., confirmed quantity) Availability check results  These three tables together represent the logical sales order: VBAK for what the order is globally, VBAP for the lines, and VBEP for when and how much is delivered.  In addition, SD orders have many related tables:  Conditions (pricing): KONV in ECC, and condition tables + pricing result structures in S/4HANA, storing line- and header-level pricing details like discounts, surcharges, taxes, freight. Partners: VBPA for partner functions at header and item level (sold-to, ship-to, payer, bill-to, etc.). Texts: STXH/STXL and SD text determination tables, which store long texts linked to the sales order and its items. Status: VBUK (header status) and VBUP (item status) carry more granular status information. Document flow: VBFA links one document to another (e.g., sales order → delivery → invoice) by storing preceding and subsequent document references.  For purchasing (MM), a similar pattern is used, but with different tables:  EKKO – purchasing document header EKPO – purchasing document item EKET – purchasing document schedule lines  For example, a purchase order is in EKKO (overall supplier, PO type, currency, dates), its lines in EKPO (materials or services, quantities, prices per item), and its delivery schedule per item in EKET.  Production orders (PP) and process orders are stored using order master and operation/component tables, such as:  AUFK – order master data (header: order number, type, plant, status, controlling area) AFKO – header data for production orders (for make-to-order or make-to-stock production) AFPO – order item or material data AFVC – operations (routing steps of the order) RESB – reservations/components assigned to the order  These PP tables follow the same conceptual structure: a single order number (AUFNR) links header (what is being produced, at what plant, basic dates and status) to operations and components that define how the order will be executed.  Financial documents created by orders (such as billing documents from SD or GR/IR postings from MM) are stored in FI tables:  BKPF – accounting document header BSEG – accounting line items  Those FI entries are linked back to logistics documents via reference fields (e.g., VBELN, EBELN, or AUFNR) or via the document flow tables.  From a technical perspective, all of this rests on these core principles:  Client and document-number-based keys Almost every business table has a client field MANDT as part of the primary key. Orders are uniquely identified by numbers:  Sales: VBELN Purchasing: EBELN Production: AUFNR  These keys then propagate down to item and schedule-level tables:  VBELN + POSNR for SD items EBELN + EBELP for MM items AUFNR + operation number (VORNR) for PP operations  Normalization SAP is highly normalized: general info (like customers, materials, plants) is stored once in master data tables (KNA1, LFA1, MARA, MARC, etc.), and the orders only reference them via keys. This keeps redundancy low but results in a large number of table joins to get a complete picture.  Status and document flow Instead of copying extensive status information into many records, SAP uses dedicated status tables (VBUK, VBUP, JEST, JCDS for status and change documents) and document flow tables (VBFA for SD) to trace how an order evolves over time: creation, confirmation, delivery, billing, and settlement.  Configuration tables and customizing The behavior of how orders are stored and processed is not hard-coded in the data model alone; customizing tables (in the T* and V* namespace like TVAK, T161, T003, etc.) define document types, number ranges, item categories, and status profiles. The actual order tables then use type codes (e.g., AUART, BSART, AUFART) that point to these configuration records.  In S/4HANA, the underlying storage mechanism changed technically (many classic tables are now compatibility views over HANA-optimized tables or CDS views, and aggregates/indices were simplified), but the logical order structure is intentionally kept very similar for business continuity. Tables such as VBAK, VBAP, EKKO, EKPO, and AUFK still exist from an application perspective, even when technically they can be views on column-store tables with different physical names.  In summary, SAP stores orders via a generic and reusable pattern:  One header table per order type (sales, purchase, production, etc.) with global attributes One or more item tables linked via document number and item number Optional schedule-line tables for date/quantity breakdowns Separate tables for pricing, partners, texts, status, and document flow Strong linking to master data via IDs instead of repeated descriptive fields  This structured, relational design allows SAP to support complex order lifecycles, multiple languages and currencies, cross-module integration, and auditing, while keeping the core concept of an order consistent across SD, MM, PP, and FI/CO.
5|30: In SAP ERP, orders are not usually stored as a single big record, but instead are split across multiple specialized database tables that are linked together by keys such as client, document number, and item number. Each functional area (like SD for sales orders or MM for purchase orders) has its own main header and item tables, plus a range of related detail tables. At a high level, SAP follows a normalized, relational data model where the database stores relatively lean, well-structured records, and the richer business logic is handled in the application layer.  For sales orders in the SD module, the two central application tables are VBAK and VBAP. VBAK holds the order header information, one record per sales document, such as the sales document number (VBELN), document type, sales organization, customer, order date, and overall status fields. VBAP holds the item-level lines of the same sales order, with one record per item. Each VBAP record is linked to the header by VBELN and is distinguished by the item number POSNR, which is typically a 6-digit field like 000010, 000020, and so on. Together, the header and item tables form the backbone of how SAP stores a sales order.  Instead of repeating text and long descriptions in the header and item tables, SAP stores most variable texts in separate text tables. For sales orders this is done through the standard text interface, often stored in tables like STXH and STXL (or newer text solutions) that hold text header and text lines. The link between an order and its texts is done with a combination of object keys like the document number, language, and text IDs (for example, header note, item note, shipping instructions). When an end user displays a sales order in the SAP GUI, the application layer reads the main VBAK/VBAP records and then pulls related text records as needed.  Condition records and pricing details are also kept in separate structures, not mixed directly into the order header or items. The pricing result of an order is stored in tables such as KONV where each record represents a single pricing condition applied to a particular document and item (for example, base price, discount, freight). The key fields connect it to VBELN and POSNR along with a condition type. This design lets SAP reuse the same pricing engine across different document categories and keeps the main order tables smaller and more stable.  Status information is similarly split out. While VBAK and VBAP have some general status fields, detailed status handling makes use of status tables such as VBUK (overall document status) and VBUP (item status). These tables hold information like whether the order item is fully delivered, whether billing is complete, or whether any credit blocks are active. The separation of status into its own tables helps SAP avoid repeated status indicators scattered across many different structures and facilitates faster status queries.  For purchase orders in the MM module, the equivalent core tables are EKKO and EKPO. EKKO is the purchase order header, with one record per PO number, containing vendor, purchasing organization, document type, terms of payment, and similar details. EKPO is the item table, keyed by the same PO number plus item number. It contains material, quantity, price, delivery date, and account assignment references. Like SD, MM has associated partner, text, conditions, and status tables that are linked to EKKO and EKPO via keys.  Partner and address data are not duplicated fully on each document. Instead, SAP uses a combination of partner functions and centralized master data. For sales orders, partner assignments such as sold-to, ship-to, bill-to, and payer are contained in VBPA, which references business partners or customers stored in tables like KNA1 or BUT000. Actual postal address details are usually stored in centralized address tables such as ADRC. Documents only store references, so if a customer address changes, the system can reflect that change in new documents without bulk-updating historical orders.  Logically, most SAP orders have three main layers in the schema. The header layer (for example, VBAK or EKKO) holds data that is common across the entire order. The item layer (for example, VBAP or EKPO) contains data specific to individual lines. A third layer includes schedules or subitems, such as VBEP (schedule lines for SD orders) or EKET (schedule lines for MM purchase orders), which store delivery dates and planned quantities over time. This layered model makes it possible to support complex scenarios like multiple partial deliveries per line without changing the basic header or item structures.  In newer SAP systems like S4HANA, the underlying technical storage can move from classic row-store tables in a relational database to in-memory columnar tables in SAP HANA, but the logical data model as seen by applications is still very similar. Key tables like VBAK, VBAP, EKKO, and EKPO remain, though some index and aggregate tables have been removed or simplified. S4HANA optimizes performance using HANA features such as column storage and in-memory processing while retaining the traditional document and item paradigm.  SAP also uses generated transparent tables, views, and foreign key relationships defined in the ABAP Dictionary to describe how these order tables are structured. Each table has a primary key, foreign keys, data elements, and domains that define technical attributes such as field length and data type. The ABAP Dictionary metadata is used by both the runtime and the development environment, so when changes are made to the structure of an order table, they are centrally controlled and consistent across the application and the database.  On top of the core tables, SAP defines many views and reporting structures to make it easier to read order data. For example, some views combine header and item tables or enrich them with material or customer master data. In S4HANA, CDS views serve a similar purpose by creating semantic models over the basic order tables. These are used for analytics, Fiori apps, and APIs but still point ultimately to the underlying order tables.  All of this comes together so that an order is not a single blob in a database, but a network of normalized records spread across header, item, schedule, text, status, partner, condition, and master data tables. The user sees a coherent order in the transaction screens because the ABAP application layer orchestrates queries across these related tables, assembles them into a document image, and enforces business rules. This layered and normalized structure is central to how SAP maintains consistency, performance, and flexibility in its order processing across modules.
6|30: In SAP ERP and S/4HANA, orders are not stored as one big record in a single table. Instead, SAP uses a highly normalized, modular data model where different aspects of an order are kept in separate but linked tables. The exact tables depend on the type of order: sales orders in SD, purchase orders in MM, production orders in PP, and so on. The idea is always the same: a header table for the overall document, one or more item tables for line details, plus many related tables for conditions, schedules, texts, statuses, and accounting links.  For a sales order in the SD module, the core tables are:  Header level: VBAK This stores information that applies to the whole sales order. Examples include  Client and sales document number Document type such as standard order Sales organization, distribution channel, division Order date, requested delivery date Customer numbers sold to party, ship to party, payer, bill to Overall status fields for delivery, billing, credit checks Currency and incoterms  Each record in VBAK is one sales order header identified by the key field VBELN the sales document number. This number is the anchor used to find all related data.  Item level: VBAP This table stores the individual line items of the sales order. Each record references  VBELN the sales document number from VBAK POSNR the item number within the order  For each item, VBAP stores material number, quantity, unit of measure, plant, item category, pricing relevance flags, schedule line category, and item level statuses. Together, VBAK and VBAP represent the logical sales order document.  Schedule lines: VBEP If line items are planned to be delivered in several partial deliveries or at specific dates, SAP stores these schedules in VBEP. The primary keys are VBELN, POSNR, and ETENR schedule line number. Each record contains confirmed quantities and dates, availability check results, and delivery relevance. This allows one order item to be spread over multiple delivery dates.  Pricing conditions: KONV or PRCD elements SAP does not store the final price directly in the item table beyond some summary values. Instead, it stores the full breakdown of pricing conditions in the pricing tables. In older ECC systems, KONV is commonly used where each row represents one pricing condition for a given document item discount, surcharge, tax, freight, etc. In newer S4HANA, pricing data is often found in more modern pricing tables named PRCD elements. The link is again via document number and item number plus condition type.  Texts: STXH and STXL or long text objects Longer descriptive texts related to orders such as header texts order confirmations, item texts, shipping instructions are stored separately in SAPscript or Smart Forms text tables. The header STXH and line STXL tables are addressed using a text object and text ID that link back logically to the order document e.g. sales document number and item.  Status management: VBUK and VBUP SAP separates business statuses from the base document tables. VBUK stores header status entries such as overall delivery status, overall billing status, credit status. VBUP holds item level status values like delivery status by item, goods movement status, and billing status by item. This setup lets SAP update statuses efficiently without rewriting large main records.  Document flow: VBFA SAP tracks relationships between documents in the document flow table VBFA. When a sales order leads to a delivery and then to an invoice, VBFA stores links from predecessor to successor documents. Fields include preceding document, subsequent document, item references, and relationship category. SAP uses this for navigation in VA03 document flow and to determine what has already been delivered or billed.  Connections to logistics and accounting:  Deliveries from the order are stored in tables such as LIKP header and LIPS item, with document numbers distinct from the sales order but linked via VBFA. Billings invoices go into VBRK header and VBRP item. Those billing documents then create accounting documents stored in BKPF header and BSEG line items in Financial Accounting. Material movements related to deliveries and goods issues are stored in MKPF header and MSEG or MATDOC in S4HANA.  Purchase orders in MM follow a similar, but module specific, pattern  Header: EKKO purchase order header including document number, vendor, purchasing organization, document date, terms. Items: EKPO item data including materials or services, quantities, net price, delivery date, plant. Schedule lines: EKET planned delivery dates and quantities for each PO item. Conditions: EKKN and pricing related tables for account assignment and price conditions. Document history: EKBE goods receipts, invoice receipts, associated with the purchase order items.  Production orders in PP:  Header: AUFK or similar order master data table containing order type, controlling area, responsible cost center, and status. Operation data: AFVC operations for routing steps. Component assignments: RESB or equivalents for reservation and dependent requirements. Costs and confirmations: Various CO and PP tables such as AFKO, AFPO, and accounting tables.  Technical aspects  Primary keys: SAP uses synthetic document numbers as primary keys VBELN, EBELN, AUFNR etc. These numbers ensure uniqueness across the client. Item and schedule lines add POSNR and ETENR to make composite keys. Client separation: Nearly all business tables have a client field MANDT so that data for different clients logical systems can be isolated within the same physical database. Normalization and referential logic: SAP heavily normalizes its schema. For example, customer master data is not stored repeatedly on each order but referenced by customer numbers that point to KNA1, KNVV, etc. Material numbers reference MARA, MVKE, and other material master tables. This keeps each table focused on one domain area and reduces redundancy. Indexes and performance: SAP creates numerous secondary indexes on key fields like document number, customer, material, and dates to accelerate queries such as open order lists or order history. On HANA systems, this is further optimized with columnar storage and in memory processing. Customization: Through configuration in SPRO, SAP allows customers to extend orders with additional fields using append structures or custom tables. These can be accessed in user exits or BAdIs and are often visible via transactions like VA01 VA02 for sales orders or ME21N for purchase orders.  Conceptually, an order in SAP is therefore a logical document that lives across multiple relational tables. The header table defines the core identity of the order, item tables define the detailed contents, and many satellite tables store pricing, schedules, texts, statuses, flows, and accounting information. When an end user opens an order in the GUI or Fiori app, SAP assembles and displays information pulled and joined from all these underlying tables instead of reading a single flat record.
7|30: In SAP ERP (particularly in the classic ECC SD/MM/FI setup), an order is not stored as one big record in a single table. Instead, SAP uses a highly normalized, document-oriented data model composed of several linked tables. Think of an order as a document header with multiple items, each of which can have its own conditions, schedules, texts, and follow-on documents.  For SD sales orders (customer orders), the core technical structure looks like this at a high level:  The header of the sales order is stored in table VBAK. There is exactly one VBAK record per sales order number (field VBELN). This record contains data that applies to the whole order, such as order type (AUART), sales organization (VKORG), distribution channel, division, sold-to party, document date, overall status fields, and various control flags. Conceptually, VBAK answers the question: What kind of order is this, and who is it for at the global level?  The individual line items are stored in table VBAP. There is one VBAP record per combination of order number (VBELN) and item number (POSNR). These records contain information specific to each item: material number (MATNR), order quantity (KWMENG), plant (WERKS), item category, pricing relevancy flags, item-level status, and references to preceding documents (for example, an inquiry or quotation). Together, VBAK and VBAP form the backbone of the SD order.  Around these two core tables, SAP uses a set of related tables to model all aspects of the order:  Schedule lines are stored in VBEP. Each line item can have one or more schedule lines (VBELN, POSNR, and schedule line number ETENR), which specify requested delivery dates, confirmed quantities, and availability check results. This is where SAP breaks down the item quantity over time.  Conditions (pricing, surcharges, discounts, taxes, freight, etc.) are stored in KONV in classic ECC. Each KONV entry is linked to the order via a document and item reference (for example KNUMV in the header, then VBELN and POSNR at item level depending on the release). KONV contains condition type (KSCHL), condition value, currency, scale information, and calculation details. In S/4HANA, pricing data is partly restructured and some views/tables are replaced, but the conceptual idea remains: pricing is stored separately from the basic order header/item.  Partners (sold-to, ship-to, bill-to, payer, and any additional partner functions) are stored in tables like VBPA for sales documents. VBPA entries are linked to the order via VBELN and optionally POSNR, and they include the partner role (PARVW) and the partner number (KUNNR, LIFNR, etc.). This enables multiple roles and multiple partners per document or per item.  Texts such as header and item texts are stored in the generic SAP text system rather than directly in VBAK or VBAP. Typically, they are stored in STXH (header) and STXL (lines) and referenced logically via text object, text ID, and key (often including VBELN/POSNR). The SD application retrieves these through standard text function modules, not by direct table access in normal business logic.  Status information is distributed across several tables. There are so-called status fields in VBAK and VBAP (overall status, delivery status, billing status, credit status, etc.), and more granular object statuses in JEST, JCDS when using the cross-application status management. This allows SAP to track whether an order is open, partially delivered, fully billed, technically completed, and so on, without changing the core structural design of the order tables.  Document flow is stored in table VBFA, which links preceding and subsequent documents: for example inquiry to quotation to sales order to delivery to billing document. VBFA entries contain the preceding document number and item, the succeeding document number and item, and the relationship category (like reference type). This is how SAP can show a complete document chain for an order.  From the MM (purchasing) side, purchase orders are structurally similar but use different tables. The purchase order header is in EKKO, and the line items are in EKPO. Conditions are in the MM condition tables (historically also KONV, with MM-specific keys), schedule lines in EKET, and text data in the same generic text infrastructure (STXH/STXL). As with SD, there are partner functions, account assignments, statuses, and history stored in additional tables such as EKKN (account assignment) and EKBE (PO history for goods receipts and invoice receipts).  Key technical principles about how SAP stores orders:  It is document-centric: Orders are documents with stable numbers (VBELN for SD, EBELN for POs) that act as primary keys linking many tables.  It is normalized: Instead of one wide record, SAP uses multiple tables for header, item, schedule, conditions, texts, partners, and document flow. This reduces redundancy and supports flexible configuration.  It is generic: The same basic concept and some of the same tables or frameworks (status, texts, conditions, document flow) are reused for many document types (orders, deliveries, billings, etc.), which is why the table designs can seem abstract or over-generic.  In S/4HANA, much of this remains conceptually the same, but the physical storage changes because the system uses the HANA in-memory database. Some classic transparent tables are replaced by compatibility views; some condition and status tables are optimized; and performance is improved by in-memory processing. However, the logical model for orders from an application perspective stays very close to the ECC structure: you still have header and item tables, schedule lines, conditions, partners, and document flow all linked via the order number.  So, when you say SAP stores an order, you can picture it as SAP creating one header record, several item records, and many related child records across multiple specialized tables, all tied together by the document number and item numbers. Business logic in ABAP (BAPIs, function modules, frameworks) handles reading and writing across these tables so end users see a single coherent order, while technically it is a network of linked database entries.
8|30: In classic SAP ERP (and largely in S/4HANA as well, just with some simplification), orders are stored using a header–item–schedule-line style data model spread across multiple related tables rather than one big order table. The exact set of tables depends on the order type: for example, sales orders use the VA* and VB* tables, purchase orders use the EKKO/EKPO set, and production orders use AUFK/AFKO/AFPO.  At a conceptual level, an order in SAP is split into several logical layers that are persisted in different tables and tied together by keys such as document number, item number, and client:  Header level: This contains information that applies to the entire order document, such as the customer or vendor, company code, sales organization or purchasing organization, document type, currency, overall status, and various dates. Technically, this is where the primary key for the order lives. For example, in SD (Sales and Distribution), the header is stored in VBAK, with field VBELN as the sales document number. In MM purchasing, the header is stored in EKKO, with field EBELN as the purchase order number. In CO/PP orders, AUFK contains the technical order header with order number AUFNR.  Item level: Each header can have multiple line items, each with its own material, quantity, pricing, account assignment, and status. These items are linked to the header by the document number and are uniquely identified by an item number. For sales orders, items live in VBAP, key fields VBELN (document) and POSNR (item). For purchase orders, items sit in EKPO with EBELN and EBELP. For production orders, AFPO stores item-level data and is linked to the order in AUFK/AFKO via AUFNR. An item inherits a lot of settings from the header, but can override or extend them.  Schedule lines and further detail: Orders often need more granular time and quantity planning than just header and item. SAP introduces schedule lines: each item can be split into multiple requested delivery dates and quantities. In SD, schedule lines are in VBEP, with key VBELN, POSNR, and ETENR (schedule line number). In purchasing, delivery schedule information is spread in tables like EKET. For manufacturing and internal orders, related detailed planning may live in specialized tables like AFVC (operations for orders) or AFVV (operation quantities and dates).  Status and administrative tracking: SAP does not only store what the order is, but also what has happened to it. Status data is tracked both at header and item level. There is a concept of overall status fields directly in tables (for example GBSTK, LFSTK, FAKSK-like fields in VBAK/VBAP for SD) and also entries in centralized status tables like JEST / JSTO for generic object statuses. These keep track of whether an order is open, partially delivered, fully invoiced, technically completed, etc. Change history is logged through change document tables (CDHDR and CDPOS), which record who changed what, when, for many business objects including orders.  Customizing and reference data: Many behaviors of orders do not sit directly on the order record itself but are inferred from customizing tables. For example, the meaning of a document type (like sales order type OR or purchase order type NB) is defined in configuration tables in the background (e.g., TVAK in SD for sales document types, T161 in MM for purchase document types). These tables tell the system which screens to show, which number ranges to use, which follow-on documents are allowed, and how pricing, delivery, and billing should behave. The order entries store only the document type code and other keys, while the logic comes from these customizing records.  Number ranges and technical keys: Every order document type is linked to a number range object, controlling how document numbers are assigned and guaranteed to be unique. These number ranges are stored in dedicated customizing tables (like NRIV). The actual orders then just carry the final generated number in the header table (VBELN, EBELN, AUFNR, etc.). Client field MANDT in nearly every table ensures that data is logically separated per client/tenant.  Relationships with other documents: Orders in SAP rarely live in isolation. SAP stores references between documents in specific fields, allowing it to build a document flow. For a sales order, the reference to a preceding quotation or contract may be stored at the item level (e.g., VBAP-VGBEL/VGPOS). In general, VBFA manages the document flow relationships in SD, linking predecessors and successors (order → delivery → invoice). In purchasing and logistics, similar reference fields and tables tie together purchase requisitions, purchase orders, goods receipts, and invoices.  Indexes and performance structures: Because these core order tables can become very large, SAP maintains many secondary index tables and database views that make searching faster. For example, tables like VAPMA/VAPVB for SD or specialized views in S/4HANA are used for reporting and selection. In S/4HANA, some of the old aggregate and index tables have been removed and replaced with on-the-fly views on the underlying line-item tables, but the logical structure from the application perspective still looks like header–item–schedule.  Module-specific flavors: Sales orders (SD): Header: VBAK, key VBELN Items: VBAP, key VBELN, POSNR Schedule lines: VBEP, key VBELN, POSNR, ETENR Document flow: VBFA Statuses: status fields in VBAK/VBAP plus JEST/JSTO for generic status objects Purchasing orders (MM): Header: EKKO, key EBELN Items: EKPO, key EBELN, EBELP Schedules: EKET History (goods receipts, invoices): EKBE Production / internal orders (PP/CO): Technical order header: AUFK, key AUFNR Production order header/additional: AFKO Items (for manufacturing orders): AFPO Operations: AFVC  Statuses: JEST/JSTO and status fields, plus various PP/CO tables  Storage in the database itself: Technically, SAP is an ABAP application server running on top of a relational database (Oracle, HANA, SQL Server, etc.). Each of the tables mentioned (VBAK, VBAP, EKKO, etc.) is a physical or logical table in that database. Classic systems stored all of this row-by-row; with HANA, columnar storage and in-memory processing are used under the hood, but to the ABAP layer the tables still look like relational tables. SAP defines these tables in the Data Dictionary (SE11), which controls their physical database representation. Keys, foreign keys, and indexes are defined there as well.  In summary, SAP stores orders as a network of related records: a single order is not one row but a combination of header, multiple items, potential schedule lines, status entries, document-flow records, and many customizing references. The main linking mechanism is the order number and item number across standardized header and item tables that are specific to the application area (sales, purchasing, production, controlling), but the underlying principle is always the same: normalized, modular tables that separate shared, header-wide information from per-line and per-schedule details, with extensive status and relationship tracking layered on top.
9|30: In classic SAP ERP (and in S/4HANA with some simplifications), customer orders are not stored as a single monolithic record, but as a set of related tables that together represent the order header, its items, and all associated details. The basic idea is always header → items → item details, with relational keys tying it all together.  For a standard SD sales order in SAP ERP:  The order header is stored primarily in table VBAK. Each row in VBAK represents one sales document (for example a sales order, quotation, contract) and is keyed by the sales document number, field VBELN. The header contains data that is common to the entire order, such as  Client (MANDT) Sales document number (VBELN) Document type (AUART) Sales organization, distribution channel, division Sold to party, ship to party, payer, bill to party (KUNNR and related partner fields) Order date, requested delivery date Overall status fields for the order Currency and pricing date  The order items are stored in table VBAP. Each row in VBAP represents one item (a position) of the sales document and is keyed by VBELN (document number) plus POSNR (item number). VBAP holds information specific to a line item, such as  Material number Ordered quantity Item category Plant, storage location Item status fields Item level pricing relevance, schedule line category, etc.  Each item can have multiple schedule lines representing how the quantity is split across delivery dates and sometimes locations. These are stored in VBEP, keyed by VBELN, POSNR, and ETENR (schedule line number). VBEP typically contains  Confirmed quantities Requested and confirmed delivery dates Availability check results  Pricing conditions that belong to the order (for example base price, discounts, surcharges, taxes) are typically in KONV in classic ECC. Each pricing condition line is linked to the document via fields such as KNUMV (pricing document number) and can further reference VBELN and POSNR. In S/4HANA, pricing data is partly restructured and exposed through new CDS views and different tables but the conceptual link remains the same: multiple condition lines are associated with each order item and sometimes header.  Partners and addresses for the order, beyond simple Sold to / Ship to fields in VBAK, are in table VBPA. VBPA is keyed by client, document number, item (possibly 000000 for header level), and partner function (for example AG for sold to, WE for ship to). This provides the flexible partner determination concept.  Texts maintained at header or item level (for example internal notes, customer facing order text) are typically stored generically in STXH and STXL or, in newer systems, in text cluster tables. The order references these via text object and ID, not by directly embedding the text in VBAK or VBAP.  On the logistics execution and billing side, follow on documents are stored similarly but in their own header and item tables. Outbound deliveries (linked to the order) are in LIKP (header) and LIPS (items), using the delivery number as key. Billing documents are in VBRK (header) and VBRP (items). Linkages between orders, deliveries, and invoices are captured via reference fields (for example VBRP-VGBEL and VGBEL/VGPOS type fields) and via document flow.  The document flow itself captures the lifecycle of an order from quotation to order to delivery to billing and potentially to accounting documents. This is stored in table VBFA in ECC. Each record in VBFA represents a relationship between a preceding and a subsequent document, keyed by the document numbers and item numbers, plus the category and flow type. This allows SAP to show the chain of related documents from any starting point.  From the database perspective, SAP uses a client field MANDT to separate tenants within the same physical database, so all these tables are typically client dependent. The primary keys combine the client with document number and line identifiers to ensure uniqueness.  In S/4HANA, the underlying data model is technically simplified and optimized for HANA, but the conceptual structure for orders is similar. Some historically separated tables are replaced or flattened, some are represented as compatibility views, and new ABAP CDS views sit on top to provide a more semantic model. From an application or reporting standpoint you still think in terms of header, item, schedule line, conditions, partner, and document flow.  For other types of orders in SAP, the same general pattern applies but with different specific tables  Purchase orders (MM module) are in EKKO for header and EKPO for items. Further details like account assignment are in EKKN, and delivery schedules in EKET. Production orders (PP) are stored in AUFK (order master) with operation level details in AFVC and confirmations in AFKO/AFRU and related tables. Maintenance orders (PM) also use AUFK and related structures, with PM specific enhancements.  In each of these, SAP separates  Order wide data in a header table Position specific data in an item or operation table Further detail in additional tables (schedule lines, account assignments, confirmations, conditions, texts, partners)  and glues everything together through well defined primary key and foreign key relationships along with reference fields for document chains. The application layer (ABAP programs, function modules, BAPIs, and OData services) then handles reading and writing across these multiple tables so that end users experience one coherent order object, even though it is physically distributed in the database.
10|30: In classic SAP ERP (and still conceptually in S/4HANA), orders are not stored as one big record but as a set of related tables that together represent the document. SAP follows a very normalized, modular design: there is usually a header table, one or more item tables, and various detail tables for conditions, schedules, texts, and status. The technical keys that tie everything together are document number fields and item numbers. In Sales and Distribution (SD), a sales order is stored mainly in table VBAK (header) and VBAP (items). VBAK holds data that applies to the whole order: sales document type, sales organization, customer numbers, overall dates, currency, overall status, and so on. Each record in VBAK is uniquely identified by the sales document number field VBELN. Items of the order are stored in VBAP. Every item line of an order is one entry in VBAP, also keyed by VBELN plus the item number field POSNR. VBAP holds material numbers, quantities, item categories, pricing-relevant flags, delivery plant, and other item-specific data. Around these core tables, SAP uses additional tables for specialized aspects. Pricing conditions for each item and for the header are stored in KONV (in S/4HANA this is partly replaced/virtualized, but the conceptual idea is the same). Delivery schedules and requested or confirmed dates are stored in VBEP, again keyed by the same document and item number, plus a schedule line number. Texts that users see attached to the order (e.g., header or item texts) are stored in the generic text tables STXH and STXL, which are linked logically to the order via object keys and text IDs. Status information is split into system and user status, often stored in VBUK and VBUP for SD documents; these tables hold status flags like whether the order is completely delivered, billed, or blocked. In Materials Management (MM), a purchase order is stored similarly with a header table EKKO and an item table EKPO. EKKO is keyed by EBELN, the purchase order number, and carries vendor, purchasing organization, document type, overall terms, and validity data. EKPO links each item via EBELN and item number EBELP and holds the material, plant, quantity, delivery date, and account assignment references. There are associated tables like EKET for schedule lines, EKKN for account assignments, and condition tables for pricing and freight. Internally, SAP applications never access the underlying database tables directly in business logic; they use ABAP function modules, BAPIs, or classes that encapsulate document creation, change, and read logic. When you create an order via VA01 or ME21N, these application layers validate data and then write consistent records into the multiple tables belonging to the document. Document numbers (VBELN, EBELN, etc.) are assigned via number range objects configured in customizing, ensuring uniqueness and often reflecting specific business or legal requirements. SAP also keeps a change history for many order types, using change document tables (for example CDHDR and CDPOS) where each modification to critical fields is logged with old and new values, time stamps, and user IDs. This allows audit trails without mixing history into the main transaction tables. In S/4HANA, technically the storage may use HANA column-store tables, views, and compatibility views, but the logical structure remains similar: a clear separation into header, item, schedule, condition, text, and status entities, all connected through consistent keys. So, SAP does not store an order as a single blob. Instead, it decomposes the document into multiple normalized tables, linked by document and item numbers, and manages them through consistent application logic, providing both flexibility for extensions and reliability for transactional processing.

1|33: Scavenging and improvising is usually cheaper than buying anything purpose-made. The absolute bottom-cost approach is to skip a traditional wooden or metal case entirely and just create a safe, powered frame for the modules. Use a free or scrap enclosure: an old drawer, a strong cardboard box, a shoe box lid, or a thrift-store briefcase or toolbox. Then source a pair of used or very cheap aluminum mounting rails or, cheaper still, make crude “rails” from straight wood strips or scrap metal angle stock drilled to accept M3 screws. Mount the modules directly into those strips; they do not have to be perfect as long as they are aligned enough for the mounting holes to catch. For power, instead of a dedicated Eurorack power supply and bus board, use a repurposed laptop brick or high-current 12V switching supply combined with a cheap DC-DC converter board that can generate +12V and -12V from a single brick (or use two bricks if necessary). Then make your own bus wiring: daisy-chain ribbon cable or, cheaper still, hand-wire flying leads with keyed IDC connectors or 10/16-pin headers to each module, carefully matching the polarity to avoid damage. Fasten everything to the inside of the scrap box with screws, zip ties, or even hot glue for strain relief so nothing moves or shorts. Keep the power supply fully enclosed and insulated; leave ventilation openings and keep mains wiring untouched or handled only in a fully enclosed off-the-shelf supply to avoid shock hazards. If you already own a multimeter and soldering iron, you can do this with mostly found materials plus only the absolutely necessary new parts: a cheap DC supply or laptop brick, a small DC-DC converter, a few connectors, some ribbon cable, and screws. This approach is ugly and not as durable as a proper case, but in terms of pure cost, a scavenged container, DIY rails from scrap, and a hacked-together low-voltage power system using surplus parts is about as cheap as it gets while still being functional and reasonably safe.
2|33: Use whatever you can get for free or nearly free and only spend on the things that absolutely must be proper: rails (or at least threaded strips) and a safe power supply. The cheapest practical route is usually scavenging and improvising. Start with an old wooden box, drawer, small bookshelf, or even scrap plywood or OSB someone is throwing away. If rails are still too expensive, you can mount modules directly into hardwood strips: pre drill holes spaced to match panel holes and use wood screws, knowing it will be less convenient but basically free.  For power, the absolute cheapest route that is still sane is a used or surplus Eurorack power module or flying bus system rather than designing a mains powered supply yourself. Use a decent external DC brick that provides the correct voltage and amperage, then feed that into a simple bus board or passive flying bus cables. Many people sell homemade or leftover bus boards cheaply; you can even use stripboard or perfboard to build one if you know what you are doing with low voltage wiring. Avoid wiring anything directly to mains if you are not experienced and do not try to build a barebones open frame mains PSU just to save a few dollars; the risk is not worth it.  Use basic hardware store parts for everything else: simple wood screws or small angle brackets to attach the rails, cheap handles from a discarded case or drawer, and leftover paint or no finish at all. Skip fancy sliding nuts, go for the cheapest threaded strips or bulk M3 nuts you can find. The case does not need to be pretty, just square and sturdy enough to hold modules without flexing.  In short, the cheapest approach is to salvage the enclosure completely, buy only the cheapest safe power option and mounting hardware, and accept that the result will be ugly, heavy, and not very portable. What you absolutely should not cheap out on is electrical safety: always use a reputable low voltage supply (ideally with an external wall wart or laptop style brick), a properly fused and protected power module or distribution board, and correct polarity cables so the only thing you are sacrificing is aesthetics and convenience, not your modules or your safety.
