4|33: The absolute cheapest way is to forget about buying anything marketed for Eurorack and instead treat it as a DIY woodwork and power project using generic parts. Use scrap wood, a cheap tool like a handsaw, and the lowest-cost power option that is still safe.  1. Frame and rails without rails Instead of buying metal rails, you can mount modules directly into a wooden frame:  – Find free or nearly free wood: old shelves, IKEA leftovers, discarded furniture, or pallets. Cut two side panels and two crossbars for each row. – Skip proper rails: measure 3U height (128.5 mm) and 84HP width (~427 mm) and mark drill points for your modules directly in the front crossbars. – Use cheap wood screws into the wood to hold modules. To avoid damaging module panels, you can use nylon washers or tiny pieces of rubber cut from an old bike tube under the screw heads. If you want threaded strips, you can use cheap M3 T-nuts hammered into the backside of the wood. – If you can find any kind of scrap aluminum angle or slotted rail at a metal recycler, you can upgrade and use that instead of wood as a pseudo-rail.  2. Power as cheaply as possible but safely Power is where many people overspend or under-think. The cheapest reasonably safe path is usually a used or surplus switching brick plus a DIY busboard.  – Use a surplus 12 V or 15 V DC laptop/LED strip power brick from a local thrift store, electronics recycler, or your own junk drawer. Many are a few dollars and are already certified and fused. – Build a simple linear regulator or DC-DC step converters for ±12 V from that brick if needed, or search for surplus dual-output bench-supply modules. If you only need +12 V modules at first, you can run with just a +12 V line and 0 V and add negative later. – Make a DIY busboard from stripboard or perfboard: run thick copper traces or wire for +12 V, -12 V, and 0 V; solder on cheap 10- or 16-pin right-angle headers. Use proper orientation markings and a fuse per rail if possible. – Use cheap ribbon cable and IDC connectors to make your own power ribbons. IDC plugs and flat cable bought in bulk are usually far cheaper than pre-made Eurorack cables.  3. Case structure from whatever is free – Build a simple open-back box. It does not need to be pretty: two side cheeks, a bottom, and a top lip. You can even screw the rails (or rail-substitutes) directly into an existing wooden crate, toolbox, or drawer. – People have successfully made cases out of:   – Old briefcases or attache cases   – Toolbox lids   – Wine crates and fruit boxes   – Broken guitar pedalboards – The cheapest approach is to start with a free or thrift-store box that is already close in size, then only add wood strips where you need to mount modules and power.  4. Hardware sourcing strategies – Avoid music stores and Eurorack-branded hardware until you absolutely must use them. – Get M3 or M2.5 screws from a general fastener store or online bulk supplier; they are far cheaper than anything sold as module screws. – Re-use old PC power supplies for their metal cases and sometimes the 12 V rail (though ATX supplies can be noisy and require a dummy load; still, the metal PSU enclosure itself is very handy for mounting a DIY supply safely). – Ask local makerspaces, schools, or repair shops for scrap parts. Aluminum angle, old rack rails, and bus wire are often free.  5. Ultra-barebones workflow – Start with one row only: a 3U, 84HP strip of wood with modules screwed to it, powered by a single laptop brick and a perfboard busboard, all bolted into a free wooden crate. – Leave the back open, run wiring visibly, and do not worry about cosmetics. As long as power is correctly wired (red stripe to -12 V, good strain relief, no exposed mains wiring), it is completely usable. – Upgrade only when necessary: swap the wood rails for proper rails once you can afford them, replace a noisy DC-DC converter later, add a lid only once you start traveling.  6. Safety notes (do not cheap out here) – Never expose mains AC wiring. If you need to rectify mains yourself, buy an enclosed, certified PSU module and mount it so nobody can touch the AC terminals. If that is too much cost, stick with external power bricks that keep mains out of the case. – Add inline fuses or resettable polyfuses on each rail between the PSU and your busboard. – Double-check polarity on every module connector before powering up; one reversed ribbon can cost more than your entire DIY case.  In practice, the lowest-cost builds many people manage are: – Free or scrap wood box – Salvaged rails or just wood strips as rails – Used laptop brick plus DIY busboard on perfboard – Bulk screws and IDC connectors  That can get you a working Eurorack case for almost no money beyond a soldering iron, some wire, and a bit of time, with the main expense being whatever minimal, safe power solution you choose.

1|34: Italy is generally safe, but there are some practical security concerns to keep in mind. The most common problem is petty crime, especially in crowded tourist areas, on public transportation, and around major train stations like Roma Termini, Milano Centrale, and Napoli Centrale. Pickpockets and bag snatchers work in teams and often use distraction tactics, like bumping into you, asking for signatures or directions, or staging minor commotions. Keep valuables out of back pockets, use a money belt or inside pockets for passports and most cash, and carry bags in front of you with closures zipped and a hand on them in crowds. Be cautious of people trying to help with luggage, ticket machines, or ATMs if they seem overly insistent, and avoid leaving bags hanging on the back of chairs at outdoor cafes.  There are also common tourist scams. You might encounter people offering friendship bracelets, roses, or trinkets and then aggressively demanding payment once you accept. Others may pose as officials checking tickets, or taxi drivers may overcharge by not using the meter or taking long routes from airports and train stations. To reduce risk, only use licensed taxis from official ranks or reputable ride apps where available, confirm prices before getting in if no meter is used, and buy tickets from official counters, machines, or verified websites. Be careful at ATMs attached to busy tourist sites; use those in banks when possible and shield your PIN.  Personal safety is usually not a major issue, but situational awareness still matters, especially at night. In large cities, certain neighborhoods around main stations can feel rough after dark with more aggressive touts or intoxicated people. Stick to well lit, busier streets, and consider taking a taxi or rideshare rather than walking alone late at night in unfamiliar areas. Violent crime against tourists is rare, but harassment can occur, particularly for women traveling alone, ranging from catcalls to unwanted attention. Setting firm boundaries, staying in populated areas, and trusting your instincts about leaving a bar, club, or group is important.  Other security related concerns are more about safety than crime. Road safety can be an issue; driving styles may seem aggressive, scooters weave through traffic, and in cities like Rome or Naples pedestrians do not always have clear right of way in practice. Use marked crossings but also watch drivers, and be very cautious if renting a car, especially on narrow rural roads or coastal routes. On beaches and in popular nightlife areas, keep an eye on your drink to avoid tampering, and do not leave valuables unattended on the sand. For accommodation, use hotel safes for passports and extra cash, lock doors and windows, and avoid letting unknown people follow you into buildings.
