1|35: In Rust, Arc from the standard library is a carefully engineered atomic reference-counted pointer. Building a custom Arc-like type is mostly an educational exercise, because the real Arc is highly optimized and subtle, but you can approximate its behavior with a few core ideas: a heap-allocated inner structure, an atomic reference count, and safe interfaces that follow Rust’s ownership rules.  High-level idea  You want a type, say MyArc<T>, that  Holds a pointer to some shared heap allocation containing both T and a reference count  Increments the count when cloned  Decrements the count when dropped, and frees the allocation when the count reaches zero  Uses atomic operations so multiple threads can safely clone and drop it concurrently  Basic layout  You usually separate the inner allocation from the smart pointer wrapper. A common pattern is an inner struct, often called Inner<T> or ArcInner<T>:  struct Inner<T> {     ref_count: std::sync::atomic::AtomicUsize,     value: T, }  Then your smart pointer stores a non-owning pointer to Inner<T>:  pub struct MyArc<T> {     ptr: *const Inner<T>, }  You cannot store Inner<T> directly by value inside MyArc because then each MyArc would have its own ref_count and value. Instead you put Inner<T> on the heap and share a pointer.  Creating a new instance  The constructor takes ownership of a T and allocates an Inner<T> on the heap. Box is the simplest way to allocate:  impl<T> MyArc<T> {     pub fn new(value: T) -> MyArc<T> {         let inner = Box::new(Inner {             ref_count: std::sync::atomic::AtomicUsize::new(1),             value,         });          let ptr = Box::into_raw(inner);          MyArc { ptr }     } }  At this point we have exactly one MyArc, so the reference count is initialized to 1.  Cloning  Clone must create a new MyArc pointing to the same Inner<T> and increment the ref_count atomically. To do this safely, you use atomic fetch_add with Ordering::Relaxed or a stronger ordering depending on your requirements. A simplified version might be  impl<T> Clone for MyArc<T> {     fn clone(&self) -> MyArc<T> {         unsafe {             let inner = &*self.ptr;             inner.ref_count.fetch_add(1, std::sync::atomic::Ordering::Relaxed);         }          MyArc { ptr: self.ptr }     } }  The unsafe block is required because we are dereferencing a raw pointer. The design invariant is that self.ptr must always point to a valid Inner<T> as long as there is at least one MyArc alive.  Dropping and deallocation  Drop must decrement the reference count and, if it reaches zero, deallocate Inner<T> and run T’s destructor. The core logic is  impl<T> Drop for MyArc<T> {     fn drop(&mut self) {         unsafe {             let inner = &*self.ptr;              if inner.ref_count.fetch_sub(1, std::sync::atomic::Ordering::Release) == 1 {                 std::sync::atomic::fence(std::sync::atomic::Ordering::Acquire);                 drop(Box::from_raw(self.ptr as *mut Inner<T>));             }         }     } }  There are two important details here  We use fetch_sub to decrement, and check if the previous value was 1. If so, this MyArc is the last owner, so we must free the allocation.  We use Release on decrement and Acquire fence on deallocation to ensure memory ordering is correct: this matches a common pattern in lock-free reference counting.  Accessing the inner value  Arc<T> implements Deref<Target = T> so users can treat it like &T. You can do the same  impl<T> std::ops::Deref for MyArc<T> {     type Target = T;      fn deref(&self) -> &T {         unsafe { &(*self.ptr).value }     } }  This is safe because  As long as a MyArc exists, the Inner<T> is kept alive by the reference count.  Deref only gives shared references &T, and MyArc is Send + Sync only if T meets appropriate bounds. For a minimal version you can skip those trait impls or mirror what std::sync::Arc does more carefully.  Thread safety and trait bounds  The whole reason to use atomics is to allow multiple threads to share a MyArc<T>. To be fully correct, you need to implement Send and Sync similarly to std::sync::Arc  MyArc<T> is Send if T is Send + Sync  MyArc<T> is Sync if T is Sync  That generally requires unsafe impl blocks with where bounds, because the compiler cannot infer them automatically from raw pointers  unsafe impl<T: Send + Sync> Send for MyArc<T> {} unsafe impl<T: Send + Sync> Sync for MyArc<T> {}  You should be sure this is correct based on how MyArc is used. It mirrors std’s guarantees  MyArc<T> is safe to share between threads as long as all access to the shared T happens through shared references and T itself is safe to be shared.  Pitfalls  Memory ordering  The exact memory orderings used in Arc are subtle. For educational use, you can copy what the standard library does Release on decrement, Acquire or AcqRel on increment as needed, plus fences when the count hits zero. Using Relaxed everywhere is often incorrect for a general shared-ownership type.  Double free or leaks  You must ensure that Box::from_raw is called exactly once for each Box::into_raw. That only happens when the count drops from 1 to 0.  Any bug in the reference counting can lead to use-after-free or leaks.  Raw pointers and unsafe blocks  Because you store a raw pointer, a lot of the implementation uses unsafe. You must maintain an internal invariant that ptr always points to a valid, properly initialized Inner<T> while count > 0.  No mutable access  Like Arc<T>, your MyArc<T> should not give out &mut T from shared owners because that would break aliasing rules. If you want mutation, you need interior mutability types like Mutex<T> or RwLock<T> around T.  Why you usually should not roll your own in production  The real Arc in std or in Arc-based crates has years of optimization and subtle correctness work behind it, including  Careful layout for cache efficiency and alignment  Optimized atomics  Weak references (Arc::downgrade and Weak<T>)  Support for unsized types  Edge-case handling around panics and partial initialization  So in production, you almost always use std::sync::Arc instead of a custom implementation. But building a toy MyArc is a great exercise to understand  How ownership and lifetimes can be modeled manually  How atomic reference counting works  Why unsafe is necessary under the hood of many safe abstractions  Summary outline of a minimal custom Arc  Define an Inner<T> with AtomicUsize ref_count and value: T  MyArc<T> stores *const Inner<T>  new allocates Box<Inner<T>>, sets ref_count to 1, converts Box into raw pointer  Clone increments ref_count atomically and returns another MyArc pointing at the same ptr  Drop decrements ref_count atomically, and if it hits zero, converts ptr back into Box and drops it  Implement Deref to get &T from MyArc<T>  Optionally implement Send and Sync safely based on T’s bounds  If you implement exactly that, you will have a simple but working custom Arc-like type in Rust.
2|35: In Rust, Arc from the standard library is already highly optimized and very subtle, so building your own custom Arc is mostly a learning exercise or something you do to add special behavior, like custom allocation, inline metadata, or debugging hooks. Conceptually, Arc is just three pieces: a heap allocation that stores a reference count plus the actual data; a way to atomically adjust the count when cloning and dropping; and a way to deallocate the allocation only when the last owner goes away.  At a high level, a custom Arc-like type looks like this in spirit  struct MyArcInner<T> {     refcount: AtomicUsize,     value: T, }  struct MyArc<T> {     ptr: NonNull<MyArcInner<T>>,     marker: PhantomData<MyArcInner<T>>,  // for drop checking and variance }  You allocate MyArcInner on the heap when you create a new MyArc, set the refcount to 1, and then store the raw pointer in MyArc. When you clone the MyArc, you atomically increment the refcount; when you drop a MyArc, you atomically decrement, and if it hits zero, you drop T and free the allocation. The tricky parts are all around safety, atomic ordering, and layout.  Here is a simplified outline using only core ideas and avoiding unsafe details as much as possible conceptually. In actual code, unsafe is required, but this is the structure you would follow  1. Data layout  You need a single heap block that contains both the refcount and the value T. This is important because you only want one refcount per allocation, not one per Arc handle.  struct ArcInner<T> {     refcount: AtomicUsize,     data: T, }  2. Creating a new Arc  The new function will allocate ArcInner<T> on the heap, initialize the refcount to 1, and wrap a raw pointer to it in your Arc  impl<T> MyArc<T> {     pub fn new(value: T) -> MyArc<T> {         // Allocate ArcInner with Box         let inner = Box::new(ArcInner {             refcount: AtomicUsize::new(1),             data: value,         });          // Turn Box into a raw pointer (Box guarantees non null)         let ptr = Box::into_raw(inner);          MyArc {             ptr: unsafe { NonNull::new_unchecked(ptr) },             marker: PhantomData,         }     } }  3. Cloning  Clone should bump the refcount and then return a new MyArc pointing at the same allocation. Because multiple threads might do this concurrently, you use atomics.  impl<T> Clone for MyArc<T> {     fn clone(&self) -> Self {         let inner = unsafe { self.ptr.as_ref() };         // Relaxed can be enough for pure reference counting;         // std uses more conservative orderings for soundness in all cases         inner.refcount.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed);          MyArc {             ptr: self.ptr,             marker: PhantomData,         }     } }  4. Dropping  Drop does the opposite of clone: decrement refcount, and if it reaches zero, deallocate the ArcInner. This is where you must be very careful to avoid double frees or use after free.  impl<T> Drop for MyArc<T> {     fn drop(&mut self) {         let inner = unsafe { self.ptr.as_ref() };         if inner.refcount.fetch_sub(1, Ordering::Release) == 1 {             // This was the last reference             // Acquire fence to synchronize with prior writes             fence(Ordering::Acquire);              unsafe {                 // Recreate Box to take back ownership and drop it                 Box::from_raw(self.ptr.as_ptr());             }         }     } }  The pattern fetch_sub with Release followed by fence Acquire (or an Acquire in fetch_sub on the last decrement) is about ensuring all prior writes to T are visible to the last thread that drops it. The standard library uses a similar pattern.  5. Accessing the inner value  You want MyArc to deref to T similarly to Arc. That is done by implementing Deref  impl<T> Deref for MyArc<T> {     type Target = T;      fn deref(&self) -> &Self::Target {         unsafe { &self.ptr.as_ref().data }     } }  You can add DerefMut only if you can guarantee uniqueness, which typical Arc cannot, so usually it is not provided except through special wrappers like Arc<Mutex<T>>.  6. Safety considerations  Because you are using raw pointers and manual memory management, the implementation relies on unsafe blocks. To make it sound you must ensure  The allocation is created exactly once and freed exactly once. The pointer never outlives the underlying allocation. No data race occurs when reading or writing the refcount. The layout of ArcInner<T> is stable and you do not move it after allocation. You never mutate data through multiple concurrent shared references unless it is synchronized internally.  The atomics guarantee that increments and decrements to the refcount are thread safe. Using NonNull is a good way to express non null raw pointers, and PhantomData helps Rust understand ownership and drop semantics.  7. Optional enhancements  Once you have the basic skeleton, you can extend it for various purposes  A weak pointer type similar to std::sync::Weak, which holds a non owning reference to the allocation and only lets you upgrade to MyArc if strong refcount is nonzero. This requires tracking two counters: strong and weak. Custom deallocation strategies or custom allocators, by using GlobalAlloc, allocator APIs, or external crates. Inline metadata such as type ids, reference id numbers for debugging, or extra state used by your program. Reference counted handles for FFI objects, where you need to call some external release function instead of simply dropping with Box.  8. Why not roll your own in production  The standard Arc is battle tested, correct in edge cases, and uses careful memory orderings that have been reviewed extensively. Rolling a custom Arc is easy to get mostly right but hard to get perfectly right, especially with weak references, cross thread interactions, and panic safety.  In practice, you generally do one of these  Use std::sync::Arc directly. Wrap Arc in a newtype if you want to add methods or invariants while still delegating memory management to Arc. Use existing crates that already offer variations, such as intrusive or arena backed reference counting.  But as an educational exercise, building a small Arc clone is excellent for learning unsafe, atomics, and ownership at a low level. The key ideas are single shared heap allocation, atomic reference counting, careful drop semantics, and enforcing that all user facing operations remain safe even though the internals use unsafe.
3|35: In Rust, Arc from std::sync::Arc is a thread-safe, atomically reference-counted smart pointer. Building a custom Arc-like type is mainly an exercise in understanding three pieces: reference counting, allocation/layout, and memory ordering/thread-safety. Below is a conceptual explanation and a sketch of how you might build one. This is advanced unsafe Rust, so it is mostly for learning; in real code you should almost always use Arc.  High-level idea  You want a type, say MyArc<T>, that  Holds a pointer to heap-allocated storage containing T and a reference count Increments the count when you clone it Decrements the count when it is dropped Destroys T and frees memory when the count reaches zero Is Send + Sync if T is Send + Sync, with atomic refcount operations  Overall memory layout  A simple layout is a separate heap allocation that stores both metadata (the refcount) and the value T:  struct Inner<T> {     refcount: AtomicUsize,     value: T, }  Then MyArc<T> just stores a non-null pointer to Inner<T>:  pub struct MyArc<T> {     ptr: NonNull<Inner<T>>,     // PhantomData<T> not strictly necessary with NonNull<Inner<T>>, but often kept }  Because MyArc only holds a pointer to existing allocated memory, cloning is cheap; you just bump the refcount.  Creating a new MyArc  When you construct a new MyArc, you  Allocate space for Inner<T> Construct Inner<T> with refcount set to 1 and value set to T Store its pointer in MyArc  Example sketch:  impl<T> MyArc<T> {     pub fn new(value: T) -> MyArc<T> {         let boxed = Box::new(Inner {             refcount: AtomicUsize::new(1),             value,         });          // Convert Box to raw pointer; Box ensures it is non-null         let ptr = unsafe { NonNull::new_unchecked(Box::into_raw(boxed)) };         MyArc { ptr }     } }  Cloning: increment refcount  Cloning must use an atomic increment so that thread races are safe. A simple implementation is  impl<T> Clone for MyArc<T> {     fn clone(&self) -> Self {         let inner = unsafe { self.ptr.as_ref() };         let old = inner.refcount.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed);         // Optionally, you can add debug assertions about overflow         MyArc { ptr: self.ptr }     } }  Ordering::Relaxed is usually enough for reference counting itself, as Arc uses more nuanced orderings internally for full correctness guarantees across operations. For a learning implementation, this is a reasonable simplification, but for production you need to read the Arc documentation and related RFCs to copy its semantics.  Dropping: decrement and free  When MyArc is dropped, you need to  Atomically decrement the refcount If the new count is zero, deallocate the Inner<T> and run T s destructor  Implementation sketch  impl<T> Drop for MyArc<T> {     fn drop(&mut self) {         // Safety: ptr is always valid as long as refcount > 0         let inner = unsafe { self.ptr.as_ref() };          if inner.refcount.fetch_sub(1, Ordering::Release) == 1 {             // This was the last reference             // Acquire fence to ensure all other writes are visible before we drop T             std::sync::atomic::fence(Ordering::Acquire);              unsafe {                 // Reconstruct Box so Rust can drop value and free memory                 let _boxed: Box<Inner<T>> = Box::from_raw(self.ptr.as_ptr());                 // _boxed is dropped here, running T s Drop and freeing memory             }         }     } }  The Release/Acquire pair is what Arc uses to synchronize destruction with other threads that may still be accessing the data before their last reference goes away.  Accessing the inner value  You want to access &T from &MyArc<T> and possibly &mut T from &mut MyArc<T> (though mutable access is tricky for a shared type).  impl<T> std::ops::Deref for MyArc<T> {     type Target = T;      fn deref(&self) -> &T {         // Safety: as_ref returns a shared reference to Inner<T> that outlives self         let inner = unsafe { self.ptr.as_ref() };         &inner.value     } }  Because MyArc shares ownership, you generally only provide immutable access (just like Arc). Interior mutability (e.g., via Mutex<T> or RwLock<T>) is how you usually handle mutation.  Thread-safety bounds  You must choose under what conditions MyArc<T> is Send and Sync. Arc uses  impl<T: Send + Sync> Send for Arc<T> {} impl<T: Send + Sync> Sync for Arc<T> {}  You can adopt the same constraints with unsafe impls, because you are promising that your implementation behaves like a proper atomic ref-counted pointer.  unsafe impl<T: Send + Sync> Send for MyArc<T> {} unsafe impl<T: Send + Sync> Sync for MyArc<T> {}  Any mistake in reference-counting or memory ordering can cause use-after-free, double-free, or data races, so these unsafe impls are only valid if your logic is correct.  Why using Arc is preferred  Arc in the standard library is heavily optimized, battle-tested, and correctly handles a lot of subtle memory ordering details. It also  Supports weak references via Weak<T>, preventing certain kinds of cycles Uses an optimized layout and carefully chosen atomics Has many small design details like partial equality, downcasting, etc.  If you need custom behavior (like a different allocation strategy, custom deallocation hooks, arena allocation, etc.), you might wrap Arc rather than reimplement it.  Common educational variations  Custom non-thread-safe Rc: use Cell<usize> or plain usize instead of Atomics, and constrain it to !Send and !Sync. This is much simpler and a great first step.  Refcount-only struct: store a refcount separate from the data, to understand aliasing and lifetimes first.  Feature-limited Arc: implement only new, clone, drop, and Deref for a minimal Arc to focus on refcount logic.  Summary steps  Define an Inner<T> with AtomicUsize refcount and T value Allocate Inner<T> on the heap and store a raw pointer in MyArc<T> On new: create Inner with refcount = 1 On clone: use fetch_add to increment the refcount On drop: use fetch_sub; if it hits 1 to 0, fence and then Box::from_raw to drop T and free Implement Deref to access &T Use unsafe impl Send/Sync only with appropriate T bounds  If you want, I can walk through a complete minimal implementation with all code in one block and some tests showing it behaves like Arc.
4|35: In Rust, Arc from std::sync is already a carefully engineered atomic reference-counted pointer, but exploring how to build a simplified custom Arc is a good way to understand ownership, reference counting, and concurrency. Below is a conceptual explanation of how you might design one, step by step, without trying to fully re-implement all the unsafe subtleties in the standard library.  At a high level, an Arc does two things  It owns some heap-allocated data of type T It maintains a shared reference count in an atomic integer so that multiple threads can hold cloned Arcs to the same data safely  When the last Arc is dropped, it deallocates both the data and the refcount structure.  Core data layout  A simple design is to allocate a single heap block that contains both the reference count and the T value. Conceptually  struct Inner<T> {     refcount: AtomicUsize,     data: T, }  Your custom Arc will be a thin pointer to this Inner<T> on the heap. For example  struct MyArc<T> {     ptr: *const Inner<T>, }  We use a raw pointer because we need manual control over allocation and deallocation. The public API will expose only shared borrows to T, such as ampersand T, to enforce thread-safe shared access.  Creating a new instance  The new function should allocate an Inner<T> on the heap, set the reference count to 1, and store the pointer.  impl<T> MyArc<T> {     pub fn new(value: T) -> MyArc<T> {         let inner = Box::new(Inner {             refcount: AtomicUsize::new(1),             data: value,         });         let ptr = Box::into_raw(inner);         MyArc { ptr }     } }  At this point, there is exactly one owner of the data, and the reference count is 1.  Cloning and reference counting  The key behavior of Arc is that cloning it does not clone the underlying data T, but instead increments the shared refcount. Implementing Clone requires an atomic increment on refcount, because different threads might be cloning or dropping at the same time.  impl<T> Clone for MyArc<T> {     fn clone(&self) -> Self {         unsafe {             let inner = ampersand *self.ptr;             inner.refcount.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed);         }         MyArc { ptr: self.ptr }     } }  Here we use fetch_add on AtomicUsize. In a production-quality Arc, more careful memory orderings are chosen for correctness and performance; for learning, Relaxed can illustrate the basic pattern, though for real concurrent use you would want at least Acquire or Release semantics on some operations.  Dropping and deallocation  When an Arc instance is dropped, we need to decrement the refcount, and if it hits zero, free the heap allocation and drop T. That logic lives in Drop.  impl<T> Drop for MyArc<T> {     fn drop(&mut self) {         unsafe {             let inner = ampersand *self.ptr;             if inner.refcount.fetch_sub(1, Ordering::Release) == 1 {                 std::sync::atomic::fence(Ordering::Acquire);                 drop(Box::from_raw(self.ptr as *mut Inner<T>));             }         }     } }  The typical pattern for a correct Arc is fetch_sub with Release ordering, followed by an Acquire fence when the count reaches zero. This ensures that all writes to data are visible to the final drop. The Box::from_raw reconstructs the Box so that Rust will handle dropping T and freeing the memory.  Accessing the inner data  To let users read the inner value, implement Deref so ampersand MyArc<T> coerces to ampersand T  impl<T> std::ops::Deref for MyArc<T> {     type Target = T;      fn deref(&self) -> ampersand T {         unsafe {             ampersand (*self.ptr).data         }     } }  This provides shared read-only access to the underlying data. If T is Sync, then ampersand T is safe to share across threads.  Thread safety  To behave like std::sync::Arc, your custom type must be Send and Sync when T is Send and Sync appropriately. Typically  unsafe impl<T: Send + Sync> Sync for MyArc<T> {} unsafe impl<T: Send + Sync> Send for MyArc<T> {}  These unsafe impls say that MyArc<T> may be sent to and shared across threads when T itself is safe to do so.  Subtleties and caveats  This design omits many details that the standard Arc handles carefully  Memory ordering subtleties on the reference count to ensure correctness on all platforms Support for weak references ArcWeak that do not keep the data alive but can be upgraded to Arc if the data still exists Layout optimizations and niche optimizations Pinning, downcasting, and integration with other standard traits and APIs Handling unsized types like dyn Trait Interior mutability patterns, where the data itself can be mutated safely across threads using Mutex, RwLock, or Atomic types  As a learning exercise, your MyArc should be considered experimental and not used as a drop-in replacement for std::sync::Arc in production. But building it forces you to understand  How Box::new and Box::into_raw and Box::from_raw manage heap memory Why raw pointers and unsafe blocks are needed when you step outside Rusts automatic lifetime management How AtomicUsize and memory orderings synchronize operations between threads How Drop and Clone interact with manually managed resources  Putting it together, a minimal custom Arc is  use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicUsize, Ordering}; use std::ops::Deref;  struct Inner<T> {     refcount: AtomicUsize,     data: T, }  pub struct MyArc<T> {     ptr: *const Inner<T>, }  impl<T> MyArc<T> {     pub fn new(value: T) -> MyArc<T> {         let inner = Box::new(Inner {             refcount: AtomicUsize::new(1),             data: value,         });         let ptr = Box::into_raw(inner);         MyArc { ptr }     } }  impl<T> Clone for MyArc<T> {     fn clone(&self) -> Self {         unsafe {             let inner = ampersand *self.ptr;             inner.refcount.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed);         }         MyArc { ptr: self.ptr }     } }  impl<T> Deref for MyArc<T> {     type Target = T;      fn deref(&self) -> ampersand T {         unsafe { ampersand (*self.ptr).data }     } }  impl<T> Drop for MyArc<T> {     fn drop(&mut self) {         unsafe {             let inner = ampersand *self.ptr;             if inner.refcount.fetch_sub(1, Ordering::Release) == 1 {                 std::sync::atomic::fence(Ordering::Acquire);                 drop(Box::from_raw(self.ptr as *mut Inner<T>));             }         }     } }  unsafe impl<T: Send + Sync> Send for MyArc<T> {} unsafe impl<T: Send + Sync> Sync for MyArc<T> {}  In practice, you should prefer std::sync::Arc, but understanding a skeleton like this explains how Arc works under the hood and how Rust enables shared ownership with thread safety while still avoiding data races through its type system and atomics.
5|35: In Rust, Arc is a thread safe reference counted smart pointer that lets multiple owners share the same heap allocated value. Building a custom Arc like type yourself is a good way to understand how Arc works internally, but it is also easy to get wrong and cause undefined behavior. So it is usually done as a learning exercise, not for production, unless you really know what you are doing.  At a high level, an Arc like type needs three ingredients:  1. A heap allocation that stores both the reference count and the value being shared 2. Atomic operations to increment and decrement the count safely across threads 3. Correct memory ordering and destructor logic so that the value is dropped exactly once when the last handle goes away  A minimal design looks like this conceptually  You define an inner struct that lives on the heap and contains the refcount and the data. This is usually something like  struct ArcInner<T> {     refcount: AtomicUsize,     data: T, }  Then your user facing type is essentially a pointer to that inner allocation  pub struct MyArc<T> {     ptr: NonNull<ArcInner<T>>,     marker: PhantomData<ArcInner<T>>, }  You use NonNull so that your type is covariant and so that Option<MyArc<T>> can use the Null pointer optimization. PhantomData is needed to tell the compiler about the ownership and variance of T.  Creating a new instance allocates ArcInner on the heap, initializes the atomic counter to 1, and stores the pointer in MyArc  impl<T> MyArc<T> {     pub fn new(value: T) -> MyArc<T> {         let inner = Box::new(ArcInner {             refcount: AtomicUsize::new(1),             data: value,         });         let ptr = NonNull::from(Box::leak(inner));         MyArc { ptr, marker: PhantomData }     } }  The leak is used so that Box does not automatically free the memory; you are going to free it manually when the refcount hits zero.  Cloning the MyArc increments the refcount atomically and returns a new MyArc pointing to the same inner allocation  impl<T> Clone for MyArc<T> {     fn clone(&self) -> Self {         let inner = unsafe { self.ptr.as_ref() };         let old = inner.refcount.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed);         // If old was 0 here, it would be a use after free bug. In a correct design, this should not happen.         MyArc { ptr: self.ptr, marker: PhantomData }     } }  Dropping a MyArc decrements the refcount. If the count reaches zero, you drop T and free the inner allocation  impl<T> Drop for MyArc<T> {     fn drop(&mut self) {         let inner = unsafe { self.ptr.as_ref() };         if inner.refcount.fetch_sub(1, Ordering::Release) == 1 {             // This thread is the last owner, so we must synchronize with other threads             std::sync::atomic::fence(Ordering::Acquire);             unsafe {                 // Rebuild a Box so Rust can drop T and free the memory                 let _ = Box::from_raw(self.ptr.as_ptr());             }         }     } }  The subtle part here is the memory ordering. The standard library Arc uses Release on decrement and Acquire fence before dropping, so all writes to the data done by any thread that held an Arc before the last one is dropped become visible before the destructor runs. Using Relaxed everywhere would compile but might break the memory model.  Access to the inner data is usually given via Deref, so you can use MyArc<T> like a regular shared reference  impl<T> std::ops::Deref for MyArc<T> {     type Target = T;     fn deref(&self) -> &T {         unsafe { &self.ptr.as_ref().data }     } }  This is safe because Arc is immutable by default; only shared references are exposed. If you want to allow mutation, you need interior mutability, such as putting a Mutex<T> or RwLock<T> inside.  You also need to think about Send and Sync. The type should be Send if T is Send and Sync if T is Send and Sync in a typical Arc like design. A simple way is  unsafe impl<T: Send + Sync> Send for MyArc<T> {} unsafe impl<T: Send + Sync> Sync for MyArc<T> {}  Unsafe here is required because you are promising the compiler the thread safety properties of your type; the compiler cannot derive them automatically since you are using raw pointers and unsafe code.  A few important caveats and possible bugs to watch out for when writing a custom Arc  If you ever decrement the refcount below zero or increment after it has hit zero, you have a use after free bug. If you use incorrect memory ordering, you may see data races or subtle visibility issues across threads. If you call Box::from_raw with a pointer that did not originate from Box::into_raw, you will double free or corrupt the allocator. If you forget PhantomData, your type might have incorrect variance or drop semantics.  The real std::sync::Arc type is more complex. It handles weak references via a separate weak refcount, supports downcasting to unique when the count is 1 in some operations, has optimizations for unsized types, and is tuned for performance and correctness in highly concurrent workloads. It also uses carefully chosen orderings and layout tricks.  If your goal is to learn, you can  Search for How Arc is implemented in Rust and read blog posts or educational crates that implement a mini Arc. Look at the Rust standard library source code for Arc in library core or alloc. The real implementation is heavily commented and uses some tricks but follows the same core idea. Try writing a simplified version that only works in single threaded code first by using a non atomic usize and then upgrade to AtomicUsize.  If your goal is production code, you almost certainly want to use std::sync::Arc or a crate like arc swap instead of rolling your own, because it is extremely easy to introduce subtle undefined behavior. Using the standard type gives you battle tested correctness and good performance while still matching the mental model you developed by understanding the custom implementation.
6|35: In Rust, Arc from the standard library is a thread-safe reference-counted pointer with atomic operations. Recreating a simplified custom Arc is a good way to understand how it works internally. Conceptually, there are three main pieces: a heap-allocated inner structure that holds the value and the reference count, a pointer type that points to that inner structure, and implementations of Clone and Drop that manipulate the reference count correctly.  First, you define the heap-allocated inner structure. It needs to store both the reference count and the value T. You want the reference count to be an atomic integer so multiple threads can safely increment and decrement it.  For example, conceptually:  struct ArcInner<T> {     ref_count: AtomicUsize,     value: T, }  Then you define your public Arc type as a thin pointer wrapper around ArcInner<T>:  pub struct MyArc<T> {     ptr: *mut ArcInner<T>, }  You usually construct it via a new function that allocates ArcInner<T> on the heap and initializes its ref_count to 1. Box::new allocates on the heap, and Box::into_raw turns it into a raw pointer, which you store in MyArc.  The core logic is in Clone and Drop. In Clone, you want to increase the reference count. Because multiple threads may clone the same MyArc at the same time, you must use atomic operations. The general pattern is to use fetch_add on the AtomicUsize with Ordering::Relaxed or similar (standard Arc uses more careful ordering for correctness guarantees). The cloned MyArc just copies the pointer and increments the count.  In Drop, you want to decrease the reference count and, if it hits zero, deallocate the inner allocation and drop T. You again use an atomic fetch_sub to get the previous count; if the previous count was 1, you are the last owner and should free the memory. You turn the raw pointer back into a Box and let it drop, which drops value and deallocates the heap.  You also need to implement Deref so that MyArc<T> behaves like &T when used. Deref should take &self and return &T by taking the pointer, dereferencing it to ArcInner<T>, and returning a reference to its value field.  Safety is the tricky part. You use raw pointers inside MyArc, but the public API should be safe. All unsafe code is contained in new, Deref, Clone, and Drop where you convert between raw pointers and references or Boxes. You must ensure that the refcount logic is correct to avoid double frees or leaks. That means never decrementing below zero, never using a freed pointer, and ensuring that once refcount is zero the allocation is never accessed again.  Another subtle part is choosing memory orderings for the atomic operations. For a learning, toy implementation, Relaxed is often used in examples, but a production-quality implementation needs stronger orderings and careful reasoning about data races and visibility across threads. The standard library Arc implementation is heavily optimized and carefully reasoned about; replicating it exactly is nontrivial.  A minimal conceptual outline is:  1) Define ArcInner<T> with AtomicUsize and T. 2) Define MyArc<T> holding a *mut ArcInner<T>. 3) Implement new to allocate ArcInner<T> on the heap and set ref_count to 1. 4) Implement Clone: atomically increment ref_count and return a new MyArc with the same pointer. 5) Implement Drop: atomically decrement ref_count; if it was 1 before decrement, turn the pointer back into a Box and drop it. 6) Implement Deref<Target = T> to get &T from &MyArc<T>.  You can also extend this with conveniences like a strong_count method, weak references (like Arc::downgrade), or sending across threads by implementing Send and Sync where appropriate. But for a basic custom Arc, the essential lesson is how to manage a shared heap allocation with an atomic reference count and correct Clone and Drop semantics in Rust.
7|35: In Rust you almost never need to build your own Arc because std::sync::Arc is very well implemented and heavily optimized. But explaining how you could conceptually build a custom Arc is a good way to understand how Arc works under the hood.  At a high level an Arc is just two things:  A reference-counted allocation that holds - the actual value T - a shared atomic counter telling how many Arcs point to this allocation  A lightweight handle that lives on the stack and points to that shared allocation and updates the counter when cloned or dropped.  Conceptually the heap layout is something like:  [ ArcInner<T> ] where ArcInner<T> has at least: - count: AtomicUsize - data: T  So a simplified custom Arc might look like this:  use core::sync::atomic::{AtomicUsize, Ordering}; use std::ptr::NonNull; use std::alloc::{alloc, dealloc, Layout};  struct ArcInner<T> {     count: AtomicUsize,     data: T, }  pub struct MyArc<T> {     ptr: NonNull<ArcInner<T>>, }  The MyArc handle just stores a non-null pointer to ArcInner<T>. We allocate ArcInner<T> on the heap when we create a new MyArc:  impl<T> MyArc<T> {     pub fn new(value: T) -> MyArc<T> {         // Compute layout for ArcInner<T>         let layout = Layout::new::<ArcInner<T>>();          unsafe {             let raw = alloc(layout) as *mut ArcInner<T>;             if raw.is_null() {                 std::alloc::handle_alloc_error(layout);             }              // Write the initial contents into the allocated memory             raw.write(ArcInner {                 count: AtomicUsize::new(1),                 data: value,             });              MyArc { ptr: NonNull::new_unchecked(raw) }         }     }      pub fn get_ref(&self) -> &T {         unsafe { &self.ptr.as_ref().data }     } }  The key operations are clone and drop. Clone increments the atomic counter; drop decrements it and, if it hits zero, deallocates the whole ArcInner and runs T's destructor.  impl<T> Clone for MyArc<T> {     fn clone(&self) -> Self {         let inner = unsafe { self.ptr.as_ref() };         // Increase strong count. Ordering is subtle; Release/Acquire is common         inner.count.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed);         MyArc { ptr: self.ptr }     } }  impl<T> Drop for MyArc<T> {     fn drop(&mut self) {         unsafe {             let inner = self.ptr.as_ref();             if inner.count.fetch_sub(1, Ordering::Release) == 1 {                 // This thread is dropping the last reference                 std::sync::atomic::fence(Ordering::Acquire);                  let layout = std::alloc::Layout::new::<ArcInner<T>>();                 // First drop the data                 let raw = self.ptr.as_ptr();                 std::ptr::drop_in_place(raw);                 // Then free the allocation                 std::alloc::dealloc(raw as *mut u8, layout);             }         }     } }  This is a minimal sketch; real Arc has more features and more careful memory ordering.  Important points and caveats:  Ownership and safety - MyArc must be Send + Sync when T is Send + Sync, and the correct impls must be added. - We must be sure that data is only dropped once when the last reference is gone. - The use of unsafe pointers and raw allocation means you must be meticulous to avoid double free, use after free, and data races.  Atomic ordering - Reference counting in a concurrent context requires atomic operations. - Standard Arc uses specific orderings (Acquire, Release, Relaxed) so that mutations of shared data become visible across threads once the last reference is dropped or acquired. - The fence in Drop is used to pair with the Release decrement so that memory operations before destruction are properly synchronized.  Layout and allocation - Using std::alloc directly is low level. In a custom implementation you could also use Box<ArcInner<T>> to simplify, which removes some unsafe allocation logic:  struct MyArc<T> {     ptr: NonNull<ArcInner<T>>, }  impl<T> MyArc<T> {     pub fn new(value: T) -> Self {         let boxed = Box::new(ArcInner {             count: AtomicUsize::new(1),             data: value,         });         MyArc { ptr: NonNull::from(Box::leak(boxed)) }     } }  impl<T> Drop for MyArc<T> {     fn drop(&mut self) {         unsafe {             let inner = self.ptr.as_ref();             if inner.count.fetch_sub(1, Ordering::Release) == 1 {                 std::sync::atomic::fence(Ordering::Acquire);                 // Recreate Box to drop and deallocate                 drop(Box::from_raw(self.ptr.as_ptr()));             }         }     } }  This version uses Box::leak to obtain a stable pointer and Box::from_raw to reclaim and free it; that still needs unsafe but avoids direct Layout and alloc calls.  Why you should usually not roll your own - The standard Arc is heavily tested, battle hardened, and optimized. - Getting the atomic orderings and corner cases right is tricky; subtle bugs may only appear under high concurrency and are hard to reproduce. - A custom Arc is only justified if you have special needs (custom allocators, embedded no_std environment, debug experiments, learning, etc.).  Common extensions a real implementation might add - A weak count and Weak handles, which let you hold a non owning pointer that can tell if the Arc data is still alive. - In place formatting for debugging, downcasting, etc. - Niche optimizations for space and performance.  To summarize: - A custom Arc is a heap allocation containing an atomic reference count and the value T. - The Arc handle is a pointer to that allocation that increments the count on clone and decrements it on drop. - When the count reaches zero, the allocation is destroyed and freed. - Implementing this correctly requires unsafe code and careful use of atomic operations; it is valuable as a learning exercise but should not replace std::sync::Arc in normal code.
8|35: In Rust you almost never need to build your own Arc, but doing a simplified version is a great way to understand how Arc works internally. The core ideas are reference counting, atomic operations for thread safety, and shared ownership of heap-allocated data. I’ll walk through building a minimal, educational Arc-like type, ignoring some of the tricky edge cases that the real std::sync::Arc handles.  First, conceptually, an Arc is a pointer to a heap allocation that looks like this:  struct Inner<T> {     ref_count: AtomicUsize,     data: T, }  When you clone the Arc, you increment ref_count. When an Arc is dropped, you decrement ref_count. If it reaches zero, you free Inner<T>.  Here is a minimal implementation outline. This is not production quality, but it is enough to show the mechanics.  use std::ops::Deref; use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicUsize, Ordering}; use std::ptr::NonNull; use std::alloc::{alloc, dealloc, Layout};  struct Inner<T> {     ref_count: AtomicUsize,     data: T, }  pub struct MyArc<T> {     ptr: NonNull<Inner<T>>, }  impl<T> MyArc<T> {     pub fn new(value: T) -> MyArc<T> {         // Allocate space for Inner<T>         let layout = Layout::new::<Inner<T>>();         unsafe {             let raw = alloc(layout) as *mut Inner<T>;             if raw.is_null() {                 std::alloc::handle_alloc_error(layout);             }              // Place Inner<T> into the allocation             raw.write(Inner {                 ref_count: AtomicUsize::new(1),                 data: value,             });              MyArc { ptr: NonNull::new_unchecked(raw) }         }     }      fn inner(&self) -> &Inner<T> {         unsafe { self.ptr.as_ref() }     } }  // Cloning increases the ref count impl<T> Clone for MyArc<T> {     fn clone(&self) -> MyArc<T> {         let inner = self.inner();         // Relaxed is OK here in most Arc designs for refcounting         let old = inner.ref_count.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed);         // Optionally you could debug assert that old > 0         MyArc { ptr: self.ptr }     } }  // Dropping decreases the ref count, deallocating on last drop impl<T> Drop for MyArc<T> {     fn drop(&mut self) {         let inner = self.inner();         if inner.ref_count.fetch_sub(1, Ordering::Release) == 1 {             // We were the last owner. Acquire fence pairs with Release above             std::sync::atomic::fence(Ordering::Acquire);              unsafe {                 // Read the pointer and deallocate                 let layout = std::alloc::Layout::new::<Inner<T>>();                  // Manually drop the data first                 std::ptr::drop_in_place(self.ptr.as_ptr());                  // Free the memory                 dealloc(self.ptr.as_ptr() as *mut u8, layout);             }         }     } }  // Deref so MyArc<T> can be used like &T impl<T> Deref for MyArc<T> {     type Target = T;     fn deref(&self) -> &T {         &self.inner().data     } }  This MyArc type has the essential behavior of Arc  new creates a heap allocation containing Inner<T> with ref_count set to 1 and the stored value Clone increments ref_count Drop decrements ref_count and frees memory when it hits 0 Deref lets you use it like a shared reference to T  Key points and subtleties  Thread safety Because multiple threads can own clones of the same MyArc, ref_count must be AtomicUsize with appropriate ordering. In the minimal version above  fetch_add with Relaxed is used on clone because you just need to ensure atomicity, not a particular visibility ordering for the data itself fetch_sub with Release plus a fence with Acquire before deallocation is a common pattern to synchronize with other threads that might still see the object The memory ordering details are subtle, but the pattern is the same as in the real Arc implementation.  Layout and unsafe We allocated memory manually so we needed to  Ask for a Layout that matches Inner<T> Call alloc Construct Inner<T> using write Drop the inner value and call dealloc on the layout when ref_count reaches zero These steps are all unsafe because mistakes can easily cause undefined behavior. The standard Arc wraps all of this in a safe interface.  Send and Sync To be Send and Sync like real Arc, we need trait bounds  unsafe impl<T: Send + Sync> Send for MyArc<T> {} unsafe impl<T: Send + Sync> Sync for MyArc<T> {}  This encodes the rule that you can only share MyArc across threads when T itself is safe to share across threads.  No weak references A custom Arc that matches std::sync::Arc fully would also support Weak references, which are non owning pointers to the same allocation. They use a second atomic counter for weak refcount so that the allocation can stay alive as long as there are either strong or weak references. Implementing Weak requires adding  A second AtomicUsize for weak_count Logic to keep the allocation alive while weak_count > 0, even when ref_count is zero An upgrade operation from Weak to Arc that checks whether ref_count is nonzero  Why build a custom Arc  Educational purposes: to understand ownership, lifetimes, and concurrency Custom behavior: for specialized arenas or embedded environments where you want tight control Experimentation: exploring different memory orderings, statistics on refcounts, or debugging tools  But for real world code, always prefer std::sync::Arc unless you have very strong reasons not to. Its implementation is well tested, heavily optimized, and handles a number of edge cases that a naive reimplementation might miss, such as layout optimizations, aliasing concerns, panic safety, and subtle memory ordering issues.  Summary  A minimal custom Arc in Rust is  A heap allocated Inner<T> with atomic ref_count and stored T A handle MyArc<T> that holds a non null pointer to Inner<T> Clone increments ref_count, Drop decrements it and frees when it hits zero Deref exposes an immutable reference to the inner T Careful use of atomics and unsafe memory management is required to be both correct and thread safe  Studying and writing such a custom Arc is valuable for understanding how Rust provides safe shared ownership across threads on top of low level primitives.
9|35: To build a custom Arc in Rust, you are essentially re‑implementing thread‑safe reference counting with shared ownership over heap‑allocated data. The standard library Arc<T> is highly optimized and very tricky to implement correctly, so a custom version is mostly for learning or very specialized use cases. Conceptually, there are four main pieces you need to design: the allocation layout, the reference count, the clone / drop behavior, and the thread‑safety guarantees.  At a high level, a simplified Arc<T> consists of a heap allocation that stores both a reference count and the value T. Every Arc<T> instance you hold is really just a pointer to this shared allocation. Cloning an Arc increments the counter, dropping an Arc decrements it, and when the count reaches zero you free the allocation and run T’s destructor.  The usual pattern is to define an inner allocation struct like:  struct ArcInner<T> {     ref_count: AtomicUsize,     value: T, }  This struct always lives on the heap. Your public Arc<T> type then contains a NonNull<ArcInner<T>> or *const ArcInner<T> pointer. NonNull is safer because it is guaranteed not to be null and integrates well with ownership rules, but a raw pointer also works if you handle it carefully in unsafe blocks.  Construction is straightforward: you allocate ArcInner<T> on the heap, set the ref_count to 1, and store the pointer in your Arc<T>.  impl<T> MyArc<T> {     pub fn new(value: T) -> MyArc<T> {         let inner = Box::new(ArcInner {             ref_count: AtomicUsize::new(1),             value,         });         MyArc {             ptr: NonNull::from(Box::leak(inner)),         }     } }  Leaking the Box gives you a stable pointer whose lifetime you now manage manually. Alternatively, you can convert from Box to a raw pointer using Box::into_raw and then wrap it in NonNull.  Clone must increase the reference count atomically. You use Ordering::Relaxed for basic reference counting when you only need correctness, not a happens‑before relationship on reads and writes of the inner value. In many cases Arc uses Acquire/Release or stronger orderings around operations that interact with weak counts, but for a minimal learning implementation you can keep it simple.  impl<T> Clone for MyArc<T> {     fn clone(&self) -> Self {         let inner = unsafe { self.ptr.as_ref() };         inner.ref_count.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed);         MyArc { ptr: self.ptr }     } }  Drop must decrement the counter and, when it hits zero, free the allocation and drop the inner value. This is where the unsafe logic is concentrated, because you must not touch the allocation after you have freed it, and you must ensure exactly one thread performs the final drop.  impl<T> Drop for MyArc<T> {     fn drop(&mut self) {         let inner = unsafe { self.ptr.as_ref() };         if inner.ref_count.fetch_sub(1, Ordering::Release) == 1 {             std::sync::atomic::fence(Ordering::Acquire);             unsafe {                 let _boxed = Box::from_raw(self.ptr.as_ptr());                 // when _boxed goes out of scope, T is dropped and memory freed             }         }     } }  The usual pattern for correctness is Release when decrementing and an Acquire fence on the thread that sees the counter go to zero. This pairs with the Release to create a happens‑before relationship, ensuring all writes to value are visible before destruction. For a toy single‑threaded or non‑synchronizing version you might be tempted to use Relaxed, but that’s incorrect for a fully general multi‑threaded Arc.  The value accessors must provide shared references to T. Because any number of MyArc<T> can exist at the same time, you can only expose &T, not &mut T. The simplest API is:  impl<T> std::ops::Deref for MyArc<T> {     type Target = T;     fn deref(&self) -> &T {         unsafe { &self.ptr.as_ref().value }     } }  This lets you treat MyArc<T> like a shared reference in most contexts. Because you are using immutable shared references, the compiler guarantees there are no data races on T itself unless T contains interior mutability and you use it incorrectly.  If you want to mimic the standard Arc exactly, you also need weak references that do not keep the allocation alive but allow upgrading to a strong Arc if the data is still alive. This requires a second counter for weak references, plus more complex rules about when to free memory. A common layout is:  struct ArcInner<T> {     strong: AtomicUsize,     weak: AtomicUsize,     value: T, }  Strong counts keep the value alive. Weak counts, plus strong counts, keep the allocation alive. When strong goes to zero, you drop T but keep the allocation until weak also goes to zero. Weak::upgrade increments strong if it is nonzero and returns Some(Arc), otherwise returns None.  In terms of safety, any custom Arc implementation will necessarily use unsafe code, because you are managing the lifetime of a heap allocation shared by multiple owners. The unsafe boundaries should be narrow and clearly documented. You must guarantee:  You only free the allocation exactly once when the last owner goes away You never dereference a pointer after its allocation has been freed You implement the atomic ordering correctly so that all threads see consistent memory  Missteps here can lead to use‑after‑free bugs, double frees, or subtle data races that only show up under heavy concurrency.  There are a few additional design considerations if you want production‑quality behavior.  You might want to put ArcInner<T> behind a pointer that is pointer‑width aligned and minimize padding for cache friendliness. You may want to support unsized types (like Arc<str> or Arc<[T]>) with some custom allocation layout. You might implement into_inner or try_unwrap to extract the inner T when there is only one strong reference. You might add debug assertions to check that ref_count never underflows.  For learning purposes, though, a minimal example with a single AtomicUsize, Clone, Drop, and Deref is enough to understand how Arc works. The key ideas are  Move the refcount and value into a single heap allocation shared by all owners Use atomics to change refcounts safely across threads Use unsafe carefully to manage allocation and deallocation boundaries Expose a safe, ergonomic API that behaves like the standard Arc  In production, you should almost always prefer std::sync::Arc, but writing your own small version is an excellent way to grasp low‑level ownership, memory ordering, and unsafe abstractions in Rust.
10|35: In Rust, the standard Arc type is an atomically reference counted pointer that lets multiple threads share read-only access to the same value. Building a custom Arc-like type yourself mainly means re-creating three pieces: a heap allocation that stores both the data and a refcount, atomic reference counting operations, and correct Drop semantics that free the memory exactly once when the last reference disappears.  A minimal custom Arc generally looks like this conceptually:  1. You define an inner allocation layout that holds the reference count and the value T together. For example, you might have a struct Inner<T> { refcount: AtomicUsize, value: T } and then allocate Inner<T> on the heap.  2. Your custom Arc<T> itself is just a thin pointer to Inner<T>. For instance, struct MyArc<T> { ptr: *const Inner<T> }. You keep this pointer non-null and assume it always points to valid memory while at least one MyArc exists.  3. Construction: when you call MyArc::new(value), you allocate Inner<T> with refcount = 1 and store value inside. This is usually done via Box::new(Inner { refcount: AtomicUsize::new(1), value }) and then you convert the Box into a raw pointer with Box::into_raw.  4. Cloning: Arc semantics say that cloning an Arc increments the reference count so that multiple Arcs can point to the same allocation. In Clone::clone, you take self.ptr, cast it to *const Inner<T>, and do an atomic increment on (*ptr).refcount. For example, (*ptr).refcount.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed) or a stronger ordering like Ordering::AcqRel if you want stricter guarantees. Then you construct a new MyArc pointing at the same ptr.  5. Dropping: When a MyArc is dropped, you atomically decrement the reference count. If the result is nonzero, you just return; the data is still in use by other clones. If the result is zero, then this was the last reference: you must free the allocation and drop the inner value. This means taking the raw pointer, converting it back to Box<Inner<T>> with Box::from_raw, then letting that Box drop normally, which drops T and frees the memory.  6. Deref and DerefMut: To act like Arc, you implement Deref for MyArc<T> targeting T. In deref, you read self.ptr, perform an unsafe dereference, and return a shared reference to the inner value. Because the reference count ensures the Inner<T> outlives all MyArcs, this is sound as long as you never make mutable references without exclusive ownership. For a read-only Arc-like type, you usually do not implement DerefMut at all, to preserve the shared immutable semantics.  7. Thread safety: For a true Arc you must guarantee Send and Sync semantics. In standard library Arc, the pointer is Send and Sync as long as T: Send + Sync (or some related bound). Your custom Arc will need unsafe impls: unsafe impl<T: Send + Sync> Send for MyArc<T> and unsafe impl<T: Send + Sync> Sync for MyArc<T>. These are unsafe because the compiler cannot verify that your reference counting logic is correct; you promise it is.  8. Memory ordering: The simplest but slightly conservative approach is to use Ordering::SeqCst for both fetch_add and fetch_sub. A more tuned version uses Ordering::Acquire for loading and Ordering::Release when decrementing to zero, but that requires understanding of the memory model. If you are simply experimenting, SeqCst is fine, though slower.  Here is a simplified sketch of how it might look, written conceptually without quotes inside this answer:  struct Inner<T> {     refcount: AtomicUsize,     value: T, }  pub struct MyArc<T> {     ptr: *const Inner<T>, }  impl<T> MyArc<T> {     pub fn new(value: T) -> MyArc<T> {         let inner = Box::new(Inner {             refcount: AtomicUsize::new(1),             value,         });         let ptr = Box::into_raw(inner);         MyArc { ptr }     } }  impl<T> Clone for MyArc<T> {     fn clone(&self) -> MyArc<T> {         unsafe {             let inner = &*self.ptr;             inner.refcount.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed);         }         MyArc { ptr: self.ptr }     } }  impl<T> Drop for MyArc<T> {     fn drop(&mut self) {         unsafe {             let inner = &*self.ptr;             if inner.refcount.fetch_sub(1, Ordering::Release) == 1 {                 // Ensure other writes are visible before we free                 fence(Ordering::Acquire);                 drop(Box::from_raw(self.ptr as *mut Inner<T>));             }         }     } }  impl<T> Deref for MyArc<T> {     type Target = T;     fn deref(&self) -> &T {         unsafe { &(*self.ptr).value }     } }  You also often add constructors like from raw and into inner for advanced usage, and possibly weak references, which are separate refcounts allowing non-owning handles. That is essentially how std::sync::Arc and Arc::downgrade with Weak are implemented, only with more edge case handling, additional atomic fields, and strict safety guarantees.  When building a custom Arc in production code, you normally do not reimplement it yourself; you just use std::sync::Arc or the alloc crate’s Arc if you are in no_std with allocator support. Implementing your own is mainly a learning exercise in unsafe, ownership, and memory ordering. If you do so, keep these points in mind:  You must never double free. Always convert the raw pointer back to a Box exactly once when the count hits zero. You must never let the refcount wrap around, which would happen if you increment from usize::MAX. The standard library Arc treats extremely large refcounts as undefined behavior; you can follow the same assumption or add debug assertions. You must ensure that all methods that access the inner value respect aliasing rules. Shared references are fine; mutable references require exclusive access or interior mutability types like Mutex or RwLock.  By following this pattern, you get a working custom Arc, and along the way you deepen your understanding of how Rust’s standard Arc actually works under the hood.
1|36: You can build a 2D Fortune‑based Voronoi mesh in C# and clip it to a boundary in three main steps: run Fortune’s algorithm to get an unbounded diagram, convert edges into polygonal cells, and then intersect those cells with your clipping shape.  First, pick or implement a Fortune algorithm in C#. Implementing it from scratch is doable but error‑prone; if possible, start from an existing implementation. Common approaches:  Use a C# Fortune implementation from GitHub by searching for terms like csharp fortune voronoi or fortune sweep voronoi csharp. Make sure the library returns the sites and the corresponding edges or half‑edges of the diagram. If you implement it yourself, represent events and beach line with:  Priority queue for site and circle events Balanced tree or custom structure for the beach line arcs Diagram data structure with vertices, half‑edges, and faces (DCEL, Doubly Connected Edge List)  The key output you want is a planar graph: vertices with coordinates, edges between vertices, and which face each edge belongs to. Each face corresponds to a site.  Second, convert each Voronoi region to a polygon. Many Fortune implementations already link edges around each site in order, but if yours does not, you can build polygons like this:  For each site, collect all edges incident to that face. Determine the cyclic order of edges around the face (sort edges by their angle around the region center or by walking the DCEL next pointers). Extract the ordered vertex loop to form the polygon of that cell.  At this stage, cells that touch the convex hull of the input sites are unbounded. They have rays or extremely long edges; the diagram is conceptually infinite. To make it practical for a mesh, you need to clip it against a finite boundary.  Third, perform clipping against your boundary polygon or rectangle. Let the clipping region be a simple polygon B (often an axis‑aligned rectangle). For each Voronoi cell polygon P, compute the intersection P ∩ B. This yields a bounded polygon that you can treat as a mesh cell. In C#, you can use a polygon clipping library so you don’t have to implement this yourself:  Clipper library (C# port of Angus Johnson’s Clipper) – robust for polygon clipping, supports intersection, union, difference. Use the Intersection operation with P as subject and B as clip. NetTopologySuite – a more general geometry library; create Polygon geometries and call polygonA.Intersection(polygonB).  Example with Clipper (conceptual in plain text):  Create a Clipper instance. Convert your Voronoi cell polygon vertices to IntPoint list. Clipper prefers integer coordinates, so scale your doubles (e.g., multiply by 1e4) and round. Add the cell polygon as subject. Add the boundary polygon as clip. Run Execute(Intersection, ...) to get result polygons. Scale back the coordinates to doubles.  This turns each possibly unbounded region into a bounded polygon perfectly clipped to your region. You then have a nice Voronoi mesh inside the desired boundary.  Additional practical tips:  Choose an initial bounding box for the fortune algorithm that is larger than your real boundary. Many implementations require an outer rectangle; use something like slightly larger than your final clipping region to guarantee that all relevant edges are generated. When building your final mesh, you might want to triangulate clipped polygons. Libraries like Triangle.NET or a constrained Delaunay triangulation approach can be used, where each clipped cell polygon is triangulated independently. For performance, pre‑convert your boundary polygon B into the library’s geometry type once, then reuse it during intersection for each cell.  If you want a minimal workable setup:  Use an existing C# Fortune implementation that outputs faces and edges. Use Clipper or NetTopologySuite to intersect each face polygon with your clipping polygon. Optionally, store results as a mesh structure: list of vertices, list of faces (each face is an index list into the vertex array).  This approach gives you a 2D Voronoi mesh that is strictly confined to a given boundary, using Fortune’s algorithm for the diagram and a robust polygon clipper for the boundary clipping.
2|36: If you want Fortune based Voronoi in 2D with clipping to a rectangular or polygonal boundary in C#, you essentially need three pieces: an implementation of Fortune’s sweep algorithm, a robust way to construct the Voronoi cells as polygons, and then polygon clipping against your domain boundary.  A practical route in C# is to combine an existing Fortune implementation with a geometry library rather than writing everything from scratch.  High level approach  1. Generate the Voronoi diagram with Fortune’s algorithm    Use a C# implementation of Fortune’s algorithm that produces half edges or line segments for each Voronoi edge. Some options:        Using MIConvexHull    - MIConvexHull is a .NET library available via NuGet that can compute Voronoi diagrams in 2D.    - It is not hand coded Fortune, but internally it uses convex hull based duality. For many uses this is just as good. If you strictly require Fortune, you can use another library (see below), but MIConvexHull provides a robust API.    - Install via NuGet: `Install-Package MIConvexHull`    - Define a point class implementing `IVertex`:       public class Vertex : IVertex      {          public double[] Position { get; set; }          public Vertex(double x, double y)          {              Position = new double[] { x, y };          }      }     - Compute the Voronoi diagram:       var points = new List<Vertex>();      // fill points with your 2D sites       var voronoi = VoronoiMesh.Create<Vertex, VoronoiCell<Vertex, VoronoiEdge<Vertex>>>(points);     - Each cell in `voronoi.Vertices` or `voronoi.Cells` represents a region for a site. You can extract its polygon by walking its edges.     Using a direct Fortune implementation    - Search for C# Fortune implementations like LeeByron FortuneVoronoi port or other GitHub projects (for example TinyVoronoi, Fortune.NET, etc.).    - These libraries usually give you structures such as Site, Edge, and Vertex, and lists of segments that represent the Voronoi edges.    - Once you have those edges, you need to reconstruct polygons by grouping edges by cell (each site), ordering them around the site, and closing the polygon.  2. Represent Voronoi regions as polygons    After running the Voronoi routine, you want each site to have a polygon that describes its region. The steps conceptually:    - For each site, collect all Voronoi edges that belong to that site.    - Each edge has two endpoints (Voronoi vertices). For clipping, you need them ordered (counter clockwise) so that they form a simple polygon.    - Build a list of points (x,y) for each region in order.    - Infinite regions will have edges that go off to infinity; you will handle those by intersecting them with your clipping boundary in the next step.     With MIConvexHull VoronoiMesh    - Each `VoronoiCell` has a `Generator` (the original site) and a collection of `Vertices` that are the Voronoi vertices.    - You may need to sort the cell vertices angularly around the cell generator to get a proper polygon:       var center = new Vector2((float)cell.Generator.Position[0], (float)cell.Generator.Position[1]);      var polygon = cell.Vertices                        .OrderBy(v => Math.Atan2(v.Position[1] - center.Y, v.Position[0] - center.X))                        .Select(v => new Vector2((float)v.Position[0], (float)v.Position[1]))                        .ToList();  3. Define your clipping boundary    Decide what boundary you want to clip to. The simplest case is an axis aligned bounding box, but you can use any polygon.    - Rectangular boundary:      Example: minX, maxX, minY, maxY    - Polygonal boundary:      A list of points in order that define a closed polygon.  4. Clip each Voronoi polygon against the boundary    Use a robust polygon clipping library rather than writing your own clipping (especially important for numerical robustness).     The popular choice in .NET is Clipper (Clipper Library by Angus Johnson). There is a .NET version called ClipperLib or using the newer Clipper2.     With Clipper (classic)    - Install Clipper via NuGet: `Install-Package ClipperLib`    - Clipper works on integer coordinates (scaled). Multiply your float/double coordinates by a scaling factor (e.g. 1000 or 100000) and round to long.     Example outline for clipping a single cell polygon to a rectangular boundary using Clipper:     using ClipperLib;     const double scale = 1000.0;     PathD MakeRect(double minX, double minY, double maxX, double maxY)    {        return new PathD        {            new PointD(minX, minY),            new PointD(maxX, minY),            new PointD(maxX, maxY),            new PointD(minX, maxY)        };    }     var clipper = new ClipperD();     // subject polygon: the Voronoi cell    PathD subject = new PathD();    foreach (var p in polygon) // polygon is List<Vector2>    {        subject.Add(new PointD(p.X, p.Y));    }     // clip polygon: the boundary    PathD clipBoundary = MakeRect(minX, minY, maxX, maxY);     PathsD solution = new PathsD();     clipper.AddSubject(subject);    clipper.AddClip(clipBoundary);    clipper.Execute(ClipType.Intersection, FillRule.NonZero, solution);     Now solution contains one or more polygons representing the clipped Voronoi cell. If it is empty, the cell lies completely outside your boundary.     With older Clipper that uses IntPoint    - Scale and convert to IntPoint:       List<IntPoint> ToClipperPath(List<Vector2> poly, double scale)      {          return poly.Select(p => new IntPoint(              (long)Math.Round(p.X * scale),              (long)Math.Round(p.Y * scale))).ToList();      }       List<IntPoint> boundaryPath = new List<IntPoint>      {          new IntPoint((long)(minX * scale), (long)(minY * scale)),          new IntPoint((long)(maxX * scale), (long)(minY * scale)),          new IntPoint((long)(maxX * scale), (long)(maxY * scale)),          new IntPoint((long)(minX * scale), (long)(maxY * scale))      };       var subj = new List<List<IntPoint>> { ToClipperPath(polygon, scale) };      var clip = new List<List<IntPoint>> { boundaryPath };       var c = new Clipper();      c.AddPaths(subj, PolyType.ptSubject, true);      c.AddPaths(clip, PolyType.ptClip, true);       var solutionInt = new List<List<IntPoint>>();      c.Execute(ClipType.ctIntersection, solutionInt, PolyFillType.pftNonZero, PolyFillType.pftNonZero);       // convert back from IntPoint to Vector2 or your own type  5. Handle infinite Voronoi regions    Fortune style Voronoi typically has unbounded cells at the outer regions. When you clip against a finite boundary, the clipping step naturally converts these infinite polygons into finite clipped polygons.    - The raw Voronoi output might represent infinite edges with some sentinel, like endpoints at infinity or null. In practice, reconstructing polygons for these cells is easiest if you first intersect edges with a big enclosing bounding box (or your real domain boundary), then clip more precisely.    - Alternatively, if you use MIConvexHull or a library that supports bounding boxes, check if there is API to compute a Voronoi diagram constrained to a bounding box; some libraries let you specify a bounding rectangle and automatically produce clipped cells.  6. Putting it together in a pipeline    Pseudocode     Input: List of sites S, boundary polygon B (or rectangle)     // 1. Voronoi    voronoi = ComputeVoronoi(S)  // via MIConvexHull or Fortune implementation     List<CellPolygon> resultCells = new List<CellPolygon>();     foreach cell in voronoi.Cells    {        polygon = BuildCellPolygon(cell)      // order vertices into polygon        clipped = ClipPolygonToBoundary(polygon, B)         if clipped is not empty            resultCells.Add(new CellPolygon(cell.Generator, clipped))    }     return resultCells  7. Libraries and references in C#     MIConvexHull    - NuGet: MIConvexHull    - Pros: Easy Voronoi API, robust, no need to implement Fortune.    - Good if you just need a Voronoi mesh and do not care about the exact algorithm being Fortune.
