Within Initialize or LoadContent, after you have your GraphicsDevice and SpriteBatch, initialize Myra:  – Call MyraEnvironment.Game = this; if you are in the main Game class. – Create a Desktop instance: Desktop _desktop = new Desktop(); – Optionally assign a default stylesheet or theme if you load one from content.  Desktop is Myra’s root container, analogous to Gwen’s Canvas.  Initially, create a very simple UI so you can test wiring: – Create a Myra widget, like a Panel or Label. – Add it as Desktop.Root = yourRootWidget.  This gives you a minimal Myra presence without yet removing Gwen.  Step 4: Hook Myra into drawing and updating Unlike Gwen, Myra is largely handled by calling Desktop.Render and Desktop.Update(FrameTime) once per frame.  In Draw – After clearing the screen and drawing your world, but before presenting the backbuffer, call _desktop.Render();  In Update – Compute a delta time (or use the GameTime parameter) and call _desktop.Update(gameTime); or simply _desktop.Update(); depending on the Myra version.  Myra automatically queries MonoGame for mouse and keyboard state by default when you set MyraEnvironment.Game or provide InputContext. If your Intersect fork uses a custom input system, you may either: – Allow Myra to query Mouse.GetState() and Keyboard.GetState() directly, or – Manually set MyraEnvironment.MouseInfo and MyraEnvironment.KeyboardInfo based on Intersect’s input manager.  At this stage, ensure: – The project compiles. – The game runs and you can see the simple Myra widget.  Still keep Gwen active; you are verifying coexistence before migrating.  Step 5: Build a mapping from Gwen controls to Myra widgets Conceptually map common Gwen constructs to Myra constructs: – Gwen Canvas  Myra Desktop.Root (a widget, usually a Panel or Grid acting as root container) – Gwen containers like DockLayout, GridLayout, VerticalLayout  Myra widgets such as Grid, HorizontalStackPanel, VerticalStackPanel – Gwen Button  Myra TextButton or ImageTextButton – Gwen Label  Myra Label – Gwen TextBox  Myra TextBox – Gwen Checkbox  Myra CheckBox – Gwen ComboBox  Myra ComboBox – Gwen ListBox  Myra ListView or ListBox variant – Gwen WindowControl  Myra Window  Also map style and skin usage: – Gwen uses skins and renderers (e.g., a skin texture and a Skin class). – Myra uses stylesheets or themes loaded via Myra’s Resource management, with style JSONs or in‑code theme definitions.  Do this on paper or in documentation so that for each Gwen screen, you already know the Myra equivalent structures.  Step 6: Choose a migration strategy You can: – Big‑bang: Remove Gwen in one commit and rewrite all UI to Myra. Quick but risky. – Incremental: Temporarily run Gwen and Myra side by side, migrating screen by screen.  Incremental is usually safer: – Keep Gwen as the primary UI initially. – Introduce a Myra version of a specific screen (e.g., main menu) and switch code to show the Myra version instead of the Gwen one. – Once stable, remove the Gwen code for that screen.  Because both toolkits draw via SpriteBatch and the same GraphicsDevice, ensure your draw order is well defined so they don’t conflict visually.  Step 7: Create a Myra UI manager paralleling Gwen’s UI manager Intersect likely has some form of UI manager or set of classes that: – Create Gwen controls. – Maintain references to things like chat windows, inventory windows, etc. – Show/hide windows. – Respond to gameplay events.  Introduce a MyraUiManager class with responsibilities similar to the current Gwen UI manager, but purely in terms of Myra: – Holds a reference to the Desktop. – Builds widget trees for different screens (login, character select, game HUD, etc.). – Exposes methods like ShowLogin, ShowHud, ShowOptions. – Handles events like OnLoginSuccess, OnInventoryChanged, binding those to widget updates.  In code that currently talks to the Gwen UI manager, start inserting conditional paths or new calls that go through MyraUiManager instead, one feature at a time.  Step 8: Port one screen end‑to‑end as a template Pick a relatively self‑contained UI screen, for example the main menu or login window.  Find its Gwen implementation – Look for code that creates a Canvas child or WindowControl for login. – Identify how controls are laid out and what events they handle (button clicks, text entry, etc.).  Create the Myra equivalent – Create a method BuildLoginScreen() in your MyraUiManager that:   – Instantiates a Grid (or Panel) as root.   – Adds Labels, TextBoxes for username and password.   – Adds Buttons for Login, Register, Exit.   – Lays them out using Grid row/column, HorizontalStackPanel, or VerticalStackPanel.  Wire up events – Subscribe to Myra button Click events. – When clicked, call the same methods or raise the same events that Gwen code did (e.g., send login packets, show other screens).  Attach to Desktop – When you want to show the login screen: _desktop.Root = _loginRootWidget;  Temporarily use a configuration or flag to select between Gwen and Myra for this screen, so you can toggle back if something breaks.  Test thoroughly – Verify keyboard focus, tab traversal, and text input. – Check that pressing Enter triggers login, Esc cancels, etc., replicating old Gwen behavior.  Step 9: Translate Gwen’s layout patterns to Myra layout patterns Gwen and Myra both have container and layout concepts, but the APIs differ. While porting each screen, rewrite layout logic with Myra idioms:  – Absolute positions: If Gwen code sets explicit X,Y positions on controls, in Myra you can manually set Left and Top or rely on a Grid with fixed Row/Column widths and heights. – Docking: For Gwen DockLayout usage, in Myra you might use Grid with appropriate rows/columns, or Panels anchored with Alignment and proportion‑based Width/Height. – Margins and padding: Translate Gwen Margin/Padding to Myra’s margin and padding properties directly, adjusting values as needed.  You don’t have to preserve pixel‑perfect layouts; however, keep visual equivalence so that players experience minimal changes.  Step 10: Handle input focus, hotkeys, and shortcuts Check how Gwen handled hotkeys and focus, for example: – Global hotkeys for opening inventory, map, character window. – Keyboard shortcuts in text inputs. – Mouse wheel handling over lists.  In Myra, you typically: – Use Desktop.FocusedWidget to see what has keyboard focus. – Handle KeyDown or Char events via Myra’s event system if you need per‑widget behavior. – Alternatively, capture global keys in your main Update method and then call methods on the Desktop or widgets (e.g., toggling windows).  Make sure that: – Text input uses MonoGame’s text input (or Myra’s built‑in mechanisms) across platforms. – Non‑ASCII text still works if the game previously supported it.  Step 11: Style and theme migration Gwen skins define UI visuals; Myra uses stylesheets or theme files. Decide how close you want to be to the original look.  Approaches: – Approximate the Gwen skin by customizing a Myra theme, adjusting colors, fonts, and borders. – Reuse existing assets (e.g., UI texture atlas) by defining appropriate NinePatch or texture region styles in Myra. – Or intentionally adopt Myra’s default style if visual change is acceptable.  Implementation steps: – Create a Myra style definition (JSON or in code) matching your desired look. – Load it at startup and assign to Desktop or to specific widgets so you don’t hardcode style everywhere.  Step 12: Move remaining screens one by one Repeat the process you used for the first migrated screen for all other UI pieces: – Character selection. – Game HUD (health bars, mana, XP, minimap, chat, hotbar). – Inventory, equipment, spellbook. – Options, dialogs, message boxes. – Any debug or admin UI.  For each, follow this cycle: – Identify Gwen implementation. – Sketch the equivalent widget tree in Myra. – Implement using Myra containers and controls. – Wire up events to existing game logic. – Replace references and remove the old Gwen UI for that screen.  Keep the work incremental to avoid big broken states; run and test after each migrated screen.  Step 13: Remove Gwen input wiring Once all visible screens are ported, there may still be Gwen input handling present: – Code that forwards mouse and keyboard events to Gwen.Input. – Code that updates or draws a Gwen Canvas even if you don’t use it.  Search again for Gwen.Input or similar and unlink it: – Remove input handler registrations. – Delete or disable any code that sends keyboard/mouse state to Gwen.  Verify that Myra still gets input and that there are no lingering references causing compilation errors.  Step 14: Remove Gwen rendering and root controls After input paths are gone, remove Gwen rendering calls in the draw loop: – Any Canvas.Render calls or Gwen specific draw setups can be eliminated. – Any custom Gwen renderer (e.g., a Gwen renderer that wraps SpriteBatch) can be removed.  Also remove any global or static Gwen Canvas references. The Desktop and Myra widget tree now represent the entire GUI layer.  Step 15: Remove Gwen references from the project When you are sure nothing uses Gwen: – Remove Gwen assemblies or projects from the solution. – Remove Gwen entries from package references or project references. – Delete any Gwen-specific helper classes that you no longer use.  Rebuild the entire solution to confirm no missing references.  Step 16: Clean up and refactor the Myra infrastructure Once you confirm the game runs fully on Myra: – Refine your MyraUiManager structure so code is clean and maintainable. – Group common UI patterns into reusable builders or components. – Move configuration for fonts, colors, and spacing into style or config files. – Remove temporary compatibility shims introduced during the migration.  Step 17: Test across platforms and resolutions Gwen and Myra may differ in how they handle scaling and DPI, so test: – Different window sizes and fullscreen resolutions. – UI scaling settings, if Intersect has them. – Multiple platforms (Windows, Linux, etc.) where Intersect runs.  Fix layout issues by: – Using proportionally sized rows and columns in Grid (star sizing where available). – Relying on anchors, alignment, and auto‑sizing instead of hardcoded positions.  Step 18: Document the new UI layer Provide a short developer guide for future contributors: – Where the Desktop is created and how to access it. – How to add a new window or screen. – Where styles/themes are defined. – Any conventions for naming widgets and structuring layouts.  This prevents regressions back to ad‑hoc patterns and makes it easy for others to work with the Myra‑based UI.  Summary Replacing Gwen with Myra in Intersect.Client is primarily about wiring a different UI framework into the existing MonoGame loop and systematically rewriting UI screens. The key steps are: – Add Myra and initialize a Desktop from your Game. – Render and update the Desktop each frame. – For each Gwen screen, build an equivalent Myra widget tree and hook it to the same gameplay logic. – Gradually remove Gwen input, drawing, and references until only Myra remains. – Refine layout, styling, and documentation once migration is complete.  By doing this screen‑by‑screen with a well‑structured MyraUiManager, you minimize risk and end up with a modern, MonoGame‑friendly UI layer that is easier to maintain and extend than the original Gwen integration.
3|67: This is a high-level guide for migrating Intersect’s client UI from Gwen (the existing immediate-mode GUI) to Myra (a retained-mode GUI library). It focuses on concepts and steps, not exact line-by-line changes, because your specific fork, platform, and customizations may vary. Treat this as a roadmap you can adapt.  Overview of the migration  The Intersect client (Intersect.Client) currently uses Gwen.Net for:  UI system and event wiring (Windows, Panels, Labels, Buttons, TextBoxes, CheckBoxes, ListBoxes, etc.) Skinning and styling Layout Input handling (mouse, keyboard) integrated with MonoGame  Myra will replace Gwen in all these roles. The biggest conceptual differences are:  Gwen is immediate-ish and heavily event-driven per widget creation in code; Myra is also event-driven but encourages layout via widgets and optionally UI markup Gwen uses Canvas as root; Myra uses Desktop as root Gwen widgets have their own namespaces and event patterns; Myra widgets are in Myra.Graphics2D.UI with its own events and layout properties  The migration can be done in stages: introduce Myra alongside Gwen, switch one screen at a time, then remove Gwen.  Prerequisites  Have a working build of Intersect.Client from the main branch of the AscensionGameDev Intersect-Engine repo Ensure you are running on a compatible .NET/MonoGame version (Myra targets MonoGame and .NET, so Intersect’s client environment should be fine) You should be comfortable with C#, MonoGame, and reading the Intersect client source  1. Add Myra to the Intersect client project  Open Intersect.Client.csproj Add Myra via NuGet  Use your IDE or edit the csproj directly (paths will depend on your environment). For example in Visual Studio, open Package Manager Console in the Intersect.Client project and run:  dotnet add package Myra  Verify references  Rebuild Intersect.Client Confirm that Myra.Graphics2D.UI namespace is available in client files  2. Introduce a Myra Desktop into the client  Locate the core game client loop and GUI root  In Intersect, the main game loop and rendering live in something like Game1 or IntersectGame (names may change slightly depending on branch). Search in Intersect.Client for where Gwen is initialized.  Common patterns to look for:  Using Gwen-related namespaces like Gwen.Control, Gwen.Skin, Gwen.Renderer Initialization of a Gwen Canvas as the root UI Calls to gwenCanvas.Render or similar inside Draw Input routing from MonoGame (mouse, keyboard) to Gwen controls  Add Myra initialization  In the game initialization section after graphics and content are set up but before entering the main loop:  Create a Desktop instance Store it in a global or manager that your UI system can access (e.g., UiManager.MyraDesktop) Configure the Desktop to use the same MonoGame Game object and sprite batch that Intersect already uses  Pseudocode example adapted to the Intersect style (not copy-paste ready):  namespace Intersect.Client.Core {     using Myra.Graphics2D.UI;      public class IntersectGame : Game     {         private Desktop _myraDesktop;          protected override void Initialize()         {             base.Initialize();              _myraDesktop = new Desktop();              // Optionally: load a default style sheet or resources             // You might set: _myraDesktop.RenderContext = new MyraRenderContext(GraphicsDevice);         }          protected override void Draw(GameTime gameTime)         {             GraphicsDevice.Clear(Color.Black);              // Game world rendering goes here              // Draw Myra UI last             _myraDesktop.Render();              base.Draw(gameTime);         }     } }  Wire input to Myra  In your Game.Update method (or where input is processed), you need to forward input events to Myra. Typically, Myra’s Desktop reads input using Myra-specific input providers integrated with MonoGame. For Intersect you will probably:  Use MonoGame’s Mouse and Keyboard state each frame Set Desktop.MousePosition, Desktop.MouseButtons, and key states accordingly, or Use Myra’s built-in MonoGame integration (if you bring in Myra’s MonoGame specific helpers; see Myra docs/examples)  For an initial phase, you can just render an empty Desktop while keeping Gwen fully functional. This ensures Myra is not breaking the game.  3. Abstract the UI layer so Gwen and Myra can coexist temporarily  Rather than replacing Gwen everywhere at once, introduce an abstraction layer for UI screens.  Identify your UI screen classes  Look for things like:  Login and registration windows Character selection and creation screens Main HUD Dialogs, menus, popups, tooltips  These are probably derived from some base class that already encapsulates Gwen Controls, or they may directly construct Gwen widgets.  Create a minimal UI abstraction  Define interfaces in Intersect.Client that describe the behavior, not the implementation  Example:  public interface IUiScreen {     void Show();     void Hide();     void Update(GameTime gameTime); }  Then implement Gwen-based and Myra-based versions gradually.  Initially, you can keep existing Gwen implementations and introduce parallel Myra implementations for specific screens.  4. Implement a first simple Myra screen (e.g., a basic dialog)  Pick a non-critical screen such as a simple options dialog or a debug window.  Create a Myra widget tree  Use Myra.Graphics2D.UI widgets like Window, Panel, Label, TextButton.  For example:  public class MyraTestScreen : IUiScreen {     private readonly Desktop _desktop;     private readonly Window _window;      public MyraTestScreen(Desktop desktop)     {         _desktop = desktop;          _window = new Window         {             Title = Test Window,             Width = 300,             Height = 200         };          var panel = new VerticalStackPanel         {             Spacing = 8,             Padding = new Thickness(8)         };          var label = new Label { Text = Hello from Myra };                 var button = new TextButton { Text = Close };          button.Click += (s, a) => Hide();          panel.Widgets.Add(label);         panel.Widgets.Add(button);          _window.Content = panel;     }      public void Show()     {         if (!_desktop.Widgets.Contains(_window))         {             _desktop.Widgets.Add(_window);         }         _window.ShowModal(_desktop);     }      public void Hide()     {         _window.Close();     }      public void Update(GameTime gameTime)     {         // Optional per-frame logic     } }  Hook this screen into the Intersect UI manager  Wherever your game opens debug or options windows, replace one call to the Gwen version with the MyraTestScreen.  Ensure inputs go to Myra and that the window renders and responds to clicks.  5. Map Gwen concepts to Myra concepts  You will systematically replace Gwen widgets with Myra equivalents.  General mapping  Gwen Canvas  Myra Desktop (as root) or a root Panel attached to Desktop Gwen Window  Myra Window Gwen Button  Myra TextButton or Button Gwen Label   Myra Label Gwen TextBox  Myra TextBox Gwen CheckBox  Myra CheckBox Gwen ComboBox  Myra ComboBox Gwen ListBox  Myra ListBox Gwen TabControl  Myra TabControl Gwen Layout (Dock, Grid, etc.)  Myra panels (Grid, HorizontalStackPanel, VerticalStackPanel, etc.)  Event handling  Gwen uses event properties like Clicked, TextChanged, etc. Myra uses standard .NET events like Click or Changed, typically with EventHandler or EventHandler<T> signatures.  For each existing Gwen control creation code:  Identify which Gwen type is used Determine the Myra equivalent Rewrite creation and event hookup Rewrite layout and sizing logic to use Myra properties (e.g., Grid.Row, Grid.Column, HorizontalAlignment, VerticalAlignment, Proportions in panels)  6. Replace one full screen at a time  Plan an order; for example:  Simple modal dialogs (OK/Cancel boxes, message popups) Login/registration screen Character selection/creation Settings/options screen In-game HUD Special custom windows (inventory, skills, quests, etc.)  For each screen  Find the screen class that currently uses Gwen Clone its behavior but rebuild the UI using Myra widgets exclusively Ensure logic such as network callbacks, events, and state updates are not coupled to Gwen types (refactor so they depend on your screen interface or plain C# objects) Temporarily route the game to create your Myra version instead of the Gwen version Test thoroughly: layout, localization, dynamic resizing, scaling, input focus, and navigation  7. Input, focus, and modal behavior adjustments  Myra’s Desktop handles focus management and modal windows. Pay attention to:  Which controls should get focus on open (e.g., username text box in the login screen) Keyboard shortcuts and hotkeys (Enter to confirm, Escape to cancel) Tooltips (Myra supports them, but you must create and assign them differently than Gwen) Mouse wheel behavior on scrollable containers (ListBox, ScrollViewer)  Intersect may have its own input manager that decides whether game input or UI input should be processed each frame. Update that logic so that when Myra has an active modal window or when the mouse is inside certain UI regions, game input is suppressed.  8. Styling and skinning  Gwen uses skins (themes). Myra uses style sets and optionally UI markup.  Identify where Intersect sets its Gwen skin or theme (colors, fonts, etc.). Replicate the same visual style in Myra by:  Creating a Myra style set Loading fonts and textures for the new UI Configuring default styles for buttons, windows, labels, etc.  Myra supports XAML-like or JSON-like markup for UI, but you can also stick to code-based construction if that fits better with how Intersect currently builds Gwen UIs.  9. HUD and in-game overlays  The HUD is typically the most complex part of the UI in Intersect, with many small elements (health bars, skill bars, chat window, minimap, etc.).  Before converting the HUD to Myra, ensure:  World rendering plus basic Myra UI overlays work well together Z-order between world, UI, and any special effects is correct Performance impact is acceptable  Port pieces of HUD gradually:  Start with static elements like top bars or frames Then port dynamic elements (hotbars, chatbox, party frames) Finally, port highly interactive elements like drag-and-drop inventory windows  For drag-and-drop and advanced interactions, familiarize yourself with Myra’s support for drag events, mouse events, and custom widgets.  10. Cleaning up Gwen  After all major UI screens and HUD components are recreated in Myra and verified:  Search for all Gwen-related using directives and types in Intersect.Client Replace or remove all remaining uses Remove Gwen from the project references and NuGet packages Delete any Gwen-specific glue code (renderers, skins, input bridges) Run a full rebuild to ensure no Gwen symbols are left  11. Testing and edge cases  Test across resolutions and aspect ratios; Myra’s layout system may behave differently from Gwen, so verify:  Anchoring and docking of controls Scaling (if Intersect uses resolution scaling for UI) Localization with longer strings or different alphabets Input methods (mouse, keyboard, possibly gamepad)  Also test network-driven UI updates, for example:  Dialogs triggered by the server Error messages and popups UI updates on character state changes (hp, mp, buffs)  12. Optional: Using Myra UI markup to simplify UI definitions  If desired, move from code-only UI definitions to Myra markup files:  Design complex screens (login, character select, HUD segments) using Myra’s UI editor or markup syntax Load them at runtime, then attach event handlers in code This usually results in cleaner separation between layout and logic, and might make future maintenance easier than the Gwen approach  Summary migration blueprint  1. Add Myra to Intersect.Client via NuGet and set up a Desktop 2. Integrate Myra rendering in the Draw method and forward input 3. Introduce a UI abstraction so Gwen and Myra can coexist 4. Build a small Myra-based test window and hook it into the game 5. Create a mapping from Gwen widgets to Myra widgets and gradually convert screens 6. Migrate major screens one by one, testing intensively 7. Convert the HUD and advanced interactions like drag-and-drop 8. Recreate Gwen’s theme in Myra via styles and resources 9. Remove Gwen dependencies once all UI has Myra equivalents 10. Optionally adopt Myra markup for layouts  By following this staged approach, you can replace Gwen in the Intersect client with Myra with minimal downtime and the option to test and iterate on each screen instead of attempting a risky all-at-once rewrite.
4|67: This guide outlines a practical, incremental approach to replacing the Gwen UI system in the Intersect Engine client with the Myra UI framework. It focuses on understanding how Gwen is currently wired into the client, what Myra provides, and a migration path that minimizes risk while keeping the codebase maintainable.  Understand the current Gwen integration in Intersect  First, map out where and how Gwen is used in the Intersect client. In the Intersect.Client repository you will typically find Gwen usage in namespaces and files related to UI, for example something like  Intersect.Client.Interface Intersect.Client.Interface.Shared Intersect.Client.Interface.Menu Intersect.Client.Interface.Game  Look for  using Gwen using Gwen.Control using Gwen.Skin  and any references to classes like  Gwen.Renderer.OpenTK or Gwen.Renderer.SDL Gwen.Skin.Base or Gwen.Skin.TexturedBase Gwen.Control.Canvas Gwen.Control.Window, Button, Label, TextBox, etc.  Also look at where the root Gwen canvas is created and updated. Common locations  The main game window initialization logic, often in something like Game or Graphics or something similar inside Intersect.Client Any UiManager or InterfaceManager class that might own a Gwen.Canvas and is responsible for creating and updating all Gwen controls.  You want to identify  Where Gwen is initialized Where Gwen is updated each frame Where Gwen is drawn each frame Where Gwen handles input from keyboard and mouse Where layout and skinning are configured  This will define the boundaries of the Gwen dependency and show you what you must replace or adapt for Myra.  Review what Myra offers  Myra is a UI library for MonoGame and .NET. It integrates with MonoGame Game classes and uses SpriteBatch for rendering. Intersect uses MonoGame under the hood, so Myra is compatible conceptually.  Key Myra concepts you will need  Desktop: The root UI container. You assign it to your Game, then set Desktop.Root = some widget. Widgets: Common controls like Label Button TextBox ListBox Tree Grid Panel etc. Input routing: Myra integrates via Mouse and Keyboard input from MonoGame. Layout: Myra uses layout containers such as Grid StackPanel Panel etc. Skins or styles: Myra uses styles from resource files (usually .xstyle or JSON) or programmatic styling.  Confirm Intersect client is on a target framework supported by Myra (for example .NET 6 or a compatible version) and that you can reference the Myra NuGet package.  Add Myra to the Intersect client project  In the Intersect.Client project  Add the Myra package via NuGet  Using dotnet CLI from the client project folder  dotnet add package Myra  Or using Visual Studio NuGet Package Manager  Search for Myra and install the latest stable version.  After installation confirm that  Your .csproj for Intersect.Client contains a PackageReference for Myra. You can add at top of relevant files  using Myra using Myra.Graphics2D.UI  Initialize Myra in the game client  Locate the main game class that inherits from MonoGame Game. In the Intersect engine this is often something like  Intersect.Client.Core.Game or similar  Look for where Gwen is currently initialized, something like  var renderer = new Gwen.Renderer.Something(graphicsDeviceManager.GraphicsDevice) var skin = new Gwen.Skin.TexturedBase(renderer, textures) var canvas = new Gwen.Control.Canvas(skin)  You will remove or phase out this code. Instead you will integrate Myra. A typical Myra setup for MonoGame looks like  private Desktop _desktop  protected override void Initialize() {     base.Initialize()      MyraEnvironment.Game = this     _desktop = new Desktop() }  protected override void Draw(GameTime gameTime) {     GraphicsDevice.Clear(Color.CornflowerBlue)      _desktop.Render()      base.Draw(gameTime) }  In Intersect, the drawing and game loop might already be structured differently, but the idea is the same  Set MyraEnvironment.Game in initialization. Create a Desktop field that will hold the root of your UI. Call _desktop.Render in your Draw or post world rendering.  You need to ensure this call sequence matches how Intersect handles its rendering pipeline. If Intersect already has a SpriteBatch that draws game world and Gwen UI, you will adapt it as follows  Keep the game world rendering as it is. After game world is drawn, call _desktop.Render. Myra will probably create and manage its own SpriteBatch inside the Desktop, so you do not necessarily need to pass one unless you decide to integrate more deeply.  Replace basic Gwen setup with Myra Desktop management  In the current code you will likely find a central UI manager that instantiates Gwen controls and attaches them to a root canvas. For example you might see something like  public static class Interface {     public static Canvas Canvas { get; private set; }      public static void Initialize()     {         Canvas = new Canvas(skin)         Canvas.ShouldDrawBackground = false         Canvas.SetSize(screenWidth, screenHeight)          // Create windows and other controls here     } }  You will want to replace this thinking with something like  public static class Interface {     public static Desktop Desktop { get; private set; }      public static void Initialize(Game game)     {         MyraEnvironment.Game = game         Desktop = new Desktop()          // Later set Desktop.Root to main root widget     } }  Or in your Game class you might centralize this like  public class IntersectGame : Game {     private Desktop _desktop      protected override void Initialize()     {         base.Initialize()          MyraEnvironment.Game = this         _desktop = new Desktop()          // maybe call Interface.Initialize(this) which uses _desktop     }      protected override void Draw(GameTime gameTime)     {         // draw world          _desktop.Render()         base.Draw(gameTime)     } }  After you have a Desktop instance, you set Desktop.Root to a main container, for example a Panel or Grid that will act as the top-level UI layout for the game. You will now migrate each Gwen window or screen into Myra widgets contained under this root.  Map Gwen controls to Myra widgets  Go through Gwen UI code and identify each concrete control and layout used. For instance  Gwen.Control.Window Gwen.Control.Button Gwen.Control.Label Gwen.Control.TextBox Gwen.Control.ComboBox Gwen.Control.ListBox Gwen.Control.TabControl Gwen.Control.TreeControl Gwen.Control.DockBase or DockLayout Gwen.Control.HorizontalSplitter VerticalSplitter  Then determine the nearest approximate Myra widget  Window in Gwen becomes a Panel or Window in Myra depending on the version. Myra provides a Window widget in most recent versions. Button maps to Myra Button. Label maps to Myra Label. TextBox maps to Myra TextBox. ComboBox maps to ComboBox. ListBox maps to ListBox. Tabs in Gwen via TabControl can map to Myra TabControl. Trees map to Tree. Layout containers map like   DockBase to a DockPanel or manually laid out Grid.   VerticalLayout or HorizontalLayout to a VerticalStackPanel or HorizontalStackPanel.  Myra names sometimes vary slightly with versions, but the basic principle is similar.  Extract behavior before replacing UI  Before you rip out Gwen code, isolate the logic and events from the visual layer. For example, if you have  var connectButton = new Button(canvas) connectButton.Text = Connect connectButton.Clicked += (s, e) => ConnectToServer()  You want to move the ConnectToServer logic into a separate service or handler not directly tied to Gwen. For example  public class ConnectionController {     public void ConnectToServer()     {         // existing connection logic     } }  Then in both Gwen and Myra code you simply wire the UI event to that controller. During migration, this lets you parallel-run or easily replace UI without rewriting the behavior.  Create Myra equivalents of key screens  Choose one screen at a time to convert. For example, start with the main menu interface.  Find Gwen code for main menu, which typically constructs a Window or Canvas subtree representing  Game logo Buttons for Play Options Exit Maybe some status labels.  Write a Myra version of that screen, for example  public class MainMenuView {     public Widget Root { get; private set; }      public MainMenuView(ConnectionController controller)     {         var panel = new VerticalStackPanel         {             HorizontalAlignment = HorizontalAlignment.Center,             VerticalAlignment = VerticalAlignment.Center,             Spacing = 8         }          var title = new Label         {             Text = Intersect Game,             HorizontalAlignment = HorizontalAlignment.Center         }          var playButton = new TextButton { Text = Play }         playButton.Click += (s, a) => controller.ConnectToServer()          var exitButton = new TextButton { Text = Exit }         exitButton.Click += (s, a) => controller.ExitGame()          panel.Widgets.Add(title)         panel.Widgets.Add(playButton)         panel.Widgets.Add(exitButton)          Root = panel     } }  Then integrate it into the Desktop  var mainMenu = new MainMenuView(connectionController) _desktop.Root = mainMenu.Root  At this stage you might still have Gwen running for other screens, but the main menu is now using Myra instead.  Integrate input handling  Gwen typically has explicit input passing from the game to the Gwen canvas, for example  _canvas.InputMouseMoved(mouseX, mouseY, deltaX, deltaY) _canvas.InputMouseButtonDown(mouseButton) _canvas.InputMouseButtonUp(mouseButton) _canvas.InputKeyDown(key) _canvas.InputKeyUp(key)  Myra on MonoGame usually hooks directly via Desktop, often without explicit per event calls, but in some setups you route input yourself.  For Myra with MonoGame  Ensure that MyraEnvironment.Game is set to your Game instance. Myra has built-in input handlers that read Mouse and Keyboard states from MonoGame by default. If you are using custom input handling in Intersect, verify that Myra is seeing correct values by testing buttons and text input.  If you must route input manually, check Myra documentation for how to forward events, but generally the default integration is simpler than Gwen.  Rendering pipeline adjustments  Gwen used its own renderer implementation that took a GraphicsDevice and applied its own SpriteBatch logic.  With Myra your main tasks  Ensure that GraphicsDevice parameters such as viewport size and resolution are consistent with the game world. On window resize or resolution change, you may need to adjust Desktop.Bounds or update layout.  Myra Desktop usually handles resizing automatically if you set  _desktop.Bounds = new Rectangle(0, 0, GraphicsDevice.PresentationParameters.BackBufferWidth, GraphicsDevice.PresentationParameters.BackBufferHeight)  Call this in your Resize or in Update when window size changes. In Intersect, see where Gwen canvas was resized and replicate that logic to Myra Desktop.  Styling and theming  Gwen uses skins for visual appearance. Intersect likely has a Gwen skin residing in some resource folder with images and style definitions.  Myra uses stylesheets that can be JSON or binary resources. You can  Start with the default Myra theme and later customize. Create a resource through the Myra UI editor or by hand. Load style file at startup  var uiResource = MyraResource.Load<DesktopTheme>(Content.Load<RawAsset>(mytheme)) MyraEnvironment.Style = uiResource  Or use a standard approach documented by Myra. The exact API may differ by version.  To roughly match existing Gwen appearance  Export colors and fonts from Gwen skin definitions and apply them to Myra style. Replace Gwen textures with Myra nine-patch or texture regions for buttons and panels.  This part is cosmetic, so you can postpone detailed theming until your functionality works.  Incremental migration strategy  Do not attempt to translate the entire Gwen UI into Myra in one pass. Instead  Introduce Myra and Desktop while leaving Gwen in place but disabled for screens you are replacing. Pick one subsystem, for example   Main menu   Login window   Character selection   In game HUD and chat   Inventory and character windows  For each subsystem  Recreate the layout as a Myra widget tree. Wire events to existing non UI logic. Test thoroughly. Remove the corresponding Gwen code only after the Myra version is stable.  During transition you can have a configuration switch, something like  UseMyraUI = true or false  So that you can temporarily revert to Gwen if needed, but ideally you fully commit once major screens are ported.  Dealing with complex layouts and advanced Gwen features  If Intersect uses advanced Gwen features like docking, splitters, drag and drop, tooltips, you need to find Myra equivalents or reimplement features.  For docking and splitters  Use SplitPane or Grid with adjustable column or row sizes. Use DockPanel for top bottom left right docking.  For drag and drop inventories  Myra supports event handling for mouse down move up. Implement custom drag logic using   Mouse position   Capturing mouse when dragging   Changing parent of widgets or updating item grid positions.  For tooltips  Myra has Tooltip like functionality via Tooltip or by showing a small floating panel on mouse over using Widget.MouseEntered and MouseLeft events.  Remove Gwen dependencies  Once all major UI areas are migrated  Search the solution for  Gwen. using Gwen any Gwen renderer or skin references.  Delete residual Gwen related code paths. Remove Gwen packages or projects from the solution and project references. If Gwen is brought in via source, delete its folders and references from the .csproj.  Clean and rebuild to ensure there are no Gwen types left.  Update build scripts and distribution  If the engine is distributed with Gwen dlls or Gwen content  Remove Gwen assemblies from the client distribution. Add Myra dlls to your distribution if not statically linked. Ensure Myra style and font assets are included in the content pipeline.  Also update any documentation for contributors so they know the engine now uses Myra instead of Gwen for UI.  Testing and debugging tips  Check z order  If your UI does not respond to clicks, verify that  Desktop.Root is set. Bounds are correct relative to the window size. Other rendering or input layers are not swallowing events before Myra can access them.  Check performance  If you notice frame drops  Profile SpriteBatch usage, ensure you are not creating huge numbers of widgets every frame. Reuse windows and panels rather than destroying and recreating them.  Check scaling and resolution independence  If Intersect already has its own scaling strategy, make sure the UI uses relative layout rather than hardcoded pixels where possible. This helps with different resolutions.  Summary migration checklist  Identify all Gwen usage in Intersect.Client and encapsulate UI behavior away from Gwen types. Add Myra via NuGet and initialize MyraEnvironment.Game and Desktop in the main Game class. Hook Desktop.Render in Draw and adjust Desktop.Bounds to match the backbuffer. Create Myra UI equivalents for each Gwen screen, one subsystem at a time, wiring events to existing game logic. Port complex interactions such as drag and drop or tabbed layouts using Myra widgets and custom event handling. Gradually remove Gwen code and references once Myra replacements are stable. Polish styling with Myra styles to visually approximate or improve upon Gwen based UI.  By following this staged approach you keep the engine runnable throughout the transition, reduce risk, and end up with a cleaner abstraction where game logic is not tightly coupled to the specific UI library. That will make future changes or theming far easier, even beyond the move from Gwen to Myra.
5|67: Overview This guide outlines one reasonable way to replace Gwen (the immediate-mode UI wrapper used in Intersect.Client) with Myra (a retained-mode UI toolkit) in the Intersect Engine client hosted at the AscensionGameDev repository. The focus is on moving from Gwen.Net controls and layout to Myra widgets and Desktop, integrating with MonoGame, and progressively migrating individual UI windows.  The gist of the migration:  You remove Gwen references and Gwen-based UI classes from the client You add Myra to the project and initialize a Myra Desktop in the main game You reimplement Gwen windows (menus, HUDs, dialog boxes) with Myra widgets and layout files You hook up existing game logic to Myra events instead of Gwen events You incrementally replace UI screens until Gwen is no longer referenced  Preparation  Clone Intersect.Engine repository and open the Intersect.Client project in your IDE. You should be able to build and run the client as-is before changing anything.  Find where Gwen is used  In Intersect.Client, search for:  using Gwen; using Gwen.Control; using Gwen.ControlInternal; using Gwen.Skin;  You will see Gwen usage in GUI managers, panels, windows (Admin panel, Inventory, Character window, etc.). These files form the basis for your migration list.  Set a migration strategy  Because the UI is large, try a phased approach rather than a big bang  Keep existing Gwen UI running and introduce Myra alongside it in a test screen Mirror one Gwen-based window into a Myra-based version Once stable, remove the Gwen version Repeat for all windows until Gwen is completely gone  Add Myra to Intersect.Client  Add the Myra package. With NuGet in the Intersect.Client project  Add reference to Myra MonoGame integration package (for example Myra or Myra.MonoGame depending on your target and Myra version). Check the Myra GitHub readme for the recommended package.  Ensure the following namespaces will be available  using Myra; using Myra.Graphics2D.UI; using Myra.Graphics2D.Brushes; using Myra.Graphics2D.TextureAtlases;  Remove or isolate Gwen dependencies  In Intersect.Client.csproj, remove Gwen references if they are project-level dependencies. If they are still needed during transition, keep them temporarily and only remove once all Gwen-based UI has been migrated.  Examine the Gwen UI infrastructure  Intersect typically centralizes GUI setup in something like a GuiManager or similar service. Inspect where Gwen Canvas, Skin, and Renderer are created, for example  A MonoGame-based Gwen renderer A root Canvas that holds all windows Code that calls canvas.Render or equivalent inside Draw Code that calls canvas.ProcessInput or equivalent inside Update  Make notes on  Where the Gwen root control is stored How Gwen controls are created and attached How events (click, value changed, window closed) are handled  Plan how Myra will mimic that structure  Myra uses a Desktop as the root widget that manages focus, input, and rendering. You can treat Myra.Desktop as the functional replacement for Gwen.Canvas.  Bootstrap Myra in the main client Game  In the main Game subclass of Intersect.Client (often GameRoot or something similar), integrate Myra in LoadContent and Draw/Update.  Initialization example (pseudo-code, adapt to your actual class names and methods)  In your Game constructor or LoadContent  MyraEnvironment.Game = this; _desktop = new Desktop();  Optionally load a style/theme for Myra from an .xk or .json asset if you want a consistent look.  If your game uses a centralized GuiManager, store Desktop there and give the rest of the UI system an accessor to it.  Wire Myra into the Update and Draw loops  In Update(GameTime gameTime)  _desktop.Update();  In Draw(GameTime gameTime)  GraphicsDevice.Clear(Color.Black);  or existing clear code  _spriteBatch.Begin();  according to your engine _desktop.Render(); _spriteBatch.End();  Make sure Myra uses the same SpriteBatch the rest of the game uses, or a compatible setup.  Create a Myra layout as a test screen  Before migrating complex windows, make a small test widget tree to validate Myra is working.  Example  var panel = new VerticalStackPanel {   Spacing = 8,   Padding = new Thickness(10) };  var label = new Label {   Text = Hello from Myra, };  var button = new TextButton {   Text = Click Me, };  button.Click += (s, a) => {   // Trigger some simple action, like a log or toggling a variable };  panel.Widgets.Add(label); panel.Widgets.Add(button);  _desktop.Root = panel;  Run the client and check if the button and label show and respond. When this is stable, you can start migrating real Gwen UI.  Understand Gwen vs Myra conceptual differences  Gwen is largely immediate-mode style  You build controls via classes like WindowControl, Button, Label You frequently set event handlers as delegates on controls Layout is typically anchored via docking, padding, margin  Myra is retained-mode  You build widgets that remain on the Desktop You use layout containers like HorizontalStackPanel, Grid, Panel You can define UI in code or in Myra layout (xk) files You use widget event handlers similarly (Click, TextChanged, etc.)  The mapping is generally straightforward  Gwen WindowControl maps to Myra Window Gwen Button maps to Myra TextButton or ImageTextButton Gwen Label maps to Myra Label Gwen TextBox maps to Myra TextBox Gwen ListBox/TreeControl maps to Myra ListBox/Tree Gwen Canvas or Panel maps to Myra Panel/StackPanel/Grid  Migrate a single Gwen window to Myra (example workflow)  Pick a simpler UI window (for example a settings or small dialog) as your first conversion. Suppose there is a Gwen class like OptionsWindow.  Identify the Gwen class  Find the C# file, check how it  Creates the window Adds child controls Binds data or game state Subscribes to events (button.Click += ...)  Create an equivalent Myra widget class  Create a new class OptionsWindowMyra derived from Widget or simply create a method that builds and returns a Myra Window.  Example  public static Myra.Graphics2D.UI.Window CreateOptionsWindow() {   var window = new Myra.Graphics2D.UI.Window   {     Title = Options,     Width = 400,     Height = 300,     IsDraggable = true,     // other properties   };    var mainPanel = new VerticalStackPanel   {     Spacing = 6,     Padding = new Thickness(8)   };    var soundLabel = new Label { Text = Sound Volume };   var soundSlider = new HorizontalSlider   {     Minimum = 0,     Maximum = 100,     Value = currentVolume   };    soundSlider.ValueChanged += (s, a) =>   {     // Update game volume setting   };    var okButton = new TextButton { Text = OK };   okButton.Click += (s, a) =>   {     // Apply settings and close window     window.Visible = false;   };    mainPanel.Widgets.Add(soundLabel);   mainPanel.Widgets.Add(soundSlider);   mainPanel.Widgets.Add(okButton);    window.Content = mainPanel;    return window; }  Hook this window into the Desktop  When the game needs to show options, instead of creating Gwen OptionsWindow, you will instantiate CreateOptionsWindow and add it to Desktop  var optionsWindow = CreateOptionsWindow(); _desktop.Widgets.Add(optionsWindow);  If you want to open and close repeatedly, you might keep a reference to this window in a GUI manager class and toggle its Visible flag.  Map existing Gwen event handlers to Myra events  For each Gwen control  button.Clicked += OnSomeAction;  Find the corresponding places in the game where those handlers reference game state. Rewire them in Myra  myraButton.Click += (s, a) => OnSomeAction();  Remove Gwen-specific API usage such as Docking that has no direct analog  Gwen Dock enumeration may be replaced with Myra layout containers Dock.Fill  use Grid or adjust Panel to stretched alignment Dock.Top  use VerticalStackPanel and add widget at the top Dock.Left  use HorizontalStackPanel or Grid  In some cases you will need to nest Panel, HorizontalStackPanel, VerticalStackPanel, and Grid to achieve the same layout but the logic remains similar.  Use Myra layout templates for complex UI  If you want designers to modify layouts without recompiling, use Myra layout files (.xk or .json) created from MyraPad (the Myra editor). The process  Open MyraPad, design the UI visually (buttons, labels, etc.) Export a .xk layout Add that layout file to your Content project and ensure it is copied/loaded  In code  var xml = AssetManager.LoadRaw(myraOptionsLayout.xk);   pseudo var project = MyraSerialization.Load<Desktop>(xml); _desktop = project;  or load as root widget instead of building via code.  Gradual replacement for all Gwen windows  Repeat the previous pattern for each Gwen-driven UI component  HUD (health bar, mana bar, experience bar) Inventory window Character / stats window Chat window Admin panels Dialog and quest windows Crafting, trade, bank, etc.  For each  Locate Gwen-based class Recreate layout and controls with Myra widgets Rebind event handlers and data bindings Replace Gwen creation calls with Myra widget instantiation and Desktop.Widgets.Add  Input handling and focus  Gwen may have its own input router. Myra hooks into MonoGame input via Desktop.Update and MyraEnvironment, relying on Mouse and Keyboard states from MonoGame. Ensure that  Your game does not keep forwarding keyboard/mouse events exclusively to Gwen You call Desktop.Update before or after your own input handling (but not after Gwen, once removed) You decide how to handle UI focus vs. game-world input. Typically, when Desktop.HasFocusedWidget is true, you suppress game-world keyboard input.  Styling and skins  Intersect with Gwen uses skins (texture atlases, colors) for UI appearance. Myra uses  Styles loaded from resources (JSON-based) and Texture atlases for images  Strategy  Either create new Myra styles and textures approximating Gwen look Or adopt a new Myra theme for the client UI  Define theme files and set them globally or per widget tree.  Performance considerations  Myra is efficient enough for typical 2D MMO UI workloads, but  Keep the number of simultaneously visible complex windows reasonable Avoid building and discarding widgets in tight loops; reuse where possible Call Desktop.Render inside the main SpriteBatch usage in a consistent way  Remove Gwen dependencies fully  Once all Gwen-based windows are replaced and you do not rely on any Gwen types  Remove Gwen references from Intersect.Client.csproj Delete Gwen wrapper code and Gwen renderer classes Search your solution for Gwen to ensure there are no lingering references  Test edge cases  Test  Window resizing (if applicable) Switching UI language (if your localization system changes text at runtime) Resolution scaling and UI scale options Input when multiple windows overlap and focus behavior Interaction between Myra UI and in-game shortcuts (ESC, inventory key, chat key, etc.)  Adapting to Intersect-specific code  Because the engine is actively maintained, always check the latest code for  Where UI is initialized (may be in a GUIManager, Interface, or similar class) How hotkeys and input are wired to UI actions How the client obtains fonts, textures, and colors  Map these to Myra constructs  Fonts: use SpriteFont or Myra font wrappers Textures: build TextureAtlases or assign textures directly to Image widgets Colors: use Myra brushes and set widget Background/Foreground where needed  Example mapping for a typical HUD element  Suppose HUDHealthBar is a Gwen ProgressBar. You can build a similar Myra widget  var healthBar = new ProgressBar {   Minimum = 0,   Maximum = player.MaxHp,   Value = player.CurrentHp,   Width = 200,   Height = 16, };  Bind it to game update logic  healthBar.Value = player.CurrentHp;  Place it in a panel anchored to top-left of the screen. For example, set Desktop.Root to a main Grid with areas for HUD, chat, etc., and put the health bar into the top row.  Practical tips  Migrate one type of screen at a time so you always have a working client Keep Gwen and Myra side-by-side initially, but ensure they do not both consume the same input in conflicting ways Use MyraPad to quickly prototype complex dialogs and then integrate them into the engine Write thin adapter methods to translate game events (OnOpenInventory, OnShowDialog) into Desktop widget creation and visibility toggling  Summary migration checklist  Add Myra packages to Intersect.Client Initialize MyraEnvironment and create Desktop in the main Game Render Desktop in Draw and call Desktop.Update in Update Create a simple Myra test layout to confirm wiring For each Gwen window   Analyze layout and events   Rebuild with Myra widgets (code or layout file)   Reconnect event handlers to existing game logic   Replace Gwen instantiation with Myra instantiation   Remove Gwen-specific docking and canvas references Gradually delete all Gwen references and renderer code Finalize styling, scaling, and input focus handling  Following this process, you convert Intersect.Client from Gwen to Myra in a controlled, incremental way, while preserving all gameplay behavior and only replacing the presentation layer and UI framework.
6|67: Overview This guide describes an approach to migrating the Intersect Engine client from Gwen (a C# immediate mode GUI library) to Myra (a retained mode UI library built on top of MonoGame/FNA). The goal is to:  - Keep engine architecture intact as much as possible - Replace Gwen types, layout, and skinning with Myra equivalents - Gradually port UI widgets and logic  Because UI in Intersect is tightly coupled to Gwen, the migration is non-trivial. Treat this as a roadmap and pattern catalog rather than a copy-paste script.  Prerequisites - Working build of Intersect.Client from the repository - Understanding of how the current Gwen UI is structured - Basic familiarity with MonoGame (or at least the Intersect rendering layer) - Myra basics: widgets, Desktop, layout, and event handling  High-level plan - Introduce Myra as a dependency alongside Gwen - Integrate Myra rendering into the Intersect client render/update loop - Introduce mapping from Gwen concepts to Myra concepts - Incrementally replace Gwen windows and controls with Myra counterparts - Remove Gwen references once all UI elements are ported  Step 1: Add Myra to the Intersect client project - In Intersect.Client, add a reference to Myra   - If using NuGet: add package Myra to Intersect.Client   - If using source: clone the Myra repository, add the Myra project to the solution, and reference it from Intersect.Client  - Ensure Myra targets are compatible with your runtime (net framework/core used by Intersect)  - Verify that Myra content (fonts, textures) can be loaded using the same content pipeline or via raw file loading from the client content directory  Step 2: Identify Gwen integration points in Intersect.Client Search for usages of Gwen types and namespaces, e.g. - Gwen - Gwen.Control - Gwen.Skin - Gwen.Renderer  Typical areas to examine in Intersect.Client - UI initialization (where Gwen renderer and skin are initialized) - Any Screen, UiManager, or GameInterface class that holds references to Gwen Canvas or Gwen controls - Event wiring: button click handlers, text fields, etc. - The main Update and Draw methods of the client, where Gwen UI is updated and rendered  Document or list all windows, dialogs, and panels that use Gwen, for example: - Login window - Character selection window - Game HUD (status bars, chat, hotbar, etc.) - Settings and options menus  This will be your migration checklist.  Step 3: Integrate Myra into the rendering pipeline Myra is usually driven by a Desktop instance that you update and render each frame.  Core concepts to map - Gwen.Canvas ≈ Myra.Desktop - Gwen controls ≈ Myra widgets (Panel, Grid, Label, Button, TextBox, etc.) - Gwen skinning ≈ Myra UI styles and themes  In the main client Game (or equivalent class used by Intersect): - Create a field of type Myra.Graphics2D.UI.Desktop - Instantiate it during client initialization, once graphics and content are available  Pseudo-structure - In client initialization   - Load a Myra style (optional). For example, using Myra built-in styles or a custom .xk theme file stored with client UI resources   - Create a Desktop   - Assign its Root control to some initial root widget, such as a Panel or Grid that is your top-level container  - In Update   - Call desktop.Update() with appropriate GameTime or equivalent  - In Draw   - Ensure SpriteBatch is configured similarly to how Myra expects (usually immediate mode or using provided Myra draw flow)   - Call desktop.Render()  You can run Myra side by side with Gwen temporarily for testing. For example, draw Gwen UI, then Myra above it (or vice versa) until you fully migrate.  Step 4: Establish a mapping between Gwen and Myra widgets Before rewriting windows, decide how Gwen controls correspond to Myra widgets. Rough guideline: - Gwen.Canvas → Desktop.Root (some layout container, often Grid or Panel) - Gwen.Control.Base → Myra Widget - Gwen.Control.Label → Myra Label - Gwen.Control.Button → Myra TextButton or regular Button - Gwen.Control.TextBox → Myra TextBox - Gwen.Control.CheckBox → Myra CheckBox - Gwen.Control.ComboBox → Myra ComboBox - Gwen.Control.ListBox → Myra ListBox - Gwen.Control.TabControl → Myra TabControl - Gwen.Control.WindowControl → Myra Window - Gwen.Control.Menu/ContextMenu → Myra Menu / MenuItem - Gwen.Control.StatusBar/ProgressBar → Myra ProgressBar  Layout mapping - Gwen uses docking, margins, padding, and layout containers - Myra uses layout containers such as   - VerticalStackPanel / HorizontalStackPanel   - Grid   - Panel (absolute positioning)  You must decide whether to preserve exact pixel-perfect layout or take the opportunity to modernize UI layout. Using Myra Grid and StackPanels often makes complex windows easier to manage.  Step 5: Migrate a simple window first Start with a small dialog (for example a simple message box or settings subpanel) to establish a repeatable pattern.  Process pattern - Locate Gwen window class (for example, a class that creates a Gwen.WindowControl with child controls) - Recreate the same window as a Myra Window   - Create a new C# class for the Myra-based window   - Build layout using Myra widgets   - Wire the same events (button clicks, text changed, etc.) to existing engine logic  - Ensure show/hide logic is triggered by the same game events. Instead of referencing the Gwen window instance, you reference the Myra window instance.  - Temporarily keep both versions (Gwen and Myra) behind a compile-time flag or configuration, so you can switch for debugging until satisfied  Example structure for a Myra window - A Window widget with Title - Inner layout container, e.g. Grid with Rows/Columns - Labels, TextBoxes, Buttons arranged in Grid - Events like button.Click += ... or textBox.TextChanged += ...  Test - Run the client - Confirm that the Myra window appears at the appropriate time and responds correctly  Step 6: Create a central UI manager for Myra widgets Intersect already has some form of UI manager for Gwen. You can parallel this with a Myra-focused manager or adapt the existing one.  Responsibilities - Own the Desktop instance - Manage references to common windows and panels (login, character select, HUD, inventory, chat, etc.) - Provide helper methods like ShowLoginWindow, ShowInventoryWindow, ToggleChat, etc. - Handle global input routing where needed (e.g. keyboard capture when a TextBox is focused)  If the existing Gwen UI manager is tightly coupled to Gwen types, consider: - Introducing an abstract interface for UI windows and having separate Gwen and Myra implementations, then gradually move references to abstract interfaces - Or directly updating the manager to use Myra and rewriting the windows one by one, leaving Gwen only on windows not yet ported  Step 7: Replace core screens (login, character select, main HUD) After proving the approach with a small dialog, move to key UI screens.  For each screen - Inspect the existing Gwen code for layout and logic - Decide a Myra layout (a combination of Grid, Panels, and StackPanels) that approximates current UI - Recreate widgets and event handlers  Common pitfalls - Absolute vs. relative positions: if Gwen code uses explicit coordinates, Myra Panel with absolute positioning might be easiest to start with. Later, you can refactor to Grid-based, responsive layouts - Font and text rendering: ensure fonts used by Gwen are available or replicated for Myra. You may need TTF to bitmap conversion using MonoGame pipeline or Myra font loaders - Input focus: Myra handles focus internally; ensure that the main game or other subsystems do not steal focus from UI when a text box is active  Step 8: Port HUD and in-game UI overlays The HUD (health bars, mana bars, hotbars, chat box, minimap, etc.) is usually a Gwen Canvas with multiple nested controls anchored to corners.  Strategy - Create a dedicated Myra root container for HUD, for example a Grid using Rows and Columns corresponding to screen regions, or an overlay Panel that uses anchored absolute positions - Implement each HUD component as a separate Myra widget or user control-like helper class   - Example: HealthBarWidget, ManaBarWidget, HotbarWidget, ChatWidget  - Wire them to game state updates   - HP and MP update events trigger ProgressBar or custom bar controls   - Inventory and hotbar update icons/buttons   - Chat incoming messages append to ListBox or custom scrollable text view  Rendering and layering - Ensure the order of drawing is correct so HUD appears on top of world rendering - If game currently draws Gwen last, ensure Myra Desktop.Render() is called at the same stage or after equivalent world-draw calls  Step 9: Events and input migration Gwen and Myra have different event models, but conceptually they map closely.  Typical conversions - Gwen: button.Clicked += (sender, args) => ...   Myra: button.Click += (sender, args) => ...  - Gwen: textBox.SubmitPressed   Myra: textBox.TextChanged or hooking keyboard events at Desktop level  - Gwen: context menu open/close events   Myra: MenuItem.Selected, custom logic  Input routing - Ensure that the main game input system defers to Myra when UI elements need to capture keyboard/mouse, particularly for text entry, dragging, and selecting. - Myra usually intercepts input via Desktop.Update. Confirm that mouse and keyboard state passed into Myra is consistent with what the engine uses.  Step 10: Skinning and theming Gwen uses skins (texture packs + style definitions); Myra uses themes defined via resources (xk style files) and can use texture atlases as well.  Options - Start with default Myra theme for simplicity - Gradually define a custom theme to match Intersect existing look   - Create or adapt a Myra theme file (XML-based) describing colors, paddings, fonts, etc.   - Place the theme file and resource textures into the Intersect client content tree   - Load the theme at startup and assign it globally, or to individual widgets  - If Intersect uses custom Gwen textures for windows and buttons, you can cut them into Myra style textures or keep them as backgrounds for Panels and Windows via Image widgets or background images.  Step 11: Remove Gwen dependencies gradually Only after most UI has been ported should you remove Gwen.  Checklist - Confirm all primary windows and HUD elements have Myra versions and are wired correctly - Remove Gwen window creation code and any conditionals that switched between Gwen and Myra - Remove Gwen-specific fields from UI manager classes - Remove Gwen references from project files and usings  Validate that - The client builds without Gwen - No runtime errors occur from missing Gwen types or initialization  Step 12: Testing and debugging strategies UI migrations are error-prone. Use systematic testing: - Smoke tests for main flows: login, character creation, joining world, combat, inventory management, chat - Check that keyboard shortcuts, ESC menus, and popup dialogs all still work - Inspect different resolutions and windowed vs. full-screen modes  Debugging tips - Temporarily draw debug rectangles or backgrounds in Myra layout containers to visually see margins and alignment - Log focus changes and event triggers for problem widgets - Compare side-by-side screens from old Gwen version and new Myra version for alignment and aesthetics  Step 13: Optional enhancements and refinements Once Myra is in place and stable, you can - Improve layout with responsive Grids instead of absolute positions - Add animation or transition effects manually (Myra does not provide heavy animation out of the box, but you can code transitions in the game loop) - Introduce reusable user controls for common UI patterns - Localize text with the same or improved system, since Myra labels can be easily updated at runtime  Practical advice for working inside the Intersect codebase - Study existing Gwen UI code in Intersect.Client to understand where logic is intertwined with UI - When creating Myra windows, keep business logic in separate classes or services; the UI layer should bind to them or call them, not contain all logic - Use partial classes or separate files to avoid huge UI code blocks in a single file; consider building some UI in code and some from Myra UI XML if you prefer  Summary - Add Myra to Intersect.Client and wire a Desktop into the main game loop - Map Gwen canvas and controls to Myra Desktop and widgets - Start by migrating a small window, then the main screens and HUD - Introduce a robust UI manager for Myra instances - Recreate events and bindings from Gwen in Myra - Update skinning and themes to match the existing style - Remove Gwen only after all essential UI is ported and tested  Because both projects (Intersect-Engine and Myra) evolve, the precise namespaces and API calls may differ slightly from this description. Use this as a conceptual migration guide, then adapt to the exact version of each library you are working with.
