Gwen.Control.TabControl → Myra.TabControl - Layout containers (DockLayout, Grid, etc.) → Myra.Panel, Grid, HorizontalStackPanel, VerticalStackPanel  Decide on layout definition style Options - Code-based layouts: Build all UI in C# code, mirroring Gwen layout logic - Resource-based layouts: Use Myra .xmb (or alternative) files to define windows and load them at runtime A realistic approach for a first pass - Port layouts in code first for correctness - Later, migrate stable windows to Myra resource files  Step 5: Port core infrastructure from Gwen to Myra Replace Gwen renderer and skin initialization Locate Gwen initialization code in the Intersect client - Typically you will see something like   - Initialize Gwen Renderer with GraphicsDevice   - Load Gwen skin from resources   - Create root Canvas Plan how Myra takes over - You no longer need a Gwen renderer or canvas - Myra uses Desktop as the root container - Styling works via themes/stylesheets rather than Gwen skins  Create a Myra theme that approximates Gwen look - Check Myra samples for how to define and load themes - Use a basic default theme at first, do not aim for perfect visual parity early on  Wire Myra Desktop where Gwen root canvas was referenced - Any place you had a top-level Gwen canvas for showing child windows, now attach them to Desktop.Root or use containers within it  Step 6: Incrementally port individual windows and widgets Adopt a staged migration strategy rather than rewriting everything at once.  Choose a simple, low-risk window to port first For example - A simple options/settings dialog - A small status HUD panel Process - Open the Gwen-based implementation - Identify layout and controls   - Which controls exist   - What properties they use (anchors, docking, padding, visibility, etc.)   - What events are handled (button clicks, text changed, etc.)  Create a corresponding Myra class - Under the same or parallel namespace (e.g., Intersect.Client.Interface.Myra) - Create a class like OptionsWindowMyra extending a small helper base type that knows how to hook into Desktop  Replicate layout - For each Gwen layout construct, find a Myra equivalent   - Gwen.DockLayout → Myra.Grid or Panel with alignments   - Gwen.Grid → Myra.Grid   - Gwen.VerticalLayout → Myra.VerticalStackPanel   - Gwen.HorizontalLayout → Myra.HorizontalStackPanel - Keep the same basic arrangement, but be flexible with exact sizes; Myra layout rules may differ  Wire events - Replace Gwen event handlers   - gwenButton.Clicked += OnClicked; With Myra events   - myraButton.Click += (s, a) => OnClicked(); Adjust signatures as needed  Connect with game logic - Ensure any calls the game makes to the Gwen window (e.g., optionsWindow.Show(), optionsWindow.SetVolume(float)) are now routed to the Myra implementation - If using an interface abstraction, point the injection/factory to the Myra-based implementation instead of Gwen-based  Test thoroughly in-game - Confirm the window appears and behaves as expected - Fix visual alignment - Validate that closing, opening, and focus/keyboard handling work as required  Repeat for more important windows Port windows roughly in this order - Login / registration UI - Main HUD (health, mana, experience, hotbar) - Chat window - Inventory, spells, equipment, character sheet - NPC dialogue, trade, bank, shops - Admin and debug tools  After each window or group is ported - Remove or comment out its Gwen version - Replace references in the UI factory to create the Myra version  Step 7: Input and focus integration Ensure input is not double-handled - Once a given screen or window is fully Myra-based, remove or disable the corresponding Gwen controls and event hooks for that screen Focus and keyboard handling - Verify tab navigation (if used) works in Myra - Check that pressing escape or other hotkeys properly closes Myra windows, just as Gwen windows did Mouse handling - Confirm that click-through behavior matches expectations   - Example: HUD elements intercept clicks, but world clicking still works when clicking on empty UI areas If world clicking is blocked incorrectly - Adjust hit testing or event consumption rules in Myra - Make sure you recognize when the pointer is over Myra UI and suppress world input only then  Step 8: HUD and always-on UI elements HUD porting is special because it is always visible and tightly bound to game state.  Port status bars and overlays - Health, mana, XP bars - Mini-map (if present) - Compass, notifications Use Myra widgets such as - ProgressBar or custom drawn Panel with width proportional to percentage - Labels for text values  Tie updates to game state - Wherever Gwen controls were previously updated in the HUD update logic   - healthBar.Value = player.Health; Replace with Myra equivalents   - myraHealthBar.Value = player.Health; Or your custom widgets interface  Positioning - Use anchors, horizontal/vertical alignment, or fixed coordinates inside Panels depending on what Intersect previously did with Gwen - Check aspect ratios and multiple resolutions; Myra layout should be resolution-agnostic as much as possible  Step 9: Resource management and performance Ensure UI creation is not repeated every frame - Create Myra UI elements once (on screen open or game start) - Update only properties (e.g., text, value, visibility) during Update Minimize layout thrash - Avoid constantly adding/removing large numbers of widgets every frame - Use visibility toggles instead of destroy/recreate when possible Profile if available - Confirm UI rendering does not significantly impact framerate compared to the Gwen version  Step 10: Remove Gwen-specific references Once all visible UI elements are Myra-based and tested - Remove Gwen initialization code - Delete Gwen renderer, skin, and canvas setup - Remove Gwen input handlers - Remove or archive Gwen-based controls and windows Update project references - Remove the Gwen library from references (DLL, NuGet, or submodule) - Clean up any residual using Gwen.* statements Build and run to ensure no leftover dependencies  Step 11: Styling and polish Create or refine a Myra theme that matches your desired look - Colors, fonts, paddings, borders - Button hover/pressed states, textboxes, scrollbars Load theme at startup - Use Myra APIs to load your stylesheet/resource Ensure consistency - Same font sizes across HUD and windows - Consistent margins and alignments  Step 12: Documentation and maintenance Write a short internal guide for future developers - Where Myra is initialized - How to create a new window - How to add controls, bind events, and hook game logic Include notes about - Which Myra version is used - Any engine-specific helper wrappers you built (e.g., UIFactory, abstract interfaces)  Common pitfalls and how to avoid them Difference in layout semantics - Gwen dock/anchor behavior will not map 1:1 to Myra; accept small layout differences, focus on functionality first Input conflicts - Make sure only one UI framework is active at any time; during the migration, guard input forwarding with flags Direct control references from game logic - If game code references Gwen controls too deeply, you may need to introduce a middle abstraction layer to cleanly swap implementations Chasing pixel-perfect parity too early - Prioritize migrating behavior and gameplay functionality, then refine the visuals and spacing  Suggested incremental workflow summary - Integrate Myra into Intersect.Client, create Desktop, and render a basic test UI - Introduce a thin UI abstraction where possible to reduce engine-wide changes - Port one simple window from Gwen to Myra and wire it into the game - Once stable, port key windows one by one (login, HUD, inventory, chat, etc.) - Gradually remove the Gwen infrastructure as soon as each major area is fully Myra-based - Clean up references, optimize layouts, and finalize theme  By following this staged approach, you replace Gwen with Myra without breaking gameplay, and you end up with a maintainable Myra-based UI layer integrated cleanly into Intersect’s client.
8|67: Below is a conceptual guide on how to replace Gwen with Myra in the Intersect client. It focuses on locating Gwen usage, wiring Myra into the engine, migrating controls and layouts, and dealing with event/input/rendering differences. You will still need to adapt exact class names and namespaces to match the current versions of both Intersect and Myra.  Locate and isolate Gwen usage  Inspect the Intersect.Client project structure Search for references to Gwen and Gwen.Control in the Intersect.Client project. Typical places: Intersect.Client.Interface Intersect.Client.Interface.Game Intersect.Client.Interface.Menu Any GuiManager, Interface or UISystem classes that own the root Gwen canvas Anywhere that constructs a Gwen.Skin object or Gwen.Renderer Note the following while reading the code: How the root UI is created (probably a Gwen Canvas or similar) How themes/skins are loaded and applied How input is fed into Gwen (mouse, keyboard, text input) How Gwen is updated and rendered each frame How screens are organized (e.g. login, character select, in-game HUD) Create a temporary UML or a small text sketch of: What class creates/owns the UI root What UI layers exist How UI instances are activated/deactivated  Add Myra to the project  In the Intersect.Client project, add Myra via NuGet or by referencing the project If you are using .NET and NuGet, from the client project directory:  Install Myra via your package manager Ensure the correct framework version matches your client  If you are compiling Myra from source: Clone https github.com/rds1983/Myra Add the Myra project to your solution Add a project reference from Intersect.Client to Myra  Adjust the client to initialize Myra Find the main game class in the client. In older Intersect versions, this is typically a MonoGame Game subclass, often named IntersectGame, Client, or similar. This class usually: Initializes the graphics device Initializes Gwen Runs the update and draw loops Locate where Gwen is initialized. Often you will see something like:  Creation of a Gwen.Renderer based on the MonoGame graphics device Creation of a Gwen.Skin Creation of a Gwen.Canvas as the root  Remove the Gwen initialization logic and replace it with Myra setup.  Basic Myra initialization pattern  Myra is commonly used with MonoGame. A typical initialization in the Game constructor or LoadContent method looks like this, translated into Intersect style terms, not literal code  Create the MyraUI singleton or root Set MyraEnvironment.Game to your Game instance, if you use that pattern Create a Desktop instance Desktop is the top-level widget/container that receives input and draws everything Assign the created Desktop to a field in your game class, such as _uiDesktop  Example structure in pseudo-code without real quotes  In your game class constructor or Initialize  Call MyraEnvironment.Game equals this Create new Desktop instance and store into a Desktop field  In LoadContent  Optionally load UI assets (textures, fonts) for Myra if you are not using the built-in ones  In Update  Feed input state into Desktop (more details below)  In Draw  Call Desktop.Render  You must align this with how Intersect already structures its update and render.  Input integration  Gwen currently receives input from MonoGame via an input handler. You need to: Inspect where Intersect converts MonoGame MouseState, KeyboardState, and possibly TextInput events into Gwen input Replace those Gwen-oriented calls with Myra input handling  Mouse input  Myra Desktop uses MonoGame input state. If you use the built-in Myra input integration, you can simply set  Desktop.Bounds to match the viewport Desktop.MousePosition based on Mouse.GetState Desktop.HandleMouseMoved, HandleMouseDown, HandleMouseUp, etc., as needed  Or you may use MyraIntegration classes if present. Review Myra samples to see the recommended approach for the version you use.  Keyboard input  In the Game constructor, subscribe to Window.TextInput and KeyDown/KeyUp if needed Forward those events to Desktop  For example, in conceptual form  When the Window receives text input Call Desktop.OnChar with that character  When a key is pressed or released Call Desktop.OnKeyUpOrDown with the key  Focus management  Gwen has its own focus model. Myra uses Desktop.FocusedWidget. Intersect code that previously queried Gwen focus may need to be updated to use Desktop.FocusedWidget or other Myra APIs to determine whether input should be captured by UI or by the game world.  Rendering integration  Gwen rendering is usually integrated via a Gwen-specific renderer using SpriteBatch. Myra uses SpriteBatch as well, but manages its own drawing passes. General pattern in the game Draw method:  Clear the screen Draw the world (maps, entities, etc.) Begin a SpriteBatch for UI (if Myra requires manual SpriteBatch management in that version) or let Myra manage its internal SpriteBatch Call Desktop.Render End SpriteBatch if you began it manually  Check your version of Myra to see whether Desktop.Render begins/ends SpriteBatch internally or requires a SpriteBatch instance.  If Gwen currently uses a separate RenderTarget or scissor logic, map any such requirements to Myra. Myra supports clipping and layout; in most cases, you just render Desktop and it handles clipping.  Theme and visual design  Gwen skins vs Myra styles  Intersect likely uses Gwen skins (textures, XML definitions, etc). You will need to: Identify where the Gwen skin textures reside, often in a resource folder Identify how they are loaded and tied to controls Myra uses themes and style sheets defined via JSON or code. You can Create a new theme JSON file that references your textures Or initially use Myras builtin default theme to get the UI functional  Steps to start simple  Remove Gwen skin loading Let Myra use its default theme Focus on functionality first (all UI works, even if it looks different) After everything works, create a Myra theme that matches the games style and wire it up by Loading a Theme object from a JSON file Applying it to Desktop or individual widgets  Widget/control mapping  Identify Gwen controls currently used  Panels, labels, textboxes, buttons, list boxes, combo boxes Windows/dialogs for inventory, character, shop, chat, etc. Custom controls for Intersect like spell bars, hotbars, etc.  Map them to Myra widgets  Gwen Label -> Myra Label Gwen Button -> Myra TextButton or ImageTextButton Gwen TextBox -> Myra TextBox Gwen ListBox -> Myra ListView or ListBox equivalent Gwen TreeControl -> Myra TreeView Gwen WindowControl -> Myra Window  Layout containers  Gwen uses containers like DockLayout, GridLayout, VerticalLayout, etc., depending on how Intersect uses Gwen. Myra also has: HorizontalStackPanel, VerticalStackPanel Grid Panel (absolute positioning) SplitPane  For each Gwen-based UI screen  Open the code that builds its controls Identify which layout system is used Rebuild the layout with Myra equivalents  For example, if the old code did  Create a Gwen Canvas/Panel as root for that screen Dock menu to top, chat to bottom, hotbar to bottom center, etc.  You can: Create a Myra Panel or Grid as the screen root Add child widgets to the appropriate rows/columns or attach to alignment properties  Screen management and UI states  Intersect typically has multiple UI screens  Menus (main menu, login, registration) Pre-game character selection In-game HUD, inventory, craft dialog, trade dialog, etc.  With Gwen, each of these may be either: Separate canvases Separate windows created under the same root canvas Separate interface manager classes that show/hide groups of controls  With Myra Desktop, adopt one of two main strategies  Single Desktop  Use just one Desktop instance for the entire UI layer Maintain separate root containers (Panels or Windows) for each logical screen Attach/detach or show/hide containers when screens change Example for login screen Create a Panel named loginPanel, add controls for login When moving to game screen, set loginPanel.Visible to false and gameHudPanel.Visible to true  Multiple Desktop instances  Create different Desktop instances for different layers Swap the active Desktop in your game class when switching states This can be heavier but may be conceptually simpler  Decide which strategy fits Intersects existing design best  If there is a central InterfaceManager that handles screen changes, single Desktop with multiple root panels is usually cleaner  Events and logic binding  Gwen event model vs Myra  Gwen uses events like Button.Released += handler TextBox.SubmitPressed, etc.  Myra uses event patterns such as MyButton.Click += handler MyTextBox.TextChanged += handler  Migration steps  Search for Gwen event subscriptions For each one, note the logic in the handler Replace the Gwen control type with the Myra control type Subscribe to the closest Myra event  For example, a login button  Old Gwen pattern (described abstractly)  Create Gwen Button btnLogin btnLogin.Released += OnLoginButtonReleased  New Myra pattern  Create Myra TextButton loginButton loginButton.Text equals Login loginButton.Click += OnLoginButtonClick  Where OnLoginButtonClick calls the same login logic that was previously triggered by OnLoginButtonReleased.  Text input patterns  For text fields that submit on Enter In Gwen, there might be events like TextBox.SubmitPressed In Myra, use TextBox.KeyDown or Desktop.Window.KeyDown Detect Enter key and manually trigger the logic  Focus and tab ordering  If Intersect uses Gwen features for tab focus, you may need to Set TabIndex or similar properties on Myra widgets, if present Or manually move focus on key events (for example, when Tab is pressed, call Desktop.FocusNextWidget)  Complex windows: inventory, hotbars, drag and drop  These are the trickiest part.  Inventory grid  If Intersect uses Gwen to define an inventory grid with image buttons and tooltips, port it by: Using a Grid widget in Myra Create ImageButtons or custom widgets for each inventory slot Bind your item data (icon texture, quantity text) to the slot widget Subscribe to Click, MouseEnter, MouseLeave for tooltips and item actions  Drag and drop  If Gwen was used for drag and drop, examine how that logic is implemented. It might be engine-provided or custom. Myra can handle drag and drop manually On mouse down, mark the item as being dragged During mouse move, render a dragging icon at the cursor in a separate overlay panel On mouse up, detect which slot your cursor is over and drop item there This might be mostly game logic, with UI only responsible for forwarding events and giving slot rectangles.  Hotbars and spell bars  Map Gwen buttons to ImageButtons or custom widgets Add right-click, left-click, and tooltip behavior just like inventory Use a horizontal Grid or HorizontalStackPanel  Tooltips  Gwen likely had a dedicated tooltip system. For Myra, you can Create a hidden Panel or Window that contains a Label (and maybe an image) On MouseEnter of a widget, set the Panel.Visible to true and position it near the cursor On MouseLeave, hide it Optional On MouseMove, update its position to follow cursor  Adapting the architecture cleanly  Introduce an abstract UI layer  To keep the rest of the game code less dependent on the UI library, consider introducing an abstraction layer. For example, create interfaces like IButton, ILabel, ITextBox, IWindow, IPanel, IUIRoot Provide two implementations One based on Gwen (current) One based on Myra  Refactor non-UI-specific gameplay code (like the login logic or inventory logic) to depend on the interfaces rather than on Gwen directly. Then switch the implementation to Myra.  If that is too big a refactor for now, at least centralize Myra-specific code in a small number of classes, such as MyraInterfaceManager, instead of scattering Myra widgets everywhere.  Stepwise migration strategy  To reduce breakage, migrate in small steps: Start with a non-critical screen, like the main menu Implement the Myra version of that screen in parallel with Gwen Add a configuration flag or compile symbol that can switch between Gwen and Myra for that screen Once stable, move to the login and character selection Next, tackle HUD and static dialogs Last, migrate complex, interaction-heavy windows like inventory, spells, quests After everything is ported, remove Gwen and its references from the project  Practical checklist  Set up Myra in the project and verify it renders a test button over the game Route basic mouse and keyboard events to Desktop Port one simple Gwen window to Myra using simple controls and layout Verify events (click, text change) trigger the same gameplay logic as before Create a basic global theme or use defaults Port major screens one by one Port complex windows (inventory, hotbar, drag and drop, tooltips) Verify focus and input interactions with the world (e.g., clicking UI should not move the character) Remove Gwen references and dependencies from the solution  Debugging tips  If nothing shows on screen: Check that Desktop is actually being rendered after the world Ensure Desktop.Bounds matches window size Ensure the root widget of Desktop has a proper size or uses layout that fills the area  If input does not work: Confirm the game window is capturing input events Set breakpoints or logging in your Myra event handlers Verify that Desktop has Focus and that focus is not stuck on some invisible widget  If layout is strange: Start with absolute positioning Panel to verify controls appear at expected coordinates Move to Grid or StackPanel only after verifying coordinate system  Adapting to repository specifics  Because the Intersect Engine repository evolves, here is how to contextualize this guide for the current version at the given path  Open Intersect.Client project in your IDE Search for Gwen in the client project Note specific files such as Interface or GuiManager LoginWindow, CharacterWindow, HudWindow, InventoryWindow Study how these windows are constructed and how they are attached to the Gwen root Replicate their structure with Myra widgets and containers Map each event invocation from Gwen to Myra with the same game-level handler functions to avoid rewriting game logic  Once you have at least one major screen successfully running under Myra, the rest is largely repetition and refinement: replace Gwen widget construction with Myra equivalents, adapt layout, hook events, and gradually remove Gwen until the dependency is fully gone.
9|67: High-level idea You are replacing Gwen (an immediate-mode, event-driven GUI running on top of MonoGame) with Myra (a retained-mode GUI that also integrates with MonoGame). The target project is Intersect.Client, which is built on MonoGame and currently wires Gwen deeply into its UI layer. The main work is to:  – Remove Gwen references and initialization from the client – Introduce Myra initialization and content loading – Rebuild or adapt existing UI screens using Myra widgets and layouts – Replace Gwen event wiring with Myra events – Adjust the game loop to draw and update the Myra UI  The steps below assume you are comfortable reading and modifying C# and the Intersect.Client source code.  1. Analyze where Gwen is used in Intersect.Client Open the Intersect.Client solution and locate all Gwen dependencies.  Look at project references – In Intersect.Client, open the .csproj file – Locate any references to Gwen, often something like Gwen.dll, or a Gwen project reference – Note any custom Gwen wrapper or helpers located under folders like UI, Graphics, or Controls  Search in code – Search for using Gwen, using Gwen.Control, using Gwen.Skin, using Gwen.Renderer, and so on – Identify key Gwen integration points, commonly:   – The renderer (MonoGame Gwen renderer implementation)   – The root control or canvas (Gwen.Control.Canvas)   – Skin/loading code (textures for Gwen skins)   – Window, Button, Label, TextBox, etc. definitions  Map out the logical UI structure – Determine what UI layers exist: login screen, character select, HUD, inventory, chat, menus, etc. – Identify which classes build these screens; they might inherit from some base window type or be user controls using Gwen – Sketch or list the main UI trees so that you can re-create them in Myra  2. Introduce Myra to the project Add Myra via NuGet – Open Intersect.Client in your IDE – Add the Myra package to the client project:   – Using dotnet CLI: dotnet add Intersect.Client package Myra   – Or use the NuGet Package Manager in Visual Studio and install Myra into Intersect.Client  Check Myra version compatibility – Confirm that the Myra version is compatible with the MonoGame version used by Intersect.Client – If the game uses DesktopGL vs WindowsDX, confirm that Myra supports that target; Myra supports MonoGame cross-platform, so you should be fine, but double-check the README for any platform specifics  3. Remove Gwen dependencies Remove Gwen from the project file – In Intersect.Client.csproj, remove any Gwen reference or Gwen project dependency – If there is a custom Gwen renderer project (e.g., MonoGameGwenRenderer), remove it if it is not reused for anything else  Clean up using directives – Run a code-wide search for Gwen and carefully refactor:   – Remove using Gwen.* statements   – Mark all Gwen types (Canvas, Control, Button, etc.) for replacement  Decide on migration strategy – You can proceed in two ways:   – Big-bang: Remove all Gwen UI at once and build all new UI in Myra   – Incremental: Wrap Myra UI in a transitional structure while Gwen still runs, gradually porting screens – In practice, Intersect’s UI is fairly integrated, so a big-bang port for all screens may be simpler to reason about, though more disruptive  4. Initialize Myra in the game Locate game initialization code – In Intersect.Client, find the main Game class; often something like IntersectGame, GameMain, or similar – Look for where Gwen is currently initialized:   – The Gwen renderer creation   – The Canvas root being created   – Skin loading and layout loading  Insert Myra initialization – Myra typically needs a call to MyraEnvironment.Game = this; in your Game constructor or Initialize method – Example pattern in your main Game class (pseudo-structure):    – Add using Myra;   – In the Game constructor or Initialize:     MyraEnvironment.Game = this;  Establish a root desktop – Myra usually uses a Desktop as the root container for widgets – Create a field on your Game class:   – private Myra.Graphics2D.UI.Desktop _desktop; – In Initialize or LoadContent:   – _desktop = new Desktop();  Set up basic theme or styles – Optionally load a Myra UI project or a generated .xnb/.json-based UI layout for your default theme – You can use Myra’s built-in widgets without a separate skin, or you can generate and load styles if you want custom visuals  5. Wire Myra into the game loop Find the main Update and Draw methods – Open your Game class and find the Update and Draw overrides where Gwen UI logic previously existed  Replace Gwen Update logic – Remove any Gwen calls such as canvas.ProcessInput or equivalent – Myra generally integrates input via the Desktop and MyraEnvironment automatically, as long as MyraEnvironment.Game is set and MonoGame’s default input handling is available – If you are doing custom input routing, map keyboard/mouse events to Myra’s Desktop.Input via Myra’s APIs; check the Myra docs if you need to override defaults  Replace Gwen Draw logic – Remove any Gwen.Render or canvas.Draw calls – In Draw, after drawing the game world and sprites, call:   – _desktop.Render(); – Ensure the SpriteBatch that Myra uses is properly integrated. Usually Myra manages its own SpriteBatch, but verify your settings against Myra examples  6. Port window layouts from Gwen to Myra Understand how layouts were done in Gwen – Gwen often uses containers such as DockLayout, GridLayout, VerticalLayout, HorizontalLayout, etc., and manual position/size settings – Look at each UI class that inherits from Gwen.Control.Base or a derived window/control type – Note the structure, approximate layout, and logic  Map Gwen controls to Myra widgets – Rough equivalents to consider:   – Gwen Canvas or main root → Myra Desktop.Root or a top-level Panel/VerticalStack/HorizontalStack/Grid   – Gwen Label → Myra Label   – Gwen Button → Myra TextButton or ImageTextButton   – Gwen TextBox → Myra TextBox   – Gwen CheckBox → Myra CheckBox   – Gwen ComboBox → Myra ComboBox   – Gwen ListBox → Myra ListBox or ListView depending on your needs   – Gwen WindowControl → Myra Window   – Gwen MenuStrip / MenuItem → Myra Menu and MenuItem   – Gwen TabControl → Myra TabControl  Choose a layout system per screen – Myra provides layouts such as:   – Grid, VerticalStackPanel, HorizontalStackPanel, Panel, SplitPane, etc. – For each Gwen UI screen, decide which Myra layout(s) best represent the same layout semantics – Rebuild the UI tree in C# code, or use Myra’s UI editor if you prefer a visual approach and then load the resulting layout at runtime  7. Convert Gwen events to Myra events Identify Gwen event usage – In Gwen, events look like control.Clicked += delegate; or similar, and sometimes use event bindings like control.TextChanged, ItemSelected, etc. – List all event hooks for each screen: buttons, text boxes, list selections, window close events, etc.  Map to Myra’s event model – Myra’s events follow standard C# events, for example:   – button.Click += (s, a) => { ... };   – textBox.TextChanged += (s, a) => { ... };   – window.Closed += (s, a) => { ... }; – Translate the logic from the Gwen handlers directly into Myra handlers – Where Gwen events provide special arguments, inspect Myra’s event args; sometimes you need to adapt your code slightly  Consider focus and input – If you relied on Gwen-specific focus behavior, map it to Myra’s focus methods, such as: widget.SetKeyboardFocus or Desktop.FocusedWidget – Verify keyboard shortcuts or hotkeys; if you used Gwen-level input mapping, port it to MonoGame input or Myra’s specialized handling  8. Handle skins, styles, and appearance Remove Gwen skin loading – Gwen typically loads a skin from a texture atlas or uses a Skin object – Remove the Gwen skin class and loading code  Set up Myra styles or theme – Myra supports styles via resources. Common patterns:   – Use Myra default theme; it gives a basic look and feel   – Create a style JSON (or layout files) and load them using Myra UI loader – If you want to emulate the Gwen look:   – Extract colors, padding, margins from old Gwen skin definitions   – Replicate them through Myra styles or by setting properties (Background, BorderThickness, Padding, etc.) on individual widgets or container defaults  9. Replace Gwen-specific helpers and abstractions Search for custom UI helper classes – Intersect may have custom wrappers like GuiHelper, GwenControlExtensions, WindowManager, etc. – Inspect these helpers to understand what they abstract: window creation, modal behavior, message boxes, tooltips, etc.  Rebuild or adapt them for Myra – Replace Gwen-specific types in those helpers with Myra UI types – For example, a CreateWindow helper that produced a Gwen WindowControl becomes a helper that creates and configures a Myra Window – If you had custom message box classes built on Gwen, port them to Myra by creating a Myra Window with appropriate Labels and Buttons, or use Myra’s ready-made widgets if available  10. Integrate with existing game logic Ensure UI logic still talks to the same subsystems – Most non-UI logic (networking, game state, inventory, character stats) should remain unchanged – Verify that your new Myra-based UI still calls the same service classes or event pipelines: sending packets, triggering state changes, updating local models  Adapt data-binding patterns – If Gwen logic manually assigned text values, lists, or selection, continue that pattern first:   – Example: label.Text = someValue.ToString(); – Over time you can implement a more robust MVVM-like pattern if desired, but that is optional for the migration  Check modal dialogs and input blocking – For windows that used to be modal in Gwen, ensure you replicate modal behavior with Myra – Strategies include:   – Keep a reference to the current modal window and avoid processing input for background UI when it is open   – Use Myra Desktop’s ability to manage focused/active widgets and logic in your Game’s Update to block interactions with non-modal parts  11. Testing and debugging Test each major screen – Launch the client – Walk through: login, registration, character creation, character selection, in-game HUD, inventory, equipment, chat, menus, settings – Verify:   – Widgets appear correctly   – Mouse interaction is working   – Keyboard input in text fields works and respects focus   – Tab-navigation or shortcuts behave reasonably  Trace drawing and z-order issues – If some UI elements are not visible:   – Confirm they are added to Desktop.Root or another visible root container   – Check DrawOrder or ZOrder properties in Myra where appropriate  Monitor performance – Ensure that calling _desktop.Render() does not conflict with your SpriteBatch usage – Follow Myra guidelines:   – Avoid manually beginning/ending SpriteBatch around Myra’s render call unless you know what you are doing   – If required, ensure correct ordering: draw world, end world batch, render Myra  12. Clean-up and refactoring Remove any dead code – After all UI has been ported, search for Gwen again to ensure all dependencies and old helper code are gone – Remove old resource files used only by Gwen skins  Improve structure – Group Myra UI code into a clear namespace/folder hierarchy:   – Client/UI/Screens   – Client/UI/Controls   – Client/UI/Styles – Consider extracting shared UI logic into base classes or helper methods as you notice duplication  13. Optional: using the Myra UI editor If you prefer not to hand-code the UI layouts, integrate the Myra UI editor into your workflow: – Use the external Myra UI editor tool to visually design windows and screens – Export layouts to .xaml-like or JSON resources supported by Myra – In Intersect.Client, load those layouts at runtime and then:   – Find named widgets from the loaded layout   – Attach event handlers in code – This can greatly speed iteration and help replicate more complex Gwen layouts  14. Practical mapping example Imagine Intersect has an InventoryWindow based on Gwen: – Old Gwen pseudo-structure:   – class InventoryWindow : Gwen.Control.WindowControl     – Title: Inventory     – A GridLayout of item slots (buttons or custom controls)     – A Label for gold     – Events: OnItemClicked, OnClose – New Myra version:   – class InventoryWindow     – Holds a Myra Window instance or inherits from Window     – Build layout:       – Root: Grid or VerticalStackPanel       – Add a grid of buttons representing item slots       – Add a Label for gold at the bottom     – Hook events:       – Each item button.Click += OnItemClicked handler       – Window.Closed += OnClose     – Expose methods to update the inventory, similar to old Gwen logic – Add this window to the Desktop when needed:   – inventoryWindowInstance.Show(); or add to Desktop.Root.Children  15. Summary migration checklist – Add Myra via NuGet and initialize MyraEnvironment.Game – Create a Desktop and integrate it in Update/Draw – Remove Gwen references from project and code – Rebuild UI layouts using Myra widgets and layouts – Convert Gwen events to Myra events – Recreate skins/styles or accept new ones via Myra themes – Test all client UI flows – Clean up obsolete Gwen-related code and resources  By following this structured approach, you replace Gwen at the Intersect.Client layer with Myra cleanly: starting with dependency and initialization changes, then migrating each UI screen’s layout and event logic, and finally refining styling and behavior until the UX is comparable or better than the original Gwen-based UI.
10|67: High-level overview Replacing Gwen with Myra in the Intersect Client is mostly about swapping the UI framework while keeping the existing game logic and data flow intact. Conceptually, you want to:  - Remove Gwen dependencies (assemblies, using directives, and Gwen widget construction) - Introduce Myra as the new UI framework - Recreate the UI layout and widgets in Myra - Rewire events and data binding (where applicable) so the client behavior remains the same - Make sure rendering and input for the UI are correctly integrated into the game loop  This guide assumes you have a working build of Intersect and basic familiarity with C#, MonoGame, and XNA-style game loops.  Step 1: Analyze the existing Gwen integration Start by locating where Gwen is used in Intersect.Client.  Look for Gwen namespaces In the client project, search for:  using Gwen; using Gwen.Control; using Gwen.Skin; using Gwen.Renderer; using Gwen.Input; or similar Gwen-related namespaces.  Take note of:  - Where the Gwen renderer is created - Where the main Gwen UI canvas/root is instantiated - Any Gwen-specific initialization during game startup - How input events (mouse, keyboard) are passed into Gwen - How drawing of Gwen is invoked in the Draw or Render methods  Identify UI construction and layout In many Gwen-based projects, UI is created either:  - Programmatically (new WindowControl(...), new Button(...), etc.) - Or via some Gwen-specific layout/skin configs  Make a list of key Gwen UI components you must recreate in Myra:  - Main root / desktop - Windows, dialogs, message boxes - Buttons, labels, text boxes - List views, trees, tabs, progress bars - Any custom Gwen controls  Step 2: Remove Gwen references from the project Before adding Myra, cleanly remove Gwen dependencies.  Unload Gwen from project references In Intersect.Client:  - Open the project file (Intersect.Client.csproj) and remove references to Gwen and any Gwen renderer libraries (for example, Gwen.dll, Gwen.Renderer.Something.dll). - If using a package manager (NuGet, etc.), uninstall Gwen-related packages.  Clean up using directives In all client source files:  - Remove using Gwen and related namespaces. - Optionally, comment out code blocks that rely on Gwen until Myra replacements are in place.  Build once to see errors Attempt a build at this point. The compiler errors will show you the exact locations and classes where Gwen is used. Save this error list as a to-do map for what must be ported to Myra.  Step 3: Add Myra to the client project Introduce Myra as a dependency.  Add Myra via NuGet In Intersect.Client:  - Install the Myra library via NuGet (for example, using dotnet CLI or Visual Studio package manager):   - Package name is typically Myra - Ensure the version you pick matches your MonoGame / .NET version.  Check the references Verify that Intersect.Client now references Myra and that you can:  - Add using Myra; - Add using Myra.Graphics2D.UI;  Step 4: Integrate Myra with the game framework Intersect.Client is based on MonoGame/XNA-style Game. Myra is designed to integrate well with MonoGame.  Initialize Myra in Game.Initialize or LoadContent In the main Game class (often something like Intersect.Client.Core.Game or similar):  - Add MyraEnvironment.Game = this; during initialization.  Example skeleton (pseudo-style, match to your actual class):  - In the Game constructor or Initialize method, call:   MyraEnvironment.Game = this;  Create the Myra Desktop (root UI) Myra uses Desktop as the root widget, analogous to Gwen’s main canvas/root.  - Add a field:   private Desktop _desktop;  - In LoadContent or a suitable initialization method:   _desktop = new Desktop();  This Desktop will host all of your UI widgets (windows, buttons, panels, etc.).  Hook Myra into your Draw method In your Game.Draw method, after drawing the game world, render the UI:  - _desktop.Render();  This ensures Myra overlays your game view.  Step 5: Map Gwen concepts to Myra concepts To port UI code, you need a mental map between Gwen and Myra.  Gwen root vs Myra Desktop  - Gwen typically: a Canvas or root Control - Myra: Desktop  Controls  - Gwen.Control.Label → Myra.Graphics2D.UI.Label - Gwen.Control.Button → Myra.Graphics2D.UI.TextButton (or ImageButton as needed) - Gwen.Control.TextBox → Myra.Graphics2D.UI.TextBox - Gwen.Control.WindowControl → Myra.Graphics2D.UI.Window - Gwen.Control.ListBox / ListView → Myra widgets like ListBox, Tree, Grid-based custom lists - Gwen.Control.Menu → Myra widgets like HorizontalMenu or custom menu using panels and buttons  Layout  - Gwen uses docking, margins, padding, and container controls - Myra uses panels like Panel, Grid, HorizontalStackPanel, VerticalStackPanel, and supports Proportions  You do not need to perfectly replicate Gwen’s layout system; you only need to achieve the same visual and functional result.  Step 6: Re-creating core UI structure in Myra Start by recreating top-level UI elements.  Identify main UI entry point Find where the initial Gwen UI is created (for example, some UIManager, UIBuilder, or GameInterface class). That is where you will now build the Myra Desktop UI.  Create a Root widget In Myra, the Desktop needs a single Root widget which can be any widget containing the rest of the layout.  For example (pseudocode; adapt to actual syntax):  - var rootPanel = new Panel(); - _desktop.Root = rootPanel;  Build out primary containers From the old Gwen code, identify main areas like:  - Top bar / HUD - Chat window - Inventory window - Status bars - Popup windows  Translate each Gwen container to a Myra widget structure. For example, a Gwen docked panel might become a Myra Grid or VerticalStackPanel. Try to match the layout logic:  - For horizontal alignment: use HorizontalStackPanel or Grid columns - For vertical stacks: VerticalStackPanel or Grid rows - For overlays: nested Panels and setting Anchors/Margins appropriately  Step 7: Rewire events and handlers Events are where logic lives, so porting them correctly is crucial.  Find Gwen event hooks Search for Gwen events like:  - button.Clicked += ... - textBox.TextChanged += ... - window.Closed += ...  Observe:  - Which methods are called - What they modify (game state, network calls, other UI)  Map to Myra events Myra uses similar C# events for widgets:  - For a button: button.Click += (s, a) => { ... }; - For text box changes: textBox.TextChanged += ...; - For window closing/minimizing: window.Closed or custom handling if you hide instead of dispose  Copy the event handlers’ logic directly, adjusting only the event args types and widget names as needed.  Step 8: Input integration and focus Intersect already handles input for the old Gwen UI. With Myra, you usually let it process input through the integrated Desktop.  Keyboard and mouse If the game uses standard MonoGame input polling, Myra will generally work transparently as long as MyraEnvironment.Game is set and _desktop.Render is called. If there was any Gwen-specific input routing (like Gwen.Input.XNAInput), remove it.  - Remove code that manually passes mouse/keyboard events to Gwen - Ensure the game window is capturing input normally - Myra’s Desktop interacts with MonoGame via MyraEnvironment and internal hooks  Focus and typing If you had specific Gwen calls to set focus, replace them with Myra’s equivalents, for example:  - _desktop.FocusedKeyboardWidget = someTextBox;  Step 9: Rendering, skins, and theming Gwen uses skins and renderers. Myra uses stylesheets and themes.  Remove Gwen skin setup Search for Gwen.Skin and Gwen.Renderer usage such as:  - new TexturedSkin(renderer, ...) - renderer = new SomeGwenRenderer(GraphicsDevice, ...)  Remove these and their related texture loading.  Apply Myra styles Myra can use styles defined in a JSON or from code. You can:  - Start with the default built-in style - Later, load your own style file to match Intersect’s desired look  Example approach (simplified):  - In LoadContent, optionally call MyraEnvironment.LoadStyle(...) to load a .xks or .json style definition, if your chosen Myra version supports it.  For the first iteration, you can live with the default theme and focus on functionality; refine visual styling later.  Step 10: Porting complex or custom Gwen controls Some Intersect UI components might be custom Gwen widgets. For these, you have two choices:  - Re-create them as custom Myra widgets - Approximate them using combinations of built-in Myra widgets  Building custom Myra widgets You can subclass Myra widgets or create new widgets by combining basic ones.  Typical patterns:  - Composite control: create a Panel, add multiple labels/buttons, expose properties and events - Custom drawing: inherit from Widget and override rendering logic if you need custom visuals  If the Gwen control interacted deeply with game state, reuse the same game logic; just replace drawing and event-handling with Myra equivalents.  Step 11: Gradual migration strategy If Intersect has a lot of Gwen usage, migrate in stages.  Stage 1: Introduce Myra Desktop alongside Gwen (temporary)  - Keep Gwen running for most UI - Create a Myra Desktop and maybe one small screen (e.g., a simple debug overlay) to ensure Myra integration works  Stage 2: Port non-critical screens  - Port auxiliary interfaces (debug windows, minor dialogs) from Gwen to Myra - Disable or hide their Gwen counterparts  Stage 3: Port main in-game UI and menus  - Port main HUD, inventory, skills, character, chat - Replace Gwen UI calls to show/hide these elements with Myra equivalents  Stage 4: Remove Gwen completely  - When all Gwen UI has Myra equivalents and is tested, remove any remaining Gwen code, references, and assets  Step 12: Handling layout files (optional advanced) Myra supports loading UI from JSON or XML definitions created with MyraPad. If you want a more data-driven approach:  - Use MyraPad to design layouts for screens like main menu, character screen, etc. - Save them as .xnb or JSON (depending on the pipeline) - In code, load them and set _desktop.Root to the loaded layout  This decouples layout and styling from code and may make it easier to iterate on UI design without recompiling the client.  Step 13: Testing and debugging Once basic porting is done:  - Verify that all core UI flows function: logging in, character select, in-game HUD, chat, inventory management, settings, exiting - Confirm that keyboard input goes to UI controls when they are focused and to the game when they are not, as intended - Check common edge cases: resizing the window (if supported), alt-tabbing, lost focus, device resets - Check how Myra UI behaves on different resolutions and aspect ratios  Performance considerations Myra is generally lightweight, but you should:  - Ensure you are not recreating UI every frame (only once or when needed) - Avoid heavy per-frame layout recalculations if unnecessary  Step 14: Cleaning and refactoring Once everything runs under Myra:  - Remove any dead code that was only for Gwen - Simplify any temporary shims used during migration - Organize UI-related classes into a clear structure (e.g., a UI or GUI namespace with screens, windows, and controls)  Example mapping walkthrough (conceptual) Imagine you had a Gwen-based login window.  Previously with Gwen (conceptually):  - var window = new WindowControl(canvas) { Title = "Login" }; - var userLabel = new Label(window) { Text = "Username" }; - var userText = new TextBox(window); - var passLabel = new Label(window) { Text = "Password" }; - var passText = new TextBox(window) { IsPassword = true }; - var loginButton = new Button(window) { Text = "Login" }; - loginButton.Clicked += OnLoginClicked;  With Myra:  - var loginWindow = new Window { Title = "Login" }; - var grid = new Grid(); - grid.ColumnsProportions.Add(new Proportion(ProportionType.Auto)); - grid.ColumnsProportions.Add(new Proportion(ProportionType.Fill)); - grid.RowsProportions.Add(new Proportion(ProportionType.Auto)); - grid.RowsProportions.Add(new Proportion(ProportionType.Auto)); - grid.RowsProportions.Add(new Proportion(ProportionType.Auto)); - var userLabel = new Label { Text = "Username" }; - grid.Widgets.Add(userLabel); grid.SetGridPosition(userLabel, 0, 0); - var userText = new TextBox(); - grid.Widgets.Add(userText); grid.SetGridPosition(userText, 1, 0); - var passLabel = new Label { Text = "Password" }; - grid.Widgets.Add(passLabel); grid.SetGridPosition(passLabel, 0, 1); - var passText = new TextBox { PasswordChar = '*' }; - grid.Widgets.Add(passText); grid.SetGridPosition(passText, 1, 1); - var loginButton = new TextButton { Text = "Login" }; - loginButton.Click += (s, a) => OnLoginClicked(userText.Text, passText.Text); - grid.Widgets.Add(loginButton); grid.SetGridPosition(loginButton, 1, 2); - loginWindow.Content = grid; - _desktop.Widgets.Add(loginWindow);  The event handler OnLoginClicked can reuse your existing login logic.  Practical tips for this specific repository Since Intersect-Engine is open-source, you can:  - Clone the repo and use IDE search tools to quickly map Gwen usage locations - Consider creating a feature branch like feature/myra-ui so you can iterate without breaking main - Start with one simple screen, commit, then move to the next  Because the engine is community-maintained, if you intend to contribute this back upstream, keep changes logically grouped, add comments explaining new Myra patterns, and avoid mixing unrelated refactors with the Gwen→Myra transition.  Summary  - Remove Gwen references and renderer/skin setup - Add Myra through NuGet and initialize MyraEnvironment.Game - Create a Desktop and assign it as your main UI root - Rebuild UI in Myra by mapping Gwen controls and layouts to Myra widgets and containers - Reattach all UI event handlers to Myra widgets, preserving game logic - Render the Desktop in Game.Draw and rely on Myra for input handling - Gradually migrate screens until no Gwen references remain, then clean up  With this roadmap, you can systematically transition the Intersect Client from Gwen to Myra while preserving behavior and enabling future UI improvements.

1|69: Let’s break AI‑powered training into three parts: foundations, tools, and a simple project you can actually build.  Foundations you need to understand  Start with what “AI‑powered training” means. It usually refers to using AI to:  – Adapt learning content to each learner – Generate practice questions, feedback, and explanations – Analyze learner performance and recommend what to learn next – Automate parts of content creation: slides, quizzes, summaries, scenarios  The core AI concepts behind this are:  Machine learning basics  – Supervised learning: Train a model using input–output pairs. Example: Given past learners’ quiz results and outcomes, predict who needs help. – Unsupervised learning: Find patterns without labels. Example: Group learners into clusters based on behavior. – Reinforcement learning: An agent tries actions and learns from rewards. Example: A system that experiments with different content sequences and learns which ordering boosts retention.  Large language models (LLMs)  – These are the engines behind tools like ChatGPT. – They are good at text generation: explanations, examples, scenarios, role‑plays, quizzes, feedback. – They can understand instructions and context: You can pass them a learner profile, current topic, and ask them to generate personalized content.  Key ideas for learning design  Even with AI, good pedagogy matters more than fancy models.  – Learning objectives: Be explicit about what the learner should be able to do (not just know) after the training. – Chunking: Break content into small, focused segments. – Retrieval practice: Make learners recall, not just read. – Spaced repetition: Revisit material over time, especially the hard parts. – Feedback: Give clear, actionable, timely feedback.  AI should enhance these principles, not replace them.  Core tools and building blocks  You do not need to build your own model from scratch to start.  Hosted LLMs and APIs  – OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, etc. let you send prompts and receive text, images, or structured outputs. – You can ask them to:   – Generate learning objectives   – Draft lesson content at different levels   – Create examples, analogies, case studies   – Generate quizzes, flashcards, and explanations   – Simulate role‑plays: practice conversations with an AI “character” (manager, customer, patient, etc.)  Embeddings and retrieval  – Embeddings turn text into vectors so you can search semantically (by meaning, not just keywords). – With a vector database, you can:   – Feed your existing manuals, policies, or textbooks into an AI assistant.   – Let learners ask questions and get answers grounded in your training content, not just generic internet knowledge.  Analytics and personalization  – Use simple models first: even basic statistics and dashboards can show you:   – Which topics most learners fail   – How long people spend per module   – Where they drop off or disengage – Later, you can add ML to:   – Predict who is likely to struggle   – Recommend the next best module for each learner   – Adapt question difficulty automatically  A step‑by‑step project to learn by doing  Here is a concrete roadmap you can follow to “learn AI‑powered training” by actually building a small system.  Phase 1: Manual plus AI (no coding required)  Goal: Use AI to supercharge how you design and deliver training, even with basic tools.  Pick a topic you know reasonably well: it could be Excel basics, sales conversations, new‑hire onboarding, safety training, or a programming language.  Then:  Define learners and objectives  – Describe a learner persona: background, goals, constraints. – Write clear learning objectives for a short module. – Use an LLM to refine them: Ask it to rewrite objectives in action‑oriented terms.  Develop content with AI assistance  – Ask the AI to outline a 30–60 minute course that hits your objectives. – For each section, ask it to draft:   – Explanations at basic and advanced levels   – Realistic examples from your industry   – Short case studies or scenarios   – A summary in 5 key points  Generate practice and feedback  – Ask AI to generate different forms of practice:   – Multiple‑choice questions with explanations   – Short answer questions and ideal answers   – Role‑play dialogues learners might encounter on the job   – Reflection prompts: questions that make learners think, not just recall  Personalize tone and difficulty  – Ask the AI to rewrite the same explanation:   – For absolute beginners   – For experienced professionals   – For non‑technical managers  This phase teaches you prompt design and how AI can speed up instructional design.  Phase 2: Interactive AI tutor (light coding or no‑code)  Goal: Turn static content into an AI‑augmented learning experience.  You have two options: no‑code platforms or light coding.  No‑code / low‑code approach  Use tools that let you connect LLMs through visual workflows. Typical pattern:  – Input: learner question or progress data – Logic: choose what to do   – If learner is stuck on concept X, generate extra explanation and practice about X.   – If learner scored below threshold on quiz, trigger a “remediation path.” – Output: AI‑generated content, hints, or recommendations  Light coding approach  If you can code a bit (Python or JavaScript), try this architecture:  – Front‑end: a simple web page where learners log in and:   – See the next lesson   – Take quizzes   – Ask questions via chat – Back‑end:   – Stores learner progress and answers   – Calls the LLM API to generate:     – Tailored explanations     – Hints for quiz questions     – Extra practice questions similar to ones they missed  Example behaviors you can implement:  – Adaptive help: When a learner gets a question wrong, send their answer plus the correct explanation to the LLM and ask it to generate a custom hint, not just the solution. – Variable difficulty: Based on recent accuracy, adjust the difficulty of next questions by telling the LLM: Generate a more challenging problem that tests the same concept.  Phase 3: Data and personalization  Goal: Use learner data to continuously improve the training.  Start capturing basic data:  – Engagement: time on each page, modules started/completed – Performance: quiz scores, number of attempts per question – Behavior: which optional modules they choose, which explanations they request  Use this data to:  – Identify problem spots: questions most people get wrong or content they skip. – Refine prompts: If you see people misunderstand the same concept, feed their wrong answers to the LLM and ask: Why might learners be confused by this? Then update explanations. – Personalize learning paths:   – If they are advanced: skip the basics; generate a diagnostic test and then a fast‑track path.   – If they struggle: slow down, add more examples, use simpler language, and increase spaced repetition.  Concepts to explore as you advance  Once you are comfortable with the above, you can deepen your AI skills.  Prompt engineering  – Structure prompts with:   – Role: You are an expert trainer in X.   – Task: Explain concept Y to a learner who already knows Z.   – Constraints: Use simple language, give two examples, end with a self‑check question. – Iterate: Test with real learners and tune your prompts based on where they still struggle.  Retrieval‑augmented generation (RAG)  – Store all your training content in a vector database. – When learners ask a question, the system retrieves relevant paragraphs and passes those to the LLM. – This keeps answers aligned with your policies, procedures, and domain knowledge instead of generic internet content.  AI‑driven assessment  – Use AI to grade short answers or essays with rubrics. – Have the AI provide structured feedback: what was good, what is missing, a suggestion to improve the answer.  Ethics, fairness, and limitations  Understanding what AI must not do is part of learning AI‑powered training.  – Privacy: Do not log sensitive personal data unless you have clear consent and secure storage. – Transparency: Tell learners when they are interacting with AI. – Bias: AI can contain biases from its training data; review its content for stereotypes or unfair assumptions. – Over‑reliance: Remind learners that AI is a helper, not the only authority; encourage critical thinking.  A simple progression plan for you  Here is a practical learning path you can follow personally over a few weeks.  Week 1: Conceptual  – Learn fundamentals of LLMs, basic ML, and instructional design. – Use an AI assistant to help you rewrite an existing training module you have.  Week 2: Content and prompts  – Design one focused micro‑course, fully supported by AI content. – Experiment with prompts to generate varied explanations, quizzes, and role‑plays.  Week 3: Interactivity  – Build a small interactive experience with no‑code or a simple front‑end plus LLM API. – Add logic for hints, extra practice, and level‑appropriate explanations.  Week 4: Data and iteration  – Run a small pilot with a few learners. – Collect feedback and usage data. – Refine your prompts, sequences, and content based on real outcomes. 2|69: AI powered training means using artificial intelligence to make learning more personalized, adaptive, and efficient. Think of it as combining good instructional design with data, algorithms, and automation so that each learner gets the right content at the right time in the right way.  Here is a simple way to understand and start with AI powered training as a non-technical practitioner.  First, understand the core ideas  AI in training usually does four big things:  Personalization: The system adapts difficulty, pace, and content based on each learner’s behavior, performance, and preferences. For example, if someone struggles with a concept, the system gives more practice and simpler explanations; if they master it quickly, it skips ahead.  Recommendation: Like a streaming service suggests movies, AI can recommend the next course, lesson, or resource based on a learner’s role, past activities, skills, and goals.  Automation: AI can generate practice questions, summaries, feedback, and even draft lesson outlines. That lets instructors focus on high-value work like mentoring and designing better experiences.  Analytics and prediction: AI can detect patterns such as who is at risk of dropping out, which concepts cause confusion, or which types of content are most effective. This supports data-informed improvements.  Second, get clear on your goals  Before tools or algorithms, decide what you want AI to help with. Common goals include:  Improve learner engagement and completion rates Shorten time to competence for new hires Make compliance or mandatory training less painful and more targeted Scale coaching and feedback without hiring many more trainers Identify and close specific skill gaps in a workforce  Write goals in plain, measurable terms. For example: Improve course completion from 60 percent to 80 percent in six months, or reduce the average onboarding ramp-up time from 90 to 60 days.  Third, learn the basic building blocks  You do not need to become a programmer, but a light understanding of how AI systems work will help you use them effectively.  Data: This is everything the system sees. In training, that includes learner profiles, quiz responses, time spent on activities, click paths, text answers, job performance metrics, and content metadata.  Models: These are mathematical structures that learn from data. Different types do different jobs: recommendation models suggest the next item; language models generate text; classification models group learners or predict who needs help.  Feedback loops: AI systems get better when they are updated with new data. For example, if learners consistently skip certain recommended modules, the model can learn that those recommendations are not helpful.  Fourth, start with easy applications  You can add AI to training step by step without building everything from scratch.  Use AI to create content: Language models can draft lesson outlines, write explanations in different tones, generate multiple versions of quiz questions, or create role-play scenarios. You still need to review for accuracy and clarity, but this speeds up design.  Use AI for adaptive assessments: Instead of a fixed quiz, use tools that adjust questions based on learner performance. Early correct answers lead to harder questions; repeated mistakes lead to simpler questions or revisiting prerequisites.  Use AI for micro recommendations: In your learning platform, configure or adopt tools that suggest Just-in-time resources: a short video, job aid, or article based on what someone is doing or struggling with.  Use AI for support: Chatbot style helpers can answer common questions about the training content, provide hints during exercises, or help explain difficult concepts in different ways.  Fifth, design AI powered learning journeys  When you design a course or program, think in terms of an adaptive path rather than a single linear path.  Define key competencies: What skills or knowledge should learners demonstrate at the end? Break these into observable behaviors or objectives.  Map content to competencies: For each competency, list which lessons, activities, examples, and assessments help teach or measure it.  Set rules and signals: Decide what signals indicate mastery or struggle. Signals might be quiz scores, time spent, number of hints used, or self-assessed confidence.  Define adaptive rules: If a learner scores below a threshold on a topic, they get extra practice and alternative explanations. If they show mastery quickly, they can skip redundant content or move to enrichment.  Over time, as you gather more data, you can replace some of these hand-crafted rules with learned models, but rules are a good start.  Sixth, pick tools wisely instead of chasing hype  You can implement AI powered training with a mix of:  Existing learning platforms that include AI features such as personalized recommendations, adaptive quizzes, or learning analytics.  General AI tools such as language models that you connect to your content creation workflow or to your learning platform via APIs.  Custom solutions only if you have clear needs that off-the-shelf tools cannot meet and you have technical capacity.  When evaluating tools, consider:  Data ownership and privacy: Who owns learner data? Can you export it? Is it handled according to your regulatory requirements?  Explainability: Can you understand why the system made a recommendation, or is it a black box? For high-stakes training, you want some interpretability.  Integration: Does it work with your LMS, HR system, or content repository? Manual copying of data will quickly become painful.  Control: Can you adjust rules, override recommendations, or customize how models behave for your context?  Seventh, keep humans in the loop  AI should augment, not replace, instructors and learning designers.  Trainers focus on coaching, discussion, motivation, and handling nuance. AI handles repetitive tasks, basic feedback, and pattern detection.  Use instructor dashboards: Provide trainers with analytics that highlight which learners are struggling, which topics cause misunderstanding, and which resources are most effective.  Give learners control: Let them see recommended paths, but allow them to override, request more practice, or slow down. This preserves agency and trust.  Eighth, pay attention to ethics and quality  Avoid bias: If your data reflects only a subset of your learners (for example, high performers from one region), your AI may make poor or unfair suggestions for others.  Transparency: Tell learners when AI is involved, what data is collected, and how recommendations are made.  Accuracy: AI generated content can be confidently wrong. Always review critical material, especially in safety, legal, medical, or compliance contexts.  Impact: Measure not just quiz scores, but real-world performance and satisfaction. AI powered does not automatically mean better.  Ninth, build a basic workflow to start  Here is a simple starter workflow you can use:  Select a single course or training program to pilot. Ideally, something with clear objectives and enough learners to generate data.  Baseline measurement: Capture current metrics: completion rates, average scores, learner feedback, time to competence.  Add AI in one or two places: Use AI tooling to help create more varied practice questions and explanations. Enable or integrate a simple recommendation engine or adaptive quiz.  Collect data: Monitor how learners interact with the new system. Are they spending less time but getting similar or better results? Are they more engaged?  Iterate: Adjust rules, content, and AI configurations based on what you observe. Do not assume the first setup is optimal.  Compare to baseline: Quantify improvements. Use this to decide whether and how to expand AI use to other programs.  Tenth, deepen your skills progressively  If you want to go further into AI powered training, build skills in three areas.  Instructional design: The better your learning objectives, assessments, and content structure, the more effective your AI will be. AI amplifies both good and bad design.  Data literacy: Learn to read basic analytics, understand A/B testing, and interpret dashboards. You do not need calculus, but you should be comfortable with questions like What does this chart actually tell me about learner behavior.  Working with AI tools: Practice writing clear prompts, critically reviewing AI outputs, and giving feedback to improve quality. This is as much a communication skill as a technical one.  Putting it all together as a simple example  Imagine you are building AI powered training for new customer support agents.  You map the core skills: product knowledge, empathy, troubleshooting steps, and systems navigation.  You create a content library: short videos, interactive walkthroughs, example calls, and job aids.  You use AI to generate realistic chat and email scenarios for practice, with varied customer moods and issues.  You deploy an adaptive assessment that increases scenario complexity as agents perform well, and offers hints or review modules when they struggle.  You add a chatbot helper inside the training environment that can answer questions like How do I check a customer’s subscription status or Explain this policy in simpler terms.  You track metrics like average handling time on simulated calls, quality scores, and post-training performance on the job. You refine both the content and the AI logic over time.
