3|72: Heart failure is a clinical syndrome in which the heart is unable to pump blood adequately to meet the body’s metabolic needs, or can do so only with increased filling pressures. It is not a single disease but a final common pathway of many cardiac problems.  We say a patient has heart failure when:  They have typical symptoms: breathlessness on exertion or at rest, orthopnea (shortness of breath when lying flat), paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (waking up gasping for air), fatigue, reduced exercise tolerance, ankle or leg swelling, abdominal distension from fluid, rapid weight gain from fluid retention.  And there is objective evidence of cardiac dysfunction: reduced ejection fraction on echocardiography, dilated or hypertrophied chambers, impaired relaxation and high filling pressures, raised natriuretic peptides (BNP or NT‑proBNP), signs of pulmonary congestion or cardiomegaly on chest X‑ray, or hemodynamic evidence on catheterization.  Types: Systolic heart failure (heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, HFrEF): impaired contraction; LVEF usually below 40 percent. Diastolic heart failure (heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, HFpEF): impaired relaxation and filling; LVEF 50 percent or higher but stiff ventricle and raised filling pressures. Right‑sided, left‑sided, or biventricular involvement can occur.  Common causes of heart failure: Ischemic heart disease and prior myocardial infarction: loss of viable myocardium reduces contractility. Long‑standing hypertension: pressure overload leads to hypertrophy, stiffness, and later systolic dysfunction. Valvular heart disease: aortic stenosis, aortic or mitral regurgitation causing pressure or volume overload. Cardiomyopathies: dilated, hypertrophic, or restrictive, from genetic, viral, toxic, metabolic, or idiopathic causes. Arrhythmias: persistent tachycardia, atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, or complete heart block. Congenital heart disease: shunts or structural defects. Other: pericardial disease (constrictive pericarditis, tamponade), severe anemia, thyrotoxicosis, chronic lung disease (leading to cor pulmonale).  How systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) can cause heart failure: SLE is a systemic autoimmune disease that can affect virtually all layers of the heart and the vasculature, producing multiple potential pathways to heart failure.  Myocarditis: Immune‑mediated inflammation of the myocardium can occur in SLE. Inflammatory infiltrates and myocyte necrosis reduce contractility and lead to a dilated cardiomyopathy picture. Patients can present with acute or subacute heart failure, arrhythmias, and elevated cardiac enzymes. Chronic or recurrent myocarditis can lead to persistent systolic dysfunction and HFrEF.  Coronary artery disease and ischemic cardiomyopathy: SLE markedly increases the risk of premature atherosclerosis due to chronic inflammation, vasculitis, dyslipidemia, steroid use, and endothelial dysfunction. This can cause myocardial infarction at a young age. Repeated or large infarcts cause ischemic cardiomyopathy and systolic heart failure. Coronary vasculitis, though less common, can also compromise perfusion.  Valvular disease (Libman‑Sacks endocarditis): SLE can produce sterile vegetations, most often on the mitral and aortic valves. These can lead to valvular regurgitation; chronic volume overload from significant mitral or aortic regurgitation eventually causes ventricular dilation and failure. Valvular thickening and dysfunction can also develop from chronic inflammation.  Pericardial disease: Pericarditis is common in SLE. Recurrent or chronic pericardial inflammation may cause large effusions leading to tamponade, which produces acute hemodynamic failure. Over time, pericarditis can lead to constrictive pericarditis, where a stiff pericardium restricts diastolic filling, causing a form of right‑sided and global heart failure with preserved ejection fraction.  Pulmonary hypertension: SLE can cause pulmonary arterial hypertension via vasculopathy, thromboembolism (including antiphospholipid antibody syndrome), and interstitial lung disease. Chronic elevation of pulmonary artery pressures leads to right ventricular hypertrophy, dilation, and right‑sided heart failure.  Conduction and rhythm abnormalities: Inflammation, fibrosis, or ischemia of the conduction system in SLE can cause bradyarrhythmias or tachyarrhythmias. Sustained tachycardia or uncontrolled atrial fibrillation can lead to tachycardia‑induced cardiomyopathy and heart failure.  Drug‑related cardiotoxicity: Some drugs used in SLE, as well as comorbid conditions, can be cardiotoxic. Anthracyclines (if used for associated malignancy), high‑dose cyclophosphamide, and certain biologics rarely may contribute to myocardial damage. Chronic high‑dose steroids exacerbate hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia, and obesity, indirectly promoting heart failure.  Management of heart failure in general: Management has three key goals: relieve symptoms, improve quality of life and function, and reduce hospitalizations and mortality. Treatment is tailored to the type of heart failure (HFrEF versus HFpEF), etiology, comorbidities, and severity.  General nonpharmacologic measures: Fluid and salt control: moderate sodium restriction, and fluid restriction in those with hyponatremia or severe congestion. Daily weights: to detect fluid retention early; seek review if sudden weight gain over a few days. Lifestyle: smoking cessation, limit alcohol, weight control, vaccination (influenza, pneumococcal), moderate physical activity and cardiac rehabilitation when stable. Management of comorbidities: optimal control of hypertension, diabetes, sleep apnea, anemia, thyroid disease, kidney disease. Patient education: recognizing early signs of decompensation, adherence to medications and follow‑up.  Pharmacologic treatment of HFrEF (reduced ejection fraction, unless contraindicated): ACE inhibitor or ARB or ARNI: cornerstone therapy to reduce mortality and hospitalizations. ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan) is often used instead of an ACE inhibitor in appropriate patients. Evidence‑based beta‑blockers: such as carvedilol, bisoprolol, or metoprolol succinate, titrated slowly to target or maximally tolerated doses. Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist: spironolactone or eplerenone for NYHA class II–IV with appropriate renal function and potassium levels. SGLT2 inhibitor: such as dapagliflozin or empagliflozin, now standard in HFrEF regardless of diabetes status. Diuretics: loop diuretics like furosemide or bumetanide to control congestion and edema; dose adjusted to symptoms and weight. Other options in selected patients: ivabradine (if sinus rhythm with high heart rate despite beta‑blocker), hydralazine plus nitrates (especially in those intolerant of ACEI/ARB or in selected ethnic groups), digoxin in some with persistent symptoms or atrial fibrillation.  Nonpharmacologic and device therapy: Cardiac resynchronization therapy: for selected patients with reduced EF, wide QRS, and persistent symptoms despite optimal medical therapy. Implantable cardioverter‑defibrillator: for primary or secondary prevention of sudden cardiac death in those with severe systolic dysfunction. Revascularization: PCI or CABG in ischemic cardiomyopathy when there is viable myocardium and significant coronary disease. Valve surgery or percutaneous interventions: for severe valvular disease contributing to heart failure. Advanced therapies: LVAD and heart transplantation in end‑stage, refractory heart failure despite optimal therapy.  Management of HFpEF: Focuses on aggressive control of contributing factors: blood pressure, ischemia, atrial fibrillation, obesity, diabetes, sleep apnea, and valvular disease. Diuretics are used to control congestion. SGLT2 inhibitors have emerging roles in HFpEF as well. Lifestyle interventions and exercise training are critical. There is less evidence that ACEI, ARB, or beta‑blockers improve mortality specifically in HFpEF, but they may be indicated for comorbidities.  Specific considerations for SLE‑related heart failure: Treat the underlying lupus activity: High‑dose glucocorticoids and immunosuppressive therapy (such as cyclophosphamide, mycophenolate mofetil, azathioprine, or biologics like rituximab) are used for active myocarditis, severe pericarditis, or vasculitis, guided by rheumatology. Hydroxychloroquine is usually continued unless contraindicated, as it improves long‑term SLE outcomes and may be cardioprotective; rare hydroxychloroquine cardiomyopathy must be considered if unexplained heart failure and conduction disease occur after long‑term use.  Manage specific cardiac manifestations: Myocarditis: combination of standard heart failure therapy plus immunosuppression for active inflammation. Monitor with echocardiography and biomarkers; cardiac MRI or biopsy in selected cases. Libman‑Sacks valvular disease: if mild and asymptomatic, close follow‑up. If causing significant regurgitation or heart failure symptoms, treat heart failure medically and consider surgical or percutaneous valve intervention in collaboration with cardiothoracic surgery. Pericarditis and effusion: NSAIDs and colchicine for mild cases; steroids and immunosuppressants for severe or refractory disease. Large effusions causing tamponade require urgent pericardiocentesis or surgical window. Constrictive pericarditis may ultimately need pericardiectomy. Pulmonary hypertension: evaluate with echocardiography and right‑heart catheterization. Treat lupus activity, anticoagulate when antiphospholipid syndrome is present, and consider targeted pulmonary vasodilators according to pulmonary hypertension subtype. Coronary artery disease: aggressive risk factor control (lipids, blood pressure, glucose, smoking), antiplatelets when indicated, statins, and revascularization if appropriate. Arrhythmias: manage with rate or rhythm control, anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation, and consider devices if indicated.  Medication choices in SLE patients with HF must account for: Renal involvement (lupus nephritis) affecting dosing and risk of hyperkalemia with ACEI, ARB, or MRA. Drug interactions between heart failure therapies and immunosuppressants. Infection risk with immunosuppression; decompensations may be triggered by sepsis. Thrombotic risk in antiphospholipid syndrome, requiring careful anticoagulation.  In summary, heart failure is a syndrome of impaired cardiac pumping and filling, diagnosed by characteristic symptoms and objective evidence of cardiac dysfunction. Its causes are diverse, including ischemic, hypertensive, valvular, myocardial, and pericardial diseases. SLE can cause heart failure through myocarditis, accelerated atherosclerosis and infarction, valvular lesions, pericardial disease, pulmonary hypertension, arrhythmias, and treatment‑related toxicity. Management combines standard heart failure therapies with disease‑specific treatment of SLE manifestations, close coordination between cardiology and rheumatology, and careful control of comorbidities and risk factors.
4|72: Heart failure means the heart is unable to pump enough blood to meet the body’s needs, or can do so only with raised filling pressures. It is a clinical syndrome, not a single disease. You say someone has heart failure when there is a combination of typical symptoms, typical physical signs, and usually objective evidence of cardiac dysfunction on tests.  Definition and when to call it heart failure You call it heart failure when:  The patient has typical symptoms such as: – Breathlessness, especially on exertion or when lying flat (orthopnea) – Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, waking up at night gasping for air – Fatigue and reduced exercise tolerance – Swelling of legs, ankles, or abdomen (peripheral edema, ascites) – Rapid weight gain from fluid retention  And there are typical signs such as: – Elevated jugular venous pressure (JVP) – Lung crackles (pulmonary edema) – Peripheral edema, sacral edema – Enlarged or displaced apex beat, third heart sound (S3) – Hepatomegaly, tender liver from congestion  Plus objective evidence on investigations, for example: – Echocardiogram showing reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (HFrEF), or structural heart disease, or diastolic dysfunction (HFpEF) – Elevated natriuretic peptides (BNP or NT-proBNP) – Chest X-ray showing pulmonary congestion, cardiomegaly – Other imaging or hemodynamic evidence of increased filling pressures  If a patient has symptoms and signs compatible with HF and no better alternative explanation, and tests support cardiac dysfunction, you call it heart failure.  Main causes of heart failure Common broad causes include:  Ischemic heart disease Coronary artery disease leading to myocardial infarction causes loss of functioning myocardium, ventricular remodeling, and reduced contractility.  Hypertension Long-standing high blood pressure causes left ventricular hypertrophy, stiffens the ventricle, and eventually leads to systolic and/or diastolic failure.  Valvular heart disease Aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, mitral regurgitation, and other valvular lesions lead to chronic volume or pressure overload and ultimately HF.  Cardiomyopathies – Dilated cardiomyopathy: idiopathic, familial, alcohol, viral, peripartum – Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy – Restrictive cardiomyopathy, including infiltrative diseases such as amyloidosis  Arrhythmias and conduction disease Persistent tachyarrhythmias can cause tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy; bradyarrhythmias and heart block can also impair cardiac output.  Congenital heart disease Certain congenital lesions, if unrepaired or with residual defects, can lead to HF.  High-output states Severe anemia, thyrotoxicosis, AV fistulas, and beriberi can rarely cause high-output HF in susceptible hearts.  How systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) can cause heart failure SLE is a multisystem autoimmune disease that can involve all layers of the heart and blood vessels. It contributes to HF through several pathways, often overlapping.  Myocarditis SLE can cause inflammatory involvement of the myocardium. Inflammation, edema, and myocyte necrosis lead to reduced contractility and sometimes dilated cardiomyopathy. Clinically, this can present as new HF with or without chest pain, arrhythmias, or cardiogenic shock.  Coronary artery disease and accelerated atherosclerosis People with SLE have a much higher risk of premature atherosclerosis due to chronic inflammation, immune mechanisms, and frequent use of corticosteroids. They can develop ischemic heart disease and myocardial infarction at a young age, which then leads to ischemic cardiomyopathy and HF.  Valvular disease (Libman–Sacks endocarditis) Nonbacterial verrucous endocarditis can affect mainly the mitral and aortic valves. This may lead to significant regurgitation or, less often, stenosis. Chronic significant valvular lesions lead to volume or pressure overload and HF.  Pericardial disease Pericarditis is common in SLE. Large pericardial effusions may cause tamponade with acute hemodynamic compromise. Chronic or recurrent pericarditis can rarely progress to constrictive pericarditis, limiting diastolic filling, raising venous pressures, and mimicking or causing HF.  Pulmonary hypertension and right heart failure SLE can cause pulmonary arterial hypertension, chronic thromboembolic disease (especially with antiphospholipid antibodies), and interstitial lung disease. Increased pulmonary vascular resistance increases right ventricular afterload, causing right-sided HF.  Drug-related cardiotoxicity Some drugs used in SLE, like high-dose steroids, can worsen hypertension, diabetes, and dyslipidemia (indirectly promoting CAD). Cyclophosphamide and other chemotherapeutic/immunosuppressive agents can have direct myocardial toxicity in some settings.  Renal disease and volume overload Lupus nephritis causes salt and water retention, hypertension, and anemia. Volume overload, high blood pressure, and anemia all increase cardiac workload, unmasking or worsening HF.  Management of heart failure in general Management goals are to relieve symptoms, improve quality of life, reduce hospitalizations, and improve survival. Treatment is tailored to whether it is HFrEF or HFpEF, and to the underlying cause.  General measures – Patient education: daily weight monitoring, recognizing decompensation – Lifestyle: low-sodium diet, fluid restriction in selected patients, smoking cessation, alcohol moderation or abstinence, exercise and cardiac rehabilitation as tolerated – Vaccinations: influenza, pneumococcal  Pharmacologic therapy for HFrEF (reduced ejection fraction) – RAAS blockade: ACE inhibitors or ARBs, or ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan) as first-line foundational therapy – Beta-blockers: evidence-based agents such as bisoprolol, metoprolol succinate, or carvedilol, titrated slowly – Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists: spironolactone or eplerenone – SGLT2 inhibitors: dapagliflozin or empagliflozin for HFrEF regardless of diabetes status – Diuretics: loop diuretics like furosemide for symptom relief in congestion; thiazides can be added in resistant cases – Other: ivabradine in selected patients with sinus rhythm and high heart rate; hydralazine plus nitrates in certain populations or when ACEI/ARB/ARNI are not tolerated; digoxin in some patients with persistent symptoms or AF with rapid ventricular response  Non-pharmacologic and device therapies – Cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) for wide QRS with dyssynchrony and low EF – Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) for primary or secondary prevention of sudden cardiac death in appropriate HFrEF patients – Revascularization (PCI or CABG) in significant coronary disease contributing to HF – Valve repair or replacement for severe valvular lesions causing HF – Advanced options: LVAD or heart transplantation in end-stage HF not responsive to optimal medical and device therapy  Management of HFpEF (preserved EF) – Aggressive treatment of hypertension, atrial fibrillation, and ischemia – Diuretics for symptom control of congestion – SGLT2 inhibitors have shown benefit in HFpEF in reducing hospitalizations – Weight loss, treatment of sleep apnea, and management of diabetes and renal disease – No single drug class has the same mortality benefit as in HFrEF, so focus is on comorbidities and congestion control  Management of heart failure specifically in SLE In SLE-related HF, you treat both the heart failure itself and the underlying lupus activity.  General HF therapy Use standard HF therapy based on EF and clinical status: ACEI/ARB/ARNI, beta-blockers, mineralocorticoid antagonists, SGLT2 inhibitors, and diuretics, unless contraindicated. Monitor renal function and electrolytes carefully, especially because SLE often involves the kidneys.  Control of SLE disease activity – High-dose corticosteroids and sometimes pulse steroids for acute severe myocarditis or pericarditis – Additional immunosuppressive agents such as cyclophosphamide, mycophenolate mofetil, azathioprine, or biologics (e.g., rituximab, belimumab) depending on organ involvement and severity – Close coordination between cardiology and rheumatology  Address specific cardiac manifestations – Myocarditis: aggressive immunosuppression plus standard HF therapy, sometimes mechanical support in fulminant cases – Libman–Sacks endocarditis: anticoagulation may be indicated if there is associated antiphospholipid syndrome or risk of embolism; valve surgery if severe regurgitation or stenosis – Pericardial disease: NSAIDs, colchicine, or steroids for pericarditis; pericardiocentesis for tamponade; pericardiectomy if constriction develops – Pulmonary hypertension: specific pulmonary vasodilators (endothelin receptor antagonists, PDE5 inhibitors, prostacyclin analogs) plus immunosuppression if active SLE and anticoagulation where thromboembolic disease is present  Risk factor and comorbidity management – Rigorous control of blood pressure, lipids, and glucose – Encourage smoking cessation and physical activity tailored to tolerance – Minimize chronic steroid doses when possible to reduce metabolic side effects – Treat anemia and manage lupus nephritis to reduce volume and pressure burden on the heart  Long-term follow-up Patients with SLE and HF need regular follow-up with echocardiography to assess ventricular function, valve status, and pulmonary pressures, as well as continuous monitoring of lupus activity and renal function. Early detection and management of cardiac involvement in SLE can prevent progression to irreversible heart failure.  In summary, heart failure is diagnosed when typical symptoms and signs are supported by evidence of cardiac dysfunction. Its causes are diverse, but in SLE specifically, HF usually arises from lupus-related myocarditis, accelerated coronary disease, valvular lesions, pericardial disease, pulmonary hypertension, renal-related volume and pressure load, and treatment-related toxicity, and it is managed by combining standard HF therapy with targeted immunosuppression and careful control of comorbidities.
5|72: Heart failure is a clinical syndrome in which the heart cannot pump enough blood to meet the body’s needs, or can do so only at the expense of raised filling pressures. It is not a single disease but a final common pathway of many cardiac conditions.  Clinically, you say a patient has heart failure when all three elements line up:  There is a typical history: breathlessness on exertion or at rest, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, fatigue, reduced exercise tolerance, ankle swelling, abdominal distension, early satiety. There are objective signs of cardiac dysfunction: elevated JVP, pulmonary crackles, peripheral edema, S3 gallop, cardiomegaly, low blood pressure in advanced cases, or imaging/biomarker evidence (echocardiogram showing reduced ejection fraction or structural disease, or elevated BNP/NT‑proBNP). Other causes of these symptoms (like isolated lung disease, anemia, renal failure, obesity alone) have been reasonably excluded.  We describe heart failure in a few key ways:  By ejection fraction Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF): LVEF less than 40 percent. Heart failure with mildly reduced EF (HFmrEF): EF 40–49 percent. Heart failure with preserved EF (HFpEF): EF 50 percent or higher, but with objective evidence of diastolic dysfunction or raised filling pressures.  By time course Acute decompensated heart failure: sudden or rapidly worsening symptoms/signs, often requiring urgent treatment. Chronic heart failure: long‑standing, usually stable but with possible episodes of decompensation.  Common causes of heart failure  Ischemic heart disease Myocardial infarction and chronic coronary artery disease are leading causes. Infarction leads to loss of contractile myocardium, ventricular remodeling, dilation, and reduced systolic function.  Hypertension Long‑standing uncontrolled hypertension causes left ventricular hypertrophy, increased stiffness, and eventually systolic and/or diastolic dysfunction.  Valvular heart disease Aortic stenosis, mitral regurgitation, aortic regurgitation, and others alter pressure or volume loading on the ventricles, leading over time to chamber dilation, hypertrophy, and failure.  Cardiomyopathies Dilated cardiomyopathy (idiopathic, familial, viral, toxic such as alcohol or anthracyclines, peripartum) leads to systolic failure. Hypertrophic and restrictive cardiomyopathies often present with diastolic heart failure.  Arrhythmias and conduction disease Persistent tachyarrhythmias (e.g., atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, SVT) can cause tachycardia‑induced cardiomyopathy. Bradyarrhythmias or heart block can cause low output and precipitate HF.  Other systemic causes Pulmonary hypertension and right heart strain from lung disease. Obesity, diabetes, thyroid disease (hyper or hypo), severe anemia, and chronic kidney disease can all contribute.  How systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) can cause heart failure  SLE is a systemic autoimmune disease that can involve any cardiac structure. Heart failure in SLE is usually multifactorial. Mechanisms include:  Myocarditis Autoimmune inflammation of the myocardium is a direct cardiac manifestation of SLE. Inflammatory infiltration and myocyte necrosis lead to reduced contractility, arrhythmias, and dilated cardiomyopathy. This can cause HFrEF and sometimes acute severe decompensation.  Coronary artery disease SLE is associated with accelerated atherosclerosis due to chronic inflammation, immune complex deposition, steroid use, dyslipidemia, and other traditional risk factors. Younger women with SLE can develop premature ischemic heart disease and myocardial infarction, leading to ischemic cardiomyopathy.  Valvular disease (Libman‑Sacks endocarditis) SLE can cause sterile vegetations or thickening of valves, especially the mitral and aortic valves. Over time this may lead to significant valvular regurgitation or, less commonly, stenosis, causing volume or pressure overload and, eventually, HF.  Pericardial disease Pericarditis is common in SLE. Large, recurrent effusions or chronic constrictive pericarditis impair ventricular filling, causing right‑sided or biventricular failure symptoms. Cardiac tamponade is an emergency manifestation that can be seen in SLE.  Pulmonary hypertension SLE‑associated pulmonary arterial hypertension or chronic thromboembolic disease can overload the right ventricle, leading to right‑sided heart failure.  Medication and comorbidity effects Long‑term high‑dose corticosteroids can predispose to hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia, and atherosclerosis. Cyclophosphamide, anthracyclines, and some biologics used in severe SLE can be cardiotoxic and contribute to cardiomyopathy. Renal involvement (lupus nephritis) and consequent volume overload, hypertension, and uremia further stress the heart and worsen HF.  Putting it together, an SLE patient may develop HF because of direct myocardial inflammation, ischemic heart disease, valvular lesions, pericardial or pulmonary vascular disease, and general cardiovascular risk amplification by SLE and its treatment.  Management of heart failure in general  Management has three parallel goals: relieve symptoms, improve survival and reduce hospitalizations, and address underlying cause.  General measures and lifestyle Sodium restriction tailored to severity, often moderate restriction in chronic HF. Fluid restriction in patients with hyponatremia or severe congestion. Daily weight monitoring and education to recognize early decompensation. Avoid NSAIDs and drugs that worsen HF (e.g., certain calcium‑channel blockers in HFrEF, some antiarrhythmics). Smoking cessation, alcohol moderation or abstinence if alcohol‑related cardiomyopathy, regular but appropriate exercise for stable patients. Vaccinations (influenza, pneumococcal, COVID) to reduce infection‑triggered decompensation.  Pharmacologic therapy for HFrEF (core, unless contraindicated) ACE inhibitor or ARB or ARNI to reduce afterload, prevent remodeling, and improve survival. Evidence‑based beta‑blocker (e.g., bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate) started low and titrated up. Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (spironolactone or eplerenone). SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) regardless of diabetes status. Loop diuretics (e.g., furosemide) for symptom relief and congestion control. Additional options in selected patients: hydralazine plus nitrates (especially in those who cannot tolerate ACEI/ARB/ARNI or in some ethnic groups), ivabradine for patients with sinus rhythm and high resting heart rate despite beta‑blocker, digoxin in certain cases.  HFpEF and HFmrEF management Focus on controlling blood pressure, treating ischemia, managing atrial fibrillation, diuretics for congestion, and addressing obesity, diabetes, and sleep apnea. Some medications (SGLT2 inhibitors, MRAs, ARNI in selected HFmrEF/HFpEF) show benefit in outcomes but the effect size is generally less dramatic than in HFrEF.  Device and advanced therapies Implantable cardioverter‑defibrillator (ICD) for primary or secondary prevention of sudden cardiac death in appropriate HFrEF patients. Cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) for symptomatic HFrEF with wide QRS and dyssynchrony. Mechanical circulatory support (LVAD) and heart transplantation in selected advanced, refractory cases.  Treatment of reversible or precipitating causes Revascularization for significant coronary artery disease (PCI or CABG) when appropriate. Surgical or transcatheter correction of significant valvular lesions. Rate or rhythm control of atrial fibrillation, treatment of other arrhythmias. Tight control of blood pressure, diabetes, thyroid disorders, and anemia. Treatment of infection, pulmonary embolism, or other acute precipitants.  Specific aspects of heart failure management in SLE  Treat the underlying SLE activity High disease activity with myocarditis, pericarditis, or vasculitis requires immunosuppression. Corticosteroids are typically used for acute myocarditis or pericarditis, often combined with steroid‑sparing agents like azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil, or cyclophosphamide in severe cases. Biologic therapies (e.g., rituximab, belimumab) may be considered in refractory SLE; cardiac effects and risks need careful assessment.  Standard HF therapy still applies Most HF medications (ACEI/ARB/ARNI, beta‑blockers, MRAs, SGLT2 inhibitors, diuretics) are used similarly as in non‑SLE patients, with attention to renal function and blood pressure, which can be more labile due to nephritis or vasculitis.  Address SLE‑specific cardiac lesions Active myocarditis: requires both HF drugs and immunosuppression; diagnosis is often supported by cardiac MRI and sometimes biopsy. Pericarditis and pericardial effusion: manage with NSAIDs and colchicine for mild cases (if kidney function allows) plus SLE control; large effusions with tamponade may need pericardiocentesis or pericardial window. Constrictive pericarditis: may require pericardiectomy if chronic and hemodynamically significant. Libman‑Sacks endocarditis: anticoagulation may be indicated particularly if there is antiphospholipid syndrome or prior embolic events; significant regurgitation may eventually need valve surgery. Pulmonary arterial hypertension: treat with standard PAH therapies (endothelin receptor antagonists, PDE5 inhibitors, prostacyclin analogues) along with SLE control and HF management.  Risk factor modification and monitoring Aggressively manage cardiovascular risk factors given the high atherosclerotic burden in SLE: statins, blood pressure control, smoking cessation, weight and glucose management. Regular echocardiographic surveillance in patients with high SLE activity, long‑standing disease, or established cardiac involvement, to detect early dysfunction. Balance immunosuppressive therapy and steroid dose to control SLE while minimizing long‑term cardiometabolic complications.  In summary, heart failure is diagnosed when typical symptoms and signs of congestion or low output are present together with objective evidence of cardiac dysfunction and no better alternative explanation. Many conditions cause HF, but in SLE it often arises from a combination of myocarditis, ischemic heart disease, valvular lesions, pericardial disease, pulmonary hypertension, and treatment‑related or comorbidity‑related factors. Management combines guideline‑directed heart failure therapy with rigorous control of SLE activity and cardiovascular risk, tailored to the specific cardiac lesion and overall organ involvement.

Mechanisms by which SLE leads to HF  Myocarditis Immune-mediated inflammation of the myocardium can cause acute systolic dysfunction, arrhythmias, and cardiogenic shock. Patients present with chest pain, dyspnea, new heart failure signs, and elevated troponin/BNP; echo shows global hypokinesis, sometimes pericardial effusion. Accelerated atherosclerosis and coronary artery disease SLE markedly increases risk of premature coronary artery disease due to chronic inflammation, immune complex deposition, endothelial dysfunction, traditional risk factors, and steroid exposure. Myocardial infarction from coronary disease damages myocardium and can progress to chronic ischemic cardiomyopathy and heart failure.  Hypertension and renal disease Lupus nephritis, steroids, and chronic kidney disease contribute to hypertension, which drives LV hypertrophy and HFpEF, and later systolic HF. Volume overload from renal dysfunction can precipitate decompensated heart failure.  Valvular disease Libman–Sacks endocarditis Sterile vegetations on mitral and aortic valves can lead to significant regurgitation, causing volume overload and eventual LV dysfunction. Valves may also be affected by secondary antiphospholipid syndrome, leading to thickening and dysfunction. Arrhythmias and conduction disease SLE-associated myocarditis, fibrosis, or coronary disease can cause atrial fibrillation, flutter, or ventricular arrhythmias, as well as conduction blocks. Persistent tachycardia or bradycardia can worsen heart failure.  Sometimes heart failure in SLE is also drug related, for example from anthracycline chemotherapy used for lupus-related malignancy, or long-term high-dose steroids indirectly through hypertension and metabolic effects.  Management of heart failure in general  Management has two layers: treat the heart failure syndrome itself and correct the underlying cause, including the SLE component when relevant.  General measures Salt restriction usually about 2 grams sodium per day in symptomatic patients Fluid restriction in hyponatremia or advanced HF Daily weight monitoring and education on recognizing fluid overload Avoidance of NSAIDs and other drugs that worsen HF Vaccinations influenza, pneumococcal, COVID to reduce infection-triggered decompensation Smoking cessation, moderation or avoidance of alcohol, regular but tailored physical activity  Pharmacologic therapy for HFrEF reduced ejection fraction, typically LVEF ≤ 40 percent  Four foundational drug classes if tolerated ACE inhibitor or ARB or ARNI sacubitril valsartan if symptomatic and stable, which reduces mortality and hospitalization Evidence-based beta-blocker such as carvedilol, bisoprolol, or metoprolol succinate, started low and uptitrated Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist spironolactone or eplerenone for further mortality reduction SGLT2 inhibitor dapagliflozin, empagliflozin for mortality and hospitalization benefit regardless of diabetes status  Additional options based on profile Loop diuretics such as furosemide, torsemide, bumetanide for volume overload; Control of underlying SLE Assessment of lupus activity: complement levels, anti-dsDNA, other autoantibodies, inflammatory markers, evaluation for nephritis. If myocarditis or active inflammatory cardiac disease is present, initiate immunosuppression, typically High-dose corticosteroids intravenous methylprednisolone pulses followed by tapering oral prednisone Plus a steroid-sparing immunosuppressant such as mycophenolate mofetil, azathioprine, or cyclophosphamide depending on severity, organ involvement, and guidelines Refractory cases may require biologics such as rituximab in selected settings. For pericarditis and small effusions, NSAIDs and colchicine are often used in nonrenal, stable patients; however in SLE with renal disease or HF, choices must be individualized. Close collaboration between cardiology and rheumatology is essential.  Management of cardiovascular risk Aggressive treatment of hypertension with ACEI ARB ARNI, calcium-channel blockers, or others as appropriate, keeping in mind renal status. Lipid management with statins due to high atherosclerotic risk. Monitoring and treatment of diabetes and metabolic syndrome, especially in patients on long-term steroids. Smoking cessation and lifestyle modifications. Careful steroid use: use lowest effective dose, taper when possible, and favor steroid-sparing agents to reduce long-term cardiovascular harm.  Heart failure-specific therapy in SLE Use standard HF drugs unless contraindicated by renal dysfunction, hyperkalemia, severe hypotension, or drug interactions. Monitor renal function and electrolytes closely, particularly when combining ACEI ARB ARNI and MRAs in patients with lupus nephritis. Adjust diuretics based on volume status and kidney function. Consider anticoagulation if there is atrial fibrillation, LV thrombus, or antiphospholipid antibodies with prior thrombosis. Evaluate regularly for ischemia; perform coronary imaging if angina, troponin elevations out of proportion to myocarditis, or high risk is present. Address SLE-related valvular disease with echocardiographic surveillance; intervene surgically or via transcatheter approaches when valvular lesions become severe and symptomatic.  Monitoring and follow-up Repeat echocardiography to track LV function, valvular status, and pericardial effusions. Serial natriuretic peptides BNP NT-proBNP can help track HF status, while lupus serologies guide SLE activity. Education of the patient on recognizing flare versus HF decompensation, since both may present with fatigue and dyspnea but have different implications.  In concise terms, call it heart failure when there are compatible symptoms and signs plus objective evidence of cardiac dysfunction. SLE can cause heart failure through myocarditis, accelerated CAD, valvular and pericardial disease, hypertension from renal involvement, and chronic inflammation leading to cardiomyopathy. Management requires standard, guideline-directed heart failure therapy plus aggressive control of SLE activity and cardiovascular risk factors, with joint care from cardiology and rheumatology.
7|72: Heart failure means the heart is unable to pump enough blood to meet the body’s needs, or it can do so only with raised filling pressures. It is a clinical syndrome, not a single disease: you recognize it by a typical combination of symptoms and signs, supported by investigations.  In simple terms, the pump is weak, stiff, or both. You say a patient has heart failure when all three are present Typical symptoms • Breathlessness, especially on exertion or when lying flat • Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (waking at night gasping for air) • Fatigue, exercise intolerance, reduced effort capacity • Ankle swelling, abdominal distension, early satiety  Typical signs • Elevated jugular venous pressure, peripheral edema • Lung crackles, third heart sound (S3), displaced apex beat • Hepatomegaly, ascites in more advanced cases  Objective evidence of cardiac dysfunction • Echocardiogram showing reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) or impaired relaxation / increased filling pressures (HFpEF) • Elevated natriuretic peptides (BNP or NT-proBNP) • Structural heart disease, such as dilated or hypertrophied chambers, significant valve disease  Without objective evidence, you describe it as suspected heart failure; with objective evidence, you confirm the diagnosis and classify it (HFrEF, HFmrEF, HFpEF) according to ejection fraction.  Major causes of heart failure • Ischemic heart disease: prior myocardial infarction, chronic ischemia leading to ventricular remodeling and systolic dysfunction. • Hypertension: chronic pressure overload causing left ventricular hypertrophy, stiffness, and eventually failure. • Valvular heart disease: aortic stenosis / regurgitation, mitral regurgitation, etc., causing volume or pressure overload. • Cardiomyopathies: dilated, hypertrophic, restrictive; genetic, viral, alcoholic, peripartum, etc. • Arrhythmias: chronic tachycardia, atrial fibrillation with fast ventricular response, bradycardias with low output. • Congenital heart disease and right-sided causes: pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale. • Metabolic / systemic: thyroid disease, anemia, chronic kidney disease, diabetes, obesity.  How systemic lupus erythematosus SLE can cause heart failure SLE is a multisystem autoimmune disease and can involve the heart in several ways, any of which can lead to heart failure over time or during flares  Myocarditis Autoimmune inflammation of the myocardium causes myocyte injury, edema, and impaired contractility. This can present as acute systolic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, arrhythmias, and cardiogenic shock in severe cases. If persistent or recurrent, it leads to a dilated cardiomyopathy.  Coronary artery disease and accelerated atherosclerosis SLE, especially with long-standing inflammation and steroid use, markedly increases the risk of premature coronary artery disease. Myocardial infarction causes scarred, akinetic segments, reducing left ventricular function and predisposing to ischemic cardiomyopathy and chronic heart failure.  Valvular disease Libman–Sacks endocarditis SLE can cause sterile vegetations, thickening, and regurgitation (often of the mitral or aortic valve). Significant regurgitation leads to chronic volume overload, chamber dilation, and eventually heart failure.  Pericardial disease Pericarditis and pericardial effusion are common in SLE. Constrictive pericarditis or large effusions with tamponade can cause a form of heart failure due to impaired filling. Chronic constriction may mimic right-sided or biventricular heart failure.  Pulmonary hypertension SLE-associated pulmonary arterial hypertension, chronic thromboembolic disease, or interstitial lung disease can lead to right ventricular pressure overload, right heart failure, edema, and exercise intolerance.  Indirect or treatment-related factors • Long-term glucocorticoids: dyslipidemia, hypertension, diabetes, weight gain, all promoting heart failure. • Renal involvement (lupus nephritis): fluid overload, hypertension, and anemia. • Antiphospholipid syndrome overlap: recurrent thrombosis, myocardial infarction, pulmonary embolism.  Overview of management of heart failure in the context of SLE Management has two parallel aims treat heart failure according to standard guidelines, and treat the underlying SLE-related cardiac pathology and systemic disease.  General principles of heart failure management 1. Lifestyle and education • Sodium restriction, appropriate fluid control in congested patients • Daily weights and self-monitoring for early detection of decompensation • Smoking cessation, alcohol moderation, exercise within tolerance • Vaccinations (influenza, pneumococcal) to reduce infection-triggered decompensation  2. Guideline-directed medical therapy GDMT for HFrEF (Adjust for kidney function, blood pressure, and drug interactions, especially with immunosuppressants) • ACE inhibitor or ARB or ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan) to reduce afterload, improve remodeling, and symptoms. • Evidence-based beta-blocker (carvedilol, bisoprolol, metoprolol succinate) to improve survival and reduce arrhythmias. • Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (spironolactone, eplerenone) for further mortality benefit and diuresis. • SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) now first-line for HFrEF, regardless of diabetes. • Loop diuretics (furosemide, bumetanide) for symptomatic fluid overload. • Additional agents as needed (ivabradine, hydralazine–nitrate, vericiguat) in selected patients.  3. HFpEF and HFmrEF • Focus on controlling blood pressure, heart rate, ischemia, and comorbidities. • Diuretics for symptom relief from congestion. • SGLT2 inhibitors have emerging evidence for benefit in HFpEF.  4. Device and advanced therapies • Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator ICD for low EF and high arrhythmic risk. • Cardiac resynchronization therapy CRT for LBBB with reduced EF and symptoms. • Mechanical circulatory support and transplantation for refractory end-stage heart failure.  SLE-specific management in heart failure 1. Myocarditis • Confirm with echo, cardiac MRI, biomarkers troponin, and occasionally biopsy. • High-dose corticosteroids (e.g., IV methylprednisolone pulses followed by oral taper) plus steroid-sparing immunosuppressants (cyclophosphamide, mycophenolate) depending on severity. • Standard HF therapy as tolerated (ACEi/ARB/ARNI, beta-blocker, diuretics) once hemodynamically stable.  2. Coronary artery disease and MI • Aggressive risk factor control: statins, blood pressure, glucose; minimize long-term steroid exposure if possible. • Standard ACS management (antiplatelets, statins, revascularization) plus SLE control. • Long-term HF management if LV dysfunction remains.  3. Valvular lesions (Libman–Sacks and others) • Regular echocardiographic follow-up. • Anticoagulation if there is coexistent antiphospholipid syndrome or high thromboembolic risk. • Surgical or transcatheter repair/replacement if severe regurgitation or stenosis with symptoms or LV dysfunction. • Perioperative planning with rheumatology for immunosuppression and infection prophylaxis.  4. Pericardial disease • NSAIDs and colchicine for uncomplicated pericarditis, if renal function permits. • Corticosteroids for SLE-related pericarditis, especially with systemic flare. • Pericardiocentesis for tamponade; pericardiectomy for chronic constriction.  5. Pulmonary hypertension and right heart failure • Evaluate with echocardiography and right-heart catheterization. • Treat underlying lung disease or thromboembolism. • PAH-targeted therapy (endothelin receptor antagonists, PDE5 inhibitors, prostacyclin analogues) in specialized centers. • Optimize SLE control to reduce inflammation-driven vascular disease.  Drug and interaction considerations in SLE with HF • NSAIDs and some COX-2 inhibitors can worsen renal function and fluid retention; use cautiously. • Glucocorticoids promote fluid retention and hypertension; use lowest effective dose and taper when possible. • Some immunosuppressants (e.g., cyclophosphamide) require careful monitoring of kidney function and infection risk, which indirectly impact HF stability. • Monitor for QT prolongation and arrhythmias when combining drugs that affect conduction or electrolytes.  In summary, heart failure is a clinical syndrome of inadequate cardiac output and/or elevated filling pressures, diagnosed by symptoms, signs, and objective evidence of cardiac dysfunction. SLE can cause heart failure through myocarditis, accelerated atherosclerosis and infarction, valvular lesions, pericardial disease, pulmonary hypertension, and treatment-related metabolic effects. Management combines standard guideline-directed therapies for heart failure with tailored immunosuppression and treatment of the specific SLE-related cardiac lesion, in close collaboration between cardiology and rheumatology.
8|72: Heart failure is a clinical syndrome in which the heart is unable to pump blood sufficiently to meet the body’s metabolic demands, or can do so only at the cost of raised filling pressures. It is not a single disease but a final common pathway of many cardiac conditions.  When to call it heart failure You say a patient has heart failure when all three elements are present:  1. Typical symptoms    These include one or more of the following:    • Breathlessness, especially on exertion, lying flat (orthopnea), or waking at night gasping for air (paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea)    • Fatigue, exercise intolerance, weakness    • Peripheral edema (swollen legs, ankles), weight gain from fluid retention, abdominal distension    • Reduced effort capacity, easy fatigability  2. Typical signs on examination    Common findings include:    • Tachycardia, low blood pressure (in advanced cases)    • Elevated jugular venous pressure    • Basal lung crepitations from pulmonary congestion    • Peripheral edema, sacral edema, ascites    • Enlarged, displaced apex beat, S3 gallop rhythm  3. Objective evidence of cardiac dysfunction    You should demonstrate structural or functional heart abnormality, for example:    • Reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (HFrEF)    • Normal or near-normal EF with evidence of impaired relaxation or raised filling pressures (HFpEF)    • Enlarged ventricles or atria, valvular disease, wall motion abnormalities on echocardiogram    • Elevated natriuretic peptides (BNP or NT‑proBNP)  If symptoms or signs are present but no cardiac dysfunction is demonstrable, be cautious about labeling it heart failure; look for alternative explanations like anemia, lung disease, obesity, or deconditioning.  Causes of heart failure Common categories are:  Ischemic heart disease    Chronic coronary artery disease or previous myocardial infarction cause loss of viable myocardium, ventricular remodelling, and systolic dysfunction.  Hypertension    Long-standing uncontrolled high blood pressure leads to left ventricular hypertrophy, stiff ventricle, diastolic dysfunction, and eventually systolic failure.  Valvular heart disease    Aortic stenosis or regurgitation, mitral regurgitation or stenosis can cause pressure or volume overload, leading to ventricular dilatation and failure.  Cardiomyopathies    • Dilated cardiomyopathy (idiopathic, familial, alcohol, viral, peripartum, chemo‑induced)    • Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (often genetic)    • Restrictive cardiomyopathy (amyloidosis, infiltrative disease)  Arrhythmias    Persistent tachyarrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, supraventricular tachycardia, or frequent ectopy can cause tachycardia‑induced cardiomyopathy; bradyarrhythmias can reduce cardiac output.  Right heart and pulmonary causes    Pulmonary hypertension, chronic lung disease (cor pulmonale), pulmonary embolism, congenital shunts.  Metabolic and systemic causes    Diabetes, thyroid disease (hyper- or hypothyroidism), severe anemia, thiamine deficiency, obesity.  How systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) causes heart failure SLE is a chronic autoimmune disease with multi‑organ involvement, including the heart. It can lead to heart failure via multiple mechanisms, often overlapping:  Myocarditis    The immune system attacks the myocardium, causing inflammatory infiltrates, myocyte necrosis, and edema. Consequences:    • Global or regional systolic dysfunction    • Dilated and weakened ventricles    • Arrhythmias due to inflamed conduction tissue    This can present acutely with chest pain, dyspnea, and elevated cardiac biomarkers, or insidiously with progressive heart failure.  Pericardial disease    Pericarditis is common in SLE. Mechanisms toward heart failure include:    • Large pericardial effusions causing tamponade: impaired ventricular filling and reduced stroke volume    • Recurrent or chronic pericarditis leading to constrictive pericarditis: stiff pericardium restricts diastolic filling, mimicking right‑sided heart failure  Coronary artery disease and accelerated atherosclerosis    Patients with SLE, especially with long disease duration, chronic inflammation, and corticosteroid use, develop premature atherosclerosis. This leads to:    • Myocardial infarction    • Chronic ischemic cardiomyopathy    with resulting systolic dysfunction and heart failure similar to non‑SLE ischemic heart disease.  Valvular involvement (Libman–Sacks endocarditis)    SLE can cause sterile vegetations on valves, commonly mitral and aortic. Over time this leads to:    • Regurgitant lesions (mitral or aortic regurgitation)    • Occasionally stenotic lesions    Volume or pressure overload from valvular disease triggers ventricular dilatation and eventual heart failure.  Pulmonary hypertension    Can result from:    • SLE‑associated pulmonary vasculopathy    • Chronic pulmonary emboli, especially in those with antiphospholipid syndrome    • Interstitial lung disease    Consequences include right ventricular hypertrophy, dilation, and right‑sided heart failure.  Antiphospholipid syndrome and microvascular disease    Antiphospholipid antibodies may cause:    • Recurrent coronary thrombosis or microinfarcts    • Cardiomyopathy from repeated small ischemic insults  Drug toxicity    Medications used in SLE can rarely contribute:    • Long‑term high‑dose steroids worsen hypertension, diabetes, and dyslipidemia, all of which accelerate atherosclerosis    • Certain immunosuppressants might have indirect cardiovascular effects  In many SLE patients, heart failure is multifactorial: some combination of myocarditis, ischemia, hypertension, valvular disease, and pulmonary hypertension.  Management of heart failure in general Management follows two parallel tracks: treating the syndrome of heart failure and addressing the underlying cause (in this case, SLE and its specific cardiac lesion).  General approach to heart failure (especially HFrEF)  Non‑pharmacologic    • Salt restriction and cautious fluid restriction in volume‑overloaded patients    • Daily weight monitoring to detect fluid retention early    • Smoking cessation, alcohol moderation or cessation    • Vaccination (influenza, pneumococcal)    • Supervised exercise and cardiac rehabilitation when stable  Core pharmacologic therapy for HFrEF (reduced EF)    • ACE inhibitor or ARB or ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan) to reduce afterload and reverse remodeling    • Evidence‑based beta‑blocker (carvedilol, bisoprolol, metoprolol succinate) to reduce mortality and improve function    • Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (spironolactone or eplerenone)    • SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) even without diabetes    • Loop diuretics (furosemide, bumetanide) for symptom relief and volume control    • For selected patients: hydralazine plus nitrates (especially in Black patients or those intolerant of ACEI/ARB), ivabradine, digoxin  Device and procedural therapy    • Cardiac resynchronization therapy in patients with LBBB and reduced EF    • ICD for primary or secondary prevention of sudden cardiac death    • Revascularization (PCI or CABG) when ischemia is a major driver    • Valve repair or replacement for significant valvular disease    • Advanced therapies: LV assist devices or transplantation in refractory end‑stage HF  Management nuances in HFpEF    • Focus on optimizing blood pressure, controlling heart rate, managing ischemia, treating atrial fibrillation, controlling volume with diuretics, and addressing comorbidities (obesity, diabetes, sleep apnea)  Specific management when SLE is the cause The strategy depends on the specific cardiac manifestation.  SLE myocarditis    • High‑dose corticosteroids (e.g., IV methylprednisolone followed by oral taper) once infection is excluded    • Additional immunosuppressive therapy in severe or refractory cases (cyclophosphamide, mycophenolate, azathioprine, or others as guided by rheumatology)    • Standard HF therapy (ACEI/ARB/ARNI, beta‑blockers, diuretics, etc.) as tolerated    • Careful monitoring for arrhythmias; treat with appropriate antiarrhythmics or devices if needed  Pericardial disease    • Acute pericarditis: NSAIDs if renal function allows, colchicine, and often low‑to‑moderate dose steroids for SLE control    • Large effusion with tamponade physiology: urgent pericardiocentesis and hemodynamic support    • Constrictive pericarditis: diuretics for symptoms; pericardiectomy if symptoms are severe and persistent  Coronary artery disease in SLE    • Manage similarly to other patients with MI or ischemia: antiplatelets, statins, beta‑blockers, ACEI/ARB    • Revascularization when indicated    • Aggressive control of risk factors: blood pressure, lipids, glucose, smoking cessation    • Optimize SLE control to reduce chronic inflammation, which contributes to atherosclerosis  Valvular disease (Libman–Sacks or others)    • Regular echocardiographic monitoring    • Anticoagulation may be indicated in some patients, especially if there is concomitant antiphospholipid syndrome or embolic events    • Valve surgery (repair or replacement) when regurgitation or stenosis becomes severe and symptomatic, with pre‑ and post‑operative immunosuppression tailored to disease activity  Pulmonary hypertension and right heart failure    • Evaluate for and treat underlying causes: chronic thromboembolic disease, interstitial lung disease, active vasculitis    • Pulmonary vasodilator therapy in appropriate types of pulmonary arterial hypertension (endothelin receptor antagonists, PDE‑5 inhibitors, prostacyclin analogs) in specialist centers    • Diuretics for volume overload; In summary, heart failure is defined clinically by symptoms, signs, and objective cardiac dysfunction. SLE can cause heart failure through myocarditis, coronary disease, valvular lesions, pericardial disease, pulmonary hypertension, and renal‑driven hypertension and volume overload. Management combines standard heart failure therapy with aggressive control of lupus activity and targeted treatment of whichever cardiac structures are affected.
10|72: Heart failure is a clinical syndrome in which the heart is unable to pump enough blood to meet the body’s needs, or can do so only at the cost of abnormally high filling pressures. It is not a single disease but a final pathway of many cardiac problems.  When to call it heart failure Clinically, we call it heart failure when three things line up:  There are typical symptoms Such as shortness of breath on exertion or when lying flat, waking up gasping at night, leg or ankle swelling, rapid fatigue, reduced exercise tolerance, abdominal swelling, early satiety, or weight gain from fluid.  There are typical signs on exam Such as elevated jugular venous pressure, lung crackles from pulmonary congestion, peripheral edema, S3 gallop, hepatomegaly, ascites, or cool extremities in advanced low-output states.  There is objective evidence of cardiac dysfunction This usually comes from echocardiogram, showing either: Reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (HFrEF, often ≤40%) Preserved or mildly reduced EF but evidence of diastolic dysfunction, elevated filling pressures, structural heart disease such as LV hypertrophy, left atrial enlargement, or raised natriuretic peptides (HFpEF / HFmrEF).  So you say a patient has heart failure when symptoms and/or signs of congestion or low output are present, and you can reasonably attribute these to cardiac dysfunction rather than something else (like anemia, lung disease, kidney failure alone, or venous insufficiency), ideally supported by echo or natriuretic peptides.  Common causes of heart failure Ischemic heart disease Myocardial infarction and chronic coronary artery disease are among the most common causes; repeated or large infarcts weaken the myocardium.  Hypertension Long-standing uncontrolled hypertension leads to LV hypertrophy, then stiffening, diastolic dysfunction, and eventually systolic dysfunction.  Cardiomyopathies Dilated cardiomyopathy (genetic, viral, alcoholic, peripartum, toxic such as anthracyclines) Hypertrophic and restrictive cardiomyopathies Infiltrative diseases (amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, hemochromatosis).  Valvular heart disease Aortic stenosis or regurgitation, mitral regurgitation or stenosis, congenital lesions can chronically overload the heart.  Arrhythmias Persistent tachyarrhythmias like atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, atrial flutter, SVT, or frequent PVCs/VT can lead to tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy.  Right-sided/secondary causes Pulmonary hypertension from lung disease, pulmonary embolism, or left-sided HF leading to cor pulmonale.  Others Endocrine (thyroid disease, diabetes), nutritional deficiencies, chronic kidney disease, HIV, chemotherapy, radiation.  How systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) can cause heart failure SLE can involve the heart in multiple ways, each of which can lead to HF. Mechanisms include:  Myocarditis Inflammation of the heart muscle due to immune complex deposition and complement activation. Can cause global LV dysfunction, reduced ejection fraction, arrhythmias. Presents with chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations, elevated troponin, and abnormal echo.  Pericardial disease progressing to constriction or tamponade Pericarditis is common in SLE; recurrent or chronic inflammation can cause thickened, fibrotic pericardium (constrictive pericarditis), which impairs diastolic filling and leads to signs and symptoms of right-sided HF. Large effusions with tamponade cause reduced cardiac output and can mimic or precipitate HF physiology.  Coronary artery disease and accelerated atherosclerosis SLE itself, plus chronic steroid therapy, dyslipidemia, and inflammation, accelerate atherosclerosis. Premature coronary artery disease leads to myocardial infarction, ischemic cardiomyopathy, and chronic left ventricular dysfunction, causing HFrEF.  Valvular disease (Libman–Sacks endocarditis) Nonbacterial vegetations on mitral or aortic valves can cause regurgitation. Chronic significant regurgitation leads to volume overload and ultimately HF.  Pulmonary hypertension Due to pulmonary vasculopathy, chronic thromboembolism, interstitial lung disease, or association with antiphospholipid syndrome. Causes right ventricular failure and systemic congestion.  Hypertension and renal disease Lupus nephritis can lead to chronic kidney disease and secondary hypertension, which further strain the heart, leading to LV hypertrophy and HFpEF or HFrEF over time.  Medication-related cardiotoxicity Some drugs used in SLE (e.g., cyclophosphamide, high-dose steroids indirectly via metabolic effects, or certain other immunosuppressants) can contribute to cardiomyopathy, though this is less common and regimen-specific.  So SLE can cause HF through direct myocardial inflammation, chronic pressure/volume overload, vascular disease, and treatment-related toxicity.  Management of heart failure in the context of SLE Management has two parallel arms: treating HF according to standard cardiology guidelines and treating the underlying SLE activity or comorbidity driving the HF.  1. General management of heart failure The approach depends on whether it is HFrEF, HFpEF, or right-sided HF, but typical components include:  Lifestyle and non-pharmacologic Sodium restriction tailored to congestion severity. Fluid restriction in significant hyponatremia or advanced HF. Daily weight monitoring, education on recognizing worsening symptoms. Smoking cessation, limiting alcohol, optimizing body weight. Appropriate physical activity / supervised rehab once stable.  Pharmacologic therapy for HFrEF (reduced EF) Key evidence-based drug classes: RAAS inhibition: ACE inhibitors or ARBs, or ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan) for suitable patients. Beta-blockers with HF indication (e.g., bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate). Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (spironolactone, eplerenone). SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) regardless of diabetes for HFrEF. Loop diuretics (furosemide, bumetanide, torsemide) and sometimes thiazides for congestion relief. In select patients: ivabradine, hydralazine plus nitrates (especially in those who cannot tolerate ACEi/ARB/ARNI or certain ethnic groups per guidelines), digoxin.  Pharmacologic therapy for HFpEF Control blood pressure aggressively, treat ischemia, manage atrial fibrillation and other arrhythmias, optimize volume with diuretics, manage comorbidities (obesity, diabetes, sleep apnea). SGLT2 inhibitors now have evidence for benefit in HFpEF as well.  Devices and advanced therapies Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) for primary or secondary prevention in HFrEF with low EF and appropriate survival expectation. Cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) in selected patients with LBBB and wide QRS plus reduced EF and symptoms. Mechanical circulatory support (LVAD) or heart transplantation in end-stage HF, considering SLE activity and organ involvement.  2. Specific management when HF is due to SLE Identify the mechanism and drive therapy accordingly, always balancing immunosuppression against infection and other risks.  SLE myocarditis Confirm as possible with echo, cardiac MRI, and sometimes biopsy. Treat active lupus: high-dose corticosteroids (e.g., IV methylprednisolone pulses, then tapering oral steroids), plus steroid-sparing immunosuppressants such as cyclophosphamide, mycophenolate mofetil, or others per rheumatology guidance. Add standard HF therapy (RAAS blockade, beta-blocker, diuretics) once hemodynamically stable. Monitor for arrhythmias and conduction disorders.  Pericarditis and constrictive pericarditis Acute pericarditis: NSAIDs and colchicine if renal function and other factors allow; for active lupus-related pericarditis, add corticosteroids and immunosuppressives. Refractory or recurrent disease: consider azathioprine, mycophenolate, or biologics (e.g., rituximab) depending on the overall SLE picture. Constrictive pericarditis: if truly constrictive and persistent, pericardiectomy may be needed after optimizing inflammation and SLE control. Tamponade: urgent pericardiocentesis.  Coronary artery disease and MI in SLE Treat acute MI per standard protocols (reperfusion via PCI if indicated, antiplatelets, statins, beta-blockers unless contraindicated, RAAS inhibitors), but carefully consider bleeding risk, thrombosis risk (especially with antiphospholipid antibodies), and SLE-related vasculitis. Aggressive secondary prevention: high-intensity statin, tight BP and glucose control, smoking cessation, weight management, regular exercise as tolerated. For ischemic cardiomyopathy, follow HFrEF guidelines.  Valvular disease (Libman–Sacks) Manage significant regurgitation or stenosis per usual valvular guidelines. Anticoagulation may be indicated, especially with antiphospholipid antibodies or prior embolic events. Valve surgery may be needed for severe symptomatic lesions.  Pulmonary hypertension and right-sided HF Evaluate cause: V/Q scan or CT to assess chronic thromboembolic disease, echocardiography and right heart catheterization for hemodynamics, screen for interstitial lung disease. If SLE vasculopathy: immunosuppression plus PAH-specific therapy (endothelin receptor antagonists, phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors, prostacyclin analogues) under specialist care. Anticoagulate where there is antiphospholipid syndrome or chronic thromboembolic disease. Manage right HF with careful diuresis, oxygen, and avoidance of factors that worsen pulmonary pressures.  Renal disease and hypertension Treat lupus nephritis with appropriate immunosuppression (mycophenolate, cyclophosphamide etc.) plus RAAS blockade for both renal and cardiac protection if tolerated. Control blood pressure tightly, usually with RAAS inhibitors, calcium channel blockers, beta-blockers, and diuretics as needed. Dose-adjust HF medications for renal function and watch electrolytes closely.  Multidisciplinary care Optimal management of HF in SLE usually requires close collaboration among cardiology, rheumatology, nephrology, and sometimes pulmonology and hematology. Monitoring for treatment-related toxicity is critical: steroids, immunosuppressants, and HF drugs all have potential adverse effects.  In summary, heart failure is diagnosed when there are compatible symptoms and signs supported by objective evidence of cardiac dysfunction. SLE can cause HF via myocarditis, pericardial disease, valvular lesions, accelerated atherosclerosis, pulmonary hypertension, renal-related hypertension, and treatment toxicity. Management always includes guideline-directed HF therapy plus targeted control of SLE activity and its specific cardiovascular complications, coordinated in a multidisciplinary manner.
1|73: Pan-searing is one of the best and most reliable ways to cook salmon because it gives you crisp, flavorful skin and a tender, moist interior with very little fuss. Start with salmon fillets that are patted dry with paper towels; moisture is the enemy of good browning. Season generously with salt and a bit of freshly ground pepper. Use a heavy skillet, ideally cast iron or stainless steel, and heat a thin layer of high smoke point oil like avocado, canola, or grapeseed over medium to medium high heat until it shimmers. Place the salmon skin side down and then do not move it for several minutes. This lets the skin render and crisp and also helps build a good sear without sticking. Adjust the heat so the oil is gently sizzling but not smoking aggressively. Cook mostly on the skin side, about two thirds of the total time, until you can see the color of the cooked salmon rising up the sides and the flesh turning opaque about halfway to three quarters of the way. Then gently flip and cook just another minute or two on the flesh side to finish. Aim for a slightly translucent center; salmon continues to cook off the heat, and overcooking quickly dries it out. For extra flavor, you can add a knob of butter, crushed garlic, and a sprig of thyme or dill in the last minute, basting the top with the foaming butter. Rest the fillets a couple of minutes before serving. This method highlights the natural richness of salmon and works with simple sides like steamed vegetables, rice, or a lemony salad.
2|73: For most home kitchens, the best all‑around way to cook salmon is to pan‑sear it on the stovetop and finish it gently if needed. Start with fillets that are close to room temperature and very dry on the surface; pat them thoroughly with paper towels so they can brown instead of steam. Season simply with salt and a bit of pepper. Heat a neutral oil with a high smoke point in a heavy skillet, ideally cast iron or stainless steel, over medium to medium‑high heat until the oil shimmers. Place the salmon in the pan skin side down if it has skin, laying it away from you to avoid splatter. Press lightly for the first 10 to 20 seconds so the skin stays flat. Let it cook mostly on that first side without moving it; the skin will crisp and the flesh will slowly turn opaque from the bottom up. When the fish is about two‑thirds opaque, reduce the heat to medium‑low, add a small knob of butter plus a smashed garlic clove and a sprig of a fresh herb like thyme or dill, and gently baste the top of the salmon with the foaming butter. Flip once only near the end if you want light browning on the top, or leave it skin side down the entire time for maximum crisp skin. Pull it from the pan when the center is still slightly translucent and just beginning to flake; it will finish cooking from residual heat. This method gives you a contrast of crisp exterior and tender, juicy interior, works with or without skin, and takes only 6 to 10 minutes depending on thickness. Serve immediately with a squeeze of lemon and any simple side, like roasted vegetables or a fresh salad, to highlight the salmon rather than hide it under heavy sauces.
3|73: For consistently great salmon with minimal fuss, pan-searing followed by a short roast in the oven works beautifully. Start by bringing the salmon to room temperature for 15–20 minutes and patting it very dry with paper towels; dry surface is crucial for a good sear. Season simply with salt and a little pepper, and if you like, rub on a thin film of neutral oil or a mix of oil and softened butter. Use a heavy skillet, ideally cast iron or stainless steel, and heat a small amount of high-smoke-point oil over medium-high until it shimmers. Place the salmon in the pan skin-side down if it has skin and immediately use a spatula to press gently for 10–15 seconds so the skin stays flat and crisp instead of curling. Let it cook mostly undisturbed so the skin renders and turns crisp, usually 4–6 minutes depending on thickness, lowering the heat slightly if the oil starts to smoke excessively. Once the skin is well browned and the flesh has turned opaque about two-thirds of the way up the sides, carefully flip the fillets. You can finish on the stovetop at medium to medium-low, or slide the pan into a preheated 375–400°F 190–205°C oven to finish gently. Depending on thickness, it may only need 3–6 more minutes. The salmon is done when it flakes easily with a fork but is still moist and slightly translucent in the very center, around 120–125°F 49–52°C for medium. Remove from heat just before it reaches your target because carryover heat will finish the cooking. Rest it a few minutes before serving. During the last minute or two you can add a knob of butter, some smashed garlic, and a few herb sprigs to the pan, basting the fish with the foaming butter for extra flavor. Finish simply with a squeeze of lemon, a drizzle of good olive oil, or a spoonful of herb sauce like chimichurri or dill yogurt so the taste of the salmon stays front and center.

7|73: For most home kitchens, the best way to cook salmon is a simple pan-sear followed by a brief finish in the oven, which gives you a crisp exterior and tender, moist interior with very little guesswork. Bring the salmon to room temperature for about 15–20 minutes and pat it completely dry, especially the skin if it’s on. Preheat your oven to around 375–400°F and place an oven-safe skillet on the stove over medium-high heat with a tablespoon of oil. When the oil shimmers, place the salmon in the pan skin side down if it has skin, or presentation side down if it does not. Gently press it for the first 10–15 seconds so it doesn’t curl, then let it sear undisturbed until the edges turn opaque and the skin is deep golden and crisp. This usually takes about 3–5 minutes depending on thickness. Carefully flip the salmon, then slide the whole pan into the hot oven. This will usually take another 3–6 minutes. Rest it for a couple of minutes out of the oven so the juices redistribute. Finish with a squeeze of lemon, a small knob of butter that melts over the top, and some fresh herbs like dill, chives, or parsley.
