URETERS  Anatomy and location The ureters are muscular tubes (25–30 cm) that convey urine from renal pelvis to urinary bladder. They are retroperitoneal. They begin at the ureteropelvic junction at the renal pelvis, descend on the psoas major, cross the pelvic brim at the level of the sacroiliac joint, then run along the lateral pelvic wall to enter the bladder obliquely at the posterolateral angles of the trigone. On the right, the ureter lies behind the duodenum and is crossed by the right colic and ileocolic vessels; on the left, it is crossed by left colic vessels and is posterior to the sigmoid colon. In males, the ureter passes under the vas deferens; in females, under the uterine artery (water under the bridge). Physiologically important narrowings where stones often lodge: ureteropelvic junction, where ureter crosses pelvic brim, and ureterovesical junction.  Arteries and veins Blood supply is segmental along its course from nearby vessels: in the abdomen mainly from renal, gonadal, and common iliac arteries; in the pelvis from superior and inferior vesical arteries, uterine artery in females, and middle rectal and vaginal branches as variants. These branches form a longitudinal network along the ureter. Venous drainage parallels arteries: renal, gonadal, common iliac, and vesical veins drain the ureter.  Nerve supply Innervation arises from renal, aortic, hypogastric, and pelvic plexuses. Sympathetic fibers come from T10–L2; parasympathetic fibers from the pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4). Pain afferents from the upper ureter travel with sympathetic fibers to T10–L2, so colicky pain is referred from flank to groin; lower ureter pain may be referred to scrotum, labia, or inner thigh.  Histology The ureter wall has three main layers. Mucosa: lined by transitional epithelium (urothelium) with several layers of cells, including surface umbrella cells that are highly specialized, over a lamina propria of dense connective tissue. Muscularis: in the upper two-thirds, inner longitudinal and outer circular layers of smooth muscle; in the lower third (near bladder), an additional outer longitudinal layer is present. Adventitia: connective tissue with blood vessels, nerves, and adipose tissue attaching the ureter to surrounding structures. There is no serosa except for short intraperitoneal segments.  Physiology The ureters actively transport urine from the kidneys to the bladder via peristaltic contractions of smooth muscle initiated by pacemaker cells near the renal pelvis. Peristalsis is modulated by autonomic innervation and local stretch. The oblique intramural course through the bladder wall acts as a functional valve: as bladder pressure rises during filling or voiding, the ureteric orifices are compressed, preventing vesicoureteral reflux.  URINARY BLADDER  Anatomy and location The urinary bladder is a hollow muscular organ in the lesser pelvis, posterior to the pubic symphysis. In adults, when empty, it lies in the pelvis; as it fills, it can extend into the lower abdomen. In males: the bladder lies anterior to the rectum and superior to the prostate. In females: it lies anterior to the vagina and inferior to the uterus. The peritoneum covers the superior surface and forms pouches: rectovesical pouch in males, vesicouterine pouch in females. The bladder has an apex (pointing toward the pubic symphysis, attached by the median umbilical ligament), a base (posterior surface), a superior surface, and two inferolateral surfaces. Internally, the mucosa is folded except in the trigone, a smooth triangular area between the ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice.  Arteries and veins Arterial supply comes mainly from branches of the internal iliac artery: superior vesical arteries (branches of the umbilical artery), inferior vesical arteries in males, and vaginal/inferior vesical branches in females. In the neck and adjacent urethra, prostatic arterial branches in males are important. Venous drainage forms a vesical venous plexus that drains into internal iliac veins. In males, it communicates with the prostatic plexus.  Nerve supply The bladder is innervated by the vesical plexus, derived from the inferior hypogastric plexus. Parasympathetic fibers arise from pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4) and provide motor supply to the detrusor muscle and inhibitory input to the internal urethral sphincter (in males), promoting emptying. Sympathetic fibers originate from T11–L2 via hypogastric nerves; they facilitate storage by relaxing the detrusor and contracting the internal sphincter. Afferent fibers carrying pain and fullness sensations follow different routes: pain from the superior bladder tends to follow sympathetic (T11–L2); from the inferior bladder, parasympathetic (S2–S4). Conscious sensation of fullness is integrated via pelvic splanchnics.  Histology The bladder wall has four principal layers. Mucosa: transitional epithelium (urothelium) over a lamina propria of fibroelastic connective tissue. When empty, epithelium appears multilayered and folded; when distended, it thins to fewer layers. Submucosa: often not sharply demarcated; fibroelastic tissue, vessels, and nerves. Muscularis (detrusor muscle): three layers of smooth muscle not completely distinct, classically described as inner longitudinal, middle circular, and outer longitudinal. At the neck, the circular muscle is thickened to form the internal urethral sphincter, especially prominent in males. Adventitia/serosa: on the superior surface, a serosa of peritoneum; elsewhere, an adventitia of connective tissue.  Physiology The bladder functions as a low-pressure reservoir and, with the urethra, as a conduit for urine excretion. Filling (storage phase): as urine enters, detrusor muscle remains relaxed (sympathetic beta-receptor and somatic control) while the internal urethral sphincter and external urethral sphincter remain contracted (sympathetic alpha-receptors and somatic pudendal nerve, respectively). Compliance allows large volume with minimal rise in pressure. Voiding (micturition): controlled reflexly via the pontine micturition center and spinal sacral segments. Afferent stretch signals from bladder wall via pelvic splanchnic nerves trigger parasympathetic efferents (S2–S4) to contract detrusor and relax internal sphincter, while voluntary relaxation of external sphincter (pudendal nerve) allows urine flow. Higher cortical centers can facilitate or inhibit this reflex within limits.  URETHRA  Anatomy and location The urethra differs significantly between males and females. Female urethra: about 4 cm long, runs from the internal urethral orifice at the bladder neck to the external urethral orifice in the vestibule between labia minora, anterior to the vaginal opening. It is embedded in the anterior vaginal wall and passes through the urogenital diaphragm and perineal membrane. Male urethra: about 18–20 cm long, divided into prostatic, membranous, and spongy (penile) parts. It runs from the internal urethral orifice at the bladder neck through the prostate (prostatic urethra), passes through the external urethral sphincter and perineal membrane (membranous urethra), then through the corpus spongiosum of the penis (spongy urethra) to the external orifice at the glans. It is both urinary and reproductive, receiving ducts from the prostate and bulbourethral glands.  Arteries and veins Female urethra: supplied by branches of the internal pudendal and vaginal arteries; venous drainage to corresponding veins and internal pudendal/inferior vaginal plexuses. Male urethra: prostatic and membranous parts receive branches from inferior vesical and middle rectal arteries; spongy urethra from the internal pudendal artery (especially the artery of the bulb). Venous drainage from the prostatic urethra goes to prostatic venous plexus; from the spongy urethra to deep dorsal vein of the penis and internal pudendal veins.  Nerve supply In both sexes, the external urethral sphincter is supplied by the pudendal nerve (S2–S4), providing voluntary somatic control. Autonomic innervation parallels bladder innervation via the vesical and prostatic plexuses. In males, sympathetic fibers (T11–L2 via hypogastric plexus) innervate the internal urethral sphincter at the bladder neck, particularly important in ejaculation to prevent retrograde flow of semen into bladder. Sensory innervation of the urethra is via pudendal and branches of the perineal nerves; distal urethra in both sexes has somatic sensory supply.  Histology Female urethra: near the bladder, the epithelium is transitional, changing to pseudostratified or stratified columnar along its course and to stratified squamous nonkeratinized near the external opening. The lamina propria contains a venous plexus and mucous glands (urethral glands). Smooth muscle layers are present proximally; more distally, striated muscle fibers from the urogenital diaphragm form the external sphincter. Male urethra: prostatic urethra is lined mainly by transitional epithelium. Membranous and spongy urethra are lined by pseudostratified or stratified columnar epithelium, except near the external meatus, where it becomes stratified squamous. Mucous glands of Littre open into the lumen, particularly in the spongy portion. The surrounding corpus spongiosum is erectile tissue with vascular sinuses.  Physiology The urethra is the final conduit for urine excretion and, in males, for semen. Continence depends on tonic contraction of the internal (in males) and external urethral sphincters and urethral smooth muscle tone, modulated by autonomic and somatic innervation. During voiding, urethral resistance falls as sphincters relax and urethral smooth muscle may contract in a coordinated manner with detrusor contraction, producing a laminar flow of urine. In males, the urethra also participates in ejaculation, with complex coordination of smooth and striated muscle activity.  INTEGRATED RENAL SYSTEM PHYSIOLOGY Although each part has its own structure, textbook physiology emphasizes their integrated function. Kidneys filter blood, reabsorb needed substances, secrete wastes and regulate blood pressure, osmolarity, and acid–base status. Ureters and bladder act as low-pressure conduct and storage components, using smooth muscle peristalsis and compliant walls under autonomic control. The urethra and sphincters provide controlled outlet resistance, enabling continence and voluntary initiation of micturition. Neural circuits from spinal cord to brainstem and cortex integrate afferent signals from stretch receptors with efferent sympathetic, parasympathetic, and somatic outputs, coordinating filling and emptying phases. This organization, from detailed microanatomy (nephrons, urothelium, smooth muscle layers, sphincters) to systemic roles (fluid–electrolyte balance, blood pressure, excretion), is how standard anatomy, histology, and physiology textbooks describe the renal and lower urinary tract.
2|93: I will organize this by major components of the renal system as usually done in standard textbooks (e.g., Moore, Snell, Junqueira, Guyton/Boron): kidneys, ureters, urinary bladder, and urethra. For each, I will go through gross anatomy (location, vessels, nerves), histology, then key physiology.  KIDNEYS  Anatomy: location, relations, vessels, nerves The kidneys are paired retroperitoneal organs in the posterior abdominal wall, on either side of the vertebral column. In the adult, they lie approximately from T12 to L3 vertebral levels; the right kidney is usually slightly lower than the left due to the liver. Each kidney has a superior and inferior pole, medial and lateral borders, and an anterior and posterior surface. The hilum is on the medial border and transmits (from anterior to posterior): renal vein, renal artery, and renal pelvis/ureter, plus lymphatics and nerves.  Posterior relations include the diaphragm, psoas major, quadratus lumborum, and transversus abdominis muscles, and the 12th rib (both sides) plus the 11th rib on the left. The kidneys are embedded in perirenal fat, enclosed by the renal (Gerota’s) fascia, and surrounded externally by pararenal fat.  Arterial supply derives from the right and left renal arteries, direct branches of the abdominal aorta just below the origin of the superior mesenteric artery (roughly L1–L2). Each renal artery divides into segmental arteries at the hilum, which further branch into interlobar arteries (running between pyramids), arcuate arteries (arching over the base of pyramids), and interlobular (cortical radiate) arteries. Afferent arterioles arise from interlobular arteries and lead to glomerular capillaries; efferent arterioles exit the glomerulus. In cortical nephrons, efferent arterioles form peritubular capillaries; in juxtamedullary nephrons, they form the vasa recta descending into the medulla.  Venous drainage broadly mirrors the arterial tree: interlobular veins drain to arcuate veins, then to interlobar veins, and into the renal vein. The left renal vein crosses anterior to the aorta and posterior to the superior mesenteric artery; it also typically receives the left gonadal and left suprarenal veins. The right renal vein is shorter and drains directly into the inferior vena cava.  Lymph from the kidneys drains mainly to lumbar (aortic and caval) lymph nodes.  Innervation is via the renal plexus, which contains sympathetic fibers from the lesser and least splanchnic nerves (T10–L1 segments) and parasympathetic fibers primarily from the vagus nerve. Sympathetic fibers regulate vasoconstriction and renin release and convey visceral pain. Sensory afferents travel back mainly with sympathetics to the T10–L1 spinal levels.  Histology Each kidney is divided into cortex and medulla. The cortex contains renal corpuscles and the proximal and distal convoluted tubules, with cortical collecting tubules. The medulla consists primarily of parallel arrays of loops of Henle, collecting ducts, and vasa recta, organized into pyramids.  The functional unit is the nephron, plus its associated collecting duct. A nephron is composed of:  Renal corpuscle: a glomerulus (fenestrated capillary tuft) enclosed by Bowman’s capsule. Bowman’s capsule has a parietal layer of simple squamous epithelium and a visceral layer of podocytes. Between them is the urinary space. The filtration barrier is formed by fenestrated endothelium, the glomerular basement membrane (thick, fused basal lamina), and podocyte slit diaphragms.  Proximal convoluted tubule (PCT): lined by simple cuboidal epithelium with a prominent brush border (dense microvilli), many lysosomes, numerous mitochondria, and extensive basolateral infoldings; cytoplasm appears acidophilic.  Loop of Henle: thin limbs (descending and ascending) lined by simple squamous epithelium with few organelles; thick ascending limb lined by cuboidal cells with many mitochondria and basolateral infoldings but no brush border.  Distal convoluted tubule (DCT): shorter, cuboidal cells, fewer microvilli (no well-developed brush border), more distinct lumens in histological sections, and less eosinophilic than PCT.  Juxtaglomerular apparatus: located at the vascular pole of the renal corpuscle. It comprises macula densa cells in the distal tubule (tightly packed cells sensing tubular NaCl), juxtaglomerular (granular) cells in the wall of the afferent arteriole (modified smooth muscle cells containing renin granules), and extraglomerular mesangial cells.  Collecting system: collecting tubules and collecting ducts are lined by simple cuboidal to columnar epithelium; principal cells (pale, with centrally located nuclei) and intercalated cells (darker, involved in acid–base regulation) can be distinguished.  Medullary interstitium has interstitial cells, vasa recta, and an increasing osmolality from outer to inner medulla.  Physiology The kidneys maintain homeostasis of water, electrolytes, and acid–base status, excrete metabolic wastes and foreign substances, regulate blood pressure, and perform endocrine functions.  At the level of the renal corpuscle, glomerular filtration occurs driven by net filtration pressure (glomerular hydrostatic pressure minus opposing forces such as Bowmans capsule hydrostatic pressure and plasma oncotic pressure). Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is determined by net filtration pressure and filtration coefficient and is regulated by intrinsic (autoregulation via myogenic response and tubuloglomerular feedback) and extrinsic (sympathetic, hormonal) mechanisms.  In the PCT, the bulk of filtered Na+, water, bicarbonate, glucose, amino acids, and many solutes are reabsorbed via active and secondary active transport processes. Water follows solutes osmotically; the PCT is highly permeable to water. It also secretes various organic acids and bases and drugs.  The loop of Henle, especially long-loop (juxtamedullary) nephrons, establishes the corticomedullary osmotic gradient by the countercurrent multiplier mechanism. The descending thin limb is highly permeable to water and relatively impermeable to solutes, while the thick ascending limb is impermeable to water but actively reabsorbs Na+, K+, and Cl−. This separation of solute and water movements generates a hyperosmotic medulla.  The DCT and collecting duct provide fine-tuning of Na+, K+, H+, and water balance. The early DCT continues NaCl reabsorption (via NaCl cotransport) and is relatively impermeable to water. The late DCT and cortical collecting ducts are under aldosterone (enhancing Na+ reabsorption and K+ secretion) and are variably permeable to water under antidiuretic hormone (ADH). Intercalated cells secrete H+ or HCO3−, regulating acid–base balance.  The vasa recta act as countercurrent exchangers, preserving the medullary gradient while supplying blood. The juxtaglomerular apparatus regulates GFR and systemic blood pressure via renin secretion, generating angiotensin II and aldosterone.  The kidneys produce erythropoietin (from peritubular interstitial cells), convert vitamin D to its active form (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3), and secrete renin. They also metabolize various hormones and contribute to gluconeogenesis.  URETERS  Anatomy: location, relations, vessels, nerves The ureters are muscular tubes (~25–30 cm long) that convey urine from renal pelvis to bladder. They are retroperitoneal and descend on the psoas major muscles, crossing the pelvic brim at the level of the common iliac bifurcation, then course anteromedially in the pelvis to reach the posterolateral aspect of the urinary bladder.  They exhibit three classical constrictions: at the ureteropelvic junction, where they cross the pelvic brim over the iliac vessels, and at the ureterovesical junction where they pass obliquely through the bladder wall. These are common sites for ureteric stone impaction.  Arterial supply is segmental and derived from multiple sources along their course: renal arteries (upper third), gonadal (testicular or ovarian) arteries, abdominal aorta, and common iliac branches (mid), and branches from internal iliac artery (e.g., superior and inferior vesical, uterine, vaginal arteries) in the pelvis. These arteries form longitudinal anastomoses along the ureter. Venous drainage parallels the arteries, draining to renal, gonadal, and internal iliac veins.  Lymphatic drainage is to lumbar (para-aortic) nodes for the upper ureter and to iliac nodes (common, external, internal) for the lower ureter.  Innervation arises from the renal, aortic, and hypogastric plexuses. Sympathetic fibers originate from T10–L2 segments; parasympathetic fibers from the pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4) in the distal ureter. Pain from upper ureter refers to T10–L2 dermatomes (flank, abdomen); from lower ureter, pain may refer to the groin, scrotum/labia, or medial thigh.  Histology The ureter wall has three main layers: mucosa, muscularis, and adventitia.  Mucosa: lined by transitional epithelium (urothelium), which is stratified and specialized. Superficial facet cells (umbrella cells) have large, dome-shaped surfaces facing the lumen and can flatten/stretch. Beneath are several layers of polygonal and basal cells. The lamina propria is dense fibroelastic connective tissue. There is no distinct submucosa.  Muscularis: in the upper two-thirds, an inner longitudinal and outer circular layer of smooth muscle. In the lower third, an additional outer longitudinal layer appears (thus three layers). These muscle layers are not perfectly discrete but follow this general pattern.  Adventitia: composed of connective tissue containing blood vessels, lymphatics, and autonomic nerves and anchors the ureter to surrounding tissues.  Physiology The ureters conduct urine from the renal pelvis to the bladder by intrinsic peristaltic contractions of their smooth muscle, not by gravity alone. Pacemaker cells in the proximal ureter or renal pelvis initiate rhythmic waves of contraction. Stretch of the ureteric wall by urine promotes peristaltic wave frequency.  The oblique intramural course through the bladder wall and the flap-valve mechanism formed by the mucosa and muscle layers help prevent vesicoureteral reflux during bladder contraction. Sympathetic and parasympathetic innervation modulate smooth muscle tone but the basic peristaltic activity is myogenic.  URINARY BLADDER  Anatomy: location, relations, vessels, nerves The bladder is a distensible muscular reservoir situated in the lesser pelvis, posterior to the pubic symphysis. When empty, it lies largely within the pelvis; when full, it can expand into the lower abdomen. It has an apex (anterior), a base or fundus (posterior), a superior surface, and an inferolateral surface on each side. The neck of the bladder narrows inferiorly and is continuous with the urethra.  In males, the bladder lies anterior to the rectum, separated by the rectovesical pouch and related to the seminal vesicles and vas deferens. The neck rests on the prostate. In females, the bladder is anterior to the vagina and uterus; the uterovesical pouch lies between bladder and uterus.  Arterial supply mainly comes from branches of the internal iliac artery. Superior vesical arteries supply the anterosuperior regions; in males, inferior vesical arteries supply the fundus and neck; in females, analogous branches arise from the vaginal and uterine arteries. Additional contributions may come from obturator and inferior gluteal arteries.  Venous drainage forms the vesical venous plexus in the submucosal and perivesical tissues, which drains into internal iliac veins. In males, vesical and prostatic venous plexuses communicate. Lymph drains primarily to external iliac, internal iliac, and sacral lymph nodes, depending on the region.  Innervation derives from the inferior hypogastric (pelvic) plexus. Parasympathetic fibers (pelvic splanchnic nerves, S2–S4) supply the detrusor muscle and are inhibitory to the internal urethral sphincter (mainly relevant in males). Sympathetic fibers from T11–L2 via hypogastric nerves predominantly innervate bladder neck and trigone, facilitating continence. Afferent fibers for fullness and pain also travel via these pathways. Somatic innervation to the external urethral sphincter and pelvic floor is via the pudendal nerve (S2–S4).  Histology The bladder wall has mucosa, muscularis (detrusor), and adventitia/serosa.  Mucosa: lined by transitional epithelium (urothelium). When empty, the mucosa forms folds (rugae), except in the smooth trigone area. Urothelium here is similar to the ureter but may be thicker. Under the epithelium is a lamina propria of dense fibroelastic connective tissue with abundant vessels, continuing as a submucosa in some regions.  Muscularis (detrusor muscle): arranged in poorly defined inner longitudinal, middle circular, and outer longitudinal layers of smooth muscle. These layers blend but collectively form the detrusor muscle. At the bladder neck, the circular fibers are more prominent and contribute to the internal urethral sphincter especially in males.  Externally, most of the bladder is covered by adventitia; the superior surface is covered by peritoneum (serosa) reflecting onto adjacent organs.  Physiology The bladder’s main function is storage and periodic expulsion of urine. During the storage phase, sympathetic activity predominates: detrusor muscle remains relaxed (beta-adrenergic effects), and the internal urethral sphincter and bladder neck are contracted (alpha-adrenergic effects). Somatic input via the pudendal nerve contracts the external urethral sphincter and associated pelvic floor muscles.  During the voiding (micturition) phase, parasympathetic activity dominates: pelvic splanchnic nerves cause detrusor contraction and relaxation of the internal sphincter; voluntary relaxation of the external sphincter via inhibition of pudendal activity allows urine to pass. The micturition reflex involves afferent stretch receptors in the bladder wall, spinal cord reflex arcs, and higher centers (pontine micturition center and cortex) that modulate initiation and inhibition.  The trigone, a triangular region between the ureteric orifices and internal urethral orifice, has smooth mucosa and is more sensitive to stretch; it plays an important role in sensing fullness and initiating the reflex.  URETHRA  Anatomy: location, segments, vessels, nerves The urethra conducts urine from the bladder to the exterior. It differs significantly in males and females.  Female urethra: about 4 cm long, straight, and lies anterior to the vaginal wall, from bladder neck to external urethral orifice in the vestibule between the labia minora. It passes through the pelvic floor and the perineal membrane.  Arterial supply is from branches of the vaginal and internal pudendal arteries; venous drainage parallels these arteries to internal pudendal and vaginal veins. Lymph drains primarily to internal iliac and some inguinal lymph nodes.  Innervation is via the pudendal nerve (somatic), autonomic fibers from the vesical plexus, and perineal branches. The external urethral sphincter is a voluntary striated muscle encircling the urethra as it passes through the urogenital diaphragm.  Male urethra: about 18–20 cm long, with three main parts:  Prostatic urethra: passes through the prostate gland, receives the openings of the ejaculatory ducts and prostatic ducts.  Membranous (intermediate) urethra: the shortest, passes through the external urethral sphincter and perineal membrane.  Spongy (penile) urethra: traverses the corpus spongiosum of the penis to the external urethral meatus at the glans.  Arterial supply: prostatic urethra from inferior vesical and middle rectal branches; membranous and proximal spongy from internal pudendal branches; distal spongy from dorsal artery of penis. Venous drainage follows to prostatic and internal pudendal venous plexuses.  Lymph drains to internal iliac nodes for proximal segments; distal penile urethra drains to deep inguinal nodes.  Innervation is via prostatic plexus (sympathetic and parasympathetic) and the pudendal nerve for the external sphincter. The external urethral sphincter is skeletal muscle under voluntary control.  Histology The urethral epithelium transitions along its length.  In females, near the bladder neck, it is lined by transitional epithelium, becoming stratified or pseudostratified columnar, and then stratified squamous nonkeratinized near the external orifice. The lamina propria is vascular and contains urethral glands (mucous-secreting). A muscular layer with inner longitudinal and outer circular smooth muscle is present proximally, blending with striated muscle of the external sphincter distally.  In males, the prostatic urethra is lined mainly by transitional epithelium. Distally, epithelium becomes pseudostratified or stratified columnar in membranous and most of the spongy urethra; the terminal fossa navicularis features stratified squamous epithelium continuous with the external skin. Numerous mucous-secreting urethral glands (glands of Littre) empty into the lumen, especially in the spongy urethra. Bulbourethral glands (Cowper’s) are in the deep perineal pouch and secrete mucus into the proximal spongy urethra.  Physiology The urethra provides a controlled outlet for urine and, in the male, also serves as a conduit for semen.  Continence depends on the internal urethral sphincter (mainly in males at the bladder neck, under autonomic control) and the external urethral sphincter of striated muscle under voluntary somatic control. In females, the external sphincter, together with pelvic floor muscles and urethral wall tone, is especially important for continence because there is no well-developed internal sphincter.  During storage, sympathetic tone helps maintain contraction of the internal sphincter (in males) and high urethral resistance; somatic pudendal activity maintains external sphincter contraction. During micturition, coordinated relaxation of these sphincters with detrusor contraction allows urine flow.  In males, during ejaculation, sympathetic activation closes the internal urethral sphincter to prevent retrograde ejaculation into the bladder and coordinates contraction of reproductive ducts and accessory glands; somatic contractions of bulbospongiosus muscle aid semen expulsion.  INTEGRATED RENAL SYSTEM PHYSIOLOGY  Overall, the renal system regulates:  Fluid and electrolyte balance via filtration, reabsorption, and secretion in nephrons, and storage/controlled release in bladder and urethra.  Acid–base balance via bicarbonate reabsorption and hydrogen ion secretion, particularly in PCT and collecting ducts.  Blood pressure via renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system and volume regulation.  Erythropoiesis via erythropoietin.  Calcium and phosphate homeostasis via active vitamin D formation.  Coordination of tubular transport mechanisms, medullary osmotic gradients, hormonal modulation (ADH, aldosterone, ANP, PTH), and the lower urinary tract reflexes produces the final urine volume and composition and the timing and pattern of its excretion.
3|93: I will give you a textbook‑style overview, moving region by region through the renal system: kidneys, ureters, urinary bladder, and urethra. For each, I will cover gross anatomy and relations, blood supply and innervation, followed by key histology and physiology.  KIDNEYS  Anatomy and location The kidneys are paired retroperitoneal organs on the posterior abdominal wall, roughly from T12 to L3 vertebrae. The right kidney is slightly lower because of the liver; the left is usually a bit higher.  Posterior relations include the diaphragm, psoas major, quadratus lumborum, transversus abdominis muscles, and subcostal, iliohypogastric, and ilioinguinal nerves. Superiorly they are capped by suprarenal (adrenal) glands. Anterior relations differ right vs left: the right kidney contacts the liver, duodenum (second part), and hepatic flexure of the colon; the left kidney contacts the stomach, spleen, pancreas, jejunum, and splenic flexure of the colon.  Each kidney has a convex lateral border and a concave medial border with the renal hilum. From anterior to posterior in the hilum lie classically: renal vein, renal artery, renal pelvis (and then ureter). Internally, the kidney cortex lies peripherally and extends into the medulla as columns of Bertin between medullary pyramids. Each pyramid ends in a papilla that drains into a minor calyx, then major calyces, then renal pelvis.  Arterial supply Each kidney is supplied by a renal artery, usually a single branch from the abdominal aorta at about L1–L2. The right renal artery is longer and passes posterior to the inferior vena cava. Variations such as accessory (supernumerary) renal arteries are common.  Within the hilum, the renal artery divides into segmental arteries supplying surgical segments of the kidney. Commonly five segmental branches are described: superior (apical), superior (apical), superior (apical), but standard textbooks list apical, superior, middle, inferior, and basal (or similar; naming varies); the important point is that segments are end‑artery territories.  Segmental arteries give rise to interlobar arteries running between pyramids in the renal columns, then arcuate arteries arching over the bases of pyramids at the corticomedullary junction, and then interlobular (cortical radiate) arteries running toward the kidney surface. Afferent arterioles arise from interlobular arteries and supply glomerular capillaries.  Efferent arterioles from cortical glomeruli form peritubular capillary networks around cortical tubules; efferent arterioles from juxtamedullary glomeruli descend to form vasa recta, long straight vessels that run into the medulla and are critical for countercurrent exchange.  Venous drainage Venous return generally mirrors arteries in reverse order: peritubular capillaries and vasa recta drain to interlobular veins, then arcuate veins, then interlobar veins, then the renal vein. There is no segmental vein system analogous to the segmental arteries.  The left renal vein is longer and passes anterior to the aorta and posterior to the superior mesenteric artery; it receives tributaries such as the left gonadal vein and left suprarenal vein. The right renal vein is shorter and drains directly into the inferior vena cava without significant large tributaries.  Innervation Renal innervation is via the renal plexus, derived chiefly from the least splanchnic nerve (T12) and upper lumbar splanchnic nerves (L1–L2). Sympathetic fibers are predominantly vasomotor, regulating renal blood flow and renin secretion. Pain fibers from the kidney travel back via T10–L1 spinal segments, explaining referred pain to the costovertebral angle, flank, and sometimes anterior abdominal wall.  Parasympathetic innervation is relatively sparse and is carried mainly via the vagus nerve and, in some descriptions, pelvic splanchnic fibers to distal ureter and lower tract rather than to renal parenchyma.  Histology The kidney is covered by a fibrous capsule and has a cortex and medulla.  Cortex: Contains renal corpuscles and convoluted portions of nephrons. A renal corpuscle comprises a glomerulus and Bowman capsule. The glomerulus is a tuft of fenestrated capillaries; Bowman capsule has a visceral layer of podocytes with foot processes and slit diaphragms, and a parietal layer of simple squamous epithelium. The urinary (Bowman) space lies between them.  The filtration barrier has three layers: fenestrated endothelium, glomerular basement membrane (fused laminae rarae and densa), and podocyte slit diaphragm. Supporting cells include mesangial cells, which provide structural support, phagocytose debris, and modulate filtration surface area.  Tubules: The proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) has simple cuboidal epithelium with a tall brush border (microvilli), abundant mitochondria, and many basolateral infoldings; it stains intensely eosinophilic. The loop of Henle has thin segments with simple squamous epithelium and thick segments (especially thick ascending limb) with simple cuboidal cells. The distal convoluted tubule (DCT) has smaller, less eosinophilic cuboidal cells with fewer microvilli.  Collecting system: Collecting tubules and collecting ducts are lined by simple cuboidal to columnar epithelium; principal cells and intercalated cells can be distinguished. Papillary ducts of Bellini open at papillae.  Juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA): Located at the vascular pole of the corpuscle where the DCT contacts the afferent arteriole. It includes macula densa cells in the DCT (tall, closely packed cells sensing tubular NaCl), juxtaglomerular (granular) cells in the wall of the afferent arteriole (modified smooth muscle cells containing renin granules), and extraglomerular mesangial cells.  Physiology Nephron function: Each nephron performs filtration, reabsorption, secretion, and excretion.  Glomerular filtration: Hydrostatic pressure in the glomerular capillaries drives plasma ultrafiltrate across the filtration barrier into Bowman space, forming the primary filtrate. The glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is about 125 mL/min in an adult, regulated by afferent and efferent arteriolar tone, systemic blood pressure, and hormonal factors. Autoregulation via the myogenic response and tubuloglomerular feedback maintains relatively constant GFR over a range of pressures.  Tubular reabsorption and secretion: PCT reabsorbs the bulk (about two thirds) of filtered water, sodium, chloride, bicarbonate, glucose, amino acids, and many other solutes, largely via active transport coupled to Na K ATPase and secondary active transporters, with water following osmotically. It also secretes organic acids and bases.  The loop of Henle, particularly in juxtamedullary nephrons, generates a medullary osmotic gradient via countercurrent multiplication: the thick ascending limb actively reabsorbs Na K 2Cl but is impermeable to water, diluting tubular fluid; the thin descending limb is water‑permeable but relatively solute‑impermeable, allowing water to leave and concentrating the tubular fluid. Vasa recta act as countercurrent exchangers, preserving the gradient.  The DCT and collecting duct fine‑tune ion and water balance under hormonal influence. Aldosterone increases Na reabsorption and K secretion in principal cells. Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) increases water permeability of collecting ducts via insertion of aquaporin‑2 channels, concentrating urine. Parathyroid hormone (PTH) and calcitriol regulate calcium and phosphate handling.  The JGA via renin release initiates the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS), important for blood pressure regulation and sodium homeostasis. The kidney also produces erythropoietin, promoting red blood cell production, and contributes to vitamin D activation (1 alpha hydroxylase activity).  URETERS  Anatomy and location Ureters are paired muscular tubes about 25–30 cm long, conveying urine from renal pelvis to urinary bladder. They are retroperitoneal for most of their course.  Abdominal part: Arises from the renal pelvis at the ureteropelvic junction, descends on the psoas major muscle, crosses anterior to the common iliac or external iliac arteries near the pelvic brim.  Pelvic part: Runs along the lateral pelvic wall, anterior to the internal iliac arteries. In males, the ureter passes under the vas (ductus) deferens near the bladder. In females, it passes inferior to the uterine artery near the lateral fornix of the vagina, summarized as water (ureter) under the bridge (uterine artery).  There are three classical physiologic narrowings: ureteropelvic junction, where the ureter crosses the pelvic brim, and the ureterovesical junction (entry into bladder). These are common sites for obstruction by ureteric calculi.  Arterial supply Blood supply is segmental and longitudinal, derived from many sources along its course:  Upper segment: Renal arteries. Middle segment: Gonadal (testicular or ovarian) arteries, aorta, and sometimes common iliac arteries. Lower segment: Branches from internal iliac arteries, such as superior and inferior vesical arteries, uterine artery in females, and middle rectal arteries.  Small branches run longitudinally in the adventitia; damage to these can endanger ureteral viability.  Venous drainage Venous drainage parallels arterial supply: upper part to renal veins, middle to gonadal and other nearby veins, and lower part to vesical and internal iliac veins.  Innervation Innervation is via the renal, aortic, and hypogastric plexuses. Sympathetic fibers mainly arise from T10–L2 segments; parasympathetic fibers from the vagus (upper) and pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4) in the pelvis.  Pain fibers from the ureter travel with sympathetic fibers back to T11–L2, leading to characteristic colicky pain radiating from the flank to groin and into external genitalia as a stone descends.  Histology Ureter wall has three principal layers: mucosa, muscularis, and adventitia.  Mucosa: Lined by transitional epithelium (urothelium), a stratified epithelium specialized for stretch, with umbrella cells on the surface. Underlying lamina propria is fibroelastic connective tissue. In contrast to the bladder, ureter typically lacks a well‑defined muscularis mucosa.  Muscularis: In the upper two thirds, there are two smooth muscle layers: inner longitudinal and outer circular. In the lower third near the bladder, an additional outer longitudinal layer appears, so the arrangement becomes inner longitudinal, middle circular, outer longitudinal.  Adventitia: Connective tissue with blood vessels, lymphatics, and nerves anchoring the ureter to surrounding structures.  Physiology The ureter propels urine from kidney to bladder by intrinsic rhythmic peristaltic contractions of smooth muscle. Pacemaker activity in the proximal ureter initiates peristaltic waves that move distally; rate can increase with increased urine flow or certain hormones.  Autonomic innervation modulates but does not generate peristalsis; peristalsis persists after denervation. The ureterovesical junction functions as a one‑way valve, as the ureter enters the bladder obliquely through the bladder wall; when the bladder contracts, the intramural segment is compressed, preventing vesicoureteral reflux.  URINARY BLADDER  Anatomy and location The bladder is a distensible muscular reservoir in the lesser pelvis, posterior to the pubic symphysis. When empty, it lies entirely in the pelvis; when full, it may expand into the lower abdomen.  In males, the bladder lies superior to the prostate and anterior to the rectum; seminal vesicles and vas deferens are related posteriorly. In females, the bladder is anterior to the vagina and uterus; the uterus lies superior and posterior to it.  Regions: Apex (directed toward the pubic symphysis, continuous with the median umbilical ligament, remnant of the urachus), body, fundus (posterior wall), and neck (inferior portion leading into the urethra). The trigone is a smooth triangular area on the internal base, bounded by the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice; it is embryologically distinct and more firmly attached to underlying structures.  Arterial supply Superior vesical arteries, branches of the umbilical artery (from internal iliac), supply the superior portion. In males, the inferior vesical artery (from internal iliac) supplies the fundus and neck; in females, the vaginal arteries often serve a similar role. Additional branches from obturator and inferior gluteal arteries contribute.  Venous drainage A rich vesical venous plexus drains the bladder, located in the pelvic fascia. In males, it communicates with the prostatic venous plexus; drainage ultimately goes to internal iliac veins. In females, it drains to the internal iliac veins via vesical and vaginal venous plexuses.  Innervation The bladder receives innervation from the vesical plexus, derived from the inferior hypogastric plexus.  Parasympathetic fibers (pelvic splanchnic nerves S2–S4) are motor to detrusor muscle and inhibitory to the internal urethral sphincter. They mediate bladder contraction during micturition.  Sympathetic fibers (T11–L2 via hypogastric nerves) are primarily inhibitory to detrusor and excitatory to the internal sphincter, promoting urine storage.  Somatic innervation of the external urethral sphincter is via the pudendal nerve (S2–S4), allowing voluntary control.  Afferent fibers for bladder filling sensations run with pelvic splanchnics; pain fibers from the superior bladder travel with sympathetics (T11–L2), and those from the inferior bladder travel with parasympathetics (S2–S4).  Histology The bladder wall has mucosa, submucosa, muscularis (detrusor), and adventitia or serosa.  Mucosa: Lined by transitional epithelium (urothelium), capable of marked stretching; surface umbrella cells form a barrier with uroplakin plaques. Underlying lamina propria is rich in elastic fibers.  Muscularis: The detrusor muscle consists of three incompletely separated smooth muscle layers: inner longitudinal, middle circular, and outer longitudinal. In the trigone, muscle fibers are more densely arranged and interlaced; the trigone mucosa is smoother and firmly attached.  Outer covering: Most of the superior surface is covered by peritoneum (serosa). The rest has adventitia connecting it to surrounding tissues.  Physiology The bladder serves as a low‑pressure reservoir for urine and plays a central role in micturition (urination).  Filling phase: As urine enters, the detrusor muscle remains relaxed (detrusor inhibition) and the internal urethral sphincter remains contracted under sympathetic influence. The bladder is highly compliant; intravesical pressure rises only slightly over a large volume range. Somatic pudendal activity keeps the external sphincter contracted.  Micturition reflex: At a threshold volume (often 300–400 mL in adults), stretch receptors in the bladder wall send afferent impulses via pelvic nerves to the sacral spinal cord and higher centers. Parasympathetic efferents then cause detrusor contraction and internal sphincter relaxation. In infants, this is a spinal reflex; in adults, pontine and cortical centers exert voluntary control, permitting or delaying voiding by modulating parasympathetic outflow and pudendal activity.  During voiding, detrusor contracts strongly, intraabdominal pressure may increase with abdominal muscle contraction, and both internal and external sphincters relax, allowing urine flow through the urethra.  URETHRA  Anatomy and location The urethra conveys urine from bladder to exterior. Its anatomy differs significantly between males and females.  Female urethra: About 4 cm long, runs anteroinferiorly from the internal urethral orifice at the neck of bladder to the external urethral orifice in the vestibule, between clitoris and vaginal opening. It passes embedded in the anterior vaginal wall and through the pelvic floor and perineal membrane. It is relatively straight and short, predisposing to ascending urinary tract infections.  Male urethra: About 18–20 cm long and divided into preprostatic (intramural), prostatic, membranous, and spongy (penile) segments.  Intramural (preprostatic): Short segment within the bladder neck, surrounded by internal urethral sphincter. Prostatic: Passes through the prostate gland. The urethral crest and seminal colliculus are landmarks; openings for prostatic ducts and ejaculatory ducts enter here. Membranous: Passes through the external urethral sphincter and perineal membrane; the shortest but least distensible segment. Spongy (penile): Runs in the corpus spongiosum of the penis to the external urethral orifice at the glans. Bulbourethral gland ducts open into the proximal part of this segment.  Arterial supply Female urethra: Mainly branches from internal pudendal and vaginal arteries. Male urethra: Intramural and prostatic parts receive branches from inferior vesical and middle rectal arteries. The spongy urethra is supplied by branches of internal pudendal artery, especially the artery of the bulb and urethral branches.  Venous drainage Parallels the arterial supply, draining into vesical, prostatic, pudendal, and vaginal plexuses as appropriate, ultimately to internal iliac veins.  Innervation Somatic: External urethral sphincter innervated by the pudendal nerve (S2–S4), permitting voluntary control of continence.  Autonomic: In males, sympathetic fibers (via hypogastric plexus) supply the internal urethral sphincter, especially important in ejaculation to prevent retrograde flow of semen into the bladder. Parasympathetic fibers (pelvic splanchnics) contribute to urethral mucosal and periurethral gland function.  Afferent fibers convey sensations of flow and irritation.  Histology Female urethra: Proximal segment is lined by transitional epithelium, which changes to stratified or pseudostratified columnar, and then to nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium near the external orifice. A lamina propria rich in elastic tissue and venous plexuses underlies the epithelium. Surrounding smooth muscle layers are continuous with the bladder detrusor, and striated muscle from the urogenital diaphragm forms part of the external sphincter.  Male urethra: Epithelial lining varies by segment.  Prostatic urethra: Mostly urothelium (transitional), with openings of prostatic glands. Membranous and proximal spongy urethra: Lined by pseudostratified or stratified columnar epithelium. Distal spongy urethra and fossa navicularis: Lined by nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium continuous with external skin.  The lamina propria contains mucous urethral glands (glands of Littre), especially in the spongy urethra. Smooth muscle is continuous with bladder, and striated muscle of external sphincter surrounds membranous portion.  Physiology The urethra conducts urine during micturition and in males also conducts semen during ejaculation.  Continence: Maintained by tonic activity of the internal urethral sphincter (sympathetic) and external urethral sphincter (somatic via pudendal nerve), as well as pelvic floor muscles. During filling, outlet resistance exceeds bladder pressure; during voiding, sphincters relax and detrusor pressure rises to exceed outlet resistance.  In males, coordinated closure of the internal urethral sphincter during ejaculation prevents retrograde ejaculation and ensures antegrade flow of semen.  INTEGRATED RENAL SYSTEM PHYSIOLOGY  Beyond each part individually, the renal system as a whole maintains fluid and electrolyte balance, acid–base balance, blood pressure, and excretes metabolic waste products and foreign substances.  The kidneys adjust GFR, tubular reabsorption, and secretion to regulate extracellular fluid volume, osmolarity, and composition (Na, K, Ca, phosphate, H, HCO3). They produce hormones and enzymes (renin, erythropoietin, 1 alpha hydroxylase) that integrate with endocrine and cardiovascular systems.  Ureters provide unidirectional transport of urine via peristalsis. The bladder acts as a compliant reservoir that allows intermittent voiding with voluntarily controlled timing. The urethra and its sphincters provide controlled outlet resistance, allowing continence and coordinated emptying.  This framework matches the structure typically presented in standard anatomy and physiology textbooks: gross anatomy and relations, vascular and nerve supply, histology of walls and specialized structures, and key physiological roles of each component of the renal system.
4|93: I’ll organize this as a systems‑to‑microscopic walkthrough, in a way that corresponds closely to standard human anatomy, histology, and physiology textbooks (e.g., Moore, Snell, Junqueira, Guyton/Boron). I will go component by component: kidneys, ureters, urinary bladder, and urethra, and for each: location and gross anatomy, blood supply and drainage, innervation, histology, and key physiology.  RENAL SYSTEM OVERVIEW The renal system includes two kidneys, two ureters, the urinary bladder, and the urethra. Its main functions are excretion of metabolic waste, regulation of water and electrolyte balance, regulation of acid–base balance, endocrine functions (renin, erythropoietin, active vitamin D), and storage and periodic elimination of urine.  KIDNEYS  Location and gross anatomy The kidneys are paired retroperitoneal organs in the posterior abdominal wall. They lie on either side of the vertebral column, roughly from T12 to L3, with the right kidney slightly lower than the left due to the liver. Each kidney has an upper and lower pole, medial and lateral borders, and anterior and posterior surfaces. The hilum is on the medial border, transmitting the renal vein (anterior), renal artery (middle), and renal pelvis/ureter (posterior), plus lymphatics and nerves. Internally, each kidney has an outer cortex and inner medulla. The medulla is divided into renal pyramids, with bases toward the cortex and apices forming renal papillae projecting into minor calyces. The cortex extends between pyramids as renal columns. Cortex plus medullary pyramid(s) associated with it form a renal lobe; the functional unit is the nephron. The renal sinus contains the renal pelvis, calyces, vessels, nerves, and fat.  Arterial supply Renal arteries arise from the abdominal aorta at about L1–L2. Each renal artery divides into segmental arteries near the hilum (apical, superior, middle, inferior, and sometimes posterior segmental branches described in surgical anatomy). Segmental arteries give interlobar arteries that run between pyramids in the renal columns. At the corticomedullary junction, interlobar arteries form arcuate arteries that arch over the bases of pyramids. From arcuate arteries arise interlobular (cortical radiate) arteries that ascend into the cortex. Afferent arterioles branch from interlobular arteries to supply glomerular capillaries. Efferent arterioles exit glomeruli; in cortical nephrons they form peritubular capillaries; in juxtamedullary nephrons they form vasa recta running into the medulla.  Venous drainage Blood returns via venous vessels generally paralleling arteries. Interlobular (cortical radiate) veins drain to arcuate veins. Arcuate veins drain into interlobar veins. Interlobar veins converge to form renal veins, which drain into the inferior vena cava (left renal vein is longer and passes anterior to the aorta, deep to the superior mesenteric artery).  Innervation Renal nerves are from the renal plexus, derived mainly from the least splanchnic nerve (T12) and lumbar splanchnic nerves (L1–L2), with contributions from the aorticorenal and celiac plexuses. Sympathetic fibers: cause vasoconstriction of renal vessels, modulate renin secretion from juxtaglomerular cells, and regulate sodium and water reabsorption indirectly. Visceral afferent fibers travel with sympathetics to T10–L1 segments; pain can be referred to flank, lower thoracic, and upper lumbar regions. Parasympathetic supply is relatively minor and arises mainly from the vagus (though its functional role in renal parenchyma is limited compared with sympathetics).  Histology The kidney is encased in a dense irregular connective tissue capsule. Cortex: contains renal corpuscles and the initial portions of the tubular system. Renal corpuscle consists of the glomerulus (capillary tuft) and Bowman’s capsule. Bowman’s capsule has a parietal layer of simple squamous epithelium and a visceral layer formed by podocytes, whose interdigitating foot processes form filtration slits over the glomerular basement membrane. The glomerular filtration barrier has three layers: fenestrated glomerular endothelium, thick basal lamina, and filtration slits between podocyte foot processes bridged by slit diaphragms. Mesangial cells lie between capillary loops; they provide structural support, phagocytosis, and modulation of capillary flow. Tubular segments: Proximal convoluted tubule (PCT): in cortex, lined by simple cuboidal epithelium with prominent brush border (long microvilli), extensive basolateral infoldings, and abundant mitochondria; lumen often appears fuzzy in microscopy. Proximal straight tubule (thick descending limb): similar to PCT but somewhat less developed brush border. Thin limb of loop of Henle (descending and ascending portions in medulla): lined by simple squamous epithelium; minimal organelles; permeabilities differ along the limb regionally. Thick ascending limb (TAL): simple cuboidal cells with many mitochondria but lacking brush border. Distal convoluted tubule (DCT): in cortex, simple cuboidal epithelium with fewer microvilli, more distinct lumen, abundant mitochondria; specialized transport machinery; part of the juxtaglomerular apparatus. Connecting tubule and cortical collecting duct: simple cuboidal epithelium; principal cells and intercalated cells appear. Collecting ducts: in medulla become larger and more columnar toward papillary ducts of Bellini; clear cell borders and pale cytoplasm; principal and intercalated cells. Juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA): formed by Macula densa: modified DCT cells at the vascular pole of the renal corpuscle; cells are taller and closely packed. Juxtaglomerular (granular) cells: modified smooth muscle cells in the wall of the afferent arteriole (and sometimes efferent), containing renin granules. Extraglomerular mesangial cells (Lacis cells) between macula densa and arterioles.  Physiology Filtration The kidneys receive about 20 to 25 percent of cardiac output. Glomerular filtration is driven by net filtration pressure across the glomerular capillaries and is characterized by a relatively high hydrostatic pressure due to the arrangement of afferent and efferent arterioles. The filtration barrier is selectively permeable: freely filters water and small solutes; largely restricts proteins and cells. Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is tightly regulated by autoregulation (myogenic response, tubuloglomerular feedback) and hormonal and neural inputs.  Reabsorption and secretion PCT reabsorbs the majority of filtered water, sodium, bicarbonate, glucose, amino acids, and other solutes via active and passive transport, driven largely by the Na⁺/K⁺‑ATPase on basolateral membranes; it also secretes organic acids and bases. Loop of Henle establishes the corticomedullary osmotic gradient via countercurrent multiplication. The descending thin limb is highly permeable to water but relatively impermeable to solutes; the ascending limbs (especially thick ascending limb) reabsorb Na⁺, K⁺, and Cl⁻ but are impermeable to water. DCT and collecting ducts fine‑tune salt and water balance under hormonal control (aldosterone, antidiuretic hormone, atrial natriuretic peptide). Intercalated cells regulate acid–base status by secreting H⁺ or HCO₃⁻.  Concentration and dilution of urine Countercurrent multiplication in loops of Henle, countercurrent exchange in vasa recta, and variable water permeability in collecting ducts (ADH‑dependent) together permit excretion of either dilute or concentrated urine.  Endocrine functions Juxtaglomerular cells release renin in response to decreased renal perfusion pressure, sympathetic stimulation, or decreased NaCl at macula densa. Renin activates the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system, influencing blood pressure and volume. Peritubular fibroblast‑like cells produce erythropoietin, which stimulates red blood cell production in bone marrow. Proximal tubule cells express 1‑alpha hydroxylase and convert 25‑hydroxyvitamin D to 1,25‑dihydroxyvitamin D (active vitamin D). The kidney also produces prostaglandins and contributes to gluconeogenesis.  URETERS  Location and gross anatomy Ureters are muscular tubes (approximately 25 to 30 cm) conveying urine from renal pelvis to urinary bladder. They begin at the renal pelvis at the hilum and descend retroperitoneally on the psoas major muscle. They cross anterior to the common iliac or external iliac arteries near the pelvic brim, then continue in the pelvic cavity to enter the urinary bladder posterolaterally at an oblique angle. Classic sites of ureteric constriction are: ureteropelvic junction, crossing of the pelvic brim over the iliac vessels, and ureterovesical junction. These are important for stone impaction.  Arterial supply Segmental and longitudinal; no single continuous artery. In the abdomen, branches come from renal arteries, gonadal (testicular/ovarian) arteries, and branches of the abdominal aorta. In the pelvis, branches arise from common and internal iliac arteries, superior and inferior vesical arteries, uterine and vaginal arteries (in females), and middle rectal arteries. Small arterial branches form a rich network in the adventitia; clinically, the ureter must be mobilized with its adventitia to preserve blood supply.  Venous drainage Veins follow the arteries: drain into renal, gonadal, and internal iliac venous systems depending on segment.  Innervation Ureters are supplied by ureteric nerve plexuses from renal, aortic, superior and inferior hypogastric plexuses. Sympathetic fibers mainly from T10–L2 segments (via splanchnic nerves and lumbar sympathetic chain). Parasympathetic fibers from pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4) in the pelvic part. Visceral afferents conveying pain travel mainly with sympathetics in the upper part (referred pain to flank, groin, and lower abdomen) and with parasympathetics in the lower part. Ureteric peristalsis is myogenic (intrinsic pacemaker properties of smooth muscle) and modulated by autonomic input.  Histology Wall of ureter has three principal layers: mucosa, muscularis, and adventitia. Mucosa: transitional epithelium (urothelium) overlying a lamina propria of dense irregular connective tissue. Urothelial cells include basal cells, intermediate cells, and large superficial umbrella cells. The mucosa is thrown into longitudinal folds, giving a star‑shaped lumen in cross‑section when empty. Muscularis: inner longitudinal and outer circular layers of smooth muscle in the upper two‑thirds; in the lower third a third, outer longitudinal layer is typically present. Smooth muscle bundles are not perfectly circular but form helices. Adventitia: connective tissue containing blood vessels, lymphatics, and nerves; blends with surrounding retroperitoneal tissue.  Physiology The ureter transports urine from the kidney to the bladder by peristaltic waves of smooth muscle contraction, initiated by pacemaker cells in the proximal ureter or renal pelvis. Autonomic innervation modulates the frequency and strength of contractions, but does not initiate them. The oblique intramural course through the bladder wall acts as a functional valve, preventing vesicoureteral reflux when bladder pressure rises during filling and voiding.  URINARY BLADDER  Location and gross anatomy The urinary bladder is a hollow muscular organ in the lesser pelvis, posterior to pubic symphysis. In males: bladder lies anterior to rectum; its neck is superior to the prostate; the seminal vesicles and vas deferens lie posteriorly. In females: bladder is anterior to the uterus and vagina. Regions: apex (toward pubic symphysis), body, fundus (posterior wall), and neck (inferior). The internal urethral orifice is at the neck. Trigone: smooth triangular area on the posterior internal surface, bounded by the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice. Unlike the remainder of the bladder, the trigone is smooth even in the empty state. Capacity: usually around 400 to 600 mL in adults; desire to void begins at lower volumes. The bladder is external to the peritoneal cavity but its superior surface is covered by peritoneum (more extensively in females due to the uterovesical pouch).  Arterial supply Superior vesical arteries (branches of the umbilical artery from internal iliac) supply the superior part. In males, inferior vesical arteries supply the fundus and neck; in females, the same regions are mainly supplied by branches of vaginal arteries. Other contributions may arise from obturator and inferior gluteal branches of the internal iliac artery.  Venous drainage Vesical venous plexus drains the bladder; in males this plexus also receives blood from the prostate, seminal vesicles, and ductus deferens. Vesical plexus drains to internal iliac veins. The venous plexuses are clinically relevant for spread of malignancy and pelvic surgery.  Innervation Bladder innervation is via vesical plexus from the inferior hypogastric (pelvic) plexus. Parasympathetic fibers from pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4) innervate detrusor muscle and are responsible for bladder contraction during micturition; they also open the internal urethral sphincter in males. Sympathetic fibers from T11–L2 (via hypogastric nerves) primarily facilitate storage by relaxing detrusor and promoting contraction of the internal urethral sphincter (especially in males). Somatic innervation to the external urethral sphincter and pelvic floor is via the pudendal nerve (S2–S4), allowing voluntary control. Afferent fibers for bladder filling and pain travel with both parasympathetic and sympathetic pathways.  Histology Mucosa: transitional epithelium (urothelium), thicker than in ureter, with umbrella cells containing uroplakins that form rigid plaques, protecting underlying tissues from urine and allowing stretch. Underlying lamina propria with rich vasculature and some elastic fibers. Submucosa: in some descriptions, not clearly distinct; often lamina propria and submucosa grouped. Muscularis (detrusor muscle): three not sharply defined layers of smooth muscle: inner longitudinal, middle circular, and outer longitudinal. They form a functional syncytium responsible for powerful contractions. At the neck of the bladder there is a thickening of circular muscle fibers functioning as the internal urethral sphincter (more distinct in males). Adventitia/serosa: adventitia lines most of the external surface, consisting of connective tissue with vessels and nerves; serosa (peritoneum) covers the superior surface. Trigone: mucosa is firmly anchored to underlying smooth muscle; few folds; urothelium is thinner but still transitional.  Physiology Bladder has two functions: storage and periodic emptying of urine. Storage phase: sympathetics predominate (relax detrusor, contract internal sphincter), pudendal somatic activity keeps external sphincter contracted. Bladder compliance allows large volume increases with minimal pressure rise. Filling activates stretch receptors in the wall, sending signals to sacral spinal cord and higher centers. Conscious awareness of fullness develops as volume increases. Micturition reflex: a spinal reflex modulated by higher centers. When threshold volume is reached, parasympathetic efferents cause detrusor contraction and relaxation of internal sphincter; voluntary relaxation of external sphincter via pudendal inhibition allows voiding. In adults, cortical and pontine centers exert voluntary control over initiation and suppression of the reflex. Bladder outlet resistance and pelvic floor support are important for continence; pathology here leads to incontinence or retention.  URETHRA  Location and gross anatomy The urethra conducts urine from bladder to exterior; it also conducts semen in males. Male urethra: about 18 to 20 cm; divided into prostatic, membranous, and spongy (penile) parts. Prostatic urethra: passes through prostate gland; receives openings of ejaculatory ducts and prostatic ducts. Membranous urethra: passes through urogenital diaphragm; surrounded by external urethral sphincter. Spongy urethra: runs within corpus spongiosum of penis; terminates at external urethral orifice at the glans. Female urethra: about 3 to 4 cm; passes from internal urethral orifice at bladder neck, descending anterior to the vagina, and opens at the external urethral orifice in the vestibule between clitoris and vaginal opening.  Arterial supply Male urethra: prostatic part from inferior vesical and middle rectal branches; membranous and spongy parts from branches of internal pudendal artery (including dorsal artery of penis). Female urethra: supplied by branches of internal pudendal and vaginal arteries.  Venous drainage Venous drainage parallels arteries: venous plexuses communicate with prostatic venous plexus in males and with vesical and vaginal plexuses in females; ultimately drain to internal iliac veins.  Innervation Male and female urethrae receive autonomic fibers from the prostatic (in males) or vesical and uterovaginal plexuses (in females) derived from inferior hypogastric plexus. Somatic innervation of the external urethral sphincter is via the pudendal nerve (S2–S4), enabling voluntary control of continence. Sensory fibers convey touch, pressure, and pain; in females and in distal male urethra, innervation via pudendal nerve is particularly important.  Histology Male urethra Prostatic urethra: lined mostly by transitional epithelium; continuous with bladder urothelium. Lamina propria contains openings of prostatic ducts. Membranous urethra: epithelium transitions to stratified or pseudostratified columnar. Spongy urethra: predominantly pseudostratified or stratified columnar epithelium, except in the fossa navicularis (distal end) where it becomes nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium. The surrounding corpus spongiosum is erectile tissue with venous sinuses, CT, and smooth muscle. Mucous glands (glands of Littre) open into the lumen of spongy urethra. Female urethra Proximal part may show patches of transitional epithelium, but most of its length is lined by nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium with some areas of pseudostratified or stratified columnar epithelium. The lamina propria is rich in elastic fibers and venous plexuses; small mucous glands are present, some analogous to prostatic tissue. The external urethral sphincter region has skeletal muscle fibers circularly arranged around the urethra.  Physiology The urethra provides a low‑resistance pathway for urine outflow but must also allow competent closure to maintain continence. Internal urethral sphincter (mainly in males) consists of smooth muscle at the bladder neck under autonomic control; it prevents retrograde ejaculation and contributes to continence. External urethral sphincter is skeletal muscle, voluntarily controlled via pudendal nerve; it allows conscious control over micturition. During storage phase, urethral smooth and striated muscles are tonically active; during voiding, coordinated relaxation of sphincters and contraction of bladder is required. In males, urethral physiology is integrated with ejaculation: rhythmic contractions of bulbospongiosus and other perineal muscles expel semen.  INTEGRATED RENAL PHYSIOLOGY SUMMARY The kidneys filter blood, reabsorb needed solutes and water, secrete certain substances, and excrete waste as urine. The ureters passively conduct urine by coordinated peristaltic activity of their smooth muscle layers. The bladder acts as a compliant reservoir with a powerful muscular wall, under complex neural control to allow voluntary, socially appropriate voiding. The urethra conducts urine to the exterior and, in males, also semen, with sphincteric mechanisms and pelvic floor muscles providing fine voluntary and reflex control.  This anatomical, histological, and physiological organization, as described in standard textbooks, underlies the clinical presentations of renal and lower urinary tract diseases, and explains the sites and patterns of referred pain, patterns of obstruction, and functional disturbances such as incontinence and retention.
5|93: I will give a structured, textbook-style overview of the renal system, moving from gross anatomy and neurovascular supply, to histology, then physiology, for each major component: kidneys, ureters, urinary bladder, and urethra. I will aim for the level of a standard medical school text (e.g., Moore, Snell, Junqueira, Guyton/Boron).  KIDNEYS  Anatomy and location The kidneys are paired retroperitoneal organs in the posterior abdominal wall. They lie on either side of the vertebral column, roughly from T12 to L3, with the right kidney usually slightly lower due to the liver. Each kidney has a superior and inferior pole, medial and lateral borders, and an anterior and posterior surface. The hilum is on the medial border and contains (from anterior to posterior) renal vein, renal artery, and renal pelvis (classically described as V A P). The hilum leads into the renal sinus, which houses the calyces, vessels, nerves, and fat.  Posterior relations include diaphragm, psoas major, quadratus lumborum, and transversus abdominis, plus 12th rib on both sides and 11th rib on the left. Subcostal, iliohypogastric, and ilioinguinal nerves pass posterior to the kidneys. The kidneys are surrounded by fibrous capsule, perirenal fat, renal fascia (Gerota fascia), and pararenal fat (from deep to superficial).  Arteries Each kidney receives a renal artery from the abdominal aorta at approximately L1–L2. The right renal artery is usually longer and passes posterior to the inferior vena cava. Near the hilum, each renal artery divides into segmental arteries, which are end arteries supplying specific renal segments (apical, superior, middle, inferior, and sometimes posterior). These give rise to interlobar arteries, which run between the pyramids in the renal columns, then arcuate arteries arch over the base of pyramids at the corticomedullary junction, and finally cortical radiate (interlobular) arteries ascend into the cortex.  From the cortical radiate arteries arise afferent arterioles, which supply the glomerular capillary tufts. The efferent arterioles then form either peritubular capillaries (in the cortex) or vasa recta (in the juxtamedullary nephrons extending into the medulla).  Veins Renal veins drain into the inferior vena cava. The left renal vein is longer, passes anterior to the aorta and posterior to the superior mesenteric artery, and receives the left gonadal and left suprarenal veins. Within the kidney, venous drainage broadly parallels the arterial tree: cortical radiate veins to arcuate veins to interlobar veins to renal vein. There are no segmental veins equivalent to segmental arteries.  Nerves Renal innervation is via the renal plexus, derived from the celiac plexus, aorticorenal ganglia, and lesser and least splanchnic nerves. Sympathetic fibers arise mainly from T10–L1 segments. These innervate afferent and efferent arterioles, juxtaglomerular apparatus, and renal tubules. Parasympathetic supply is relatively sparse and thought to be via the vagus nerve.  Visceral afferents accompanying sympathetics convey pain from the kidney and proximal ureter; referred pain is classically to flank and T10–L1 dermatomes.  Histology A kidney is divided into cortex and medulla. The cortex contains renal corpuscles and convoluted segments of nephrons; the medulla contains straight segments of the nephron and collecting ducts arranged in pyramids.  Renal corpuscle consists of: Glomerulus a tuft of fenestrated capillaries formed by afferent and efferent arterioles. Bowman capsule with a parietal layer of simple squamous epithelium and a visceral layer of podocytes. The filtration barrier includes glomerular endothelial fenestrations, glomerular basement membrane (with lamina rara interna, lamina densa, lamina rara externa), and podocyte filtration slits bridged by slit diaphragms.  Tubular components of the nephron: Proximal convoluted tubule (PCT): simple cuboidal cells with an extensive brush border (microvilli), abundant mitochondria, lateral interdigitations, and apical canaliculi. This segment fills much of the cortical tissue. Loop of Henle: thin descending and thin ascending limbs lined by simple squamous epithelium, especially in long loops of juxtamedullary nephrons; thick ascending limb (TAL) lined by cuboidal cells with extensive basolateral infoldings. Distal convoluted tubule (DCT): shorter, with lower cuboidal cells, fewer microvilli (no obvious brush border), prominent nuclei, and less eosinophilic cytoplasm than PCT. Collecting tubules and ducts: low cuboidal cells early; in medullary collecting ducts and papillary ducts of Bellini, cells become more columnar. Two main cell types: principal cells (light cells) and intercalated cells (dark cells).  Juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA): located at the vascular pole. Consists of macula densa (modified DCT cells with dense nuclei), juxtaglomerular (granular) cells in the wall of afferent arteriole (modified smooth muscle cells with renin granules), and extraglomerular mesangial cells.  Physiology Renal corpuscle supports glomerular filtration. Starling forces across the filtration barrier produce an ultrafiltrate of plasma. Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is determined predominantly by hydrostatic pressure in glomerular capillaries and the properties of the filtration barrier. Autoregulation via myogenic response and tubuloglomerular feedback (macula densa sensing NaCl in distal tubule) helps maintain relatively constant GFR despite changes in blood pressure.  PCT reabsorbs about 65–70 percent of filtered Na, water, and Cl, nearly all filtered glucose and amino acids, plus substantial bicarbonate, phosphate, and other solutes. Transport is largely driven by basolateral Na K ATPase, with various cotransporters and exchangers (e.g., Na-glucose cotransporter, Na H exchanger). It also secretes certain organic acids and bases, drugs, and metabolites.  Loop of Henle establishes and maintains the corticomedullary osmotic gradient via countercurrent multiplication. The descending thin limb is permeable to water but less to solutes; water exits, concentrating tubular fluid. The thick ascending limb is impermeable to water but actively reabsorbs Na, K, and 2Cl via the NKCC2 transporter, diluting tubular fluid and increasing medullary interstitial osmolality.  DCT and connecting tubule handle fine-tuning of Na, K, and Ca. Early DCT reabsorbs Na and Cl via NCC cotransporter; late DCT is a transition towards collecting duct properties. Aldosterone-sensitive regions mediate regulated Na reabsorption and K secretion, while parathyroid hormone promotes Ca reabsorption.  Collecting ducts regulate final urine volume and composition. Principal cells reabsorb Na (via ENaC) and secrete K, under aldosterone influence, and adjust water permeability under antidiuretic hormone (ADH) via insertion of aquaporin-2 channels. Intercalated cells handle acid-base balance: type A intercalated cells secrete H and reabsorb HCO3, while type B secrete HCO3 and reabsorb H.  Vasa recta act as countercurrent exchangers, preserving the medullary gradient while allowing perfusion.  KIDNEY PELVIS AND CALYCES  Anatomy Major calyces are formed from the union of minor calyces that receive urine from papillary ducts at renal papillae. Major calyces join to form the renal pelvis, which is funnel-shaped and lies in the renal sinus. The pelvis narrows to form the ureter at the ureteropelvic junction.  Histology Calices and pelvis are lined by urothelium (transitional epithelium) with basal, intermediate, and superficial umbrella cells. The lamina propria consists of dense connective tissue, and the muscularis typically has two layers in this region (inner longitudinal and outer circular/spiral smooth muscle), though the organization is not as regular as in ureter.  Physiology The calyces and pelvis collect urine and conduct it to the ureter via peristaltic waves generated by pacemaker cells in the proximal collecting system. Peristalsis occurs even independent of extrinsic innervation. Urothelial umbrella cells contribute to barrier function against urine and accommodate volume changes by unfolding of urothelial plaques.  URETER  Anatomy and location The ureters are muscular retroperitoneal tubes (approximately 25–30 cm long) conveying urine from renal pelvis to urinary bladder. Each ureter runs inferiorly from the renal pelvis, crosses the psoas major, and passes over the pelvic brim at the level of the bifurcation of the common iliac artery. In the pelvis, they run along the lateral pelvic wall and then course anteromedially to enter the bladder obliquely at the ureterovesical junction.  Important constrictions: at ureteropelvic junction, where ureter crosses pelvic brim (over common iliac or external iliac arteries), and at ureterovesical junction. These are typical sites for obstructing stones.  In males, the ureter passes under the vas deferens near the bladder (water under the bridge). In females, the ureter passes inferior to the uterine artery in the base of the broad ligament.
