Arterial supply Segmental from nearby arteries: renal arteries (upper third), gonadal (testicular or ovarian), abdominal aorta, common and internal iliac arteries, superior vesical, and other pelvic arteries (middle and distal ureter). These branches form a longitudinal network along the ureter, with relatively poor collateralization at some points.  Venous drainage Veins correspond to arteries and drain into renal, gonadal, and internal iliac veins.  Nerve supply Ureteric plexus is derived from renal, aortic, superior hypogastric, and inferior hypogastric plexuses. Sympathetic fibers from T10–L2 segments; parasympathetic fibers mainly from pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4) in the distal ureter. Pain fibers travel with sympathetics to T10–L2; referred pain may radiate from flank to groin, scrotum or labium majus (the route of ureteric colic).  Histology The ureter wall has three main layers: Mucosa: urothelium (transitional epithelium) overlying a dense fibroelastic lamina propria. The urothelium is stratified, with umbrella cells at the surface containing plaques and fusiform vesicles. Muscularis: in most of the ureter, inner longitudinal and outer circular smooth muscle layers. In the distal third, an outer longitudinal layer appears, so there are three layers overall. The orientation is functionally spiral in some segments, aiding peristalsis. Adventitia: fibrous connective tissue with blood vessels, lymphatics, and nerves; blends with retroperitoneal connective tissue.  Physiology The ureter conducts urine to the bladder by peristaltic contractions initiated within the renal pelvis and proximal ureter. Intrinsic pacemaker activity in the smooth muscle and local stretch-mediated depolarization propagate waves of contraction. Sympathetic activation can modulate vascular tone and may influence peristalsis; parasympathetic fibers tend to enhance peristalsis.  The oblique intramural passage through the bladder wall provides a functional valve against reflux: increasing bladder pressure compresses the intramural ureter to prevent retrograde flow (vesicoureteral reflux).  URINARY BLADDER  Anatomy and location The urinary bladder is a distensible muscular reservoir located in the lesser pelvis, posterior to the pubic symphysis. When empty, it lies largely within the pelvis; when distended, it can extend into the lower abdomen. It has an apex (pointing toward the pubic symphysis), a fundus (posterior surface), a body, and a neck (most inferior and fixed part, leading into the urethra).  Inside, the mucosa shows rugae, except in the trigone area, which is smooth and triangular, between the two ureteric orifices superiorly and the internal urethral orifice inferiorly. The male bladder is related superiorly to peritoneum and small intestine or sigmoid colon, posteriorly to rectum and seminal vesicles, and inferiorly to prostate. In females, the bladder is anterior to vagina and uterus.  Arterial supply Superior vesical arteries (from the patent part of umbilical artery, branch of internal iliac) supply the superior bladder. In males, the inferior vesical artery (branch of internal iliac) supplies the fundus and neck. In females, the vaginal artery often replaces the inferior vesical supply. Additional contributions may come from obturator and inferior gluteal arteries.  Venous drainage Vesical venous plexus drains into internal iliac veins. In males, this plexus communicates with prostatic venous plexus; in females with uterovaginal plexus.  Nerves Bladder innervation comes from the vesical plexus, part of the inferior hypogastric plexus. Parasympathetic fibers: pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4). They stimulate detrusor muscle contraction and relax the internal urethral sphincter (mainly in males), facilitating micturition. They carry visceral afferents related to bladder filling and pain from the bladder neck and trigone. Sympathetic fibers: from T11–L2 segments via hypogastric plexuses. They facilitate storage by relaxing the detrusor muscle and contracting the internal urethral sphincter. Somatic fibers: pudendal nerve (S2–S4) to external urethral sphincter, providing voluntary control.  Pain afferents from the superior bladder travel with sympathetics to T11–L2; from the inferior bladder travel with parasympathetics to S2–S4.  Histology Bladder wall layers: Mucosa: lined by transitional epithelium (urothelium) with umbrella cells, resting on a thick lamina propria of dense fibroelastic connective tissue rich in blood vessels and lymphoid elements. Rugae are formed by mucosa and submucosa when empty. Muscularis (detrusor): bundles of smooth muscle arranged in poorly defined inner longitudinal, middle circular, and outer longitudinal layers. In the region of the internal urethral orifice, these are more organized and form the internal urethral sphincter (particularly prominent in males). Adventitia or serosa: most of the bladder is covered by adventitia; the superior surface is covered by peritoneum (serosa).  Physiology The bladder functions as a low-pressure reservoir and a contractile organ for micturition. During filling, sympathetic activity predominates: detrusor relaxes, and internal sphincter (in males) contracts, aided by tonic somatic contraction of the external urethral sphincter and pelvic floor muscles. The compliance of the bladder wall allows large volume increases with minimal pressure rise (pressure-volume curve is relatively flat until high volumes).  Afferent stretch receptors signal fullness to the sacral spinal cord, forming the basis of the micturition reflex. In infants and lower animals, this is primarily a spinal reflex: bladder filling activates afferents, which via parasympathetic efferents contract the detrusor and relax the internal sphincter, causing voiding when the reflex threshold is reached.  In adults, higher brain centers (pontine micturition center and cerebral cortex) modulate this reflex. Voluntary control involves conscious inhibition or facilitation of the sacral micturition center, combined with voluntary control of the external urethral sphincter via the pudendal nerve.  URETHRA  Anatomy The urethra differs significantly between males and females.  Female urethra Short (about 4 cm), runs from the internal urethral orifice at the neck of the bladder to the external urethral orifice in the vestibule of the vagina, anterior to the vaginal opening. It passes through the deep perineal pouch and perineal membrane and lies anterior to the vagina, embedded within the anterior vaginal wall. It has close relations to the anterior vaginal wall clinically relevant for urethral catheterization and incontinence surgery.  Male urethra Longer (about 18–20 cm) and divided into: Preprostatic (intramural) urethra: in the bladder neck, surrounded by internal urethral sphincter. Prostatic urethra: traverses the prostate gland; receives ejaculatory ducts and prostatic ducts. Membranous urethra: shortest and least distensible portion; passes through the external urethral sphincter and perineal membrane. Spongy (penile) urethra: runs within the corpus spongiosum penis to the external urethral meatus at the tip of the glans; receives ducts of bulbourethral glands in the proximal segment.  Arterial supply Female urethra: branches from internal pudendal and vaginal arteries. Male urethra: prostatic branches of inferior vesical and middle rectal arteries (prostatic urethra), bulbourethral and urethral branches of internal pudendal artery (membranous and spongy urethra).  Venous drainage Veins drain to vesical, prostatic (in males), and internal pudendal venous plexuses, and ultimately to internal iliac veins.  Nerve supply Somatic innervation to the external urethral sphincter is via the pudendal nerve (S2–S4). Autonomic innervation parallels that of the bladder from the inferior hypogastric plexus and its branches: sympathetics from T11–L2 and parasympathetics from pelvic splanchnic nerves.  In males, sympathetic activation is important for closure of the internal urethral sphincter during ejaculation to prevent retrograde ejaculation.  Histology Female urethra: Proximal portion has urothelium (transitional epithelium) similar to bladder, gradually changing to stratified or pseudostratified columnar epithelium, and near the external orifice to stratified squamous epithelium (nonkeratinized). The lamina propria is rich in elastic fibers and has numerous veins and small mucous glands (urethral glands, Skene glands). Muscularis includes inner longitudinal and outer circular smooth muscle layers; near the mid-urethra, there is a periurethral striated muscle component forming part of the external urethral sphincter.  Male urethra: Prostatic urethra is lined mostly by urothelium; more distally it transitions to pseudostratified or stratified columnar epithelium. The very distal segment in the navicular fossa of the glans is lined by stratified squamous epithelium continuous with penile skin (nonkeratinized just proximally). The lamina propria contains mucous glands (glands of Littre) along the spongy urethra. The muscularis has inner longitudinal and outer circular smooth muscle proximally; the membranous urethra is surrounded by the external urethral sphincter composed of striated muscle.  Physiology The urethra provides a low-resistance channel for urine outflow during micturition and a high-resistance barrier during storage. Coordinated relaxation of the internal (mainly in males) and external urethral sphincters, as well as periurethral and pelvic floor muscles, is required for voiding. Urethral pressure is an important factor in continence, particularly in females where urethral support and sphincter function are critical.  In males, the urethra also serves as a conduit for semen during ejaculation. Sympathetic activity causes contraction of smooth muscle in the vas deferens, seminal vesicles, and prostate, and closure of the internal urethral sphincter, while somatic efferents via the pudendal nerve drive rhythmic contractions of bulbospongiosus muscle that expel semen.  SUMMARY OF FUNCTIONAL PHYSIOLOGY BY COMPONENT Kidneys filter blood, regulate volume and electrolytes, maintain acid-base balance, produce hormones (renin, erythropoietin) and activate vitamin D, and maintain osmotic balance via countercurrent mechanisms. Renal pelvis and ureter provide a peristaltic transport system for urine, with urothelium protecting underlying tissue from the hyperosmotic and potentially toxic urine. Bladder acts as a compliant reservoir and a contractile organ for controlled storage and periodic expulsion of urine, under complex autonomic and somatic control involving spinal and supraspinal centers. Urethra provides the final pathway for urine excretion and, in males, also for semen, with sphincteric mechanisms and pelvic floor support ensuring continence and coordinated voiding. 6|93: I will organize this by major components of the renal (urinary) system in a textbook-style sequence: kidneys, ureters, urinary bladder, and urethra. For each, I will move through gross anatomy with location, vessels, and nerves, then histology, then key physiology, as typically presented in standard textbooks like Moore (anatomy), Junqueira (histology), and Guyton or Boron (physiology).  KIDNEYS  Anatomy – location, relations, vessels, nerves  The kidneys are paired retroperitoneal organs in the posterior abdominal wall. They lie on either side of the vertebral column, roughly from T12 to L3, with the right kidney slightly lower due to the liver. Each kidney has superior and inferior poles, medial and lateral borders, and an anterior and posterior surface. The medial border contains the renal hilum, where structures enter and leave: from anterior to posterior, typically renal vein, renal artery, and renal pelvis (then ureter).  Posteriorly, the kidneys are related to the diaphragm and psoas major, quadratus lumborum, and transversus abdominis muscles, plus ribs (usually 11th and 12th on the left, 12th on the right). Anterior relations differ right versus left: right kidney is related to liver, duodenum, and ascending colon; left kidney to stomach, spleen, pancreas, jejunum, and descending colon.  Each kidney is surrounded by fibrous capsule, then perinephric fat, then renal fascia (Gerota), then paranephric fat. The capsule adheres but can usually be stripped off in a healthy kidney.  Renal arteries arise from the abdominal aorta at about L1–L2. Each divides into segmental arteries at the hilum, then interlobar arteries (between pyramids), arcuate arteries (arch over the base of pyramids at corticomedullary junction), and interlobular cortical radiate arteries (ascending into cortex). Afferent arterioles lead to glomerular capillaries, which drain into efferent arterioles. Efferent arterioles form either peritubular capillaries (around cortical nephrons) or vasa recta (around juxtamedullary nephrons in the medulla). Venous drainage generally parallels arteries, converging into interlobular, arcuate, interlobar, and segmental veins, then the renal vein, which drains into the inferior vena cava.  Lymph from kidneys drains to lumbar (aortic and caval) lymph nodes.  Innervation is via the renal plexus, derived from thoracic and lumbar splanchnic nerves (T10–L2). Sympathetic fibers regulate vasomotor tone and renin release; afferent sensory fibers carry pain, typically referred to T10–L2 dermatomes (flank to groin). Parasympathetic innervation is minor and largely via the vagus, with limited direct functional role compared to sympathetic control.  Histology  On gross section, the kidney shows an outer cortex and inner medulla. The cortex contains renal corpuscles (glomeruli plus Bowman capsule), proximal and distal convoluted tubules, and cortical collecting tubules. The medulla is organized into renal pyramids, containing straight tubules (loops of Henle) and collecting ducts. Each pyramid plus its overlying cortical tissue constitutes a renal lobe; within lobes, there are many lobules centered around a cortical collecting duct.  The nephron is the functional unit, consisting of renal corpuscle, proximal tubule, loop of Henle, distal tubule, and connecting tubule that drains into collecting ducts. There are cortical nephrons (short loops) and juxtamedullary nephrons (long loops extending deep into medulla), the latter crucial for urine concentration.  Renal corpuscle: a tuft of fenestrated capillaries (glomerulus) invaginated into Bowman capsule. The visceral layer of Bowman capsule is formed by podocytes with interdigitating foot processes (pedicels) separated by filtration slits bridged by the slit diaphragm (nephrin etc.). The parietal layer is simple squamous epithelium. Between capillaries are mesangial cells surrounded by mesangial matrix, involved in structural support, phagocytosis, and regulation of filtration surface.  The filtration barrier has three components: fenestrated endothelium, glomerular basement membrane (fused laminae of capillary and podocyte with negatively charged proteoglycans), and podocyte slit diaphragms. It is size- and charge-selective.  Proximal convoluted tubule (PCT): lined by simple cuboidal epithelium with an abundant brush border (microvilli), many mitochondria, and basolateral infoldings. This reflects intense active transport and reabsorption.  Loop of Henle: descending thin limb lined by simple squamous epithelium; ascending thin limb (in juxtamedullary nephrons) also squamous; thick ascending limb with cuboidal cells rich in mitochondria, but no brush border. This segment is important for active salt transport and is impermeable to water.  Distal convoluted tubule (DCT): simple cuboidal epithelium with smaller cells, fewer microvilli, and relatively more distinct luminal space; still has many mitochondria. The macula densa is a specialized segment of DCT cells where it contacts the vascular pole of its own renal corpuscle; these tall, closely packed cells sense tubular NaCl concentration.  Juxtaglomerular (JG) apparatus includes macula densa, juxtaglomerular granular cells of the afferent arteriole (modified smooth muscle cells containing renin granules), and extraglomerular mesangial cells. It regulates renin release and thus systemic blood pressure.  Collecting tubules and ducts: lined by simple cuboidal epithelium in smaller segments, transitioning to columnar in larger ducts (papillary ducts of Bellini). There are principal cells (light cells, responsive to aldosterone and ADH) and intercalated cells (dark cells, involved in acid-base regulation via H and HCO3 transport).  Physiology  Kidneys maintain homeostasis of body fluids and electrolytes, regulate blood pressure, contribute to acid-base balance, and perform endocrine functions.  Glomerular filtration: Plasma is filtered across the glomerular filtration barrier into Bowman space, forming an ultrafiltrate essentially free of cells and large proteins. Filtration is driven by net filtration pressure: glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure minus opposing forces (Bowman hydrostatic pressure and plasma oncotic pressure). Autoregulation (myogenic response and tubuloglomerular feedback via macula densa and JG apparatus) keeps renal blood flow and GFR relatively constant across a range of arterial pressures.  Tubular reabsorption and secretion: PCT reabsorbs the majority of filtered sodium, water, bicarbonate, glucose, amino acids, and other solutes, largely via Na coupled transporters and solvent drag, and secretes organic acids and bases. Loop of Henle, particularly the thick ascending limb, reabsorbs Na, K, and 2Cl via the NKCC2 transporter, contributing to the countercurrent multiplier that creates a hyperosmotic medullary interstitium, necessary for urine concentration.  DCT further fine-tunes Na, Cl, and Ca reabsorption (with PTH acting on Ca and thiazide-sensitive NaCl transport). Collecting ducts under the influence of aldosterone regulate final Na and K handling via principal cells, while ADH (vasopressin) increases water permeability via aquaporin-2 insertion, allowing water reabsorption down the medullary osmotic gradient. Intercalated cells secrete H or HCO3 and reabsorb K, contributing to acid-base balance.  Endocrine functions include renin release (starting the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system), erythropoietin production by interstitial fibroblast-like cells in response to hypoxia, and activation of vitamin D (1-alpha hydroxylation to calcitriol) in proximal tubular cells.  URETERS  Anatomy – location, course, vessels, nerves  Ureters are muscular tubes (about 25–30 cm) that conduct urine from the renal pelvis to the bladder. They are retroperitoneal throughout. Each begins as the funnel-shaped renal pelvis at the hilum, then descends on the psoas major, crosses over the pelvic brim at the sacroiliac joint (over the common or external iliac vessels), and runs along the lateral pelvic wall to enter the bladder obliquely at its posterolateral angle.  Classically, there are three anatomical constrictions: at the ureteropelvic junction, at the crossing over the pelvic brim/iliac vessels, and at the intramural part where the ureter traverses the bladder wall. These are common sites for ureteric calculi.  Blood supply is segmental from multiple sources along their course: renal arteries (upper part), gonadal arteries, abdominal aorta, common and internal iliac arteries, and in the pelvis from superior and inferior vesical arteries, uterine artery in females, and others. Arterial branches form a longitudinal network along the ureter. Venous drainage parallels arteries.  Innervation is via renal, aortic, superior hypogastric, and inferior hypogastric plexuses. Sympathetic fibers from T11–L2 and parasympathetic from pelvic splanchnics (S2–S4). Pain from the ureter is referred along T11–L2 dermatomes, classically “loin to groin.” Peristalsis is primarily myogenic, modulated by autonomic input.  Histology  The ureter wall has three main layers: mucosa, muscularis, and adventitia. There is no true submucosa.  Mucosa is lined by transitional epithelium (urothelium), a specialized stratified epithelium resistant to stretching and toxic urine. It consists of basal cells, intermediate cells, and a superficial layer of large dome-shaped umbrella cells with thickened apical membranes and tight junctions. The lamina propria is a dense fibroelastic connective tissue.  Muscularis in the upper two-thirds has an inner longitudinal and outer circular layer of smooth muscle. In the lower third (distal ureter), a third outer longitudinal layer is added. The muscle layers are not perfectly uniform around the circumference. The coordinated contraction generates peristaltic waves.  Adventitia consists of loose connective tissue with blood vessels, lymphatics, and nerves. In the pelvic portion, the ureter is surrounded by pelvic fascia and may be invested in surrounding connective tissues.  Physiology  The ureter transports urine from kidney to bladder via peristaltic waves generated by intrinsic pacemaker activity in the smooth muscle and modulated by autonomic nerves. Stretch of the ureteric wall by incoming urine initiates peristalsis. Sympathetic stimulation generally reduces peristalsic frequency and increases tone; parasympathetic can enhance peristalsis.  The oblique intramural course through the bladder wall acts as a passive flap-valve: as bladder fills and intravesical pressure rises, the intramural ureter is compressed, preventing vesicoureteral reflux. Urothelium provides a barrier to reabsorption of urinary solutes and water and protects underlying tissues from urine toxicity.  URINARY BLADDER  Anatomy – location, parts, vessels, nerves  The urinary bladder is a distensible muscular reservoir located in the lesser pelvis, posterior to the pubic symphysis and anterior to the rectum in males and anterior to the vagina and uterus in females. When empty, it lies entirely in the pelvis; when filled, it expands upward into the lower abdomen.  It has an apex (toward the pubic symphysis), a base or fundus (posterior surface), a superior surface, and two inferolateral surfaces. The neck of the bladder is the most fixed part, surrounding the internal urethral orifice and continuous with the urethra.  On the internal surface, the trigone is a smooth triangular area on the posterior inferior bladder wall, bounded by the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice. Unlike the rest of the bladder, the trigone is derived embryologically from mesonephric ducts and remains relatively smooth and less distensible.  Arterial supply is via superior vesical arteries (from the umbilical artery) to the upper bladder. In males, inferior vesical arteries supply the fundus and neck; in females, analogous branches come from vaginal and uterine arteries. Additional small branches may arise from obturator and inferior gluteal arteries. Venous drainage forms vesical venous plexuses that drain into internal iliac veins.  Lymph drains to external and internal iliac lymph nodes, and some to sacral nodes.  Innervation comes from the vesical plexus, a component of the inferior hypogastric plexus. Sympathetic fibers from T11–L2 via hypogastric nerves innervate the bladder neck and internal urethral sphincter, promoting continence. Parasympathetic fibers from pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4) supply the detrusor muscle, mediating bladder contraction and micturition. Somatic fibers from the pudendal nerve (S2–S4) innervate the external urethral sphincter (voluntary control). Sensory afferents convey fullness and pain.  Histology  The bladder wall has mucosa, muscularis (detrusor), and adventitia or serosa.  The mucosa is lined by transitional epithelium similar to ureters but somewhat thicker when empty and thinner when stretched. The lamina propria has rich vascular supply and elastic fibers. Rugae (folds) are present when the bladder is empty but disappear on filling. The trigone region has a slightly different, smoother mucosa and a more firmly attached lamina propria.  The muscularis (detrusor muscle) consists of three ill-defined layers of smooth muscle: inner longitudinal, middle circular, and outer longitudinal. These interlace to form a functional syncytium. At the bladder neck, the circular layer is better defined and contributes to the internal urethral sphincter region (especially prominent in males).  The outer covering is either adventitia (loose connective tissue anchoring to surrounding structures) or serosa (peritoneum) on the superior surface where the bladder is covered by peritoneum.  Physiology  The bladder functions as a low-pressure reservoir and a pump. As it fills, the compliant detrusor muscle allows volume increase with minimal rise in intravesical pressure (vesicoureteral valves and continence maintained). This is aided by viscoelastic properties of the wall and sympathetic-mediated relaxation of detrusor.  Micturition is a coordinated reflex. During filling, sympathetic activity (T11–L2) via beta receptors relaxes detrusor; alpha receptors constrict the internal sphincter. Somatic pudendal efferents keep the external sphincter contracted. Afferent stretch receptors in the bladder wall send signals via pelvic nerves to the sacral spinal cord and higher centers.  When threshold volume is reached, the micturition reflex is triggered: parasympathetic outflow (S2–S4) contracts detrusor and relaxes internal sphincter; voluntary relaxation of external sphincter via inhibition of pudendal nerve allows urine flow. Supraspinal centers in the pons (pontine micturition center) and cortex modulate this reflex, allowing conscious control.  URETHRA  Anatomy – male and female, vessels, nerves  The urethra conveys urine from the bladder to the exterior; in males it also carries semen.  Male urethra is about 18–20 cm and subdivided into prostatic, membranous, and spongy (penile) portions.  Prostatic urethra passes through the prostate gland. On its posterior wall is the urethral crest, with the seminal colliculus, prostatic utricle, and openings of the ejaculatory ducts. Numerous prostatic ducts also open here.  Membranous urethra passes through the urogenital diaphragm (deep perineal pouch) and is surrounded by the external urethral sphincter.  Spongy urethra runs in the corpus spongiosum of the penis to the external urethral orifice at the glans. Openings of bulbourethral glands enter the proximal spongy urethra.  Arterial supply in males comes from branches of the inferior vesical and middle rectal arteries (prostatic part), and from internal pudendal branches for distal parts. Venous drainage is to prostatic venous plexus and internal pudendal veins. Innervation includes autonomic fibers from prostatic plexus and somatic fibers from the pudendal nerve.  Female urethra is about 3–4 cm long, running from the internal urethral orifice at the bladder neck to the external urethral orifice in the vestibule between labia minora, anterior to the vaginal opening. It passes through the pelvic floor and is closely related to the anterior vaginal wall; its walls are embedded in the anterior vaginal wall connective tissue.  Blood supply is via branches of internal pudendal and vaginal arteries. Venous drainage is to internal pudendal and vaginal venous plexuses. Innervation is via the vesical plexus and pudendal nerve; somatic fibers provide voluntary control of the external sphincter.  Histology  The male urethra has regionally varying epithelium: transitional epithelium in the prostatic part (continuous with bladder), changing to pseudostratified or stratified columnar in the membranous and most of the spongy urethra, and finally to stratified squamous nonkeratinized near the external orifice (sometimes becoming keratinized on the meatus). The lamina propria contains mucous glands (urethral glands of Littre) that contribute to lubrication.  Female urethra is lined mainly by stratified squamous nonkeratinized epithelium with patches of pseudostratified columnar epithelium proximally. The lamina propria has elastic tissue, a venous plexus (contributing to urethral closure pressure), and numerous mucous glands.  Both male and female urethrae have an inner longitudinal and outer circular smooth muscle layer proximally. In the region of the external urethral sphincter, there is a ring of striated muscle (rhabdosphincter) under voluntary control. In females, this sphincter is more extensive and blends with pelvic floor muscles.  Physiology  The urethra is primarily a conduit but also a key component of continence mechanisms. Urethral pressure, maintained by smooth muscle tone, mucosal coaptation, and the submucosal vascular plexus, must exceed bladder pressure to maintain continence. Sympathetic fibers enhance smooth muscle tone of the internal sphincter region (especially in males) and proximal urethra; somatic pudendal fibers maintain contraction of the external sphincter and associated pelvic floor muscles.  During micturition, relaxation of the external sphincter and decreased sympathetic tone allow urethral resistance to fall while detrusor contracts, permitting urine flow. In males, additional skeletal muscle (bulbospongiosus) contracts rhythmically at the end of micturition and during ejaculation.  In summary, textbook treatment of the renal system integrates retroperitoneal kidneys with segmental blood supply and detailed nephron histology, peristaltic ureters and their urothelial lining, the detrusor-based reservoir function of the bladder under autonomic control, and the urethral outlet with its epithelial transitions and sphincteric mechanisms, all coordinated to filter blood, form urine, and excrete it while maintaining homeostasis and continence.
7|93: I will organize this by major components of the renal (urinary) system as typically described in standard anatomy and physiology textbooks: kidneys, ureters, urinary bladder, and urethra. For each, I will move from gross anatomy and relations to blood supply, innervation, histology, and functions/physiology.  KIDNEYS  Location and gross anatomy The paired kidneys lie retroperitoneally on the posterior abdominal wall, roughly from T12 to L3 vertebral levels. The right kidney usually lies slightly lower than the left because of the liver. Each kidney has superior and inferior poles, medial and lateral borders, and an anterior and posterior surface. The hilum is on the medial border and transmits from anterior to posterior: renal vein, renal artery, and renal pelvis (which continues as the ureter), plus lymphatics and nerves. Internally, a frontal section shows the outer renal cortex and inner renal medulla organized into renal pyramids whose apices (papillae) project into minor calyces. Multiple minor calyces join to form major calyces, which unite into the renal pelvis. The kidneys are surrounded by a fibrous capsule, perirenal fat, renal fascia, and pararenal fat. Superiorly each kidney is closely related to its suprarenal (adrenal) gland.  Arterial supply The main arterial supply is the renal arteries, branches of the abdominal aorta at about L1–L2. The right renal artery is usually longer and passes posterior to the inferior vena cava. Each renal artery divides near the hilum into segmental arteries, which are considered end arteries supplying specific renal segments. Segmental arteries give rise to interlobar arteries that run between the renal pyramids, then arcuate arteries that arch along the corticomedullary junction, and then interlobular (cortical radial) arteries that ascend into the cortex. Afferent arterioles branch from interlobular arteries to form the glomerular capillaries. Efferent arterioles exit the glomeruli; in cortical nephrons they form peritubular capillaries, while in juxtamedullary nephrons they form the vasa recta descending into the medulla.  Venous drainage Venous return roughly parallels the arterial tree: peritubular and vasa recta veins → interlobular veins → arcuate veins → interlobar veins → renal vein. The renal veins drain directly into the inferior vena cava. The left renal vein is longer and crosses anterior to the aorta and posterior to the superior mesenteric artery; it receives the left gonadal and left suprarenal veins.  Nerve supply The kidneys receive autonomic fibers via the renal plexus, which contains sympathetic fibers mainly from T10–L1 (via lesser and least splanchnic nerves and lumbar splanchnic nerves) and parasympathetic fibers primarily from the vagus nerve. Sympathetic fibers supply the renal vasculature and juxtaglomerular apparatus, mediating vasoconstriction, renin release, and contributing to pain sensation from the kidney and ureter. Parasympathetic fibers are less functionally emphasized in textbooks but may modulate vasodilation and tubular functions. Visceral afferents travel mostly with sympathetics to T10–L12 spinal levels, which explains referred pain to the flank and lower thoracic dermatomes.  Histology At low magnification, the renal cortex shows numerous renal corpuscles and convoluted tubules, while the medulla shows straight tubules and collecting ducts arranged in parallel. Renal corpuscle: consists of a tuft of fenestrated capillaries (glomerulus) invaginated into Bowman capsule. The visceral layer of Bowman capsule is formed by podocytes with interdigitating foot processes, creating filtration slits bridged by slit diaphragms. The parietal layer is simple squamous epithelium. The filtration barrier includes fenestrated endothelium, a thick fused glomerular basement membrane (lamina rara interna, lamina densa, lamina rara externa), and the podocyte slit diaphragm. The mesangial cells lie between capillary loops and have contractile, phagocytic, and supportive roles.  Tubular system Proximal convoluted tubule (PCT): found in cortex, lined by simple cuboidal epithelium with a prominent brush border of long microvilli, abundant mitochondria, and basolateral infoldings; this correlates with high reabsorptive activity. Loop of Henle: thin descending and thin ascending limbs lined by simple squamous epithelium, and a thick ascending limb lined by simple cuboidal cells with many mitochondria and less prominent brush border. Distal convoluted tubule (DCT): simple cuboidal epithelium, fewer and shorter microvilli (no obvious brush border), paler cytoplasm, smaller cells. The macula densa is a specialized segment of DCT adjacent to the vascular pole of its own glomerulus, with tall, densely packed cells. Collecting ducts: begin as connecting tubules, merge into cortical and medullary collecting ducts, then papillary ducts (ducts of Bellini). Lined by simple cuboidal to columnar epithelium. Principal cells (light cells) regulate water and sodium balance under ADH and aldosterone; intercalated cells (dark cells) regulate acid base balance.  Juxtaglomerular apparatus This includes the macula densa of the DCT, juxtaglomerular (granular) cells in the wall of the afferent arteriole (modified smooth muscle cells containing renin granules), and extraglomerular mesangial cells. It is crucial in regulating blood pressure and GFR.  Physiology Main functions: excretion of metabolic wastes, regulation of fluid and electrolyte balance, acid base balance, blood pressure regulation, endocrine functions, and gluconeogenesis. Glomerular filtration: blood pressure in glomerular capillaries drives filtration across the filtration barrier into Bowman space. The net filtration pressure is determined by glomerular hydrostatic pressure, Bowman capsule hydrostatic pressure, and plasma oncotic pressure. GFR is tightly regulated by renal autoregulation (myogenic mechanism and tubuloglomerular feedback via macula densa), sympathetic tone, and hormones (angiotensin II, ANP, etc.). Tubular reabsorption and secretion: PCT reabsorbs most of filtered water, sodium, bicarbonate, glucose, and amino acids and secretes some organic ions. The loop of Henle establishes the corticomedullary osmotic gradient via countercurrent multiplication: descending limb is water permeable but relatively impermeable to solutes; thick ascending limb is impermeable to water but actively reabsorbs Na+, K+, and Cl−. The DCT and collecting duct fine tune sodium, potassium, hydrogen, and water handling under hormonal control. Aldosterone increases Na+ reabsorption and K+ secretion in principal cells. ADH increases water permeability of late DCT and collecting ducts via insertion of aquaporin 2, concentrating the urine. Intercalated cells secrete hydrogen ions or bicarbonate to maintain acid base balance. Endocrine roles: kidneys secrete renin (from juxtaglomerular cells) initiating the renin angiotensin aldosterone system, erythropoietin (stimulating RBC production), and activate vitamin D (conversion of 25 OH vitamin D to calcitriol via 1 alpha hydroxylase), affecting calcium and phosphate homeostasis.  URETERS  Location and gross anatomy The ureters are muscular retroperitoneal tubes, about 25 to 30 cm long, carrying urine from the renal pelvis to the urinary bladder. Each arises from the renal pelvis at the ureteropelvic junction, passes inferiorly on the psoas major muscle, crosses the pelvic brim at the level of the common iliac or external iliac arteries, and enters the pelvis. In the pelvis, the ureter runs anteromedially to reach the posterolateral angle of the bladder, then passes obliquely through the bladder wall. In males the ureter lies posterior to the ductus deferens near the bladder. In females the ureter runs close to the uterine artery (water under the bridge) near the lateral fornix of the vagina. There are three classical narrowings: at the ureteropelvic junction, at the pelvic brim (where it crosses the iliac vessels), and at the ureterovesical junction; these are common sites for ureteric stones.  Arterial supply Ureteric blood supply is segmental from multiple sources along its course: renal arteries (upper part), gonadal arteries, abdominal aorta, and common or external iliac arteries (mid part), and superior and inferior vesical arteries, uterine arteries, or middle rectal arteries in the pelvis (lower part). These branches form a longitudinal anastomotic chain along the ureter.  Venous drainage Venous drainage roughly parallels arterial supply: upper ureter drains to renal and gonadal veins; middle segments to gonadal and common iliac veins; lower segments to vesical, uterine, or internal iliac veins.  Nerve supply The ureters receive autonomic innervation from renal, aortic, superior hypogastric, and inferior hypogastric plexuses. Sympathetic fibers derive from T10–L2 spinal segments; parasympathetic fibers from pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4) and, more proximally, from vagal contributions. Visceral afferent pain fibers from the upper ureter travel with sympathetics to T10–L2, causing referred pain to the flank, lower abdomen, and groin. Pain from the distal ureter may refer to the scrotum or labia majora.  Histology The ureter wall has three main layers: mucosa, muscularis, and adventitia. Mucosa: lined by transitional epithelium (urothelium), ranging from two or three cell layers in a collapsed ureter to more layers when distended. The superficial layer contains large dome shaped umbrella cells with specialized apical membranes for permeability barrier and stretch. The lamina propria is dense connective tissue with elastic fibers but no distinct submucosa. Muscularis: proximal two thirds typically show an inner longitudinal and outer circular layer of smooth muscle. In the distal third, an additional outer longitudinal layer appears. These layers produce peristaltic contractions that propel urine. Adventitia: connective tissue containing blood vessels, lymphatics, and nerves; it blends with surrounding retroperitoneal tissue.  Physiology The ureters actively propel urine from the renal pelvis to the bladder via intrinsic peristaltic waves generated by pacemaker cells in the proximal renal pelvis. Peristalsis is modulated by autonomic input but does not require it; ureteric smooth muscle has myogenic rhythmicity. The oblique passage of the ureter through the bladder wall creates a functional flap valve: as bladder fills and pressure rises, the intramural ureter is compressed, preventing vesicoureteral reflux. Ureters are sensitive to distension and obstruction; pain is mediated by visceral afferents traveling with sympathetics.  URINARY BLADDER  Location and gross anatomy The bladder is a hollow muscular organ located in the lesser pelvis when empty, but it rises into the suprapubic region as it fills. It has an apex (pointing toward the pubic symphysis), a body, a fundus or base (posterior surface), and a neck that leads into the urethra. In males, the neck of the bladder lies above the prostate; the fundus is related to the rectum and separated by the rectovesical pouch. In females, the bladder lies anterior to the vagina and uterus; the uterovesical pouch lies between bladder and uterus. Internally, most of the bladder mucosa is thrown into folds (rugae) except for the trigone, a smooth triangular area defined by the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice. The trigone is more firmly attached to the underlying detrusor muscle and has different embryologic origins.  Arterial supply The main arterial supply is from branches of the internal iliac artery. Superior vesical arteries (from the patent part of the umbilical artery) supply the superior bladder. In males, the inferior vesical artery supplies the fundus and neck; in females, vaginal arteries often fulfill this role. Additional contributions may come from obturator and inferior gluteal arteries.  Venous drainage Vesical venous plexuses surround the bladder and drain into internal iliac veins. In males, this plexus communicates with the prostatic venous plexus, which in turn communicates with vertebral venous plexuses, forming a route for metastasis.  Nerve supply The bladder receives sympathetic fibers (mainly T11–L2) via the hypogastric plexuses and parasympathetic fibers via pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4), which form the inferior hypogastric (pelvic) plexus. Parasympathetic fibers are motor to the detrusor muscle and inhibitory to the internal urethral sphincter. Sympathetic fibers are thought to facilitate storage by relaxing detrusor and contracting the internal urethral sphincter, particularly in males. Afferent fibers for bladder filling and pain travel with both sympathetic and parasympathetic pathways; stretch receptors in the bladder wall initiate the micturition reflex via S2–S4 spinal segments.  Histology The bladder wall has mucosa, muscularis (detrusor), and adventitia or serosa. Mucosa: lined by transitional epithelium (urothelium), thicker than in ureter with more cell layers in an empty bladder. The umbrella cells at the surface form a strong barrier to urine with specialized plaques and tight junctions. The lamina propria contains dense connective tissue, vessels, and sometimes a thin discontinuous muscularis mucosa. Muscularis: the detrusor muscle consists of interlacing bundles of smooth muscle fibers traditionally described as inner longitudinal, middle circular, and outer longitudinal layers, though these are not sharply distinct. At the bladder neck, the circular fibers form the internal urethral sphincter, more pronounced in males. Outer covering: most of the bladder is covered by adventitia (connective tissue) that blends with surrounding tissues. The superior surface is covered by peritoneum, forming a serosal layer.  Physiology The bladder functions as a reservoir and expeller of urine. Its compliance allows storage of increasing volumes of urine with minimal rise in intravesical pressure up to a certain point. During filling (storage phase), sympathetic and somatic systems dominate. Sympathetic outflow (T11–L2 via hypogastric nerves) relaxes detrusor and contracts the internal sphincter. Somatic motor fibers via the pudendal nerve (S2–S4) maintain contraction of the external urethral sphincter (voluntary control). During micturition (voiding phase), stretch receptors in the bladder wall send afferent impulses to the sacral spinal cord (S2–S4) and higher centers. The pontine micturition center coordinates parasympathetic activation (pelvic splanchnic nerves) causing detrusor contraction and relaxation of the internal sphincter. Volitional relaxation of the external sphincter via inhibition of pudendal motor neurons allows urine outflow. Higher brain centers (cortex and brainstem) modulate this reflex, enabling voluntary control in healthy adults.  URETHRA  General The urethra is the terminal segment of the urinary system, conducting urine from the bladder to the exterior. It shows marked differences between males and females.  Male urethra Anatomy and location The male urethra is about 18 to 20 cm long, serving both urinary and reproductive functions. It is divided into preprostatic (intramural), prostatic, membranous, and spongy (penile) parts. Intramural urethra: short segment in the bladder neck surrounded by internal urethral sphincter. Prostatic urethra: runs through the prostate; widest and most dilatable part. On its posterior wall is the urethral crest with a central seminal colliculus where the prostatic utricle and openings of the ejaculatory ducts are located. Prostatic ducts also open into this segment. Membranous urethra: passes through the external urethral sphincter and deep perineal pouch; it is the narrowest and least distensible part except for the external meatus. Spongy urethra: traverses the corpus spongiosum of the penis. It has proximal bulbous and distal penile portions; it dilates in the glans as the navicular fossa and terminates at the external urethral orifice.  Arterial and venous supply (male) Prostatic and membranous segments receive branches from the inferior vesical and middle rectal arteries; spongy urethra from branches of the internal pudendal artery (bulbourethral and dorsal penile branches). Venous drainage parallels the arterial supply, draining into prostatic and internal pudendal venous plexuses and then internal iliac veins.  Nerve supply (male) Prostatic urethra is innervated by prostatic plexus (from inferior hypogastric plexus). The membranous and spongy urethra receive somatic sensory and motor fibers via the pudendal nerve, and autonomic fibers via cavernous nerves. Sensation from the distal urethra travels via the dorsal nerve of the penis, a branch of pudendal.  Histology (male) The epithelium changes along the course: Intramural and prostatic urethra: mainly urothelium (transitional epithelium). Distal to prostate: transitions to pseudostratified or stratified columnar epithelium. Terminal portion in the fossa navicularis: stratified squamous nonkeratinized, continuous with external penile skin (keratinized squamous). The lamina propria contains mucus secreting urethral glands (of Littre), most numerous in the spongy urethra. In the membranous part, the external urethral sphincter surrounds the urethra, consisting of striated muscle fibers. In the spongy part, the urethra is surrounded by erectile tissue (corpus spongiosum) with venous sinuses.  Physiology (male) The male urethra conducts urine during micturition and semen during ejaculation. Internal urethral sphincter contraction during ejaculation (mediated by sympathetics) prevents retrograde flow of semen into the bladder. Coordinated relaxation of external sphincter and contraction of pelvic floor muscles assist in urine expulsion and post void stripping of the urethra.  Female urethra Anatomy and location The female urethra is about 3 to 4 cm long, running from the internal urethral orifice at the bladder neck to the external orifice in the vestibule between the labia minora, anterior to the vaginal opening. It runs anteroinferiorly embedded in the anterior vaginal wall, passing through the deep perineal pouch and perineal membrane. There is no long intraprostatic segment; the urethra is relatively straight and short, which has clinical implications for urinary tract infections and catheterization.  Arterial and venous supply (female) Branches of the vaginal and internal pudendal arteries supply the female urethra. Venous drainage is via a urethral venous plexus to the vaginal and internal pudendal veins, then to the internal iliac veins.  Nerve supply (female) Autonomic innervation arises from the vesical and vaginal plexuses (derivatives of inferior hypogastric plexus). Somatic innervation and sensory supply to the external sphincter and distal urethra are via the pudendal nerve. Sensory fibers convey information about urine flow and local irritation.  Histology (female) The epithelium starts as transitional epithelium near the bladder neck, soon changing to stratified or pseudostratified columnar epithelium, then to nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium near the external orifice. The lamina propria is rich in elastic fibers and venous plexuses, giving the distal urethra an erectile quality. Surrounding the urethra is an outer layer of smooth muscle (inner longitudinal, outer circular) continuous with the bladder, and more externally, striated muscle fibers of the external urethral sphincter in the deep perineal pouch. Numerous paraurethral glands (Skene glands) open into the urethra or near the external orifice.  Physiology (female) The female urethra provides the conduit for urine from the bladder to the exterior and participates in urinary continence. Continence depends on the tonic activity of the striated external urethral sphincter (pudendal nerve), urethral wall elastic tissues and venous plexus, and the support of the pelvic floor and endopelvic fascia. Changes in these supports (for example after childbirth or with aging) can lead to stress urinary incontinence.  INTEGRATED RENAL SYSTEM PHYSIOLOGY  Across all these components, textbook physiology emphasizes coordinated function: Kidneys filter blood, adjust composition of body fluids, and secrete hormones. Ureters transport urine by peristalsis, with anti reflux valve mechanisms at the bladder. Bladder stores urine at low pressure and expels it under voluntary and reflex control. Urethra provides a controlled outlet, with distinct sphincteric mechanisms (internal smooth muscle and external striated muscle) and sex specific adaptations. The detailed gross anatomy, vascular arrangements, innervation, histology, and organ level functions are tightly integrated, and this is how the renal system is usually presented in standard textbooks of anatomy, histology, and physiology.
8|93: I’ll give you an integrated, textbook-style overview, moving from gross anatomy to histology to physiology, for the main components of the renal system: kidneys, ureters, urinary bladder, and urethra.  KIDNEYS  Location and gross anatomy The kidneys are paired retroperitoneal organs in the posterior abdominal wall. Each lies on the psoas major and quadratus lumborum muscles, roughly between T12–L3 vertebral levels. The right kidney is slightly lower than the left because of the liver. The hilum of each kidney lies on the medial border and transmits the renal vein anteriorly, renal artery in the middle, and renal pelvis/posterior structures posteriorly.  They are surrounded by, from inside out: renal capsule (dense connective tissue), perinephric fat, renal fascia (Gerota fascia), and paranephric fat. Internally, each kidney has a cortex (outer granular region) and medulla (inner, composed of renal pyramids). The tip of each pyramid forms a papilla that drains into a minor calyx, then major calyx, then the renal pelvis, and finally the ureter.  Arterial supply The renal arteries arise from the lateral aspect of the abdominal aorta at about L1–L2. Each renal artery divides near the hilum into segmental arteries, which are considered end arteries supplying specific vascular segments of the kidney. Within the kidney, the usual sequence is: segmental arteries → interlobar arteries (between pyramids in renal columns) → arcuate arteries (arch along cortico–medullary junction) → interlobular arteries (radiate into cortex) → afferent arterioles → glomerular capillaries → efferent arterioles → peritubular capillaries or vasa recta.  Venous drainage The venous pattern mirrors the arterial: peritubular capillaries and vasa recta drain into interlobular veins → arcuate veins → interlobar veins → renal vein. The left renal vein is longer and passes anterior to the aorta and posterior to the superior mesenteric artery. The right renal vein is shorter and drains directly into the inferior vena cava.  Innervation The kidneys receive sympathetic fibers from the least splanchnic nerve via the aorticorenal and renal plexuses (roughly T10–L1 segments). Pain from the kidney is referred to the flank and sometimes to the groin in this dermatomal distribution. Parasympathetic innervation is relatively minor and largely via the vagus nerve. Autonomic fibers regulate renal vascular tone and renin release but tubular transport is predominantly hormonally controlled.  Histology The functional unit is the nephron, consisting of: Renal corpuscle: glomerulus and Bowman capsule. The glomerulus is a tuft of fenestrated capillaries; Bowman capsule has a parietal layer of simple squamous epithelium and a visceral layer of podocytes (cells with interdigitating foot processes forming filtration slits). The glomerular filtration barrier has fenestrated endothelium, glomerular basement membrane, and podocyte slit diaphragms. Proximal convoluted tubule (PCT): lined by simple cuboidal epithelium with a prominent brush border (microvilli), many mitochondria, and extensive infolding for active transport and reabsorption. Loop of Henle: thin descending and ascending limbs lined by simple squamous epithelium; thick ascending limb lined by cuboidal epithelium rich in transporters (notably Na K 2Cl cotransporter) and mitochondria. Distal convoluted tubule (DCT): simple cuboidal epithelium, less brush border than PCT; functions in selective reabsorption and secretion. Collecting tubules and collecting ducts: start with simple cuboidal epithelium and become more columnar in larger ducts; contain principal cells (Na and water balance) and intercalated cells (acid–base regulation). The juxtaglomerular apparatus is composed of the macula densa (specialized DCT cells sensing NaCl), juxtaglomerular cells in the afferent arteriole (modified smooth muscle cells secreting renin), and extraglomerular mesangial cells.  Physiology Glomerular filtration: Blood enters glomerular capillaries under high pressure; ultrafiltrate passes across the filtration barrier into Bowman space. Filtration is governed by Starling forces and is quantified as GFR, which depends on renal blood flow, filtration coefficient, and net filtration pressure. Autoregulation (myogenic response and tubuloglomerular feedback) maintains relatively constant GFR across a range of blood pressures. Tubular reabsorption and secretion: The PCT reabsorbs the bulk of filtered water, Na, glucose, amino acids, bicarbonate, and other solutes, mainly via active transport and secondary active transport; it also secretes organic acids and bases. The loop of Henle establishes a hyperosmotic medullary interstitium via countercurrent multiplication; the thick ascending limb is impermeable to water but reabsorbs Na K 2Cl, diluting tubular fluid. The DCT and collecting duct fine-tune electrolyte and water balance under hormonal control: aldosterone increases Na reabsorption and K secretion in principal cells; antidiuretic hormone (ADH) increases water permeability in the collecting ducts via insertion of aquaporin 2 channels; parathyroid hormone increases Ca reabsorption in the DCT. The kidneys also regulate acid–base balance by reabsorbing filtered bicarbonate, secreting H, generating new bicarbonate via ammoniagenesis, and modulating phosphate buffering. They contribute to blood pressure regulation via the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system, produce erythropoietin for red cell production, and convert vitamin D to its active form, calcitriol.  URETERS  Location and gross anatomy The ureters are muscular tubes (about 25–30 cm long) transporting urine from the renal pelvis to the urinary bladder. They descend retroperitoneally on the psoas major muscle, cross the pelvic brim at the level of the common iliac vessels, then pass into the pelvis, running along the lateral pelvic wall to enter the bladder posterolaterally at an oblique angle. Clinically important constrictions, where stones often lodge, include: at the ureteropelvic junction, where they cross the pelvic brim, and at the ureterovesical junction.  Arterial supply The ureters have a segmental blood supply from nearby arteries: renal arteries in the upper abdominal portion, gonadal (testicular or ovarian) and abdominal aorta branches along the mid portion, and common and internal iliac branches (especially superior vesical, uterine, or inferior vesical arteries) in the pelvis. Arterial branches form a longitudinal anastomosing network along the ureter.  Venous drainage Veins generally parallel the arteries: drain superiorly into the renal and gonadal veins and inferiorly into the internal iliac system via vesical and uterine veins.  Innervation Innervation is from the autonomic plexuses along their course: renal, aortic, superior hypogastric, and inferior hypogastric plexuses. Sympathetic fibers come from T10–L2 segments; parasympathetic from pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4) in the pelvic portion. Pain from the ureter is referred along T10–L2 dermatomes, typically flank to groin, and can be severe in ureteric colic.  Histology The ureter wall has three main layers: Mucosa: lined by transitional epithelium (urothelium) resting on a lamina propria of dense connective tissue. Urothelium is stratified and specialized to withstand stretching and contact with urine. Muscularis: in the upper two thirds, there are inner longitudinal and outer circular smooth muscle layers. In the lower third, an additional outer longitudinal layer appears. This muscular arrangement generates peristaltic waves. Adventitia: outer connective tissue containing blood vessels, nerves, and fat, blending with surrounding tissues.  Physiology The ureters conduct urine from the kidneys to the bladder by intrinsic peristalsis. Pacemaker cells in the renal pelvis initiate rhythmic contractions, which move distally along the ureteral smooth muscle. Flow is unidirectional due to the oblique intramural course through the bladder wall: as the bladder fills and pressure rises, the intramural ureter is compressed, functioning as a physiological valve that helps prevent vesicoureteral reflux. The rate of peristalsis increases with increased urine production and can be modulated by autonomic input, though basic activity is myogenic.  URINARY BLADDER  Location and gross anatomy The bladder is a distensible muscular sac in the pelvis. When empty, it lies in the true pelvis; as it fills, it can rise into the lower abdomen. In males, it lies posterior to the pubic symphysis and anterior to the rectum, with the prostate inferior to its neck. In females, it is anterior to the vagina and uterus. The bladder has an apex (toward the pubic symphysis), a base (posterior surface), a body, and a neck (lowest part, leading to the urethra). On the internal surface of the base is the trigone, a smooth triangular area between the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice. The rest of the mucosa is folded into rugae when the bladder is empty.  Arterial supply Arterial supply is primarily from branches of the internal iliac artery. In both sexes, superior vesical arteries supply the superior portion. In males, the inferior vesical artery supplies the base and neck. In females, branches of the vaginal artery correspond to the inferior vesical supply.  Venous drainage The vesical venous plexus surrounds the bladder and drains into the internal iliac veins. In males, it communicates with the prostatic venous plexus; in females, with the uterovaginal plexus.  Innervation Innervation is via the inferior hypogastric (pelvic) plexus. Parasympathetic fibers (pelvic splanchnic nerves, S2–S4) innervate the detrusor muscle and are responsible for contraction of the bladder and relaxation of the internal urethral sphincter during micturition. Sympathetic fibers (T11–L2 via hypogastric nerves) facilitate bladder filling by relaxing the detrusor and contracting the internal urethral sphincter, especially in males. Somatic innervation of the external urethral sphincter (and part of pelvic floor support) is via the pudendal nerve (S2–S4). Sensory afferents from stretch receptors travel with both parasympathetic and sympathetic pathways.  Histology The bladder wall consists of: Mucosa: transitional epithelium (urothelium) overlying a lamina propria of fibroelastic connective tissue. When empty, the mucosa forms rugae; in the trigone, it is smoother and more firmly attached. Muscularis (detrusor muscle): three poorly defined layers of smooth muscle (inner longitudinal, middle circular, outer longitudinal) that act together to expel urine. Serosa/adventitia: the superior surface is covered by peritoneum (serosa); the rest has an adventitia of connective tissue.  Physiology The bladder stores urine and expels it during micturition. During filling, sympathetic activity predominates: detrusor muscle is relaxed, internal sphincter contracted, and somatic pudendal activity maintains contraction of the external urethral sphincter. As volume increases, stretch receptors in the bladder wall send afferent signals to the sacral spinal cord and higher centers. When micturition is initiated, voluntary relaxation of the external urethral sphincter and inhibition of sympathetic outflow occur, while parasympathetic efferents cause detrusor contraction and internal sphincter relaxation. Higher brain centers (pontine micturition center and frontal cortex) modulate this reflex, allowing conscious control in healthy adults.  URETHRA  Location and gross anatomy The urethra conducts urine from the bladder to the exterior and differs significantly between males and females. In females, the urethra is about 3–4 cm long, runs anteroinferiorly from the bladder neck, passes through the pelvic floor and perineal membrane, and opens in the vestibule between the labia minora, anterior to the vaginal opening. In males, the urethra is about 18–20 cm long and is subdivided into: prostatic urethra (within the prostate gland), membranous urethra (through the external urethral sphincter and perineal membrane), and spongy or penile urethra (within the corpus spongiosum of the penis). It serves both urinary and reproductive functions.  Arterial supply In females, the urethra receives blood from branches of the internal pudendal and vaginal arteries. In males, branches of the inferior vesical, middle rectal, and internal pudendal arteries supply different segments of the urethra.  Venous drainage Venous drainage generally parallels arterial supply, ultimately draining into internal iliac veins via pudendal, vesical, and prostatic plexuses.  Innervation Somatic innervation of the external urethral sphincter is via the pudendal nerve (S2–S4). Autonomic innervation is through pelvic and prostatic plexuses. In both sexes, parasympathetic fibers assist in sphincter relaxation during voiding, and sympathetic fibers contribute to continence by supporting internal sphincter tone (particularly in males).  Histology The lining epithelium changes along its course. Female urethra: starts with transitional epithelium near the bladder, then changes to stratified or pseudostratified columnar epithelium, and finally stratified squamous epithelium distally. The lamina propria is vascular and contains mucous glands; there is a surrounding layer of smooth muscle continuous with the bladder, plus skeletal muscle fibers in the external sphincter region. Male urethra: prostatic urethra is lined mainly by transitional epithelium; the membranous and most of the spongy urethra are lined by pseudostratified or stratified columnar epithelium, with a distal transition to stratified squamous epithelium at the fossa navicularis and external meatus. Numerous mucous glands (e.g., glands of Littre) open into the urethra, especially in the spongy segment.  Physiology The urethra provides a low-resistance pathway for urine excretion and participates in continence. Smooth muscle in the proximal urethra and internal sphincter, especially in males, is under autonomic control: sympathetic tone maintains closure during filling and ejaculation, while parasympathetic activation helps relaxation during micturition. The external urethral sphincter, composed of skeletal muscle, is under voluntary control via the pudendal nerve, allowing conscious initiation or delay of urination within functional limits. In males, the urethra also conducts semen, where coordinated closure of the bladder neck prevents retrograde ejaculation.  INTEGRATED RENAL SYSTEM PHYSIOLOGY Across all parts, the renal system functions to filter blood, regulate fluid and electrolyte balance, maintain acid–base homeostasis, control blood pressure, excrete metabolic wastes and toxins, and produce key hormones (renin, erythropoietin, active vitamin D). The kidneys generate urine; ureters, bladder, and urethra store and conduct it. Autonomic innervation and local smooth muscle properties coordinate peristalsis and micturition, while hormone-sensitive epithelial transport in nephrons determines the final composition and volume of urine.  This framework follows standard textbook organization: starting from location and gross anatomy, then vessels and nerves, then histology, and finally physiology for each major part of the renal system.
9|93: I can outline the structure part‑by‑part in a textbook‑style sequence, but to keep things usable I will group details and emphasize key patterns rather than every microscopic variant.  RENAL SYSTEM OVERVIEW The renal or urinary system includes: kidneys, ureters, urinary bladder, and urethra. For each, you can think in the standard sequence used in textbooks: gross anatomy and relations, blood and nerve supply, histology, then key physiological roles.  KIDNEYS Anatomy and location The kidneys are paired retroperitoneal organs on the posterior abdominal wall. They lie on either side of the vertebral column, roughly T12–L3, with the right kidney usually slightly lower because of the liver. Each kidney has a superior and inferior pole, medial and lateral borders, and an anterior and posterior surface. The medial border shows the hilum, where renal vessels, lymphatics, nerves, and the renal pelvis enter or leave. The posterior surface is related to the diaphragm and the psoas major, quadratus lumborum, and transversus abdominis muscles, as well as the 12th rib (and 11th rib on the left). Anterior relations differ right vs left: right kidney is related to liver, duodenum (second part), and hepatic flexure of colon; left kidney to stomach, spleen, pancreas, jejunum, and splenic flexure of colon. Each kidney is surrounded by a fibrous capsule, perirenal fat, renal fascia, and pararenal fat.  Arterial supply Each kidney is supplied mainly by a renal artery, usually a single large branch from the abdominal aorta at about L1–L2. The right renal artery typically runs posterior to the inferior vena cava. At the hilum, the renal artery divides into segmental arteries, each supplying a surgically resectable segment. A common textbook scheme describes five segments: superior (apical), superior (or upper) segment, inferior (or lower) segment, anterior superior, anterior inferior, and posterior (names vary by text). Segmental arteries branch into lobar arteries, then interlobar arteries running between renal pyramids in the columns. At the corticomedullary junction, interlobar arteries give arcuate arteries that arch over the bases of the pyramids. From arcuate arteries arise interlobular (cortical radial) arteries, which give off afferent arterioles to glomeruli. In the cortex, efferent arterioles form peritubular capillaries; those from juxtamedullary glomeruli descend as vasa recta into the medulla.  Venous drainage Renal veins emerge at the hilum anterior to the renal arteries and drain into the inferior vena cava. The left renal vein is longer, passing anterior to the aorta and posterior to the superior mesenteric artery; it receives the left gonadal and left suprarenal veins. The right renal vein is shorter and drains directly to the IVC. Within the kidney, venous drainage broadly parallels the arterial tree in reverse: interlobular veins, arcuate veins, interlobar veins, then the renal vein (there is usually no distinct segmental venous pattern described in the same surgical sense as segmental arteries).  Lymphatic drainage Lymph drains primarily to lateral aortic (lumbar) lymph nodes around the origin of the renal arteries.  Nerve supply Renal nerves are derived from the renal plexus, which receives fibers from the least splanchnic nerve and the lumbar splanchnic nerves via the aorticorenal and celiac ganglia. Sympathetic fibers are primarily vasomotor, regulate renin release, and influence tubular transport and pain pathways. Afferent pain fibers travel with sympathetic fibers, typically referring pain to the flank and costovertebral area. Parasympathetic innervation is relatively minor and often attributed to the vagus.  Histology At low magnification, the kidney shows cortex and medulla. The cortex contains renal corpuscles and convoluted tubules; the medulla contains pyramids composed mainly of straight tubules and collecting ducts. A renal corpuscle consists of the glomerulus and surrounding Bowman capsule. The glomerular capillary tuft is lined by fenestrated endothelium and surrounded by visceral epithelial cells called podocytes, which have foot processes with filtration slits bridged by slit diaphragms. The parietal layer of Bowman capsule is simple squamous epithelium. Between capillary loops lies the mesangium (mesangial cells and matrix) responsible for structural support, phagocytosis, and modulation of filtration. The filtration barrier comprises three layers: fenestrated endothelium, glomerular basement membrane (with its lamina rara interna, lamina densa, and lamina rara externa), and podocyte slit diaphragm. Proximal convoluted tubules are lined by simple cuboidal epithelium with a prominent brush border (microvilli), abundant mitochondria, and basolateral infoldings to support active reabsorption. Distal convoluted tubules have lower cuboidal cells with less prominent brush border and more distinct cell borders. The loop of Henle has thin segments lined by simple squamous epithelium and thick segments similar to distal tubule epithelium. Collecting ducts are lined by simple cuboidal to columnar epithelium composed of principal cells and intercalated cells. The juxtaglomerular apparatus, located at the vascular pole of the renal corpuscle, consists of the macula densa (specialized cells in the distal tubule wall), juxtaglomerular (granular) cells in the wall of the afferent arteriole, and extraglomerular mesangial cells.  Physiology The kidneys maintain internal homeostasis by regulating volume and osmolarity of body fluids, excreting metabolic waste products (urea, creatinine, uric acid), controlling electrolyte balance (Na, K, Ca, phosphate), and contributing to acid–base balance by hydrogen ion secretion and bicarbonate reabsorption or generation.  Glomerular filtration occurs when plasma is filtered from glomerular capillaries into Bowman space under net filtration pressure (driven by capillary hydrostatic pressure minus plasma oncotic and Bowman capsular pressures). The glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is determined by net filtration pressure and the ultrafiltration coefficient. Filtration is relatively nonselective for small solutes but excludes cells and most plasma proteins. Tubular reabsorption returns most filtered water and solutes (Na, Cl, glucose, amino acids, bicarbonate) to the blood, especially in the proximal tubule where the bulk of isoosmotic reabsorption occurs. Tubular secretion adds substances (H, K, NH4, organic acids and bases, many drugs) from peritubular blood into the tubular fluid, especially in the proximal and distal nephron segments and collecting ducts. The loop of Henle and vasa recta create and maintain a corticomedullary osmotic gradient through countercurrent multiplication and exchange, permitting concentration or dilution of urine. The distal tubule and collecting ducts fine‑tune electrolyte and water excretion under hormonal control. Aldosterone increases Na reabsorption and K and H secretion in principal and intercalated cells. Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) increases water permeability of the collecting ducts by inserting aquaporin‑2 channels, enabling water reabsorption down the medullary osmotic gradient. Atrial natriuretic peptide, parathyroid hormone, and others modulate Na, water, and Ca handling. The juxtaglomerular apparatus regulates renin secretion in response to reduced afferent arteriolar stretch, sympathetic activity, or decreased NaCl delivery to the macula densa. Renin initiates the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system, affecting blood pressure and volume. The kidneys also perform endocrine functions: they produce renin, convert 25‑hydroxyvitamin D to 1,25‑dihydroxyvitamin D (via 1 alpha hydroxylase), and secrete erythropoietin from peritubular interstitial cells in response to hypoxia.  URETERS Anatomy and location The ureters are muscular tubes, about 25 to 30 cm long, that convey urine from the renal pelvis to the urinary bladder. They are retroperitoneal. Each ureter begins at the ureteropelvic junction at the renal hilum, descends anterior to the psoas major muscle, crosses the pelvic brim near the bifurcation of the common iliac artery, and then runs in the pelvic cavity to enter the bladder obliquely at the posterolateral aspect. There are three physiologic constrictions important clinically for stone impaction: at the ureteropelvic junction, where the ureter crosses the pelvic brim (over the iliac vessels), and where the ureter enters the bladder wall (ureterovesical junction). In the pelvis, the ureter passes close to important structures; in females it passes inferior to the uterine artery (water under the bridge); in males it lies near the ductus deferens.  Arterial supply Blood supply is segmental and longitudinal, derived from multiple sources along the course of the ureter. In the abdomen, branches come from renal arteries, gonadal (testicular or ovarian) arteries, and branches of the abdominal aorta. In the pelvis, they receive branches from common iliac, internal iliac, and its branches such as superior and inferior vesical, uterine, and middle rectal arteries. These arteries form a longitudinal arterial chain along the ureter, with small penetrating branches; there is relatively poor collateral flow between segments, so stripping of the adventitia endangers blood supply.  Venous drainage Veins accompany arteries and drain to renal, gonadal, and internal iliac veins depending on segment. In the pelvis, venous drainage goes primarily into tributaries of the internal iliac venous system.  Nerve supply The ureters are innervated by autonomic fibers from renal, aortic, and hypogastric plexuses. Sympathetic fibers arise from T11 to L2 segments; parasympathetic fibers from pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4), especially to the distal ureter. Visceral afferent fibers conveying pain typically accompany sympathetic fibers to T11–L2, leading to referred pain from the flank to the groin and genital region during ureteric colic.  Histology The ureter wall has three main layers: mucosa, muscularis, and adventitia. The mucosa is lined by transitional epithelium (urothelium), a stratified epithelium specialized to tolerate stretch and toxic urine. The surface cells are large umbrella cells. Beneath the epithelium is a lamina propria of dense connective tissue. There is no distinct muscularis mucosae. The muscularis consists of smooth muscle arranged in two main layers in the upper two thirds: inner longitudinal and outer circular. In the lower third, a third outer longitudinal layer appears, so the distal ureter has three layers. These layers generate peristaltic waves that propel urine. The outer adventitia is composed of connective tissue, vessels, nerves, and fat.  Physiology The ureters conduct urine from kidneys to bladder by peristalsis and some assistance from gravity. Pacemaker regions in the proximal ureter generate rhythmic contractions. The frequency and strength of peristalsis adapt to the rate of urine flow. Smooth muscle contraction is influenced by autonomic input and local stretch (myogenic mechanism). The oblique intramural course through the bladder wall acts as a functional valve: during bladder filling and micturition, increased intravesical pressure compresses the intramural ureter, helping prevent vesicoureteral reflux.  URINARY BLADDER Anatomy and location The urinary bladder is a distensible muscular organ situated in the lesser pelvis when empty, posterior to the pubic symphysis, and it may expand into the lower abdomen when full. It has an apex directed toward the pubic symphysis, a base (fundus or posterior surface) related in males to the rectum and in females to the vagina and cervix, a superior surface covered by peritoneum, and an inferolateral surface resting on the pelvic floor. Internally, the mucosa is folded (rugae) except at the trigone: a smooth triangular area between the ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice. In males the neck of the bladder is closely related to the prostate gland; in females it rests on the pelvic diaphragm and is closely related to the urethra and anterior vaginal wall.  Arterial supply Arterial supply is mainly from branches of the internal iliac artery. In males, the superior vesical arteries (from the patent part of the umbilical artery) supply the superior portion; the inferior vesical arteries supply the fundus and neck. In females, superior vesical arteries supply the superior part and the vaginal arteries (and sometimes uterine branches) supply the rest of the bladder. There may be contributions from obturator and inferior gluteal arteries.  Venous drainage The vesical venous plexus lies around the base of the bladder. In males it is continuous with the prostatic venous plexus and drains to the internal iliac veins. In females it communicates with uterovaginal plexuses and drains similarly to internal iliac veins.  Nerve supply Innervation arises from the inferior hypogastric (pelvic) plexus. Sympathetic fibers come from the hypogastric plexuses (T11–L2 spinal segments), innervating mainly blood vessels and the internal urethral sphincter (more prominent in males). Parasympathetic fibers come from pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4) and are motor to the detrusor muscle and inhibitory to the internal sphincter. Afferent fibers for pain and distension follow different routes: in general, pain from the superior bladder travels with sympathetics (T11–L2), while from the inferior part it may travel with parasympathetics to S2–S4.  Histology The bladder has a mucosa lined by transitional epithelium, supported by a lamina propria of fibroelastic connective tissue. The mucosa forms folds when the bladder is empty. The trigone area has a smoother, more tightly adherent mucosa. The muscularis (detrusor muscle) consists of interlacing smooth muscle fibers organized into three poorly defined layers: inner and outer longitudinal layers with a middle circular layer.
