Still, you can attempt a recursive crawler by fetching the HTML, parsing links that look like either directories or file downloads, then recursing into directories until no more child links are found. The example below uses Python with requests and BeautifulSoup; it prints direct file links to stdout.  from urllib.parse import urljoin, urlparse import requests from bs4 import BeautifulSoup  start_url = "https://arcjav.arcjavdb.workers.dev/0:/001-050/%E4%B8%8A%E5%8E%9F%E4%BA%9A%E8%A1%A3/"  visited = set()  def is_same_host(base, url):     return urlparse(base).netloc == urlparse(url).netloc  def crawl(url):     if url in visited:         return     visited.add(url)      try:         resp = requests.get(url, timeout=15)         resp.raise_for_status()     except Exception as e:         print(f"Error fetching {url}: {e}")         return      content_type = resp.headers.get("Content-Type", "").lower()      if "text/html" not in content_type:         print(url)         return      soup = BeautifulSoup(resp.text, "html.parser")      links = set()     for a in soup.find_all("a", href=True):         href = a["href"].strip()         if href.startswith("#"):             continue         full = urljoin(url, href)         if not is_same_host(start_url, full):             continue         links.add(full)      file_like_exts = {         ".mp4", ".mkv", ".avi", ".mov", ".flv", ".wmv",         ".zip", ".rar", ".7z",         ".jpg", ".jpeg", ".png", ".gif", ".webp",         ".srt", ".ass", ".vtt",         ".mp3", ".flac", ".aac", ".wav"     }      def looks_like_file(link):         path = urlparse(link).path         lower = path.lower()         for ext in file_like_exts:             if lower.endswith(ext):                 return True         return False      for link in sorted(links):         if looks_like_file(link):             print(link)         else:             crawl(link)  if __name__ == "__main__":     crawl(start_url)  Notes  You may need to adjust looks_like_file and file_like_exts depending on what kind of files are hosted. Some directory index frontends distinguish folders and files by a trailing slash in the href or by specific CSS classes on anchor tags; if you inspect the page source in a browser and see such patterns, you can refine the link classification logic. If the worker uses an API endpoint (for example returning JSON with file and folder metadata), using that API instead of scraping HTML will be more robust. Remember that you must respect the sites robots.txt and terms of service, and avoid sending rapid, heavy traffic.
9|98: Since I cannot access that URL directly from here, I’ll show a general pattern in Python using requests and BeautifulSoup to recursively walk a directory-style HTTP index and collect all file URLs. You can adapt the base URL and tweak the HTML parsing depending on how that server lists directories and files.  Example Python code:  import requests from bs4 import BeautifulSoup from urllib.parse import urljoin, urlparse  BASE_URL = 'https://arcjav.arcjavdb.workers.dev/0:/001-050/%E4%B8%8A%E5%8E%9F%E4%BA%9A%E8%A1%A3/'  visited = set() file_urls = []  def is_directory_link(href):     if not href:         return False     # For many simple directory listings, directories end with '/'     return href.endswith('/')  def is_file_link(href):     if not href:         return False     # Exclude parent links and directory-style links     if href.endswith('/'):         return False     if href.startswith('?') or href.startswith('#'):         return False     return True  def crawl(url):     if url in visited:         return     visited.add(url)      resp = requests.get(url)     resp.raise_for_status()      soup = BeautifulSoup(resp.text, 'html.parser')      for a in soup.find_all('a'):         href = a.get('href')         if not href:             continue          full_url = urljoin(url, href)          # Normalize to avoid re-crawling with fragments, etc.         parsed = urlparse(full_url)         full_url = parsed._replace(fragment='').geturl()          # Skip parent directory links, if present         if a.text.strip() in ('..', '../'):             continue          if is_directory_link(href):             crawl(full_url)         elif is_file_link(href):             file_urls.append(full_url)  # Run the crawl starting from the base directory crawl(BASE_URL)  # At this point file_urls contains all discovered direct file URLs for u in file_urls:     print(u)  Notes for adapting this to your specific server  1. Directory detection    Some directory listings do not end directory names with a slash. Instead they might use icons or specific HTML structure. In that case you may need to inspect the page source in your browser and identify patterns, then adjust is_directory_link and is_file_link to use class names, icon columns, or regexes on filenames.  2. Pagination or lazy loading    If the index uses JavaScript to fetch entries dynamically, requests plus BeautifulSoup will not be enough. You would need to    Use a headless browser (e.g., Playwright or Selenium) to render the page and then extract the DOM    Or find the underlying API endpoints that the page calls (using browser dev tools Network tab) and call those endpoints directly in your script  3. File type filtering    If you only want certain file types (for example .mp4 or .zip), modify is_file_link to check extensions:     def is_file_link(href):        if not href or href.endswith('/'):            return False        allowed_ext = {'.mp4', '.mkv', '.zip', '.rar'}        from pathlib import Path        ext = Path(href).suffix.lower()        return ext in allowed_ext  4. Rate limiting and politeness    Add delays between requests (e.g., time.sleep(0.5))    Consider limiting recursion depth if the hierarchy is very deep    Respect robots.txt and any usage policies if applicable  5. Alternative: parsing JSON listings    Some Cloudflare Workers directory indexers return JSON if you hit a listing endpoint directly. If you inspect network calls and find a json endpoint that returns a structure like    files: [ { name: ..., url: ..., type: 'file' }, ... ]    you can recursively traverse that JSON instead of scraping HTML. The recursion logic would be similar: for each entry of type folder, recurse on its URL; for each entry of type file, record its url.  By adjusting the base URL and the detection logic for directories vs files, this pattern will recursively collect all direct file URLs under the given directory.
10|98: Because the site is being served by a Cloudflare Worker with an index-style HTML page, you can recursively harvest all direct file URLs by fetching the directory, parsing the links, and descending into subdirectories until you reach only files. Below is an example in Python using requests and BeautifulSoup. Adjust headers / timeouts as needed.  import requests from bs4 import BeautifulSoup from urllib.parse import urljoin, urlparse  BASE_URL = 'https://arcjav.arcjavdb.workers.dev/0:/001-050/%E4%B8%8A%E5%8E%9F%E4%BA%9A%E8%A1%A3/'  visited = set() file_urls = []  # Optional: decide how to detect files vs folders. In many of these index pages, # folders have trailing slash; files do not. We can use that heuristic.  def is_directory_link(href):     # Treat as directory if it ends with /     return href.endswith('/')   def crawl(url):     if url in visited:         return     visited.add(url)      resp = requests.get(url)     resp.raise_for_status()      soup = BeautifulSoup(resp.text, 'html.parser')      for a in soup.find_all('a', href=True):         href = a['href']          # Skip parent directory and junk         if href.startswith('#'):             continue         if href in ('../', './'):             continue          full = urljoin(url, href)          # Stay under the same origin and path tree         if not full.startswith(BASE_URL):             continue          if is_directory_link(href):             crawl(full)         else:             file_urls.append(full)   if __name__ == '__main__':     crawl(BASE_URL)     for u in file_urls:         print(u)  This script starts at the specified directory URL, recursively follows any subdirectory links (those ending in a slash), and collects direct file URLs (those without a trailing slash). When run, it prints a list of all file URLs reachable under that path. If the particular index uses a different pattern to distinguish folders from files, you can instead detect files by extension, for example by checking if the href contains .mp4, .mkv, .zip, etc.

Day 3: Create your first 2 to 3 videos Aim for done, not perfect. For a one week sprint, your advantage is speed. Pick 2 or 3 strong moments from your recordings and turn them into complete videos. Trim dead time, long silences, and loading screens. Use jump cuts to keep things moving so there is almost always something happening.  Record commentary or voiceover that respects the viewer’s time. Open quickly with what the video is about instead of long intros. For example, Today I am trying to win a match using only pistols, and it goes horribly wrong. Keep the energy up but be authentic; audiences can tell when you are faking a persona too hard.  Add simple edits: zoom-ins on funny faces or clutch moments, captions for key phrases, and sound effects sparingly. Good pacing matters more than flashy effects for your first week.  Day 4: Thumbnails, titles, and metadata A lot of new creators spend all their time on the video and almost none on the thumbnail and title, but in the first week, click-through rate matters more than your editing skills.  Thumbnail: Use a clear, readable image that works even on a small phone screen. Show one main idea, like your shocked face and a dramatic in-game scene, or large text like Only 1 HP Left. Avoid clutter. High contrast colors help the image pop.  Title: Make it searchable plus intriguing. Combine keywords and a hook, like Trying to win with no weapons in Warzone or New players keep making this mistake in Valorant. Avoid clickbait that lies; viewers will leave fast, hurting your watch time.  Description and tags: Write 2 to 3 lines about the video, including the game name and what happens. Add the game in the gaming category and select the correct title so YouTube can recommend it to people watching that game.  Day 5: Upload schedule and shorts Your one-week mission is to convince the algorithm your channel is active and consistent. Upload at least 1 main video per day for 3 to 4 days, plus 2 to 5 shorts total this week.  Turn your best 10 to 30 second moments into Shorts. Focus on one emotion: a crazy clutch, funny fail, or surprising reaction. Add vertical formatting, a strong caption on screen, and quick pacing. Shorts can blow up faster than long videos and bring your first subscribers in days.  Post your long-form videos at the same time every day, ideally when your target audience is likely online. If you are not sure, pick late afternoon or early evening in your main time zone.  Day 6: Engage and promote smartly Reply to every comment you receive this week, even if there are only a few. Ask viewers questions in the video and in the comments, like What challenge should I try next or What did I do wrong here. Engagement tells YouTube your content is worth pushing.  Share each video where people actually care about that game: small Discord servers, subreddits, or forums where self-promo is allowed, and group chats with friends. Do not spam; instead, contribute to conversations, then share your video when relevant.  On other platforms like TikTok or Instagram Reels, post your Shorts with a simple call to action in the caption like Full video on my YouTube channel and your channel name. Cross-platform views can snowball faster than waiting on YouTube alone.  Day 7: Analyze, refine, and plan your next week By the end of the week, you should have several uploads and at least a little data to look at. In YouTube Studio, study which videos have higher click-through rate and better audience retention. Ask yourself which hooks made people click and which parts cause drop-offs.  Double down on what works even if it is different from what you expected. If your funny fails short is doing better than your serious commentary, consider leaning into humor in the next batch of videos. If people like a specific game session, plan a mini series around it.  Tweak your intros: if you see people dropping off in the first 10 seconds, make the hook faster next time. Show the most exciting moment in the first few seconds, then rewind or narrate how you got there.  What to realistically expect in one week You probably will not reach thousands of subscribers immediately unless you already bring an audience from elsewhere or you hit an unusually viral short. A realistic first-week goal is something like 3 to 7 solid videos published, 5 to 30 subscribers, and a sense of what kind of content you can actually produce consistently.  What you are really building is a system: a niche, a repeatable format, a basic production pipeline, and early audience feedback. If you continue the same level of intensity beyond the first week, that is when exponential growth becomes more realistic.  In summary, treat this week as a focused experiment. Pick a tight niche, publish multiple decent-quality videos and shorts, make strong thumbnails and titles, actively engage with early viewers, and study what the data says. You will not become a big gaming YouTuber in seven days, but you can absolutely go from zero to a real, growing channel in that time if you commit hard for the week and then keep going.
4|100: Understand that one week is not enough to build a big gaming channel, but it is enough to build a strong foundation and get your first real viewers. Focus on doing a few things very well instead of trying everything.  Day 1: Define your niche and setup Pick one specific game or style of content so people know what you are about. Examples: high-energy Warzone shorts, cozy Stardew Valley lets plays, funny Fortnite clips, chill indie horror reactions, speedrun attempts in one specific game. Choose a clear channel name that matches your niche and is easy to remember. Make simple but clean channel art: a readable banner, a recognizable profile icon. Use a free tool like Canva to make them. Decide your “personality angle.” Are you calm and strategic, chaotic and funny, very educational, or story-focused? You don’t have to fake anything, but choose what you will lean into. Set up your recording and audio. Prioritize a clear microphone over ultra-high graphics. Even a budget mic can sound good if you record in a quiet room, speak close to the mic, and reduce background noise.  Day 2: Research and plan content Search your chosen game on YouTube and filter by “This week” to see what is already getting views now. Look for patterns in titles and thumbnails. Identify what is working: challenges, tips, news, funny moments, story highlights. Plan 5 to 10 video ideas you can realistically produce this week. Aim for a mix of: – Quick, short-form content like 15–60 second highlights for Shorts. – A couple of longer videos, like 5–15 minutes, that show your personality. Focus on repeatable formats: “Daily challenge,” “Trying viewer suggestions,” “Ranking X,” “I tried this weird strategy,” “Beginner guide to X in 5 minutes.”  Day 3: Record more than you need Block a few hours for recording pure gameplay. Don’t worry if you are perfect; you just need lots of raw material. Talk while playing as if someone is already watching. Comment on what you are doing, what you are thinking, and what is funny or surprising. Silence kills watch time. Keep an eye out for moments that stand out: clutch wins, fails, jump scares, funny reactions, unexpected glitches, smart plays. These become your Shorts and hooks for longer videos. Over-record. It is better to have 2–3 hours of gameplay and cut it down than barely enough.  Day 4: Edit for attention, not perfection Edit at least 3–5 Shorts and 1–2 longer videos. For Shorts: Start with the most interesting second. No long intros, logos, or “Hey guys.” People swipe in a second if bored. Add big, readable captions with strong phrases or jokes. Use quick cuts, zooms, and sound effects only when they help the moment, not just to be flashy. For longer videos: Hook in the first 3–5 seconds with a strong clip or promise, like “I tried winning without using any weapons” or “This is how I beat X boss in 60 seconds.” Cut out boring parts: long menus, loading screens, or dead air. Trim aggressively. Keep audio consistent; lower game volume when you talk. Create simple but bold thumbnails with one clear image and 2–5 words of text. Make sure it still looks good when tiny on mobile.  Day 5: Upload and optimize Upload at least 1 long video and 3–5 Shorts. Write titles that focus on curiosity or benefit, not just description. Instead of “Gameplay episode 1,” use something like “Can I survive 10 minutes with no armor in X game” or “5 early mistakes in X game that ruin your run.” Use a strong first line in the description that repeats your main keywords naturally and gives a reason to watch. Add relevant tags including the game name, game mode, and style of content like funny, competitive, guide, challenge. Make sure your channel homepage is clean: set a channel trailer (one of your best videos), add sections like “Shorts,” “Highlights,” and “Full episodes,” and write a short about section that says who you are, what you play, and what viewers can expect.  Day 6: Promote smartly and engage Share your best video and a couple of Shorts in places where people already care about that game: – Reddit communities for that game, following their self-promo rules. – Discord servers about the game or general gaming, in their self-promo or media channels. – Twitter / X, TikTok, or Instagram Reels using relevant hashtags. When you share, do not just say “Subscribe to my channel.” Instead, write a short hook that matches the clip, like “Tried winning with only pistols in Ranked… it went badly” and post the clip. Reply to every comment on your channel. Early engagement helps the algorithm and makes people more likely to return. Comment (genuinely) on videos by other small creators in your niche. Add something interesting to the conversation, not “Check out my channel.” People sometimes click through if you say something useful or funny.  Day 7: Review, adjust, and double down Open YouTube Studio and look at the first data. Check which videos have higher CTR: these are your better titles and thumbnails. Check average view duration and retention graphs to see where people drop off. Identify your best-performing video or Short from the week and ask: what specifically made it work? The idea, the hook, the pacing, the clip itself, or the title/thumbnail? Plan the next week to repeat the winning pattern: similar idea, similar format, or same style with a twist.  General principles to keep in mind when trying to grow fast Post frequently in the first week, but keep a pace you can sustain. For example, 1 long video every 2–3 days plus 1–3 Shorts per day. Even in one week, consistency matters; the algorithm learns your content style. Make every video provide something: entertainment, surprise, skill, or help. Ask yourself before uploading: if I was a random viewer who did not know me, would I watch or click away? Do not wait to “be perfect.” Imperfect but consistent content beats one “perfect” video you never finish. Use each recording session for multiple outputs. One hour of gameplay could become: one longer commentary, 3–6 Shorts, and maybe a montage. Speak clearly, bring energy, and let your personality show. In gaming, many people play the same game; your reactions, humor, and way of explaining things are what make you different. Accept that true growth takes longer than a week, but by the end of a focused week you can have: – A clean, on-brand channel. – 5–10 Shorts and a few longer videos live. – Data on what hooks and styles work. – Your first comments, maybe your first regular viewers. If you keep building from that foundation for the next few months with the same intensity and willingness to improve, real growth becomes very possible.
5|100: You cannot build a massive, stable gaming channel in one week, but you can absolutely lay a strong foundation and get your first real viewers and subscribers if you treat it like a focused sprint. Think of the week as an experiment: create a clear niche, publish fast, iterate based on data, and look for short-term discoverability boosts.  Day 0 planning before you upload anything  Pick a very specific niche instead of just gaming in general. For example: controller-only Warzone tips for beginners, cozy Stardew Valley challenge runs, horror game jump-scare compilations, speedrun practice diaries, or daily updates on a new hyped game. Specific channels grow faster than generic ones.  Define your hook in one sentence, without technical terms or fluff. Something like: I help brand-new Fortnite players win more fights in 10 minutes a day, or I show insane open-world game physics glitches every day. This helps you decide which ideas fit and which do not.  Set realistic week-one goals: publish 5–10 pieces of content, reach your first 50–100 views, and get your first comments and 5–20 subscribers. Focus on learning a repeatable process rather than going viral.  Core setup on day 1  Create your channel name, logo, and banner that visually match your niche. You can use free tools like Canva for a clean, simple identity. Make it obvious what your channel is about just from the banner text and imagery.  Write a short, clear channel description that includes what you post, who it is for, and how often you post. Include a few relevant keywords, written naturally, like tips, guides, no commentary, lets play, challenges, or the specific game names.  Decide on your upload format for the week. For a rapid one-week push, it is usually best to focus on Shorts or very tight 3–8 minute videos because they are quicker to make and algorithm-friendly.  Content strategy for just seven days  For a one-week growth sprint, you will move fast and accept that some videos will be imperfect. Quantity with focused intent is more important than perfection.  Pick one main game and do not switch games during the week. Swapping games too early confuses both viewers and the algorithm. Choose something active with proven interest: a trending new release, a popular competitive title, or a game that has a dedicated, searchable community.  Brainstorm 15–20 video concepts that fit your hook but can be executed quickly. For example:  If you are doing tips content: fastest early-game XP method, secret routes on a popular map, settings that give you an advantage, beginner mistakes to stop making. If you are doing entertainment: nasty fails montage, insane luck moments, reacting to world-record clips, trying weird challenges like playing with inverted controls. If you are doing commentary: hot takes on balance changes, reviewing unpopular opinions, breaking down pro player clips.  Check YouTube search suggestions and filters. Type your game name plus words like best, tips, how to, beginners, settings, and see what auto-completes. Filter by upload date to spot trending topics. These are great seeds for your titles because you know people are searching them.  Recording and editing approach  Aim for simple, rapid production rather than complex edits. Good audio and clear gameplay are more important than fancy effects in your first week.  Make a basic template for your videos so you do not overthink structure. For example:  For short form content: strong hook in the first 2–3 seconds, main tip or moment, a quick call to action like follow for more daily tips, then a fast-cut ending.  For long form: 5–15 second hook explaining what is in the video and why to keep watching, then structured segments, each delivering a clear tip or moment, and a simple ending inviting viewers to watch another video or subscribe.  Focus on your hook. In the first few seconds, tell or show the viewer why this video is worth their time. Examples:  I tested every shotgun so you do not have to. Here is how to win more fights even if you have bad aim. Watch how broken this new weapon actually is.  Record more than you need in one sitting, then cut down. Batch recording reduces the time you spend setting up and tearing down.  If you can, use a decent microphone and turn off background noises like keyboard clacking as much as possible. Clear audio is one of the fastest ways to look more professional instantly.  Publishing schedule during the week  Commit to a high-output schedule just for this week. For example:  Post 2–3 Shorts every day (7–20 seconds each), and 2–3 longer videos during the week (3–8 minutes). If you cannot maintain that, aim for at least 1 Short daily and 3 longer videos total.  Optimize each upload:  Use a title that states the value or curiosity clearly. Keep important words at the start. Example: Best early-game loadout for beginners in game name instead of vague titles like Crazy gameplay. Make simple custom thumbnails that are readable small. Big bold text with 2–4 words and a clear image is usually enough. You can even reuse a base template and just change the text and image. Use tags with variations of the game name, mode, and what the video shows, but do not stuff them with spam. They help a bit, but title, thumbnail, and retention matter far more.  Always write a 1–3 sentence description that repeats your core keywords naturally and adds a bit of context about what is in the video.  Shorts strategy for quick discovery  Shorts can give you views faster than long form, especially on a new channel. Treat Shorts as your reach tool and long videos as your depth tool.  For Shorts, make every second count. Cut out dead space. Start with the punchline, problem, or craziest moment first, then explain if needed.  Make themed series, not random one-offs. For example:  One broken tip per day until it gets patched. One impossible challenge attempt every day until I beat it. Rating your awful plays daily.  Put a very short, consistent call to action at the end of each Short like more daily game name tips tomorrow, follow to not miss them. Keep it quick and natural.  Audience interaction and early community building  In the first week, any sign of real human engagement is gold. You want comments, likes, and watch time more than a big sub count.  Reply to every comment quickly and with something more than just thanks. Ask follow-ups: Should I try this loadout next? What game should I break down next? This increases the chance of ongoing engagement and gives you free content ideas.  At the end of videos, ask a specific question instead of a generic please like and subscribe. Examples:  What gun should I test next What challenge should I attempt tomorrow Which setting surprised you the most  If you have friends who play the same game, share a link with a brief line about what the video covers and ask for honest feedback, not fake engagement. Feedback is more valuable than a pity like.  Use other platforms lightly but smartly. Post one or two best clips as TikToks or Instagram Reels with a note in your bio linking back to your YouTube channel. Do not get stuck trying to be big on every platform; use them as funnels.  Analyzing and adjusting during the week  Check YouTube Analytics daily, but do not obsess. Look specifically at:  Audience retention. If viewers drop off in the first 3–5 seconds, your hook is weak or misleading. Click-through rate on thumbnails and titles. If CTR is low, try more direct titles and clearer thumbnails. Traffic source. If Shorts feed impressions are climbing, keep posting similar style Shorts. If search is working, double down on similar search-focused topics.  Look at which videos get even slightly better performance. If one video gets double the watch time or more comments, make two or three follow-ups on the same idea.  End of week actions to set up longer-term growth  By the end of the week, you might have:  A small set of videos that clearly outperform the rest. A sense of what style of content you enjoy and can produce quickly. Actual data on which topics get more response.  Pause and review:  Which videos had the strongest retention Which intros worked best Which thumbnails scored higher CTR Which topics sparked comments  Use that information to define your early channel direction. Something like: viewers seem to love quick tips for beginners, or viewers are clicking on insane moments and glitches more than long commentary.  From there, commit to a sustainable schedule beyond this week. Maybe one solid long video plus 3–5 Shorts per week. Consistency over the next month matters far more than the first week alone.  Mindset: honest expectations and what success looks like in a week  You are unlikely to hit thousands of subs in seven days unless you already have editing skills, existing audience, or you hit a rare viral moment. That is not failure.  A good outcome for week one is:  You learned to produce content faster. You discovered at least one format that shows promise. You started getting real comments from strangers. You built the habit of shipping content, not just planning.  The most important decision you make after this week is whether you keep going and improve using what you learned. The creators who eventually blow up are usually the ones who made many imperfect videos, analyzed why some did better, and slowly got sharper at hooks, pacing, and understanding their audience.  So use this one-week sprint as a boot camp: niche down, publish aggressively, pay attention to what works, and build a simple system you can keep running and refining over the next months. That is how a gaming channel actually grows, even if the visible explosion seems to happen overnight.

For long-form, invest a bit more into a thumbnail: large face or character, strong emotion, bold 2–3 word text, high contrast. Don’t cram too much on it. Join a few small gaming Discords, subreddits, or communities specific to your game, and share your clips only where allowed and only where it makes sense. Don’t spam; instead, contribute, answer questions, and drop a clip when it’s actually relevant to the discussion.  On other platforms, post the same Shorts (formatted correctly) to TikTok, Instagram Reels, and maybe Twitter/X with your YouTube link in bio. Talk about what you tried, what worked best, and what you’ll do next week. It might not perform now, but later it becomes part of your story for new subscribers.  Mindset and expectations In one week, aim for these realistic milestones: fully set up channel and branding, a repeatable recording and editing process, 20–40 Shorts, 1–3 long videos, a few comments and early subscribers, and basic understanding of what resonates. Boiled down: pick one game and angle, post a lot of short, high-hook content, prioritize audio and clarity over perfection, study what performs even in tiny numbers, and be relentlessly consistent beyond the first week.

Instead of generic titles like Ranked Gameplay 1 use something like Bronze To Silver In One Day Ranked Climb Diary or I Changed This Setting And Won More Fights. Day 5: Promotion and community interaction Share your videos where your target audience already hangs out, but do it respectfully. Join small Discord servers, subreddits, and forums about your game. Day 7: Publish, refine, and set up for beyond the week Upload again, keeping quality consistent but production time manageable. Ideally you end the week with 5–10 shorts and 3–4 longer videos. That is enough content for YouTube to start testing you with small pockets of viewers.  On your channel home page, set a channel trailer or your strongest video as the featured video. Arrange your playlists so new visitors immediately see what your channel is about.  Define a schedule you can sustain after this sprint, even if it is just 2 longer videos and 3 shorts per week. One week is for launching; real growth happens by stacking consistent weeks.  Mindset and practical tips for the week Expect almost nobody to watch at first. The goal of this week is to improve your skills fast: recording, speaking, editing, thumbnails, and understanding what gets clicks.  Be on camera or use a clear voice if possible. Personality is what separates channels in saturated games. Even a basic facecam in a corner or consistent voice-over will make your content more memorable.  Keep each video focused on one clear promise: one tip, one challenge, one goal, one crazy moment. Viewers have no patience for meandering, especially for small channels.  Avoid perfectionism. Save an editing project with your intro, outro, overlays, and audio levels. Save thumbnail templates so you can swap text and images in minutes.  Leverage shorts heavily during this first week because they have a higher chance of reaching new viewers quickly. Each long video can produce multiple shorts: best clutch, funniest fail, smartest play, one key tip.  Be honest about what is working. If, for example, your funny highlight clips get almost no attention but your very simple How to win more early fights in Valorant style videos get more clicks and better retention, shift toward helping viewers improve rather than just showing gameplay.  Finally, understand that blowing up in a single week is extremely rare. What you can achieve in a week is momentum: a small base of content, a handful of real viewers, the beginnings of an identity, and the skills and system to keep going. If you treat this week like an intensive boot camp and then continue with the same energy for months, that is how channels actually grow.
8|100: Treat the week like a focused sprint: pick one specific game and one specific audience, then publish daily with aggressive short-form promotion.  Day 1 – Set up and plan Create a clean, memorable channel identity around one niche: for example, beginner-friendly Fortnite tips on console, cozy Stardew Valley playthroughs, or funny challenge runs in Minecraft. Make a simple, readable banner that clearly says who your channel is for and what you upload. Pick a profile picture that is recognizable even as a tiny icon.  Write a clear channel description that includes your niche, upload schedule for this week, and the value you offer: tips, entertainment, challenges, or guides. Example structure: I upload daily beginner-friendly [Game] guides and funny challenges. New videos every day this week.  Decide on 3–5 video ideas that can be filmed and edited quickly but have search or viral potential. Focus on hooks like Best settings for…, Beginner mistakes in…, I tried X challenge in Y game, or This weapon is broken in Season Z. Prioritize topics that people are actually searching: new patch content, trending challenges, or common problems.  Day 2 – Record and batch Record more raw footage than you need. Aim for 2–3 videos worth of material so you are not scrambling each day. When recording, speak clearly, get to the point fast, and avoid long silent stretches. Start every recording with a strong hook in the first 3–5 seconds: a surprising result, a bold claim, or a clear promise of value.  For commentary, imagine you are talking to one specific friend who loves the same game. Use a simple structure: hook, quick intro, main content, and a brief call to action like If this helps, subscribe because I am posting daily this week.  Day 3 – Edit and optimize Edit your first 1–2 videos as tightly as possible. Remove dead air, unimportant waiting times, and long menus. Add simple text captions for key moments or tips if you can do it quickly. Keep most videos between 6 and 12 minutes to maximize watchability without dragging.  Make a clickable thumbnail using strong contrast, big readable text, and close-up game visuals. The thumbnail should tell a story or create curiosity: for example a shocked character face, a crazy damage number, or a high-stakes moment. Use only a few words in big font that reinforce the hook from your title.  Write titles that are very clear, slightly emotional, and keyword rich without being spammy. Example formats: I tried winning with only [Weapon] and it was insane, The easiest way to win early games in [Game], or These settings made my aim 10x better in [Game]. Add a good description with a short summary, relevant keywords, and a simple call to subscribe.  Day 4 – Publish and cross-post shorts Upload your first main video and schedule the second one for the next day. From your existing gameplay recordings, cut multiple 15–30 second clips showing the funniest, craziest, or most clutch moments. Add simple captions and a short hook text at the start, then upload them as YouTube Shorts with relevant hashtags for the game.  Recycle those clips to TikTok, Instagram Reels, and possibly Twitter or Reddit where allowed. Wherever you post, include a short, value-driven caption and a subtle mention that your full content is on YouTube. Do not just spam your link; post clips that are good enough to stand alone as entertainment.  Day 5 – Engage and iterate Reply to every comment you get, even if it is just one word. Ask small questions in the comments and descriptions to invite interaction, like What game should I try next or Did you know about this trick. Engagement tells the algorithm that your content is active and worth suggesting.  Watch your audience retention graphs in YouTube Analytics. See where people drop off and adjust your next videos to fix those parts, such as shortening intros or moving the best moments earlier. If a particular topic gets more views or higher retention, double down and make a second video on a close variation of that idea.  Day 6 – Collab and community Join small Discords, subreddits, or communities around your game and contribute meaningfully. Share tips, answer questions, and only mention your channel when it is genuinely helpful, such as linking a guide you made that solves a specific problem. Look for other small creators with similar sizes and propose tiny collabs like reacting to each others clips, 1v1s, or duo games.  Use community posts on YouTube once you hit the eligibility threshold to ask your tiny audience what they want next: challenges, guides, or funny moments. This makes people feel involved and gives you fresh, relevant ideas.  Day 7 – Refine your best format and push By now, you should know which of your videos or shorts performed the best. Study that piece of content and make a next-level version: better hook, cleaner edit, stronger thumbnail, and more focused topic. Upload that improved video on a high-traffic time for your audience, usually afternoon or early evening in your primary region.  Post multiple Shorts cut from this new video throughout the day. Each short should have a unique hook: a surprising moment, a big fail, a huge win, or a quick tip. In the captions of those shorts, encourage viewers to check out the full video without sounding desperate.  Realistic expectations and mindset In one week you will not become huge, but you can create strong early momentum: a clean brand, a small base of videos, a handful of real fans, and some early algorithm signals. Focus on learning what works rather than chasing big numbers. Aim for small, measurable wins: your first 10 subscribers, first 100 views on a video, or first short that gets picked up.  If you can sustain even a lighter version of this pace for a few more weeks, the compounding effect can be significant. Consistent quality, clear niche, strong hooks, tight edits, and active engagement are what turn a one-week sprint into long-term growth.
9|100: Focus on what is actually possible in a week: you cannot build a huge channel, but you can build a strong foundation and get your first real viewers. Think in terms of three things only: clarity, speed, and consistency.  Day 1: Define the channel and set up Pick one specific gaming angle instead of trying to be a generic gaming channel. For example: funny Warzone clips, cozy Stardew Valley playthroughs, horror game reactions, high-level Valorant guides, challenge runs in Minecraft, or mobile game tips. The narrower and clearer your focus, the easier it is for the right audience to find you.  Create a name and visuals that match that niche. Simple, clean channel banner and logo: readable name, a key visual from the type of games you play, and a short tagline like Ranked Valorant tips daily or Relaxing farming and story games.  Set up your recording and streaming tools quickly instead of chasing perfection: OBS or Streamlabs for PC, built-in capture on consoles or a simple capture card, a basic but clear microphone, and headphones. Test audio once: game volume lower than your voice, no loud popping, no echo.  Day 2: Research and copy what works Spend a few hours searching on YouTube for your specific niche. Look at the 10–20 most recent successful videos: sort by upload date and filter by view count. Notice patterns in three areas: titles, thumbnails, and video structure.  Titles: study how they write them. Short, bold, emotional or curiosity-driven, with strong keywords: I tried the hardest Minecraft challenge, Why you KEEP losing gunfights, The most broken build right now. Do not copy exact titles, but model the format.  Thumbnails: clear subject, big readable text, high contrast, one main idea. Use a free tool like Canva. Zoom in on your face or main game element. Use 2–3 colors and short text like INSANE WIN, NO DAMAGE RUN, BRONZE TO PLAT.  Structure: first 10 seconds usually show something intense or interesting that happens later, with a quick hook: This is the match where everything went wrong or I tried beating this boss with no armor. Then it gets into the gameplay.  Day 3–5: Record and upload daily Plan to upload at least one decent video each day for the first week. They do not have to be long; 6–12 minutes is fine for most gaming content. For each video, follow a simple structure:  Open with a hook: within 5 seconds, say or show something that makes people want to stay. Tease the craziest moment or the result of the challenge.  Stay focused: cut out long load screens, boring walking, silent looting, or repeated attempts with nothing happening. Keep every 5–10 seconds interesting: a joke, a reaction, a tip, or progress.  End with a soft call to action: instead of begging, say something like If you made it this far, you probably like this kind of content, so subscribe for more [your niche] videos this week.  If you are comfortable being on camera, use a facecam. Reactions drive gaming content heavily. If you are not, use strong voiceover instead. Speak clearly and with energy: enthusiasm is more important than a perfect voice.  Day 4–6: Shorts and quick wins In one week, Shorts and clips can grow your reach faster than long videos. After recording, cut your best moments into vertical 9:16 clips of 10–30 seconds. Focus on moments with strong emotion: clutch plays, big fails, funny bugs, scary jump-scares, crazy luck.  Add captions using a tool like CapCut or built-in mobile editors. Many people watch muted, so text on screen helps. Use simple, bold captions that match what you are saying.  Post 2–5 Shorts per day from your main videos. Each Short should have a strong hook in the first second: a shout, a surprising image, or a big on-screen word like NO WAY. Put clear keywords in the title, like Valorant insane clutch, Minecraft hardcore fail, or Elden Ring no hit.  Day 5–7: Optimization and early audience Spend some time on basic SEO but do not overcomplicate it. Use clear, descriptive titles that include the game name and what makes the video special. In the description, write 2–3 sentences explaining the video and use relevant keywords naturally: game title, mode, challenge, and your niche. Add 5–10 relevant tags, including the game, mode, and content type like funny moments, guide, challenge run.  To get your first real viewers quickly, go to places where your audience already gathers: Reddit subs for your game, Discord servers, small game communities, or Twitter/X. Do not spam links. Instead, participate genuinely and only share your video when it is relevant, like Hey, I tried this crazy [boss/strat] and thought this sub might enjoy it.  Comment on other small or mid-sized channels in your niche with genuine comments that show you understand the game. Sometimes people will check your channel if your comment is helpful or funny.  Mindset and expectations In one week you are not aiming for thousands of subs; you are aiming for your first real data: which thumbnails get more clicks, which hooks keep viewers watching longer, what type of game or challenge gets the best reactions.  Check analytics lightly but not obsessively: look at click-through rate for thumbnails, audience retention graph to see where most people drop off, and which videos or Shorts get the most impressions. Then adjust: improve thumbnails that have low clicks, cut or change intros if people leave in the first 10–20 seconds.  What to avoid in your first week Do not chase too many games at once; you want repeat viewers who like seeing more of the same kind of content. Pick one primary game and maybe one backup.  Do not waste hours on tiny edits if you could make an extra video in that time. Simple cuts and clear audio beat flashy transitions.  Do not copy big creators completely. Use them as inspiration for pacing and style, but keep your own voice and personality.  Realistic goal for one week By the end of seven days you should have: a clear niche and channel identity, 5–7 full videos uploaded, 10–20 Shorts uploaded, your recording and editing workflow mostly figured out, and a small but real amount of watch time and maybe your first few subscribers and comments.  From there, growth comes from continuing the same process: upload consistently, refine based on analytics, keep improving thumbnails and hooks, and stay inside a clear niche until you build an audience that cares about you, not just the game. One week is the launch, not the finish line.
10|100: You cannot build a huge, stable gaming channel in one week, but you can absolutely lay a strong foundation and get your first real viewers and subscribers. Treat it like a one‑week sprint where you test a clear idea instead of just uploading random gameplay.  First, define a very specific focus for the week. Not just “gaming” or even “Fortnite” but something like “high‑intensity solo clutch moments in Fortnite,” “beginner friendly Elden Ring guides,” or “funny Warzone fails with friends.” A narrow theme helps people know why they should subscribe and makes it easier for the algorithm to understand your content.  Before day one, decide on one game, one style, and one type of viewer you want to attract. For example: I make short, funny, fast‑paced Fortnite shorts for casual players who like memes and crazy moments. That clarity will guide everything this week.  Day 1: Set up and research  Create your channel branding fast but decent. Use a simple, clean name that matches your focus. Make a logo and banner using a free tool like Canva. Do not obsess; you can improve later, but avoid looking like a blank or default channel.  Write a short, clear channel description. In a couple of sentences say who you are, what game(s) you focus on, and what people can expect in terms of content style and frequency.  Then research your niche for two hours instead of guessing. Search for your game plus words like funny moments, tips and tricks, beginner guide, highlights, shorts, best settings, and no commentary. Sort by recent uploads and by popularity.  Identify 5–10 channels that are near the size you want to be in a few months, not just huge creators. Study what their thumbnails look like, what video titles they use, what length performs best, what type of content gets the most views. Write down patterns: maybe short 8–12 minute guides or 20–40 second clips perform best in your niche.  Pick 3–5 video ideas that are similar in format to what is already working, but that you can execute with your personality, gameplay, or twist.  Day 2–3: Record and batch content  Your most powerful move in one week is to batch create multiple videos instead of making one at a time. Set a realistic goal like 5–7 uploads prepared in advance so you can publish consistently over the week.  Record longer sessions of gameplay focused on the ideas you picked. If you are doing highlights or funny clips, record 2–3 hours and mark the timestamps of anything interesting as you go. If you are doing guides, before recording, outline the steps so your commentary is structured, not rambling.  Even if you are shy, consider using your voice. Voice commentary usually gives better retention and connection than silent gameplay. If you are not ready yet, at least add captions and text to explain what is happening.  Day 2 is for raw recording, Day 3 is for editing. For editing, keep it simple but punchy. Cut out boring parts. Remove long downtime between fights, loading screens, or menus unless they add something funny or educational. Add basic zooms, cuts on action, and text to highlight key moments. Match the pacing of successful videos you studied.  For shorts or vertical clips, keep them 15–40 seconds with a strong hook in the first two seconds. The opening moment should instantly show something surprising, satisfying, or funny. Do not waste the first seconds with long intros or logos.  Day 4: Optimize titles, thumbnails, and metadata  Even a good video dies without a clickable thumbnail and title. You will not be perfect at this in a week, but you can get to “good enough” by copying patterns.  Look again at similar successful videos in your game. Notice word choices in titles. They usually include the game name plus a strong promise or emotion: insane, impossible, beginner guide, fastest, overpowered, try this now. Model your titles after those patterns but make them honest and relevant to your video.  Thumbnails should be clean and bold. Avoid clutter. Use one main image: a dramatic in‑game moment, your character, or your reaction face, plus 2–4 words of big, easy to read text that teases the video’s main point. Dark background with bright subject and text often stands out.  Do not write the full title in the thumbnail. The thumbnail should make people curious, and the title should finish the thought. For example, the thumbnail might show an intense fight with big text like No Way I Survive This and the title completes it with something like Surviving a 1v4 In Late Game Fortnite.  For descriptions, write 2–3 sentences summarizing the video naturally including the game name and main keywords. Do not stuff keywords. Add a couple of relevant hashtags like the game name, the game plus shorts if vertical, and something niche related.  Day 5: Upload schedule and engagement  Upload at least one video per day for the rest of the week. If you have enough content, post 1–2 shorts plus 1 longer video on at least two of the days. Shorts can help you get early impressions faster, while longer videos can convert viewers into subscribers.  When you upload, schedule your videos for times when your likely audience is online. For many gaming audiences this is late afternoon to late evening in your main time zone, and weekends often do well. You will not know your analytics yet, so just pick 1–2 consistent times and stick to them.  As soon as a video goes live, stay available for 30–60 minutes to reply to any comments. Early engagement signals can help the algorithm push your video a bit more. Encourage viewers to comment something specific, like their favorite weapon, build, or part of the video, instead of just saying like and subscribe.  Day 6: Promote smartly without spamming  In one week the main way to get extra traction is to get your content in front of existing communities without being annoying.  Join a few relevant Discord servers for your game, Reddit communities, or Twitter or other platforms where your game’s fans hang out. Before you post your video, contribute a little. Answer a question, share a tip, or comment on someone else’s clip.  When sharing your content, always add value. Instead of spamming your link with “check out my channel,” frame it around what viewers get: a quick guide for new players to beat a certain boss, a crazy clutch moment you think others will appreciate, or a settings video that helped your FPS.  You can also use shorts and vertical clips on TikTok, Instagram Reels, or YouTube Shorts to drive viewers to your main channel. Add text overlays telling people to watch the full version on your channel or to check out your other clips.  Ask a few friends who actually like games to watch your best video, like it, comment genuinely, and watch most of it. Do not buy views or subs; that just ruins your analytics and makes growth harder.  Day 7: Analyze and adjust  By the end of the week, you might only have a small number of views, but the analytics still give clues. Open your YouTube Studio and check which videos have higher click through rates and better average view duration.  Pay special attention to the first 30–60 seconds of your longer videos. If many viewers drop off quickly, your intros might be too slow. Start future videos right in the action. You can add a very short introduction after you have already grabbed attention.  If certain titles and thumbnail styles get more clicks, lean into that style in your next week. If shorts perform better, make more shorts while still testing a few longer videos.  Be honest with yourself about what felt sustainable. If daily editing burned you out, plan for 2–3 higher quality uploads per week going forward instead of trying to keep up a schedule that will make you quit.  What success looks like after one week  Realistically, in seven days as a brand‑new gaming channel, a good outcome might be 20–100 subscribers and a few videos with a couple hundred views. For a total beginner, even 10 real subscribers who comment and come back is a win. Those are the seeds of a community.  Use this week to learn the process: planning content, recording with intention, editing tight, making clickable thumbnails and titles, and talking to viewers. That skill set is what lets channels grow over months.  If you want to push even harder, you can  Focus heavily on one specific searchable problem like best beginner build, best sensitivity, how to rank up, or how to win more fights and make multiple videos around those problems. Make a mini series, like Road to Diamond over a short set of episodes, so people have a reason to watch multiple videos. Collaborate with a small streamer or creator around your size by doing a duo session, then each of you posting your own version of the highlights.  The honest bottom line is that you cannot force massive growth in a week, but you can absolutely accelerate early traction by focusing on a clear niche, making multiple decent videos, using proven formats, and actively engaging where your ideal viewers already are. Think of this week as the launch pad, not the finish line.
